demission.c: Demission De*mis"sion (?), n. [L. demissio, fr. demittere. See Demit.] 1. The act of demitting, or the state of being demitted; a letting down; a lowering; dejection. “Demission of mind.” Hammond.

demissionary.c: Demissionary De*mis"sion*a*ry (?), a. 1. Pertaining to transfer or conveyance; as, a demissionary deed.

demissive.c: Demissive De*miss"ive (?), a. [See Demiss.] Downcast; submissive; humble. [R.]

demissly.c: Demissly De*miss"ly, adv. In a humble manner. [Obs.]

demisuit.c: Demisuit Dem"i*suit` (?), n. (Mil. Antiq.) A suit of light armor covering less than the whole body, as having no protection for the legs below the thighs, no vizor to the helmet, and the like.

demit.c: Demit De*mit" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Demitted; p. pr. & vb. n. Demitting.] [L. demittere to send or bring down, to lower; de- + mittere to send. Cf. Demise.] 1. To let fall; to depress. [R.]

Demit De*mit" (?), v. i. [F. démettre to remove, se démettre to resign; dé- (L. dis-) + mettre to put, fr. L. mittere to send. Cf. Dismiss.] To lay down or relinquish an office, membership, authority, or the like; to resign, as from a Masonic lodge; -- generally used with an implication that the act is voluntary.
Demit De*mit", n. The act of demitting; also, a letter, certificate, or the like, certifying that a person has (honorably) demitted, as from a Masonic lodge.

demitasse.c: Demi-tasse ‖De*mi"-tasse" (?), n. [F., half cup.] A small cup for, or of, black coffee.

demitint.c: Demitint Dem"i*tint` (?), n. (Fine Arts) (a) That part of a painting, engraving, or the like, which is neither in full darkness nor full light. (b) The shade itself; neither the darkest nor the lightest in a composition. Also called half tint.

demiurge.c: Demiurge Dem"i*urge (?), n. [Gr. dhmioyrgo`s a worker for the people, a workman, especially the maker of the world, the Creator; dh`mios belonging to the people (fr. dh^mos the people) + 'e`rgon a work.] 1. (Gr. Antiq.) The chief magistrate in some of the Greek states.

demiurgic.c: Demiurgic Dem`i*ur"gic (?), a. [Gr. dhmioyrgiko`s.] Pertaining to a demiurge; formative; creative. “Demiurgic power.” De Quincey.

demivill.c: Demivill Dem"i*vill` (?), n. (Old Law) A half vill, consisting of five freemen or frankpledges. Blackstone.

demivolt.c: Demivolt Dem"i*volt` (?), n. [Cf. F. demi- volte.] (Man.) A half vault; one of the seven artificial motions of a horse, in which he raises his fore legs in a particular manner.

demiwolf.c: Demiwolf Dem"i*wolf` (?), n. A half wolf; a mongrel dog, between a dog and a wolf. Shak.

demobilization.c: Demobilization De*mob`i*li*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. démobilisation. See Mobilization.] (Mil.) The disorganization or disarming of troops which have previously been mobilized or called into active service; the change from a war footing to a peace footing.

demobilize.c: Demobilize De*mob"i*lize (?), v. t. [Cf. F. démobiliser.] (Mil.) To disorganize, or disband and send home, as troops which have been mobilized.

democracy.c: Democracy De*moc"ra*cy (de*mŏk"rȧ*sy̆), n.; pl. Democracies (de*mŏk"rȧ*sĭz). [F. démocratie, fr. Gr. dhmokrati`a; dh^mos the people + kratei^n to be strong, to rule, kra`tos strength.] 1. Government by the people; a form of government in which the supreme power is retained and directly exercised by the people.

democrat.c: Democrat Dem"o*crat (dĕm"o*krăt), n. [Cf. F. démocrate.] 1. One who is an adherent or advocate of democracy, or government by the people.

democratic.c: Democratic Dem`o*crat"ic (?), a. [Gr.?: cf. F. démocratique.] 1. Pertaining to democracy; favoring democracy, or constructed upon the principle of government by the people.

democratically.c: Democratically Dem`o*crat"ic*al*ly, adv. In a democratic manner.

democratism.c: Democratism De*moc"ra*tism (?), n. The principles or spirit of a democracy. [R.]

democratize.c: Democratize De*moc"ra*tize (?) v. t. To render democratic.

demodulator.c: demodulator demodulator n. (Electronics) An electronic device which extracts the modulation from a radio carrier wave, and outputs the original information-bearing signal.

demogorgon.c: Demogorgon De`mo*gor"gon (dē"mo*gôr*gŏn or dĕm"o*gôr*gŏn), n. [First mentioned by Lutatius, or Lactantius Placidus, the scholiast on Statius, perh. fr. Gr. dai`mwn god, deity + gorgo`s fierce, terrible] A mysterious, terrible, and evil divinity, regarded by some as the author of creation, by others as a great magician who was supposed to command the spirits of the lower world. See Gorgon.

demography.c: demography de*mog"ra*phy (de*mŏg"rȧfy̆), n. [Gr. dh^mos the people + -graphy.] The study of vital statistics, such as births, deaths, marriages, mortality, health, etc., in populations and subgroups of populations. -- Dem`o*graph"ic, a.

demoiselle.c: Demoiselle ‖De`moi`selle" (?), n. [F. See Damsel.] 1. A young lady; a damsel; a lady's maid.

demolish.c: Demolish De*mol"ish (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Demolished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Demolishing.] [F. démolir, fr. L. demoliri, p. p. demolitus; de- + moliri to set a thing in motion, to work, construct, from moles a huge mass or structure. See Mole a mound, and Finish.] To throw or pull down; to raze; to destroy the fabric of; to pull to pieces; to ruin; as, to demolish an edifice, or a wall.

demolisher.c: Demolisher De*mol"ish`er (?), n. One who, or that which, demolishes; as, a demolisher of towns.

demolition.c: Demolition Dem`o*li"tion (?; 277), n. [L. demolitio, fr. demoliri: cf. F. démolition. See Demolish.] The act of overthrowing, pulling down, or destroying a pile or structure; destruction by violence; utter overthrow; -- opposed to construction; as, the demolition of a house, of military works, of a town, or of hopes.

demon.c: Demon De"mon (?), n. [F. démon, L. daemon a spirit, an evil spirit, fr. Gr. dai`mwn a divinity; of uncertain origin.] 1. (Gr. Antiq.) A spirit, or immaterial being, holding a middle place between men and deities in pagan mythology.

demonetization.c: demonetization de*mon`e*ti*za"tion (?), n. The act of demonetizing, or the condition of being demonetized; specificially, the declaration by a government that something (e.g. gold or silver) is no longer the legal tender of a country; as, the demonetization of gold.

demonetize.c: demonetize de*mon"e*tize (?; see Monetary), v. t. To deprive of current value; to withdraw from use, as money.

demoniacal.c: Demoniacal Demoniac { De*mo"ni*ac (?), Dem`o*ni"a*cal (?; 277), } a. [L. daemoniacus, fr. daemon; cf. F. démoniaque. See Demon.] 1. Pertaining to, or characteristic of, a demon or evil spirit; devilish; as, a demoniac being; demoniacal practices.

demoniac.c: Demoniac De*mo"ni*ac (?), n. 1. A human being possessed by a demon or evil spirit; one whose faculties are directly controlled by a demon.

demoniacally.c: Demoniacally Dem`o*ni"a*cal*ly (?), adv. In a demoniacal manner.

demoniacism.c: Demoniacism Dem`o*ni"a*cism (?), n. The state of being demoniac, or the practices of demoniacs.

demonial.c: Demonial De*mo"ni*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a demon. [Obs.] Cudworth.

demonian.c: Demonian De*mo"ni*an (?), a. Relating to, or having the nature of, a demon. “Demonian spirits.” Milton.

demonianism.c: Demonianism De*mo"ni*an*ism (?), n. The state of being possessed by a demon or by demons.

demonic.c: Demonic De*mo"nic (?), a. [L. daemonicus, Gr. daimoniko`s.] Of or pertaining to a demon or to demons; demoniac. “Demonic ambushes.” Lowell.

demonism.c: Demonism De"mon*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. démonisme.] The belief in demons or false gods.

demonist.c: Demonist De"mon*ist, n. A believer in, or worshiper of, demons.

demonize.c: Demonize De"mon*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Demonized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Demonizing.] [Cf. LL. daemonizare to be possessed by a demon, Gr.?.] 1. To convert into a demon; to infuse the principles or fury of a demon into.

demonocracy.c: Demonocracy De`mon*oc"ra*cy (?), n. [Gr. dai`mwn demon + kra`tos strength: cf. F. démonocratie.] The power or government of demons.

demonographer.c: Demonographer De`mon*og"ra*pher (?), n. [Demon + -graph + -er.] A demonologist. [R.] Am. Cyc.

demonolatry.c: Demonolatry De`mon*ol"a*try (?), n. [Gr. dai`mwn demon + latrei`a worship,? to serve, worship: cf. F. démonolâtrie.] The worship of demons.

demonologer.c: Demonologer De`mon*ol"o*ger (?), n. One versed in demonology. R. North.

demonological.c: Demonological Demonologic { De`mon*o*log"ic (?), De`mon*o*log"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. démonologique.] Of or pertaining to demonology.

demonologist.c: Demonologist De`mon*ol"o*gist (?), n. One who writes on, or is versed in, demonology.

demonology.c: Demonology De`mon*ol"o*gy (?; 277), n. [Demon + -logy: cf. F. démonologie.] A treatise on demons; a supposititious science which treats of demons and their manifestations. Sir W. Scott.

demonomagy.c: Demonomagy De`mon*om"a*gy (?), n. [Gr. dai`mwn demon + magei`a magic.] Magic in which the aid of demons is invoked; black or infernal magic. Bp. Hurd.

demonomania.c: Demonomania De*mon`o*ma"ni*a (?), n. [Demon + mania.] A form of madness in which the patient conceives himself possessed of devils.

demonomist.c: Demonomist De*mon"o*mist (?) n. One in subjection to a demon, or to demons. [R.] Sir T. Herbert.

demonomy.c: Demonomy De*mon"o*my (?), n. [Gr. dai`mwn demon + no`mos law.] The dominion of demons. [R.] Sir T. Herbert.

demonry.c: Demonry De"mon*ry (?), n. Demoniacal influence or possession. J. Baillie.

demonship.c: Demonship De"mon*ship, n. The state of a demon. Mede.

demonstrability.c: Demonstrability De*mon`stra*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being demonstrable; demonstrableness.

demonstrable.c: Demonstrable De*mon"stra*ble (?), a. [L. demonstrabilis: cf. OF. demonstrable, F. démontrable.] 1. Capable of being demonstrated; that can be proved beyond doubt or question.

demonstrableness.c: Demonstrableness De*mon"stra*ble*ness, n. The quality of being demonstrable; demonstrability.

demonstrably.c: Demonstrably De*mon"stra*bly, adv. In a demonstrable manner; incontrovertibly; clearly.

demonstrance.c: Demonstrance De*mon"strance (?), n. [OF. demonstrance.] Demonstration; proof. [Obs.] Holland.

demonstrate.c: Demonstrate Dem"on*strate (?; 277), v. t. [L. demonstratus, p. p. of demonstrare to demonstrate; de- + monstrare to show. See Monster.] 1. To point out; to show; to exhibit; to make evident. Shak.

demonstration.c: Demonstration Dem`on*stra"tion (?), n. [L. demonstratio: cf. F. démonstration.] 1. The act of demonstrating; an exhibition; proof; especially, proof beyond the possibility of doubt; indubitable evidence, to the senses or reason.

demonstrative.c: Demonstrative De*mon"stra*tive (?), a. [F. démonstratif, L. demonstrativus.] 1. Having the nature of demonstration; tending to demonstrate; making evident; exhibiting clearly or conclusively. “Demonstrative figures.” Dryden.
Demonstrative De*mon"stra*tive, n. (Gram.) A demonstrative pronoun; as, “this” and “that” are demonstratives.

demonstratively.c: Demonstratively De*mon"stra*tive*ly (?), adv. In a manner fitted to demonstrate; clearly; convincingly; forcibly.

demonstrativeness.c: Demonstrativeness De*mon"stra*tive*ness, n. The state or quality of being demonstrative.

demonstrator.c: Demonstrator Dem"on*stra`tor (?; 277), n. [L.: cf. F. démonstrateur.] 1. One who demonstrates; specif. (a) one who proves anything with certainty, or establishes it by indubitable evidence. (b) one who shows how a certain device operates or a procedure is performed.

demonstratory.c: Demonstratory De*mon"stra*to*ry (?), a. Tending to demonstrate; demonstrative. Johnson.

demoralization.c: Demoralization De*mor`al*i*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. démoralisation.] The act of corrupting or subverting morals. Especially: The act of corrupting or subverting discipline, courage, hope, etc., or the state of being corrupted or subverted in discipline, courage, etc.; as, the demoralization of an army or navy.

demoralize.c: Demoralize De*mor"al*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Demoralized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Demoralizing.] [F. démoraliser; pref. dé- (L. dis- or de) + moraliser. See Moralize.] To corrupt or undermine in morals; to destroy or lessen the effect of moral principles on; to render corrupt or untrustworthy in morals, in discipline, in courage, spirit, etc.; to weaken in spirit or efficiency.

demosthenic.c: Demosthenic Dem`os*then"ic (?), a. [L. Demosthenicus: cf. F. Démosthénique.] Pertaining to, or in the style of, Demosthenes, the Grecian orator.

demote.c: Demote De*mote" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Demoted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Demoting (?).] [Pref. de- + mote, as in promote; cf. L. demovere to remove.] To reduce to a lower grade or rank, as in the military, one's employment, or in school; to assign to a lower position.

demotic.c: Demotic De*mot"ic (?), a. [Gr. dhmotiko`s, fr. dh^mos the people: cf. F. démotique.] Of or pertaining to the people; popular; common.

demotics.c: Demotics De*mot"ics (?), n. The department of knowledge relative to the care and culture of the people; sociology in its broadest sense; -- in library cataloguing.

demountable.c: Demountable De*mount"a*ble (?), [See De-; Mount.] Capable of being dismounted; -- said of a form of rim, for an automobile wheel, which can be removed with its tire from the wheel.

dempne.c: Dempne Demp"ne (dĕmp"nei) v. t. To damn; to condemn. [Obs.] Chaucer.

demster.c: Demster Dempster { Demp"ster (?; 215), Dem"ster (?), } n. [See Deemster.] 1. A deemster.

demulce.c: Demulce De*mulce" (?), v. t. [L. demulcere; de- + mulcere to stroke, soothe.] To soothe; to mollify; to pacify; to soften. [R.] Sir T. Elyot.

demulcent.c: Demulcent De*mul"cent (?), a. [L. demulcens, p. pr. of demulcere.] Softening; mollifying; soothing; assuasive; as, oil is demulcent.

Demulcent De*mul"cent, n. (Med.) A substance, usually of a mucilaginous or oily nature, supposed to be capable of soothing an inflamed nervous membrane, or protecting it from irritation. Gum Arabic, glycerin, olive oil, etc., are demulcents.

demulsion.c: Demulsion De*mul"sion (?), n. The act of soothing; that which soothes. Feltham.

demur.c: Demur De*mur" (de*mûr"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Demurred (de*mûrd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Demurring.] [OF. demurer, demorer, demourer, to linger, stay, F. demeurer, fr. L. demorari; de- + morari to delay, tarry, stay, mora delay; prob. originally, time for thinking, reflection, and akin to memor mindful. See Memory.] 1. To linger; to stay; to tarry. [Obs.]
Demur De*mur", v. t. 1. To suspend judgment concerning; to doubt of or hesitate about. [Obs.]
Demur De*mur", n. [OF. demor, demore, stay, delay. See Demur, v. i.] Stop; pause; hesitation as to proceeding; suspense of decision or action; scruple.

demure.c: Demure De*mure" (de*mūr"), a. [Perh. from OF. de murs (i. e., de bonnes murs of good manners); de of + murs, mours, meurs, mors, F. mœurs, fr. L. mores (sing. mos) manners, morals (see Moral); or more prob. fr. OF. meür, F. mûr mature, ripe (see Mature) in a phrase preceded by de, as de mûre conduite of mature conduct.] 1. Of sober or serious mien; composed and decorous in bearing; of modest look; staid; grave.
Demure De*mure", v. i. To look demurely. [Obs.] Shak.

demurely.c: Demurely De*mure"ly, adv. In a demure manner; soberly; gravely; -- now, commonly, with a mere show of gravity or modesty.

demureness.c: Demureness De*mure"ness (de*mūr"nĕs), n. The state of being demure; gravity; the show of gravity or modesty.

demurity.c: Demurity De*mur"i*ty (de*mūr"ĭ*ty̆), n. Demureness; also, one who is demure. Sir T. Browne.

demurrable.c: Demurrable De*mur"ra*ble (de*mûr"rȧ*b'l), a. That may be demurred to. Stormonth.

demurrage.c: Demurrage De*mur"rage (?), n. [Cf. OF. demorage delay. See Demur.] (Law) (a) The detention of a vessel by the freighter beyond the time allowed in her charter party for loading, unloading, or sailing. (b) The allowance made to the master or owner of the ship for such delay or detention.

demurral.c: Demurral De*mur"ral (?), n. Demur; delay in acting or deciding.

demy.c: Demy De*my" (?), n.; pl. Demies (#). [See Demi-.] 1. A printing and a writing paper of particular sizes. See under Paper.
Demy De*my", a. Pertaining to, or made of, the size of paper called demy; as, a demy book.

den.c: Den Den (dĕn), n. [AS. denn; perh. akin to G. tenne floor, thrashing floor, and to AS. denu valley.] 1. A small cavern or hollow place in the side of a hill, or among rocks; esp., a cave used by a wild beast for shelter or concealment; as, a lion's den; a den of robbers.
Den Den, v. i. To live in, or as in, a den.

denarcotize.c: Denarcotize De*nar"co*tize (?), v. t. To deprive of narcotine; as, to denarcotize opium. -- De*nar`co*ti*za"tion (#), n.

denarius.c: Denarius ‖De*na"ri*us (?), n.; pl. Denarii (#). [L. See 2d Denier.] A Roman silver coin of the value of about fourteen cents; the “penny” of the New Testament; -- so called from being worth originally ten of the pieces called as.

denary.c: Denary Den"a*ry (?), a. [L. denarius. See 2d Denier.] Containing ten; tenfold; proceeding by tens; as, the denary, or decimal, scale.
Denary Den"a*ry, n. 1. The number ten; a division into ten.

denationalization.c: Denationalization De*na`tion*al*i*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. dénationalisation.] The act or process of denationalizing.

denationalize.c: Denationalize De*na"tion*al*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Denationalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Denationalizing.] [Cf. F. dénationaliser.] 1. To divest or deprive of national character or rights.

denaturalize.c: Denaturalize De*nat"u*ral*ize (?; 135), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Denaturalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Denaturalizing.] [Cf. F. dénaturaliser.] 1. To render unnatural; to alienate from nature.

denature.c: Denature De*na"ture (?), v. t. [De- + nature.] To deprive of its natural qualities; change the nature of.

denay.c: Denay De*nay" (?), v. t. [See Deny.] To deny. [Obs.]

dendrachate.c: Dendrachate Den"dra*chate (?), n. [L. dendrachates; Gr. de`ndron a tree +? agate: cf. F. dendrachate, dendragate.] (Min.) Arborescent or dendritic agate.

dendriform.c: Dendriform Den"dri*form (?), a. [Gr. de`ndron tree + -form.] Resembling in structure a tree or shrub; having a branching shape.

dendrite.c: Dendrite Den"drite (?), n. [Gr. dendri`ths, fem. dendri^tis, of a tree, fr. de`ndron a tree: cf. F. dendrite.] (Min.) A stone or mineral on or in which are branching figures resembling shrubs or trees, produced by a foreign mineral, usually an oxide of manganese, as in the moss agate; also, a crystallized mineral having an arborescent form, e. g., gold or silver; an arborization.

dendritical.c: Dendritical Dendritic { Den*drit"ic (?), Den*drit"ic*al (?), } a. Pertaining to a dendrite, or to arborescent crystallization; having a form resembling a shrub or tree; arborescent.

dendrocoela.c: Dendrocoela ‖Den`dro*cœ"la (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. de`ndron tree + koi^los hollow.] (Zool.) A division of the Turbellaria in which the digestive cavity gives off lateral branches, which are often divided into smaller branchlets.

dendroidal.c: Dendroidal Dendroid { Den"droid (?), Den*droid"al (?), } a. [Gr.? treelike; de`ndron tree + e'i^dos form: cf. F. dendroïde.] Resembling a shrub or tree in form; treelike; branching.

dendrolite.c: Dendrolite Den"dro*lite (?), n. [Gr. de`ndron tree + -lite: cf. F. dendrolithe.] (Paleon.) A petrified or fossil shrub, plant, or part of a plant.

dendrologist.c: Dendrologist Den*drol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in the natural history of trees.

dendrometer.c: Dendrometer Den*drom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr. de`ndron tree + -meter: cf. F. dendromètre.] An instrument to measure the height and diameter of trees.

denegate.c: Denegate Den"e*gate (?), v. t. [L. denegatus, p. p. of denegare. See Deny.] To deny. [Obs.]

dengue.c: Dengue Den"gue (dĕṉ"ga), n. [See Note, below.] (Med.) A specific epidemic disease attended with high fever, cutaneous eruption, and severe pains in the head and limbs, resembling those of rheumatism; -- called also breakbone fever. It occurs in India, Egypt, the West Indies, etc., is of short duration, and rarely fatal.

deniable.c: Deniable De*ni"a*ble (?), a. [See Deny.] Capable of being, or liable to be, denied.

denial.c: Denial De*ni"al (?), n. [See Deny.] 1. The act of gainsaying, refusing, or disowning; negation; -- the contrary of affirmation.

denier.c: Denier De*ni"er (?), n. One who denies; as, a denier of a fact, or of the faith, or of Christ.

Denier ‖De*nier" (?), n. [F. denier, fr. L. denarius a Roman silver coin orig. equiv. to ten asses, later, a copper, fr. deni ten by ten, fr. the root of decem ten; akin to E. ten. See Ten, and cf. Denary, Dinar.] A small copper coin of insignificant value.

denigrate.c: Denigrate Den"i*grate (?), v. t. [L. denigrare; de- + nigrare to blacken, niger black.] 1. To blacken thoroughly; to make very black. Boyle.

denigration.c: Denigration Den`i*gra"tion (?), n. [L. denigratio.] 1. The act of making black. Boyle.

denigrator.c: Denigrator Den"i*gra`tor (?), n. One who, or that which, blackens.

denim.c: Denim Den"im (dĕn"ĭm), n. [Of uncertain origin.] A coarse cotton drilling used for overalls, etc.

denitration.c: Denitration Den`i*tra"tion (?), n. [Pref. de- + nitrate.] A disengaging, or removal, of nitric acid.

denitrification.c: Denitrification De*ni`tri*fi*ca"tion (?), n. The act or process of freeing from nitrogen; also, the condition resulting from the removal of nitrogen.

denitrify.c: Denitrify De*ni"tri*fy (?), v. t. [Pref. de- + nitrogen + -fy.] To deprive of, or free from, nitrogen.

denization.c: Denization Den`i*za"tion (?), n. The act of making one a denizen or adopted citizen; naturalization. Hallam.

denize.c: Denize De*nize" (de*nīz"), v. t. To make a denizen; to confer the rights of citizenship upon; to naturalize. [Obs.]

denizen.c: Denizen Den"i*zen (dĕn"ĭ*z'n), n. [OF. denzein, deinzein, prop., one living (a city or country); opposed to forain foreign, and fr. denz within, F. dans, fr. L. de intus, prop., from within, intus being from in in. See In, and cf. Foreign.] 1. A dweller; an inhabitant. “Denizens of air.” Pope.
Denizen Den"i*zen, v. t. 1. To constitute (one) a denizen; to admit to residence, with certain rights and privileges.

denizenize.c: Denizenize Den"i*zen*ize (?), v. t. To constitute (one) a denizen; to denizen. Abbott.

denizenship.c: Denizenship Den"i*zen*ship, n. State of being a denizen.

denmark.c: Denmark satin Den"mark sat"in (?). See under Satin.

dennet.c: Dennet Den"net (?), n. A light, open, two-wheeled carriage for one horse; a kind of gig. (“The term and vehicle common about 1825.” Latham.)

denominable.c: Denominable De*nom"i*na*ble (?), a. Capable of being denominated or named. Sir T. Browne.

denominate.c: Denominate De*nom"i*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Denominated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Denominating (?).] [L. denominatus, p. p. of denominare to name; de- + nominare to call by name. See Nominate.] To give a name to; to characterize by an epithet; to entitle; to name; to designate.

Denominate De*nom"i*nate (?), a. [L. denominatus, p. p.] Having a specific name or denomination; specified in the concrete as opposed to abstract; thus, 7 feet is a denominate quantity, while 7 is mere abstract quantity or number. See Compound number, under Compound.

denomination.c: Denomination De*nom`i*na"tion (?), n. [L. denominatio metonymy: cf. F. dénomination a naming.] 1. The act of naming or designating.

denominational.c: Denominational De*nom`i*na"tion*al (?), a. Pertaining to a denomination, especially to a sect or society. “Denominational differences.” Buckle.

denominationalism.c: Denominationalism De*nom`i*na"tion*al*ism (?), n. A denominational or class spirit or policy; devotion to the interests of a sect or denomination.

denominationalist.c: Denominationalist De*nom`i*na"tion*al*ist, n. One imbued with a denominational spirit. The Century.

denominationally.c: Denominationally De*nom`i*na"tion*al*ly, adv. In a denominational manner; by denomination or sect.

denominative.c: Denominative De*nom`i*na"tive (?), a. [Cf. F. dénominatif.] 1. Conferring a denomination or name.
Denominative De*nom`i*na"tive, n. A denominative name or term; denominative verb. Jer. Taylor. Harkness.

denominator.c: Denominator De*nom"i*na`tor (?), n. [Cf. F. dénominateur.] 1. One who, or that which, gives a name; origin or source of a name.

denotable.c: Denotable De*not"a*ble (?), a. [From Denote.] Capable of being denoted or marked. Sir T. Browne.

denotate.c: Denotate De*no"tate (?), v. t. [L. denotatus, p. p. of denotare.] To mark off; to denote. [Archaic]

denotation.c: Denotation De`no*ta"tion (?), n. [L. denotatio: cf. F. dénotation.] The marking off or separation of anything. Hammond.

denotative.c: Denotative De*not"a*tive (?), a. Having power to denote; designating or marking off.

denote.c: Denote De*note" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Denoted; p. pr. & vb. n. Denoting.] [L. denotare; de- + notare to mark, nota mark, sign, note: cf. F. dénoter. See Note.] 1. To mark out plainly; to signify by a visible sign; to serve as the sign or name of; to indicate; to point out; as, the hands of the clock denote the hour.

denouement.c: Denouement ‖Dé`noue`ment" (?), n. [F. dénouement, fr. dénouer to untie; pref. dé- (L. dis-) + nouer to tie, fr. L. nodus knot, perh. for gnodus and akin to E. knot.] 1. The unraveling or discovery of a plot; the catastrophe, especially of a drama or a romance.

denounce.c: Denounce De*nounce" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Denounced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Denouncing.] [F. dénoncer, OF. denoncier, fr. L. denuntiare, denunciare; de- + nunciare, nuntiare, to announce, report, nuntius a messenger, message. See Nuncio, and cf. Denunciate.] 1. To make known in a solemn or official manner; to declare; to proclaim (especially an evil). [Obs.]

denouncement.c: Denouncement De*nounce"ment (?), n. [Cf. OF. denoncement.] Solemn, official, or menacing announcement; denunciation. [Archaic]

denouncer.c: Denouncer De*noun"cer (?) n. One who denounces, or declares, as a menace.

dense.c: Dense Dense (?), a. [L. densus; akin to Gr.? thick with hair or leaves: cf. F. dense.] 1. Having the constituent parts massed or crowded together; close; compact; thick; containing much matter in a small space; heavy; opaque; as, a dense crowd; a dense forest; a dense fog.

densely.c: Densely Dense"ly, adv. In a dense, compact manner.

denseness.c: Denseness Dense"ness, n. The quality of being dense; density.

densimeter.c: Densimeter Den*sim"e*ter (?), n. [L. densus dense + -meter: cf. F. densimètre.] An instrument for ascertaining the specific gravity or density of a substance.

density.c: Density Den"si*ty (dĕn"sĭ*ty̆), n. [L. densitas; cf. F. densité.] 1. The quality of being dense, close, or thick; compactness; -- opposed to rarity.

dent.c: Dent Dent (dĕnt), n. [A variant of Dint.] 1. A stroke; a blow. [Obs.] “That dent of thunder.” Chaucer.
Dent Dent, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dented; p. pr. & vb. n. Denting.] To make a dent upon; to indent.
Dent Dent, n. [F., fr. L. dens, dentis, tooth. See Tooth.] (Mach.) A tooth, as of a card, a gear wheel, etc. Knight.

dental.c: dental den"tal (dĕn"tail), a. [L. dens, dentis, tooth: cf. F. dental. See Tooth.] 1. Of or pertaining to the teeth or to dentistry; as, dental surgery.
Dental Den"tal, n. [Cf. F. dentale. See Dental, a.] 1. An articulation or letter formed by the aid of the teeth.

dentalism.c: Dentalism Den"tal*ism (dĕn"tail*ĭz'm), n. The quality of being formed by the aid of the teeth.

dentalium.c: Dentalium ‖Den*ta"li*um (?), n. [NL., fr. L. dens, dentis, tooth.] (Zool.) A genus of marine mollusks belonging to the Scaphopoda, having a tubular conical shell.

dentary.c: Dentary Den"ta*ry (?), a. (Anat.) Pertaining to, or bearing, teeth. -- n. The distal bone of the lower jaw in many animals, which may or may not bear teeth.

dentated.c: Dentated Dentate { Den"tate (dĕn"tat), Den"ta*ted (dĕn"ta*tĕd), } a. [L. dentatus, fr. dens, dentis, tooth.] 1. (Bot.) Toothed; especially, with the teeth projecting straight out, not pointed either forward or backward; as, a dentate leaf.

dentateciliate.c: Dentate-ciliate Den"tate-cil"i*ate (?), a. (Bot.) Having the margin dentate and also ciliate or fringed with hairs.

dentately.c: Dentately Den"tate*ly (?), adv. In a dentate or toothed manner; as, dentately ciliated, etc.

dentatesinuate.c: Dentate-sinuate Den"tate-sin"u*ate (?), a. (Bot.) Having a form intermediate between dentate and sinuate.

dentation.c: Dentation Den*ta"tion (?), n. Formation of teeth; toothed form. [R.]

dented.c: Dented Dent"ed (?), a. [From Dent, v. t.] Indented; impressed with little hollows.

dentelle.c: Dentelle ‖Den*telle" (?), n. [F.] (Bookbinding) An ornamental tooling like lace. Knight.

dentelli.c: Dentelli ‖Den*tel"li (?), n. pl. [It., sing. dentello, prop., little tooth, dim. of dente tooth, L. dens, dentis. Cf. Dentil.] Modillions. Spectator.

dentex.c: Dentex ‖Den"tex (?), n. [NL., cf. L. dentix a sort of sea fish.] (Zool.) An edible European marine fish (Sparus dentex, or Dentex vulgaris) of the family Percidæ.

denticete.c: Denticete ‖Den`ti*ce"te (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. dens, dentis, tooth + cetus, pl. cete, whale, Gr.?.] (Zool.) The division of Cetacea in which the teeth are developed, including the sperm whale, dolphins, etc.

denticle.c: Denticle Den"ti*cle (?), n. [L. denticulus a little tooth, dim. of dens, dentis, tooth. See Dental, and cf. Dentelli.] A small tooth or projecting point.

denticulated.c: Denticulated Denticulate { Den*tic"u*late (?), Den*tic"u*la`ted (?), } a. [L. denticulatus, fr. denticulus. See Denticle.] Furnished with denticles; notched into little toothlike projections; as, a denticulate leaf of calyx. -- Den*tic"u*late*ly (#), adv.

denticulation.c: Denticulation Den*tic`u*la"tion (?), n. 1. The state of being set with small notches or teeth. Grew.

dentiferous.c: Dentiferous Den*tif"er*ous (?), a. [L. dens, dentis, tooth + -ferous.] Bearing teeth; dentigerous.

dentiform.c: Dentiform Den"ti*form (?), a. [L. dens, dentis, tooth + -form: cf. F. dentiforme.] Having the form of a tooth or of teeth; tooth-shaped.

dentifrice.c: Dentifrice Den"ti*frice (?), n. [L. dentifricium; dens, dentis, tooth + fricare to rub: cf. F. dentifrice. See Tooth, and Friction.] A powder or other substance to be used in cleaning the teeth; tooth powder.

dentigerous.c: Dentigerous Den*tig"er*ous (?), a. [L. dens, dentis, tooth + -gerous.] Bearing teeth or toothlike structures.

dentil.c: Dentil Den"til (?), n. [LL. dentillus, for L. denticulus. Cf. Dentelli, Denticle, Dentile.] (Arch.) A small square block or projection in cornices, a number of which are ranged in an ornamental band; -- used particularly in the Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite orders.

dentilabial.c: Dentilabial Den`ti*la"bi*al (?), a. Formed by the teeth and the lips, or representing a sound so formed. -- n. A dentilabial sound or letter.

dentilave.c: Dentilave Den"ti*lave (?), n. [L. dens, dentis, tooth + lavare to wash.] A wash for cleaning the teeth.

dentile.c: Dentile Den"tile (?), n. [LL. dentillus, for L. denticulus. See Dentil.] (Zool.) A small tooth, like that of a saw.

dentilingual.c: Dentilingual Den`ti*lin"gual (?), a. [L. dens tooth + E. lingual.] Produced by applying the tongue to the teeth or to the gums; or representing a sound so formed. -- n. A dentilingual sound or letter.

dentiloquist.c: Dentiloquist Den*til"o*quist (?), n. One who speaks through the teeth, that is, with the teeth closed.

dentiloquy.c: Dentiloquy Den*til"o*quy (?), n. [L. dens, dentis, tooth + loqui to speak.] The habit or practice of speaking through the teeth, or with them closed.

dentinal.c: Dentinal Den"ti*nal (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to dentine.

dentine.c: Dentine Den"tine (dĕn"tĭn), n. [Cf. F. dentine.] (Anat.) The dense calcified substance of which teeth are largely composed. It contains less animal matter than bone, and in the teeth of man is situated beneath the enamel.

dentiphone.c: Dentiphone Den"ti*phone (dĕn"tĭ*fōn), n. [L. dens, dentis, tooth + Gr. fwnh` sound.] An instrument which, placed against the teeth, conveys sound to the auditory nerve; an audiphone. Knight.

dentiroster.c: Dentiroster ‖Den`ti*ros"ter (?), n.; pl. Dentirostres (#). [NL., fr. L. dens, dentis, tooth + rostrum bill, beak: cf. F. dentirostre.] (Zool.) A dentirostral bird.

dentirostral.c: Dentirostral Den`ti*ros"tral (?), a. (Zool.) Having a toothed bill; -- applied to a group of passerine birds, having the bill notched, and feeding chiefly on insects, as the shrikes and vireos. See Illust. (N) under Beak.

dentiscalp.c: Dentiscalp Den"ti*scalp (?), n. [L. dens tooth + scalpere to scrape.] An instrument for scraping the teeth.

dentist.c: Dentist Den"tist (?), n. [From L. dens, dentis, tooth: cf. F. dentiste. See Tooth.] One whose business it is to clean, extract, or repair natural teeth, and to make and insert artificial ones; a dental surgeon.

dentistical.c: Dentistical Dentistic { Den*tis"tic (?), Den*tis"ti*cal (?), } a. Pertaining to dentistry or to dentists. [R.]

dentistry.c: Dentistry Den"tist*ry (?), n. The art or profession of a dentist; dental surgery.

dentition.c: Dentition Den*ti"tion (?), n. [L. dentitio, fr. dentire to cut teeth, fr. dens, dentis, tooth. See Dentist.] 1. The development and cutting of teeth; teething.

dentize.c: Dentize Den"tize (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Dentized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dentizing.] [L. dens, dentis, tooth.] To breed or cut new teeth. [R.]

dentoid.c: Dentoid Den"toid (?), a. [L. dens, dentis, tooth + -oid.] Shaped like a tooth; tooth-shaped.

denture.c: Denture Den"ture (?; 135), n. [L. dens, dentis, tooth: cf. F. denture, OF. denteure.] (Dentistry) An artificial tooth, block, or set of teeth.

denudate.c: Denudate De*nud"ate (?), v. t. [L. denudatus, p. p. of denudare. See Denude.] To denude. [Obs. or R.]

denudation.c: Denudation Den`u*da"tion (?; 277), n. [L. denudatio: cf. F. dénudation.] 1. The act of stripping off covering, or removing the surface; a making bare.

denude.c: Denude De*nude" (?), v. t. [L. denudare; de- + nudare to make naked or bare, nudus naked. See Nude.] To divest of all covering; to make bare or naked; to strip; to divest; as, to denude one of clothing, or lands; the hurricane denuded the trees.

denunciate.c: Denunciate De*nun"ci*ate (?), v. t. [L. denuntiatus, denunciatus, p. p. of denuntiare, -ciare. See Denounce.] To denounce; to condemn publicly or solemnly. [R.]

denunciation.c: Denunciation De*nun`ci*a"tion (?), n. [L. denuntiatio, -ciatio.] 1. Proclamation; announcement; a publishing. [Obs.]

denunciative.c: Denunciative De*nun"ci*a*tive (?), a. [L. denuntiativus, -ciativus, monitory.] Same as Denunciatory. Farrar.

denunciator.c: Denunciator De*nun"ci*a`tor (?), n. [L. denuntiator, -ciator, a police officer.] One who denounces, publishes, or proclaims, especially intended or coming evil; one who threatens or accuses.

denunciatory.c: Denunciatory De*nun"ci*a*to*ry (?), a. Characterized by or containing a denunciation; minatory; accusing; threatening; as, severe and denunciatory language.

denutrition.c: Denutrition De`nu*tri"tion (?), n. (Physiol.) The opposition of nutrition; the failure of nutrition causing the breaking down of tissue.

deny.c: Deny De*ny" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Denied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Denying.] [OE. denien, denaien, OF. denier, deneer, F. dénier, fr. L. denegare; de- + negare to say no, deny. See Negation.] 1. To declare not to be true; to gainsay; to contradict; -- opposed to affirm, allow, or admit.
Deny De*ny", v. i. To answer in??? negative; to declare an assertion not to be true.

denyingly.c: Denyingly De*ny"ing*ly, adv. In the manner of one denies a request. Tennyson.

deobstruct.c: Deobstruct De`ob*struct" (?), v. t. To remove obstructions or impediments in; to clear from anything that hinders the passage of fluids; as, to deobstruct the pores or lacteals. Arbuthnot.

deobstruent.c: Deobstruent De*ob"stru*ent (?), a. (Med.) Removing obstructions; having power to clear or open the natural ducts of the fluids and secretions of the body; aperient. -- n. (Med.) A medicine which removes obstructions; an aperient.

deodand.c: Deodand De"o*dand` (?), n. [LL. deodandum, fr. L. Deo dandum to be given to God.] (Old Eng. Law) A personal chattel which had caused the death of a person, and for that reason was given to God, that is, forfeited to the crown, to be applied to pious uses, and distributed in alms by the high almoner. Thus, if a cart ran over a man and killed him, it was forfeited as a deodand.

deodar.c: Deodar De`o*dar" (?), n. [Native name, fr. Skr. dēvadāru, prop., timber of the gods.] (Bot.) A kind of cedar (Cedrus Deodara), growing in India, highly valued for its size and beauty as well as for its timber, and also grown in England as an ornamental tree.

deodate.c: Deodate De"o*date` (?), n. [L. Deo to God (Deus God) + datum thing given.] A gift or offering to God. [Obs.]

deodorization.c: Deodorization De*o`dor*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of depriving of odor, especially of offensive odors resulting from impurities.

deodorize.c: Deodorize De*o"dor*ize (?), v. t. To deprive of odor, especially of such as results from impurities.

deodorizer.c: Deodorizer De*o"dor*i`zer (?), n. He who, or that which, deodorizes; esp., an agent that destroys offensive odors.

deonerate.c: Deonerate De*on"er*ate (?), v. t. [L. deoneratus, p. p. of deonerare. See Onerate.] To unload; to disburden. [Obs.] Cockeram.

deontologist.c: Deontologist De`on*tol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in deontology.

deontology.c: Deontology De`on*tol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.? gen.?, necessity, obligation (p. neut. of? it is necessary) + -logy.] The science which relates to duty or moral obligation. J. Bentham.

deoperculate.c: Deoperculate De`o*per"cu*late (?), a. (Bot.) Having the lid removed; -- said of the capsules of mosses.

deoppilate.c: Deoppilate De*op"pi*late (?), v. t. To free from obstructions; to clear a passage through. [Obs.] Boyle.

deoppilation.c: Deoppilation De*op`pi*la"tion (?), n. Removal of whatever stops up the passages. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

deoppilative.c: Deoppilative De*op"pi*la*tive (?), a. & n. (Med.) Deobstruent; aperient. [Obs.] Harvey.

deordination.c: Deordination De*or`di*na"tion (?), n. [LL. deordinatio depraved morality.] Disorder; dissoluteness. [Obs.]

deosculate.c: Deosculate De*os"cu*late (?), v. t. [L. deosculatus, p. p. of deosculari. See Osculate.] To kiss warmly. [Obs.] -- De*os`cu*la"tion (#), n. [Obs.]

deoxidation.c: Deoxidation De*ox`i*da"tion (?), n. (Chem.) The act or process of reducing from the state of an oxide.

deoxidize.c: Deoxidize De*ox"i*dize (?), v. t. (Chem.) To deprive of oxygen; to reduce from the state of an oxide.

deoxidizer.c: Deoxidizer De*ox"i*di`zer (?), n. (Chem.) That which removes oxygen; hence, a reducing agent; as, nascent hydrogen is a deoxidizer.

deoxygenation.c: Deoxygenation De*ox`y*gen*a"tion (?), n. (Chem.) The act or operation of depriving of oxygen.

depaint.c: Depaint De*paint" (?), p. p. [F. dépeint, p. p. of dépeindre to paint, fr. L. depingere. See Depict, p. p.] Painted. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Depaint De*paint", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depainted; p. pr. & vb. n. Depainting.] 1. To paint; to picture; hence, to describe; to delineate in words; to depict. [Obs.]

depardieux.c: Depardieux De*par"dieux` (?), interj. [OF., a corruption of de part Dieu, lit., on the part of God.] In God's name; certainly. [Obs.] Chaucer.

depart.c: Depart De*part" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Departed; p. pr. & vb. n. Departing.] [OE. departen to divide, part, depart, F. départir to divide, distribute, se départir to separate one's self, depart; pref. dé- (L. de) + partir to part, depart, fr. L. partire, partiri, to divide, fr. pars part. See Part.] 1. To part; to divide; to separate. [Obs.] Shak.
Depart De*part", v. t. 1. To part thoroughly; to dispart; to divide; to separate. [Obs.]
Depart De*part", n. [Cf. F. départ, fr. départir.] 1. Division; separation, as of compound substances into their ingredients. [Obs.]

departer.c: Departer De*part"er (?), n. 1. One who refines metals by separation. [Obs.]

department.c: Department De*part"ment (?), n. [F. département, fr. départir. See Depart, v. i.] 1. Act of departing; departure. [Obs.]
Department store De*part"ment store. A store keeping a great variety of goods which are arranged in several departments.

departmental.c: Departmental De`part*men"tal (?), a. Pertaining to a department or division. Burke.

departure.c: Departure De*par"ture (?; 135), n. [From Depart.] 1. Division; separation; putting away. [Obs.]

depascent.c: Depascent De*pas"cent (?), a. [L. depascens, p. pr. of depascere; de- + pascere to feed.] Feeding. [R.]

depasture.c: Depasture De*pas"ture (?; 135), v. t. & i. To pasture; to feed; to graze; also, to use for pasture. [R.]

depatriate.c: Depatriate De*pa"tri*ate (?), v. t. & i. [L. de- + patria one's country.] To withdraw, or cause to withdraw, from one's country; to banish. [Obs.]

depauperate.c: Depauperate De*pau"per*ate (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Depauperated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Depauperating (?).] [LL. depauperatus, p. p. depauperare to impoverish; L. de- + pauperare to make poor, pauper poor.] To make poor; to impoverish.
Depauperate De*pau"per*ate (?), a. [L. depauperatus, p. p.] (Bot.) Falling short of the natural size, from being impoverished or starved. Gray.

depauperize.c: Depauperize De*pau"per*ize (?), v. t. To free from paupers; to rescue from poverty. [R.]

depeach.c: Depeach De*peach" (?), v. t. [L. dépêcher. See Dispatch.] To discharge. [Obs.]

depectible.c: Depectible De*pec"ti*ble (?), a. [L. depectere to comb off; de- + pectere to comb.] Tough; thick; capable of extension. [Obs.]

depeculation.c: Depeculation De*pec`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. depeculari, p. p. depeculatus, to rob. See Peculate.] A robbing or embezzlement. [Obs.]

depeinct.c: Depeinct De*peinct" (?), v. t. [See Depaint.] To paint. [Obs.] Spenser.

depend.c: Depend De*pend" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Depended; p. pr. & vb. n. Depending.] [F. dépendre, fr. L. depend?re; de- + pend?re to hang. See Pendant.] 1. To hang down; to be sustained by being fastened or attached to something above.

dependable.c: Dependable De*pend"a*ble (?), a. Worthy of being depended on; trustworthy. “Dependable friendships.” Pope.

dependancy.c: Dependancy Dependance Dependant { De*pend"ant (?), De*pend"ance (?), n., De*pend"an*cy (?) }, n. See Dependent, Dependence, Dependency.

dependence.c: Dependence De*pend"ence (?), n. [LL. dependentia, fr. L. dependens. See Dependent, and cf. Dependance.] 1. The act or state of depending; state of being dependent; a hanging down or from; suspension from a support.

dependency.c: Dependency De*pend"en*cy (?), n.; pl. Dependencies (?). 1. State of being dependent; dependence; state of being subordinate; subordination; concatenation; connection; reliance; trust.

dependent.c: Dependent De*pend"ent (?), a. [L. dependens, -entis, p. pr. dependere. See Depend, and cf. Dependant.] 1. Hanging down; as, a dependent bough or leaf.
Dependent De*pend"ent, n. 1. One who depends; one who is sustained by another, or who relies on another for financial support or favor; a hanger-on; a retainer; as, a numerous train of dependents.

dependently.c: Dependently De*pend"ent*ly, adv. In a dependent manner.

depender.c: Depender De*pend"er (?), n. One who depends; a dependent.

dependingly.c: Dependingly De*pend"ing*ly, adv. As having dependence. Hale.

deperdit.c: Deperdit De*per"dit (?), n. [LL. deperditum, fr. L. deperditus, p. p. of deperdere; de- + perdere to lose, destroy.] That which is lost or destroyed. [R.] Paley.

deperditely.c: Deperditely De*per"dite*ly (?), adv. Hopelessly; despairingly; in the manner of one ruined; as, deperditely wicked. [Archaic]

deperdition.c: Deperdition Dep`er*di"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. déperdition.] Loss; destruction. [Archaic] Sir T. Browne.

dephase.c: Dephase De*phase" (?), v. t. (Elec.) To put out of phase, as two parts of a single alternating current.

dephlegm.c: Dephlegm De*phlegm" (?), v. t. [Pref. de- + phlegm water; cf. F. déphlegmer, déflegmer.] (O. Chem.) To rid of phlegm or water; to dephlegmate. [Obs.] Boyle.

dephlegmate.c: Dephlegmate De*phleg"mate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dephlegmated; p. pr. & vb. n. Dephlegmating.] [See Dephlegm.] (Chem.) To deprive of superabundant water, as by evaporation or distillation; to clear of aqueous matter; to rectify; -- used of spirits and acids.

dephlegmation.c: Dephlegmation De`phleg*ma"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. déflegmation.] (Chem.) The operation of separating water from spirits and acids, by evaporation or repeated distillation; -- called also concentration, especially when acids are the subject of it. [Obs.]

dephlegmator.c: Dephlegmator De*phleg"ma*tor (?), n. An instrument or apparatus in which water is separated by evaporation or distillation; the part of a distilling apparatus in which the separation of the vapors is effected.

dephlegmatory.c: Dephlegmatory De*phleg"ma*to*ry (?), a. Pertaining to, or producing, dephlegmation.

dephlegmedness.c: Dephlegmedness De*phlegm"ed*ness (?), n. A state of being freed from water. [Obs.] Boyle.

dephlogisticcate.c: Dephlogisticcate De`phlo*gis"tic*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dephlogisticated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dephlogisticating.] [Pref. de- + phlosticate: cf. F. déphlogistiguer.] (O. Chem.) To deprive of phlogiston, or the supposed principle of inflammability. Priestley.

dephosphorization.c: Dephosphorization De*phos`phor*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of freeing from phosphorous.

depict.c: Depict De*pict" (de*pĭkt"), p. p. [L. depictus, p. p. of depingere to depict; de- + pingere to paint. See Paint, and cf. Depaint, p. p.] Depicted. Lydgate.
Depict De*pict" (de*pĭkt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depicted; p. pr. & vb. n. Depicting.] 1. To form a colored likeness of; to represent by a picture; to paint; to portray.

depiction.c: Depiction De*pic"tion (?), n. [L. depictio.] A painting or depicting; a representation.

depicture.c: Depicture De*pic"ture (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depictured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Depicturing.] To make a picture of; to paint; to picture; to depict.

depilate.c: Depilate Dep"i*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depilated; p. pr. & vb. n. Depilating.] [L. depilatus, p. p. of depilare to depilate; de- + pilare to put forth hairs, pilus hair.] To strip of hair; to husk. Venner.

depilation.c: Depilation Dep`i*la"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. dépilation.] Act of pulling out or removing the hair; unhairing. Dryden.

depilatory.c: Depilatory De*pil"a*to*ry (?), a. [Cf. F. dépilatoire.] Having the quality or power of removing hair. -- n. An application used to take off hair.

depilous.c: Depilous Dep"i*lous (?), a. [Pref. de- + pilous: cf. L. depilis.] Hairless. Sir t. Browne.

deplanate.c: Deplanate De*pla"nate (?), a. [L. deplanetus, p. p. of deplanare to make level. See Plane, v. t.] (Bot.) Flattened; made level or even.

deplant.c: Deplant De*plant" (?), v. t. [Pref. de- + plan: cf. F. déplanter, L. deplantare to take off a twig. See Plant, v. t.] To take up (plants); to transplant. [R.]

deplantation.c: Deplantation De`plan*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. déplantation.] Act of taking up plants from beds.

deplete.c: Deplete De*plete" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depleted; p. pr. & vb. n. Depleting.] [From L. deplere to empty out; de- + plere to fill. Forined like replete, complete. See Fill, Full, a.] 1. (Med.) To empty or unload, as the vessels of human system, by bloodletting or by medicine. Copland.

depletion.c: Depletion De*ple"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. déplétion.] 1. The act of depleting or emptying.

depletive.c: Depletive De*ple"tive (?), a. [Cf. F. déplétif.] Able or fitted to deplete. -- n. A substance used to deplete.

deplication.c: Deplication Dep`li*ca"tion (?), n. [LL. deplicare to unfold; L. de- + plicare to fold.] An unfolding, untwisting, or unplaiting. [Obs.] W. Montagu.

deploitation.c: Deploitation Dep`loi*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. Exploitation, Deploy.] Same as Exploitation.

deplorable.c: Deplorable De*plor"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. déplorable.] Worthy of being deplored or lamented; lamentable; causing grief; hence, sad; calamitous; grievous; wretched; as, life's evils are deplorable.

deplorableness.c: Deplorableness De*plor"a*ble*ness, n. State of being deplorable.

deplorably.c: Deplorably De*plor"a*bly, adv. In a deplorable manner.

deplorate.c: Deplorate De*plo"rate (?), a. [L. deploratus, p. p. of deplorare. See Deplore.] Deplorable. [Obs.]

deploration.c: Deploration Dep`lo*ra"tion (?), n. [L. deploratio: cf. F. déploration.] The act of deploring or lamenting; lamentation. Speed.

deplore.c: Deplore De*plore" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deplored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Deploring.] [L. deplorare; de- + plorare to cry out, wail, lament; prob. akin to pluere to rain, and to E. flow: cf. F. déplorer. Cf. Flow.] 1. To feel or to express deep and poignant grief for; to bewail; to lament; to mourn; to sorrow over.
Deplore De*plore", v. i. To lament. Gray.

deploredness.c: Deploredness De*plor"ed*ness, n. The state of being deplored or deplorable. [R.] Bp. Hail.

deploringly.c: Deploringly De*plor"ing*ly, adv. In a deploring manner.

deploy.c: Deploy De*ploy" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Deployed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Deploying.] [F. déployer; pref. dé? = dés (L. dis) + ployer, equiv. to plier to fold, fr. L. plicare. See Ply, and cf. Display.] (Mil.) To open out; to unfold; to spread out (a body of troops) in such a way that they shall display a wider front and less depth; -- the reverse of ploy; as, to deploy a column of troops into line of battle.

deployment.c: Deployment Deploy { De*ploy" (?), De*ploy"ment (?), } n. (Mil.) The act of deploying; a spreading out of a body of men in order to extend their front. Wilhelm.

deplumate.c: Deplumate De*plu"mate (?), a. [LL. diplumatus, p. p. of deplumare. See Deplume.] (Zool.) Destitute or deprived of features; deplumed.

deplumation.c: Deplumation Dep`lu*ma"tion (?), n. [See Deplumate.] 1. The stripping or falling off of plumes or feathers. Bp. Stillingfleet

deplume.c: Deplume De*plume" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deplumed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Depluming.] [LL. deplumare; L. de- + plumare to cover with feathers, pluma feather: cf. deplumis featherless, and F. déplumer.] 1. To strip or pluck off the feather of; to deprive of of plumage.

depolarization.c: Depolarization De*po`lar*i*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. dépolarisation.] The act of depriving of polarity, or the result of such action; reduction to an unpolarized condition.

depolarize.c: Depolarize De*po"lar*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depolarized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Depolarizing.] [Pref. de- + polarize: cf. F. dépolarizer.] 1. (Opt.) To deprive of polarity; to reduce to an unpolarized condition.

depolarizer.c: Depolarizer De*po"lar*i`zer (?), n. (Elec.) A substance used to prevent polarization, as upon the negative plate of a voltaic battery.

depolish.c: Depolish De*pol"ish (de*pŏl"ĭsh), v. t. To remove the polish or glaze from.

depolishing.c: Depolishing De*pol"ish*ing (de*pŏl"ĭsh*ĭng), n. (Ceramics) The process of removing the vitreous glaze from porcelain, leaving the dull luster of the surface of ivory porcelain. Knight.

depone.c: Depone De*pone" (de*pōn"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deponed (-pōnd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Deponing.] [L. deponere, depositum, to put down, in LL., to assert under oath; de- + ponere to put, place. See Position, and cf. Deposit.] 1. To lay, as a stake; to wager. [Obs.] Hudibras.
Depone De*pone", v. i. To testify under oath; to depose; to bear witness. [A Scotticism]

deponent.c: Deponent De*po"nent (?), n. [L. deponenes, -entis, laying down. See Depone, v. t.] 1. (Law) One who deposes or testifies under oath; one who gives evidence; usually, one who testifies in writing.

Deponent De*po"nent, a. [L. deponens, -entis, laying down (its proper passive meaning), p. pr. of deponere: cf. F. déponent. See Depone.] (Gram.) Having a passive form with an active meaning, as certain latin and Greek verbs.

depopulacy.c: Depopulacy De*pop"u*la*cy (?), n. Depopulation; destruction of population. [R.] Chapman.

depopulate.c: Depopulate De*pop"u*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depopulated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Depopulating (?).] [L. depopulatus, p. p. of depopulari to ravage; de- + populari to ravage, fr. populus people: cf. OF. depopuler, F. dépeupler. See People.] To deprive of inhabitants, whether by death or by expulsion; to reduce greatly the populousness of; to dispeople; to unpeople.
Depopulate De*pop"u*late, v. i. To become dispeopled. [R.]

depopulation.c: Depopulation De*pop`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. depopulatio pillaging: cf. F. dépopulation depopulation.] The act of depopulating, or condition of being depopulated; destruction or explusion of inhabitants.

depopulator.c: Depopulator De*pop"u*la`tor (?), n. [L., pillager.] One who depopulates; a dispeopler.

deport.c: Deport De*port" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deported; p. pr. & vb. n. Deporting.] [F. déporter to transport for life, OF., to divert, amuse, from L. deportare to carry away; de- + portare to carry. See Port demeanor.] 1. To transport; to carry away; to exile; to send into banishment; to expel (from a region or country).
Deport De*port" (?), n. Behavior; carriage; demeanor; deportment. [Obs.] “Goddesslike deport.” Milton.

deportation.c: Deportation De`por*ta"tion (?), n. [L. depotatio: cf. F. déportation.] The act of deporting or exiling, or the state of being deported; banishment; transportation.

deportment.c: Deportment De*port"ment (?), n. [F. déportement misconduct, OF., demeanor. See Deport.] Manner of deporting or demeaning one's self; manner of acting; conduct; carriage; especially, manner of acting with respect to the courtesies and duties of life; behavior; demeanor; bearing.

deposable.c: Deposable De*pos"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being deposed or deprived of office. Howell.

deposal.c: Deposal De*pos"al (?), n. The act of deposing from office; a removal from the throne. Fox.

depose.c: Depose De*pose" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deposed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Deposing.][FF. déposer, in the sense of L. deponere to put down; but from pref. dé- (L. de) + poser to place. See Pose, Pause.] 1. To lay down; to divest one's self of; to lay aside. [Obs.]
Depose De*pose", v. i. To bear witness; to testify under oath; to make deposition.

deposer.c: Deposer De*pos"er (?), n. 1. One who deposes or degrades from office.

deposit.c: Deposit De*pos"it (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deposited; p. pr. & vb. n. Depositing.] [L. depositus, p. p. of deponere. See Depone, and cf. Deposit, n.] 1. To lay down; to place; to put; to let fall or throw down (as sediment); as, a crocodile deposits her eggs in the sand; the waters deposited a rich alluvium.

Deposit De*pos"it, n. [L. depositum, fr. depositus, p. p. of deponere: cf. F. dépôt, OF. depost. See Deposit, v. t., and cf. Depot.] 1. That which is deposited, or laid or thrown down; as, a deposit in a flue; especially, matter precipitated from a solution (as the siliceous deposits of hot springs), or that which is mechanically deposited (as the mud, gravel, etc., deposits of a river).

depositary.c: Depositary De*pos"i*ta*ry (?), n.; pl. Depositaries (#). [L. depositarius, fr. deponere. See Deposit.] 1. One with whom anything is lodged in the trust; one who receives a deposit; -- the correlative of depositor.

deposition.c: Deposition Dep`o*si"tion (?), n. [L. depositio, fr. deponere: cf. F. déposition. See Deposit.] 1. The act of depositing or deposing; the act of laying down or thrown down; precipitation.

depositor.c: Depositor De*pos"i*tor (de*pŏz"ĭ*tẽr), n. [L., fr. deponere. See Depone.] One who makes a deposit, especially of money in a bank; -- the correlative of depository.

depository.c: Depository De*pos"i*to*ry (-to*ry̆), n.; pl. Depositories (-rĭz). 1. A place where anything is deposited for sale or keeping; as, warehouse is a depository for goods; a clerk's office is a depository for records.

depositure.c: Depositure De*pos"i*ture (-tur; 135), n. The act of depositing; deposition. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

depot.c: Depot De"pot (dē"po; French da*pō"; 277), n. [F. dépôt, OF. depost, fr. L. depositum a deposit. See Deposit, n.] 1. A place of deposit for the storing of goods; a warehouse; a storehouse.

depravation.c: Depravation Dep`ra*va"tion (dĕp`rȧ*vā"shŭn), n. [L. depravitio, from depravare: cf. F. dépravation. See Deprave.] 1. Detraction; depreciation. [Obs.]

deprave.c: Deprave De*prave" (de*prāv"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depraved (de*prāvd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Depraving.] [L. depravare, depravatum; de- + pravus crooked, distorted, perverse, wicked.] 1. To speak ill of; to depreciate; to malign; to revile. [Obs.]

depravedly.c: Depravedly De*prav"ed*ly (?), adv. In a depraved manner.

depraver.c: Depraver De*prav"er (de*prāv"ẽr), n. One who depraves or corrupts.

depravingly.c: Depravingly De*prav"ing*ly, adv. In a depraving manner.

depravity.c: Depravity De*prav"i*ty (?), n. [From Deprave: cf. L. pravitas crookedness, perverseness.] The state of being depraved or corrupted; a vitiated state of moral character; general badness of character; wickedness of mind or heart; absence of religious feeling and principle.

deprecable.c: deprecable dep"re*ca*ble (?), a. [L. deprecabilis exorable.] That may or should be deprecated. Paley.

deprecate.c: deprecate dep"re*cate (dĕp"re*kāt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deprecated (-kā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Deprecating (-kā`tĭng).] [L. deprecatus, p. p. of deprecari to avert by prayer, to deprecate; de- + precari to pray. See Pray.] To pray against, as an evil; to seek to avert by prayer; to seek deliverance from; to express deep regret for; to desire the removal of. [archaic]

deprecatingly.c: Deprecatingly Dep"re*ca`ting*ly (-kā`tĭng*ly̆), adv. In a deprecating manner.

deprecation.c: Deprecation Dep`re*ca"tion (dĕp`re*kā"shŭn), n. [L. deprecatio; cf. F. déprécation.] 1. The act of deprecating; a praying against evil; prayer that an evil may be removed or prevented. [archaic]

deprecative.c: Deprecative Dep"re*ca*tive (dĕp"re*ka*tĭv), a. [L. deprecativus: cf. F. déprécatif.] Serving to deprecate; deprecatory.

deprecatory.c: deprecatory dep"re*ca*to*ry (dĕp"re*kȧ*to*ry̆), a. [L. deprecatorius.] 1. Tending to remove or avert evil by prayer; apologetic.

depreciate.c: Depreciate De*pre"ci*ate (de*prē"shĭ*āt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depreciated (de*prē"shĭ*ā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Depreciating (de*prē"shĭ*ā`tĭng).] [L. depretiatus, depreciatus, p. p. of depretiare, -ciare, to depreciate; de- + pretiare to prize, fr. pretium price. See Price.] To lessen in price or estimated value; to lower the worth of; to represent as of little value or claim to esteem; to undervalue. Addison.
Depreciate De*pre"ci*ate, v. i. To fall in value; to become of less worth; to sink in estimation; as, a paper currency will depreciate, unless it is convertible into specie.

depreciation.c: Depreciation De*pre`ci*a"tion (de*prē`shĭ*ā"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. dépréciation.] 1. The act of lessening, or seeking to lessen, price, value, or reputation.

depreciative.c: Depreciative De*pre"ci*a`tive (de*prē"shĭ*ā`tĭv or de*prē"shȧ*tĭv), a. Tending, or intended, to depreciate; expressing depreciation; undervaluing. -- De*pre"ci*a`tive*ly, adv.

depreciatory.c: Depreciatory De*pre"ci*a*to*ry (de*prē"shĭ*ȧ*to*ry̆ or de*prē"shȧ*to*ry̆), a. Tending to depreciate; undervaluing; depreciative.

depredable.c: Depredable Dep"re*da*ble (?), a. Liable to depredation. [Obs.] “Made less depredable.” Bacon.

depredate.c: Depredate Dep"re*date (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depredated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Depredating (?).] [L. depraedatus, p. p. of depraedari to plunder; de- + praedari to plunder, praeda plunder, prey. See Prey.] To subject to plunder and pillage; to despoil; to lay waste; to prey upon.
Depredate Dep"re*date, v. i. To take plunder or prey; to commit waste; as, the troops depredated on the country.

depredation.c: Depredation Dep`re*da"tion (?), n. [L. depraedatio: cf. F. déprédation.] The act of depredating, or the state of being depredated; the act of despoiling or making inroads; as, the sea often makes depredation on the land.

depredator.c: Depredator Dep"re*da`tor (?), n. [L. depraedator.] One who plunders or pillages; a spoiler; a robber.

depredatory.c: Depredatory Dep"re*da`to*ry (?), a. Tending or designed to depredate; characterized by depredation; plundering; as, a depredatory incursion.

depredicate.c: Depredicate De*pred"i*cate (?), v. t. [Pref. de- (intensive) + predicate.] To proclaim; to celebrate. [R.]

deprehend.c: Deprehend Dep`re*hend" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deprehended; p. pr. & vb. n. Deprehending.] [L. deprehendere, deprehensum; de- + prehendere to lay hold of, seize. See Prehensile.] 1. To take unawares or by surprise; to seize, as a person commiting an unlawful act; to catch; to apprehend.

deprehensible.c: Deprehensible Dep`re*hen"si*ble (?), a. That may be caught or discovered; apprehensible. [Obs.] Petty.

deprehension.c: Deprehension Dep`re*hen"sion (?), n. [L. deprehensio.] A catching; discovery. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

depress.c: Depress De*press" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depressed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Depressing.] [L. depressus, p. p. of deprimere; de- + premere to press. See Press.] 1. To press down; to cause to sink; to let fall; to lower; as, to depress the muzzle of a gun; to depress the eyes. “With lips depressed.” Tennyson.
Depress De*press", a. [L. depressus, p. p.] Having the middle lower than the border; concave. [Obs.]

depressant.c: Depressant De*press"ant (?), n. (Med.) An agent or remedy which lowers the vital powers.

depressed.c: Depressed De*pressed" (?), a. 1. Pressed or forced down; lowed; sunk; dejected; dispirited; sad; humbled.

depressingly.c: Depressingly De*press"ing*ly, adv. In a depressing manner.

depression.c: Depression De*pres"sion (?), n. [L. depressio: cf. F. dépression.] 1. The act of depressing.

depressive.c: Depressive De*press"ive (?), a. Able or tending to depress or cast down. -- De*press"ive*ness, n.

depressomotor.c: Depressomotor De*pres`so*mo"tor (?), a. (Med.) Depressing or diminishing the capacity for movement, as depressomotor nerves, which lower or inhibit muscular activity. -- n. Any agent that depresses the activity of the motor centers, as bromides, etc.

depressor.c: Depressor De*press"or (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, presses down; an oppressor.

depriment.c: Depriment Dep"ri*ment (?), a. [L. deprimens, p. pr. of deprimere. See Depress.] Serving to depress. [R.] “Depriment muscles.” Derham.

deprisure.c: Deprisure De*pri"sure (?), n. [F. dépriser to undervalue; pref. dé- (L. dis-) + priser to prize, fr. prix price, fr. L. pretium. See Dispraise.] Low estimation; disesteem; contempt. [Obs.]

deprivable.c: Deprivable De*priv"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being, or liable to be, deprived; liable to be deposed.

deprivation.c: Deprivation Dep`ri*va"tion (?), n. [LL. deprivatio.] 1. The act of depriving, dispossessing, or bereaving; the act of deposing or divesting of some dignity.

deprive.c: Deprive De*prive" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deprived (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Depriving.] [LL. deprivare, deprivatium, to divest of office; L. de- + privare to bereave, deprive: cf. OF. depriver. See Private.] 1. To take away; to put an end; to destroy. [Obs.]

depriver.c: Depriver De*priv"er (?), n. One who, or that which, deprives.

deprostrate.c: Deprostrate De*pros"trate (?), a. Fully prostrate; humble; low; rude. [Obs.]

deprovincialize.c: Deprovincialize De`pro*vin"cial*ize (?), v. t. To divest of provincial quality or characteristics.

depth.c: Depth Depth (sĕpth), n. [From Deep; akin to D. diepte, Icel. dȳpt, dȳpð, Goth. diupiþa.] 1. The quality of being deep; deepness; perpendicular measurement downward from the surface, or horizontal measurement backward from the front; as, the depth of a river; the depth of a body of troops.

depthless.c: Depthless Depth"less, a. 1. Having no depth; shallow.

depucelate.c: Depucelate De*pu"ce*late (?), v. t. [L. de + LL. pucella virgin, F. pucelle: cf. F. dépuceler.] To deflour; to deprive of virginity. [Obs.] Bailey.

depudicate.c: Depudicate De*pu"di*cate (?), v. t. [L. depudicatus, p. p. of depudicare.] To deflour; to dishonor. [Obs.]

depulse.c: Depulse De*pulse" (?), v. t. [L. depulsus, p. p. of depellere to drive out; de- + pellere to drive.] To drive away. [Obs.] Cockeram.

depulsion.c: Depulsion De*pul"sion (?), n. [L. depulsio.] A driving or thrusting away. [R.] Speed.

depulsory.c: Depulsory De*pul"so*ry (?), a. [L. depulsorius.] Driving or thrusting away; averting. [R.] Holland.

depurate.c: Depurate Dep"u*rate (?), a. [LL. depuratus, p. p. of depurare to purify; L. de- + purare to purify, purus clean, pure. Cf. Depure.] Depurated; cleansed; freed from impurities. Boyle.
Depurate Dep"u*rate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Depurated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Depurating (?).] To free from impurities, heterogeneous matter, or feculence; to purify; to cleanse.

depuration.c: Depuration Dep`u*ra"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. dépuration.] The act or process of depurating or freeing from foreign or impure matter, as a liquid or wound.

depurative.c: Depurative Dep"u*ra*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. dépuratif.] (Med.) Purifying the blood or the humors; depuratory. -- n. A depurative remedy or agent; or a disease which is believed to be depurative.

depurator.c: Depurator Dep"u*ra`tor (?), n. One who, or that which, cleanses.

depuratory.c: Depuratory Dep"u*ra*to*ry (?), a. [Cf. F. dépuratoire.] Depurating; tending to depurate or cleanse; depurative.

depure.c: Depure De*pure" (?), v. t. [F. dépurer. See Depurate.] To depurate; to purify. [Obs.]

depurgatory.c: Depurgatory De*pur"ga*to*ry (?), a. Serving to purge; tending to cleanse or purify. [Obs.] Cotgrave.

deputable.c: Deputable Dep"u*ta*ble (?), a. Fit to be deputed; suitable to act as a deputy. Carlyle.

deputation.c: Deputation Dep`u*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. députation. See Depute.] 1. The act of deputing, or of appointing or commissioning a deputy or representative; office of a deputy or delegate; vicegerency.

deputator.c: Deputator Dep"u*ta`tor (?), n. One who deputes, or makes a deputation. [R.] Locke.

depute.c: Depute De*pute" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deputed; p. pr. & vb. n. Deputing.] [F. députer, fr. L. deputare to esteem, consider, in LL., to destine, allot; de- + putare to clean, prune, clear up, set in order, reckon, think. See Pure.] 1. To appoint as deputy or agent; to commission to act in one's place; to delegate.
Depute De*pute", n. A person deputed; a deputy. [Scot.]

deputize.c: deputize dep"u*tize (dĕp"u*tīz), v. t. To appoint as one's deputy; to empower to act in one's stead; to appoint as one's substitute; to depute.

deputy.c: deputy dep"u*ty (dĕp"u*ty̆), n.; pl. Deputies (dĕp"u*tĭz). [F. député, fr. LL. deputatus. See Depute.] 1. One appointed as the substitute of another, and empowered to act for him, in his name or his behalf; a substitute in office; a lieutenant; a representative; a delegate; a vicegerent; as, the deputy of a prince, of a sheriff, of a township, etc.

dequantitate.c: Dequantitate De*quan"ti*tate (?), v. t. [L. de- + quantitas, -atis. See Quantity.] To diminish the quantity of; to disquantity. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

dequeen.c: Dequeen De*queen" (?), v. t. (Apiculture) To remove the queen from (a hive of bees).

deracinate.c: Deracinate De*rac"i*nate (de*răs"ĭ*nāt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deracinated (de*răs"ĭ*nā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Deracinating (de*răs"ĭ*nā`tĭng).] [F. déraciner; pref. dé- (L. dis) + racine root, fr. an assumed LL. radicina, fr. L. radix, radicis, root.] To pluck up by the roots; to extirpate. [R.]

deracination.c: Deracination De*rac`i*na"tion (?), n. The act of pulling up by the roots; eradication. [R.]

derain.c: Derain Deraign { De*raign", De*rain" } (?), v. t. [See Darraign.] (Old Law) To prove or to refute by proof; to clear (one's self). [Obs.]

derainment.c: Derainment Deraignment { De*raign"ment, De*rain"ment } (?), n. [See Darraign.] 1. The act of deraigning. [Obs.]

derail.c: Derail De*rail" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Derailed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Derailing.] To cause to run off from the rails of a railroad, as a locomotive. Lardner.

derailment.c: Derailment De*rail"ment (?), n. The act of going off, or the state of being off, the rails of a railroad.

derange.c: Derange De*range" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deranged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Deranging.] [F. déranger; pref. dé- = dés- (L. dis) + ranger to range. See Range, and cf. Disarrange, Disrank.] 1. To put out of place, order, or rank; to disturb the proper arrangement or order of; to throw into disorder, confusion, or embarrassment; to disorder; to disarrange; as, to derange the plans of a commander, or the affairs of a nation.

deranged.c: Deranged De*ranged" (?), a. Disordered; especially, disordered in mind; crazy; insane.

derangement.c: Derangement De*range"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. dérangement.] The act of deranging or putting out of order, or the state of being deranged; disarrangement; disorder; confusion; especially, mental disorder; insanity.

deray.c: Deray De*ray" (?), n. [OF. derroi, desroi, desrei; pref. des- (L. dis-) + roi, rei, rai, order. See Array.] Disorder; merriment. [Obs.]

derbio.c: Derbio ‖Der"bi*o (?), n. (Zool.) A large European food fish (Lichia glauca).

derby.c: Derby Der"by (?; usually? in Eng.; 85), n. 1. A race for three-old horses, run annually at Epsom (near London), for the Derby stakes. It was instituted by the 12th Earl of Derby, in 1780.

derbyshire.c: Derbyshire spar Der"by*shire spar" (?). (Min.) A massive variety of fluor spar, found in Derbyshire, England, and wrought into vases and other ornamental work.

derdoing.c: Derdoing Der*do"ing (?), a. [See Dere, v. t.] Doing daring or chivalrous deeds. [Obs.] “In derdoing arms.” Spenser.

dere.c: Dere Dere (?), v. t. [AS. derian to hurt.] To hurt; to harm; to injure. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Dere Dere, n. Harm. [Obs.] Robert of Brunne.

derecho.c: Derecho De*re"cho (?), n. [Sp. derecho straight.] A straight wind without apparent cyclonic tendency, usually accompanied with rain and often destructive, common in the prairie regions of the United States.

dereyne.c: Dereyne Dereine { De*reine, De*reyne" (?) }, v. t. Same as Darraign. [Obs.] Chaucer.

derelict.c: Derelict Der"e*lict (?), a. [L. derelictus, p. p. of derelinquere to forsake wholly, to abandon; de- + relinquere to leave. See Relinquish.] 1. Given up or forsaken by the natural owner or guardian; left and abandoned; as, derelict lands.

Derelict Der"e*lict, n. (Law) (a) A thing voluntary abandoned or willfully cast away by its proper owner, especially a ship abandoned at sea. (b) A tract of land left dry by the sea, and fit for cultivation or use.

dereliction.c: Dereliction Der`e*lic"tion (?), n. [L. derelictio.] 1. The act of leaving with an intention not to reclaim or resume; an utter forsaking abandonment.

dereligionize.c: Dereligionize De`re*li"gion*ize (?), v. t. To make irreligious; to turn from religion. [R.]

derf.c: Derf Derf (?), a. [Icel. djafr.] Strong; powerful; fierce. [Obs.] -- Derf"ly, adv. [Obs.]

deride.c: Deride De*ride" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Derided; p. pr. & vb. n. Deriding.] [L. deridere, derisum; de- + rid?re to laugh. See Ridicule.] To laugh at with contempt; to laugh to scorn; to turn to ridicule or make sport of; to mock; to scoff at.

derider.c: Derider De*rid"er (?), n. One who derides, or laughs at, another in contempt; a mocker; a scoffer.

deridingly.c: Deridingly De*rid"ing*ly, adv. By way of derision or mockery.

derision.c: Derision De*ri"sion (?), n. [L. derisio: cf. F. dérision. See Deride.] 1. The act of deriding, or the state of being derided; mockery; scornful or contemptuous treatment which holds one up to ridicule.

derisive.c: Derisive De*ri"sive (?), a. Expressing, serving for, or characterized by, derision. “Derisive taunts.” Pope. -- De*ri"sive*ly, adv. -- De*ri"sive*ness, n.

derisory.c: Derisory De*ri"so*ry (?), a. [L. derisorius: cf. F. dérisoire.] Derisive; mocking. Shaftesbury.

derivable.c: Derivable De*riv"a*ble (?), a. [From Derive.] That can be derived; obtainable by transmission; capable of being known by inference, as from premises or data; capable of being traced, as from a radical; as, income is derivable from various sources.

derivate.c: Derivate Der"i*vate (?), a. [L. derivatus, p. p. of derivare. See Derive.] Derived; derivative. [R.] H. Taylor. -- n. A thing derived; a derivative. [R.]
Derivate Der"i*vate (?), v. t. To derive. [Obs.] Huloet.

derivation.c: Derivation Der`i*va"tion (?), n. [L. derivatio: cf. F. dérivation. See Derive.] 1. A leading or drawing off of water from a stream or source. [Obs.] T. Burnet.

derivational.c: Derivational Der`i*va"tion*al (?), a. Relating to derivation. Earle.

derivative.c: Derivative De*riv"a*tive (?), a. [L. derivativus: cf. F. dérivatif.] Obtained by derivation; derived; not radical, original, or fundamental; originating, deduced, or formed from something else; secondary; as, a derivative conveyance; a derivative word.
Derivative De*riv"a*tive, n. 1. That which is derived; anything obtained or deduced from another.

derive.c: Derive De*rive" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Derived (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Deriving.] [F. dériver, L. derivare; de- + rivus stream, brook. See Rival.] 1. To turn the course of, as water; to divert and distribute into subordinate channels; to diffuse; to communicate; to transmit; -- followed by to, into, on, upon. [Obs.]
Derive De*rive" (?), v. i. To flow; to have origin; to descend; to proceed; to be deduced. Shak.

derivement.c: Derivement De*rive"ment (?), n. That which is derived; deduction; inference. [Obs.]

derm.c: -derm -derm (?). [See Derm, n.] A suffix or terminal formative, much used in anatomical terms, and signifying skin, integument, covering; as, blastoderm, ectoderm, etc.
Derm Derm (?), n. [Gr. de`rma, -atos, skin, fr.? to skin, flay: cf. F. derme. See Tear, v. t.] 1. The integument of animal; the skin.

dermal.c: Dermal Derm"al (?), a. [From Derm.] 1. Pertaining to the integument or skin of animals; dermic; as, the dermal secretions.

dermapteran.c: Dermapteran Dermaptera ‖Der*map"te*ra (?), Der*map"ter*an (?), n. (Zool.) See Dermoptera, Dermopteran.

dermatine.c: Dermatine Dermatic { Der*mat"ic (?), Der"ma*tine (?), } a. [Gr.?,?, fr.? skin.] Of or pertaining to the skin.

dermatitis.c: Dermatitis Der`ma*ti"tis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. de`rma, -atos, skin + -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the skin.

dermatogen.c: Dermatogen Der*mat"o*gen (?), n. [Gr. de`rma, -atos, skin + -gen.] (Bot.) Nascent epidermis, or external cuticle of plants in a forming condition.
Dermatogen Der*mat"o*gen (?), n. [Gr. de`rma, -atos, skin + -gen.] (Bot.) Nascent epidermis, or external cuticle of plants in a forming condition.

dermatography.c: Dermatography Der*ma*tog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. de`rma, -atos, skin + -graphy.] An anatomical description of, or treatise on, the skin.

dermatoid.c: Dermatoid Der"ma*toid (?), a. [Gr. de`rma, -atos, skin + -oid: cf. F. dermatoïde. Cf. Dermoid.] Resembling skin; skinlike.

dermatologist.c: dermatologist der`ma*tol"o*gist (?), n. One who discourses on the skin and its diseases; one versed in dermatology; especially, a physician with specialized training in dermatology, licensed to practise as a specialist in treating diseases of the skin.

dermatology.c: Dermatology Der`ma*tol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. de`rma, -atos, skin + -logy: cf. F. dermatologie.] The science which treats of the skin, its structure, functions, and diseases.

dermatopathic.c: Dermatopathic Der`ma*to*path"ic (?), a. [Gr. de`rma, -atos, skin + pa`qos suffering.] (Med.) Of or pertaining to skin diseases, or their cure.

dermatophyte.c: Dermatophyte Der*mat"o*phyte (dẽr*măt"o*fīt or dẽr"mȧ*to*fīt), n. [Gr. de`rma, -atos, skin + fyto`n plant.] (Med.) A fungus infecting and parasitic on the skin, especially one which causes disease; as, ringworm is caused by a dermatophyte.

dermestes.c: Dermestes ‖Der*mes"tes (?), n. [NL., from Gr. dermhsth`s; de`rma skin + root of? to eat.] (Zool.) A genus of coleopterous insects, the larvæ of which feed animal substances. They are very destructive to dries meats, skins, woolens, and furs. The most common species is Dermestes lardarius, known as the bacon beetle.

dermestoid.c: Dermestoid Der*mes"toid (?), a. [Dermestes + -oid.] (Zool.) Pertaining to or resembling the genus Dermestes.

dermic.c: Dermic Der"mic (?), a. 1. Relating to the derm or skin.

dermis.c: Dermis ‖Der"mis (?), n. [NL. See Derm.] (Anat.) The deep sensitive layer of the skin beneath the scarfskin or epidermis; -- called also true skin, derm, derma, corium, cutis, and enderon. See Skin, and Illust. in Appendix.

dermobranchiata.c: Dermobranchiata ‖Der`mo*bran`chi*a"ta (?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) A group of nudibranch mollusks without special gills.

dermobranchiate.c: Dermobranchiate Der`mo*bran"chi*ate (?), a. [Derm + branchiate.] (Zool.) Having the skin modified to serve as a gill.

dermohaemal.c: Dermohaemal Der`mo*hæ"mal (?), a. (Anat.) Pertaining to, or in relation with, both dermal and hæmal structures; as, the dermohæmal spines or ventral fin rays of fishes.

dermoid.c: Dermoid Der"moid (?), a. [Derm + -oid: cf. F. dermoïde.] Same as Dermatoid.

dermoneural.c: Dermoneural Der`mo*neu"ral (?), a. (Anat.) Pertaining to, or in relation with, both dermal and neural structures; as, the dermoneural spines or dorsal fin rays of fishes. Owen.

dermoptera.c: Dermoptera ‖Der*mop"te*ra (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? skin +? wing.] 1. (Zool.) The division of insects which includes the earwigs (Forticulidæ).Dermaptera -->

dermopteran.c: Dermopteran Der*mop"ter*an (?), n. (Zool.) An insect which has the anterior pair of wings coriaceous, and does not use them in flight, as the earwig.

dermopterygii.c: Dermopterygii ‖Der*mop`te*ryg"i*i (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? skin +? wing, fin, dim. of? wing.] (Zool.) A group of fishlike animals including the Marsipobranchiata and Leptocardia.

dermostosis.c: Dermostosis ‖Der`mos*to"sis (?), n. [NL., from Gr.? skin +? bone.] (Physiol.) Ossification of the dermis.

dern.c: Dern Dern (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A gatepost or doorpost. [Local Eng.] C. Kingsley.
Dern Dern, a. [See Dearn, a.] 1. Hidden; concealed; secret. [Obs.] “Ye must be full dern.” Chaucer.

derne.c: Derne Derne (?), v. t. & i. [AS. dyrnan to hide. See Dern, a., Dearn, a.] To hide; to skulk. [Scot.]

dernful.c: Dernful Dern"ful (?), a. Secret; hence, lonely; sad; mournful. [Obs.] “Dernful noise.” Spenser.

dernier.c: Dernier ‖Der`nier" (?), a. [F., from OF. darrein, derrain. See Darrein.] Last; final.

dernly.c: Dernly Dern"ly (?), adv. Secretly; grievously; mournfully. [Obs.] Spenser.

derogant.c: Derogant Der"o*gant (?), a. [L. derogans, p. pr.] Derogatory. [R.] T. Adams.

derogate.c: Derogate Der"o*gate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Derogated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Derogating (?).] [L. derogatus, p. p. of derogare to derogate; de- + rogare to ask, to ask the people about a law. See Rogation.] 1. To annul in part; to repeal partly; to restrict; to limit the action of; -- said of a law.
Derogate Der"o*gate (?), v. i. 1. To take away; to detract; to withdraw; -- usually with from.
Derogate Der"o*gate (?), n. [L. derogatus, p. p.] Diminished in value; dishonored; degraded. [R.] Shak.

derogately.c: Derogately Der"o*gate*ly, adv. In a derogatory manner.

derogation.c: Derogation Der`o*ga"tion (?), n. [L. derogatio: cf. F. dérogation.] 1. The act of derogating, partly repealing, or lessening in value; disparagement; detraction; depreciation; -- followed by of, from, or to.

derogative.c: Derogative De*rog"a*tive (?), a. Derogatory. -- De*rog"a*tive*ly, adv. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

derogatorily.c: derogatorily de*rog"a*to*ri*ly (?), adv. In a derogatory manner; disparagingly. Aubrey.
