derogatoriness.c: derogatoriness de*rog"a*to*ri*ness, n. Quality of being derogatory.

derogatory.c: derogatory de*rog"a*to*ry (?), a. Tending to derogate, or lessen in value; expressing a low opinion; expressing derogation; detracting; injurious; -- with from, to, or unto.

derotremata.c: Derotremata ‖Der`o*tre"ma*ta (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. de`ros skin +?,?, hole.] (Zool.) The tribe of aquatic Amphibia which includes Amphiuma, Menopoma, etc. They have permanent gill openings, but no external gills; -- called also Cryptobranchiata. [Written also Derotrema.]

derrick.c: Derrick Der"rick (?), n. [Orig., a gallows, from a hangman named Derrick. The name is of Dutch origin; D. Diederik, Dierryk, prop. meaning, chief of the people; cf. AS. peódric, E. Theodoric, G. Dietrich. See Dutch, and Rich.] 1. A mast, spar, or tall frame, supported at the top by stays or guys, and usually pivoted at the base, with suitable tackle for hoisting heavy weights, such as stones in building.

derringer.c: Derringer Der"rin*ger (?), n. [From the American inventor.] A kind of short-barreled pocket pistol, of very large caliber, often carrying a half-ounce ball.

dertrotheca.c: Dertrotheca ‖Der`tro*the"ca (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? beak +? box, case.] (Zool.) The horny covering of the end of the bill of birds.

dervis.c: Dervis Dervise Dervish { Der"vish (?), Der"vise (?), Der"vis (?), } n. [Per. derwēsch, fr. OPer. derew to beg, ask alms: cf. F. derviche.] 1. A Turkish or Persian monk, especially one who professes extreme poverty and leads an austere life.

derworth.c: Derworth Der"worth (dēr"wẽrth), a. [AS. deórwurþe, lit., dearworth.] Precious. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.

descant.c: Descant Des"cant (dĕs"kănt), n. [OF. descant, deschant, F. déchant, discant, LL. discantus, fr. L. dis + cantus singing, melody, fr. canere to sing. See Chant, and cf. Descant, v. i., Discant.] 1. (Mus.) (a) Originally, a double song; a melody or counterpoint sung above the plain song of the tenor; a variation of an air; a variation by ornament of the main subject or plain song. (b) The upper voice in part music. (c) The canto, cantus, or soprano voice; the treble. Grove.

Descant Des*cant" (dĕs*kănt"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Descanted; p. pr. & vb. n. Descanting.] [From descant; n.; or directly fr. OF. descanter, deschanter; L. dis- + cantare to sing.] 1. To sing a variation or accomplishment.

descend.c: Descend De*scend" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Descended; p. pr. & vb. n. Descending.] [F. descendre, L. descendere, descensum; de- + scandere to climb. See Scan.] 1. To pass from a higher to a lower place; to move downwards; to come or go down in any way, as by falling, flowing, walking, etc.; to plunge; to fall; to incline downward; -- the opposite of ascend.
Descend De*scend" (?), v. t. To go down upon or along; to pass from a higher to a lower part of; as, they descended the river in boats; to descend a ladder.

descendant.c: Descendant De*scend"ant (?), a. [F. descendant, p. pr. of descendre. Cf. Descendent.] Descendent.
Descendant De*scend"ant, n. One who descends, as offspring, however remotely; -- correlative to ancestor or ascendant.

descendent.c: Descendent De*scend"ent (?), a. [L. descendens, -entis, p. pr. of descendre. Cf. Descendant.] Descending; falling; proceeding from an ancestor or source.

descendibility.c: Descendibility De*scend`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being descendible; capability of being transmitted from ancestors; as, the descendibility of an estate.

descendible.c: Descendible De*scend"i*ble (?), a. 1. Admitting descent; capable of being descended.

descending.c: Descending De*scend"ing, a. Of or pertaining to descent; moving downwards.

descendingly.c: Descendingly De*scend"ing*ly, adv. In a descending manner.

descension.c: Descension De*scen"sion (?), n. [OF. descension, L. descensio. See Descent.] The act of going downward; descent; falling or sinking; declension; degradation.

descensional.c: Descensional De*scen"sion*al (?), a. Pertaining to descension. Johnson.

descensive.c: Descensive De*scen"sive (?), a. Tending to descend; tending downwards; descending. Smart.

descensory.c: Descensory De*scen"so*ry (?), n. [NL. descensorium: cf. OF. descensoire. See Descend.] A vessel used in alchemy to extract oils.

descent.c: Descent De*scent" (?), n. [F. descente, fr. descendre; like vente, from vendre. See Descend.] 1. The act of descending, or passing downward; change of place from higher to lower.

describable.c: Describable De*scrib"a*ble (?), a. That can be described; capable of description.

describe.c: Describe De*scribe" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Described (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Describing.] [L. describere, descriptum; de- + scribere to write: cf. OE. descriven, OF. descrivre, F. décrire. See Scribe, and cf. Descry.] 1. To represent by drawing; to draw a plan of; to delineate; to trace or mark out; as, to describe a circle by the compasses; a torch waved about the head in such a way as to describe a circle.
Describe De*scribe", v. i. To use the faculty of describing; to give a description; as, Milton describes with uncommon force and beauty.

describent.c: Describent De*scrib"ent (?), n. [L. describens, p. pr. of describere.] (Geom.) Same as Generatrix.

description.c: Description De*scrip"tion (?), n. [F. description, L. descriptio. See Describe.] 1. The act of describing; a delineation by marks or signs.

descriptive.c: Descriptive De*scrip"tive (?), a. [L. descriptivus: cf. F. descriptif.] Tending to describe; having the quality of representing; containing description; as, a descriptive figure; a descriptive phrase; a descriptive narration; a story descriptive of the age.

descrive.c: Descrive De*scrive" (?), v. t. [OF. descrivre. See Describe.] To describe. [Obs.] Spenser.

descry.c: Descry De*scry" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Descried (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Descrying.] [OE. descrien, discrien, to espy, prob. from the proclaiming of what was espied, fr. OF. descrier to proclaim, cry down, decry, F. décrier. The word was confused somewhat with OF. descriven, E. describe, OF. descrivre, from L. describere. See Decry.] 1. To spy out or discover by the eye, as objects distant or obscure; to espy; to recognize; to discern; to discover.
Descry De*scry" (?), n. Discovery or view, as of an army seen at a distance. [Obs.]

desecate.c: Desecate Des"e*cate (?), v. t. [L. desecare to cut off.] To cut, as with a scythe; to mow. [Obs.]

desecrate.c: Desecrate Des"e*crate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Desecrated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Desecrating (?).] [L. desecratus, p. p. of desecrare (also desacrare) to consecrate, dedicate; but taken in the sense if to divest of a sacred character; de- + sacrare to consecrate, fr. sacer sacred. See Sacred.] To divest of a sacred character or office; to divert from a sacred purpose; to violate the sanctity of; to profane; to put to an unworthy use; -- the opposite of consecrate.

desecrater.c: Desecrater Des"e*cra`ter (?), n. One who desecrates; a profaner. Harper's Mag.

desecration.c: Desecration Des`e*cra"tion (?), n. The act of desecrating; profanation; condition of anything desecrated.

desecrator.c: Desecrator Des"e*cra`tor (?), n. One who desecrates. “Desecrators of the church.” Morley.

desegmentation.c: Desegmentation De*seg`men*ta"tion (?), n. (Anat.) The loss or obliteration of division into segments; as, a desegmentation of the body.

desert.c: Desert De*sert" (de*zẽrt"), n. [OF. deserte, desserte, merit, recompense, fr. deservir, desservir, to merit. See Deserve.] That which is deserved; the reward or the punishment justly due; claim to recompense, usually in a good sense; right to reward; merit.

Desert Des"ert (dĕz"ẽrt), n. [F. désert, L. desertum, from desertus solitary, desert, pp. of deserere to desert; de- + serere to join together. See Series.] 1. A deserted or forsaken region; a barren tract incapable of supporting population, as the vast sand plains of Asia and Africa which are destitute of moisture and vegetation.

Desert Des"ert, a. [Cf. L. desertus, p. p. of deserere, and F. désert. See 2d Desert.] Of or pertaining to a desert; forsaken; without life or cultivation; unproductive; waste; barren; wild; desolate; solitary; as, they landed on a desert island.

Desert De*sert" (de*zẽrt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deserted; p. pr. & vb. n. Deserting.] [Cf. L. desertus, p. p. of deserere to desert, F. déserter. See 2d Desert.] 1. To leave (especially something which one should stay by and support); to leave in the lurch; to abandon; to forsake; -- implying blame, except sometimes when used of localities; as, to desert a friend, a principle, a cause, one's country. “The deserted fortress.” Prescott.
Desert De*sert", v. i. To abandon a service without leave; to quit military service without permission, before the expiration of one's term; to abscond.

deserter.c: Deserter De*sert"er (de*zẽrt"ẽr), n. One who forsakes a duty, a cause or a party, a friend, or any one to whom he owes service; especially, a soldier or a seaman who abandons the service without leave; one guilty of desertion.

desertion.c: Desertion De*ser"tion (de*zẽr"shŭn), n. [L. desertio: cf. F. désertion.] 1. The act of deserting or forsaking; abandonment of a service, a cause, a party, a friend, or any post of duty; the quitting of one's duties willfully and without right; esp., an absconding from military or naval service.

desertness.c: Desertness Des"ert*ness (?), n. A deserted condition. [R.] “The desertness of the country.” Udall.

desertrice.c: Desertrice Desertrix { De*sert"rix (?), De*sert"rice (?), } n. [L. desertrix.] A feminine deserter. Milton.

deserve.c: Deserve De*serve" (de*zẽrv"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deserved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Deserving.] [OF. deservir, desservir, to merit, L. deservire to serve zealously, be devoted to; de- + servire to serve. See Serve.] 1. To earn by service; to be worthy of (something due, either good or evil); to merit; to be entitled to; as, the laborer deserves his wages; a work of value deserves praise.
deserve de*serve" (de*zẽrv"), v. i. To be worthy of recompense; -- usually with ill or with well.

deservedly.c: deservedly de*serv"ed*ly (de*zẽrv"ĕd*ly̆), adv. According to desert (whether good or evil); justly.

deserving.c: Deserving De*serv"ing, a. Meritorious; worthy; as, a deserving person or act. -- De*serv"ing*ly, adv.

deshabille.c: Deshabille Des`ha*bille (?), n. [F. déshabillé, fr. déshabiller to undress; pref. dés- (L. dis-) + habiller to dress. See Habiliment, and cf. Dishabille.] An undress; a careless toilet.

desiccant.c: Desiccant De*sic"cant (?), a. [L. desiccans, p. pr. of desiccare. See Desiccate.] Drying; desiccative. -- n. (Med.) A medicine or application for drying up a sore. Wiseman.

desiccate.c: Desiccate Des"ic*cate (?; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Desiccated; p. pr. & vb. n. Desiccating.] [L. desiccatus, p. p. of desiccare to dry up; de- + siccare to dry, siccus dry. See Sack wine.] To dry up; to deprive or exhaust of moisture; to preserve by drying; as, to desiccate fish or fruit.
Desiccate Des"ic*cate, v. i. To become dry.

desiccation.c: Desiccation Des`ic*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. dessiccation.] The act of desiccating, or the state of being desiccated.

desiccative.c: Desiccative De*sic"ca*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. dessicatif.] Drying; tending to dry. Ferrand. -- n. (Med.) An application for drying up secretions.

desiccator.c: Desiccator Des"ic*ca`tor (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, desiccates.

desiderable.c: Desiderable De*sid"er*a*ble (?), a. Desirable. [R.] “Good and desiderable things.” Holland.

desiderate.c: Desiderate De*sid"er*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Desiderated; p. pr. & vb. n. Desiderating.] [L. desideratus, p. p. of desiderare to desire, miss. See Desire, and cf. Desideratum.] To desire; to feel the want of; to lack; to miss; to want.

desideration.c: Desideration De*sid`er*a"tion (?), n. [L. desideratio.] Act of desiderating; also, the thing desired. [R.] Jeffrey.

desiderative.c: Desiderative De*sid"er*a*tive (?), a. [L. desiderativus.] Denoting desire; as, desiderative verbs.
Desiderative De*sid"er*a*tive, n. 1. An object of desire.

desideratum.c: Desideratum ‖De*sid`e*ra"tum (?), n.; pl. Desiderata (#). [L., fr. desideratus, p. p. See Desiderate.] Anything desired; that of which the lack is felt; a want generally felt and acknowledge.

desidious.c: Desidious Desidiose { De*sid"i*ose` (?), De*sid"i*ous (?), } a. [L. desidiosus, fr. desidia a sitting idle, fr. desid?re to sit idle; de- + sed?re to sit.] Idle; lazy. [Obs.]

desidiousness.c: Desidiousness De*sid"i*ous*ness, n. The state or quality of being desidiose, or indolent. [Obs.] N. Bacon.

desight.c: Desight De*sight" (?), n. [Pref. de- + sight.] An unsightly object. [Obs.]

desightment.c: Desightment De*sight"ment (?), n. The act of making unsightly; disfigurement. [R.]

design.c: Design De*sign" (?; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Designed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Designing.] [F. désigner to designate, cf. F. dessiner to draw, dessin drawing, dessein a plan or scheme; all, ultimately, from L. designare to designate; de- + signare to mark, mark out, signum mark, sign. See Sign, and cf. Design, n., Designate.] 1. To draw preliminary outline or main features of; to sketch for a pattern or model; to delineate; to trace out; to draw. Dryden.
Design De*sign", v. i. To form a design or designs; to plan.

Design De*sign" (?), n. [Cf. dessein, dessin.] 1. A preliminary sketch; an outline or pattern of the main features of something to be executed, as of a picture, a building, or a decoration; a delineation; a plan.

designable.c: Designable Des"ig*na*ble (?), a. Capable of being designated or distinctly marked out; distinguishable. Boyle.

designate.c: Designate Des"ig*nate (?), a. [L. designatus, p. p. of designare. See Design, v. t.] Designated; appointed; chosen. [R.] Sir G. Buck.

Designate Des"ig*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Designated; p. pr. & vb. n. Designating.] 1. To mark out and make known; to point out; to name; to indicate; to show; to distinguish by marks or description; to specify; as, to designate the boundaries of a country; to designate the rioters who are to be arrested.

designation.c: Designation Des`ig*na"tion (?), n. [L. designatio: cf. F. désignation.] 1. The act of designating; a pointing out or showing; indication.

designative.c: Designative Des"ig*na*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. désignatif.] Serving to designate or indicate; pointing out.

designator.c: Designator Des"ig*na`tor (?), n. [L.] 1. (Rom. Antiq.) An officer who assigned to each his rank and place in public shows and ceremonies.

designatory.c: Designatory Des"ig*na*to*ry (?), a. Serving to designate; designative; indicating. [R.]

designedly.c: Designedly De*sign"ed*ly (?), adv. By design; purposely; intentionally; -- opposed to accidentally, ignorantly, or inadvertently.

designer.c: Designer De*sign"er (?), n. 1. One who designs, marks out, or plans; a contriver.

designful.c: Designful De*sign"ful (?), a. Full of design; scheming. [R.] -- De*sign"ful*ness, n. [R.] Barrow.

designing.c: Designing De*sign"ing, a. Intriguing; artful; scheming; as, a designing man.
Designing De*sign"ing, n. The act of making designs or sketches; the act of forming designs or plans.

designless.c: Designless De*sign"less, a. Without design. [Obs.] -- De*sign"less*ly, adv. [Obs.]

designment.c: Designment De*sign"ment (?), n. 1. Delineation; sketch; design; ideal; invention. [Obs.]

desilver.c: Desilver De*sil"ver (?), v. t. To deprive of silver; as, to desilver lead.

desilverization.c: Desilverization De*sil`ver*i*za"tion (?), n. The act or the process of freeing from silver; also, the condition resulting from the removal of silver.

desilverize.c: Desilverize De*sil"ver*ize (?), v. t. To deprive, or free from, silver; to remove silver from.

desinence.c: Desinence Des"i*nence (?), n. [Cf. F. désinence.] Termination; ending. Bp. Hall.

desinent.c: Desinent Des"i*nent (?), a. [L. desinens, p. pr. of desinere, desitum, to leave off, cease; de- + sinere to let, allow.] Ending; forming an end; lowermost. [Obs.] “Their desinent parts, fish.” B. Jonson.

desipient.c: Desipient De*sip"i*ent (?), a. [L. desipiens, p. pr. of desipere to be foolish; de- + sapere to be wise.] Foolish; silly; trifling. [R.]

desirability.c: Desirability De*sir`a*bil"i*ty, n. The state or quality of being desirable; desirableness.

desirable.c: Desirable De*sir"a*ble (?), a. [F. désirable, fr. L. desiderabilis. See Desire, v. t.] Worthy of desire or longing; fitted to excite desire or a wish to possess; pleasing; agreeable.

desirableness.c: Desirableness De*sir"a*ble*ness, n. The quality of being desirable.

desirably.c: Desirably De*sir"a*bly, adv. In a desirable manner.

desire.c: Desire De*sire" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Desired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Desiring.] [F. désirer, L. desiderare, origin uncertain, perh. fr. de- + sidus star, constellation, and hence orig., to turn the eyes from the stars. Cf. Consider, and Desiderate, and see Sidereal.] 1. To long for; to wish for earnestly; to covet.

Desire De*sire", n. [F. désir, fr. désirer. See Desire, v. t.] 1. The natural longing that is excited by the enjoyment or the thought of any good, and impels to action or effort its continuance or possession; an eager wish to obtain or enjoy.

desireful.c: Desireful De*sire"ful (?), a. Filled with desire; eager. [R.]

desirefulness.c: Desirefulness De*sire"ful*ness, n. The state of being desireful; eagerness to obtain and possess. [R.]

desireless.c: Desireless De*sire"less, a. Free from desire. Donne.

desirer.c: Desirer De*sir"er (?), n. One who desires, asks, or wishes.

desirous.c: Desirous De*sir"ous (?), a. [F. désireux, OF. desiros, fr. desir. See Desire, n.] Feeling desire; eagerly wishing; solicitous; eager to obtain; covetous.

desirousness.c: Desirousness De*sir"ous*ness, n. The state of being desirous.

desist.c: Desist De*sist" (?; 277), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Desisted; p. pr. & vb. n. Desisting.] [L. desistere; de- + sistere to stand, stop, fr. stare to stand: cf. F. désister. See Stand.] To cease to proceed or act; to stop; to forbear; -- often with from.

desistance.c: Desistance De*sist"ance (?), n. [Cf. F. desistance.] The act or state of desisting; cessation. [R.] Boyle.

desistive.c: Desistive De*sist"ive (?), a. [See Desist.] Final; conclusive; ending. [R.]

desition.c: Desition De*si"tion (?), n. [See Desinent.] An end or ending. [R.]

desitive.c: Desitive Des"i*tive (?), a. Final; serving to complete; conclusive. [Obs.] “Desitive propositions.” I. Watts.
Desitive Des"i*tive, n. (Logic) A proposition relating to or expressing an end or conclusion. [Obs.] I. Watts.

desk.c: Desk Desk (?), n. [OE. deske, the same word as dish, disk. See Dish, and cf. Disk.] 1. A table, frame, or case, usually with sloping top, but often with flat top, for the use writers and readers. It often has a drawer or repository underneath.
Desk Desk, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Desked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Desking.] To shut up, as in a desk; to treasure.

deskwork.c: Deskwork Desk"work` (?), n. Work done at a desk, as by a clerk or writer. Tennyson.

desman.c: Desman Des"man (dĕs"main), n. [Cf. Sw. desman musk.] (Zool.) An amphibious, insectivorous mammal found in Russia (Myogale moschata). It is allied to the moles, but is called muskrat by some English writers. [Written also dæsman.]

desmidian.c: Desmidian Desmid { Des"mid (?), Des*mid"i*an (?), } n. [Gr. desmo`s chain + e'i^dos form.] (Bot.) A microscopic plant of the family Desmidiæ, a group of unicellular algæ in which the species have a greenish color, and the cells generally appear as if they consisted of two coalescing halves.

desmine.c: Desmine Des"mine (?), n. [Gr. de`smh, desmo`s, bundle, fr. dei^n to bind.] (Min.) Same as Stilbite. It commonly occurs in bundles or tufts of crystals.

desmobacteria.c: Desmobacteria ‖Des`mo*bac*te"ri*a (dĕs`mo*băk*tē"rĭ*ȧ), n. pl. [Gr. desmo`s bond + E. bacteria.] See Microbacteria.

desmodont.c: Desmodont Des"mo*dont (dĕs"mo*dŏnt), n. [Gr. desmo`s bond + 'odoy`s, 'odo`ntos, tooth.] (Zool.) A member of a group of South American blood-sucking bats, of the genera Desmodus and Diphylla. See Vampire.

desmognathous.c: Desmognathous Des*mog"na*thous (?), a. [Gr. desmo`s bond + gna`qos jaw.] (Zool.) Having the maxillo-palatine bones united; -- applied to a group of carinate birds (Desmognathæ), including various wading and swimming birds, as the ducks and herons, and also raptorial and other kinds.

desmoid.c: Desmoid Des"moid (?), a. [Gr. desmo`s ligament + -oid.] (Anat.) Resembling, or having the characteristics of, a ligament; ligamentous.

desmology.c: Desmology Des*mol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. desmo`s ligament + -logy.] The science which treats of the ligaments. [R.]

desmomyaria.c: Desmomyaria ‖Des`mo*my*a"ri*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? bond +? muscle.] (Zool.) The division of Tunicata which includes the Salpæ. See Salpa.

desolate.c: Desolate ‖Des"o*late (?), a. [L. desolatus, p. p. of desolare to leave alone, forsake; de- + solare to make lonely, solus alone. See Sole, a.] 1. Destitute or deprived of inhabitants; deserted; uninhabited; hence, gloomy; as, a desolate isle; a desolate wilderness; a desolate house.
Desolate Des"o*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Desolated; p. pr. & vb. n. Desolating.] 1. To make desolate; to leave alone; to deprive of inhabitants; as, the earth was nearly desolated by the flood.

desolately.c: Desolately Des"o*late*ly (?), adv. In a desolate manner.

desolateness.c: Desolateness Des"o*late*ness, n. The state of being desolate.

desolater.c: Desolater Des"o*la`ter (?), n. One who, or that which, desolates or lays waste. Mede.

desolation.c: Desolation Des`o*la"tion (?), n. [F. désolation, L. desolatio.] 1. The act of desolating or laying waste; destruction of inhabitants; depopulation.

desolator.c: Desolator Des"o*la`tor (?), n. [L.] Same as Desolater. Byron.

desolatory.c: Desolatory Des"o*la*to*ry (?), a. [L. desolatorius.] Causing desolation. [R.] Bp. Hall.

desophisticate.c: Desophisticate De`so*phis"ti*cate (?), v. t. To clear from sophism or error. [R.] Hare.

desoxalic.c: Desoxalic Des`ox*al"ic (?), a. [F. pref. des- from + E. oxalic.] (Chem.) Made or derived from oxalic acid; as, desoxalic acid.

despair.c: Despair De*spair" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Despaired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Despairing.] [OE. despeiren, dispeiren, OF. desperer, fr. L. desperare; de- + sperare to hope; akin to spes hope, and perh. to spatium space, E. space, speed; cf. OF. espeir hope, F. espoir. Cf. Prosper, Desperate.] To be hopeless; to have no hope; to give up all hope or expectation; -- often with of.
Despair De*spair", v. t. 1. To give up as beyond hope or expectation; to despair of. [Obs.]
Despair De*spair", n. [Cf. OF. despoir, fr. desperer.] 1. Loss of hope; utter hopelessness; complete despondency.

despairing.c: Despairing De*spair"ing, a. Feeling or expressing despair; hopeless. -- De*spair"ing*ly, adv. -- De*spair"ing*ness, n.

desparple.c: Desparple De*spar"ple (?), v. t. & i. [OF. desparpeillier.] To scatter; to disparkle. [Obs.] Mandeville.

despatch.c: Despatch De*spatch" (?), n. & v. Same as Dispatch.

despecificate.c: Despecificate De`spe*cif"i*cate (?), v. t. [Pref. de- (intens.) + specificate.] To discriminate; to separate according to specific signification or qualities; to specificate; to desynonymize. [R.]

despect.c: Despect De*spect" (?), n. [L. despectus, fr. despicere. See Despite, n.] Contempt. [R.] Coleridge.

despection.c: Despection De*spec"tion (?), n. [L. despectio.] A looking down; a despising. [R.] W. Montagu.

despeed.c: Despeed De*speed" (?), v. t. To send hastily. [Obs.]

despend.c: Despend De*spend" (?), v. t. To spend; to squander. See Dispend. [Obs.]

desperado.c: Desperado Des`per*a"do (?), n.; pl. Desperadoes (#). [OSp. desperado, p. p. of desperar, fr. L. desperare. See Desperate.] A reckless, furious man; a person urged by furious passions, and regardless of consequence; a wild ruffian.

desperate.c: Desperate Des"per*ate (?), a. [L. desperatus, p. p. of desperare. See Despair, and cf. Desperado.] 1. Without hope; given to despair; hopeless. [Obs.]
Desperate Des"per*ate, n. One desperate or hopeless. [Obs.]

desperately.c: Desperately Des"per*ate*ly, adv. In a desperate manner; without regard to danger or safety; recklessly; extremely; as, the troops fought desperately.

desperation.c: Desperation Des`per*a"tion (?), n. [L. desperatio: cf. OF. desperation.] 1. The act of despairing or becoming desperate; a giving up of hope.

despicable.c: Despicable Des"pi*ca*ble (?), a. [L. despicabilis, fr. despicari to despise; akin to despicere. See Despise.] Fit or deserving to be despised; contemptible; mean; vile; worthless; as, a despicable man; despicable company; a despicable gift.

despicableness.c: Despicableness Des"pi*ca*ble*ness, n. The quality of being despicable; meanness; vileness; worthlessness.

despicably.c: Despicably Des"pi*ca*bly (?), adv. In a despicable or mean manner; contemptibly; as, despicably stingy.

despiciency.c: Despiciency Des*pi"cien*cy (?), n. [L. despicientia. See Despise.] A looking down; despection. [Obs.]

despisable.c: Despisable De*spis"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. OF. despisable.] Despicable; contemptible. [R.]

despise.c: Despise De*spise" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Despised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Despising.] [OF. despis-, in some forms of despire to despise, fr. L. despicere, despectum, to look down upon, despise; de- + spicere, specere, to look. See Spy, and cf. Despicable, Despite.] To look down upon with disfavor or contempt; to contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to have a low opinion or contemptuous dislike of.

despisedness.c: Despisedness De*spis"ed*ness, n. The state of being despised.

despiser.c: Despiser De*spis"er (?), n. One who despises; a contemner; a scorner.

despite.c: Despite De*spite" (?), n. [OF. despit, F. dépit, fr. L. despectus contempt, fr. despicere. See Despise, and cf. Spite, Despect.] 1. Malice; malignity; spite; malicious anger; contemptuous hate.

Despite De*spite" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Despited; p. pr. & vb. n. Despiting.] [OF. despitier, fr. L. despectare, intens. of despicere. See Despite, n.] To vex; to annoy; to offend contemptuously. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.
Despite De*spite", prep. In spite of; against, or in defiance of; notwithstanding; as, despite his prejudices.

despiteful.c: Despiteful De*spite"ful (?), a. [See Despite, and cf. Spiteful.] Full of despite; expressing malice or contemptuous hate; malicious. -- De*spite"ful*ly, adv. -- De*spite"ful*ness, n.

despiteous.c: Despiteous Des*pit"e*ous (?), a. [OE. despitous, OF. despiteus, fr. despit; affected in form by E. piteous. See Despite.] Feeling or showing despite; malicious; angry to excess; cruel; contemptuous. [Obs.] “Despiteous reproaches.” Holland.

despitous.c: Despitous De*spit"ous (?), a. Despiteous; very angry; cruel. [Obs.]

despoil.c: Despoil De*spoil" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Despoiled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Despoiling.] [OF. despoiller, F. dépouiller, L. despoliare, despoliatum; de- + spoliare to strip, rob, spolium spoil, booty. Cf. Spoil, Despoliation.] 1. To strip, as of clothing; to divest or unclothe. [Obs.] Chaucer.

despoliation.c: despoliation de*spo`li*a"tion (?), n. [L. despoliatio. See Despoil.] A stripping or plundering; spoliation. Bailey.

despond.c: despond de*spond" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Desponded; p. pr. & vb. n. Desponding.] [L. despondēre, desponsum, to promise away, promise in marriage, give up, to lose (courage); de- + spondēre to promise solemnly. See Sponsor.] To give up the will, courage, or spirit; to be thoroughly disheartened; to lose all courage; to become dispirited or depressed; to take an unhopeful view.

despondency.c: Despondency De*spond"en*cy (?), n. The state of desponding; loss of hope and cessation of effort; discouragement; depression or dejection of the mind.

despondent.c: Despondent De*spond"ent (?), a. [L. despondens, -entis, p. pr. of despondēre.] Marked by despondence; given to despondence; low-spirited; as, a despondent manner; a despondent prisoner. -- De*spond"ent*ly, adv.

despondingly.c: Despondingly De*spond"ing*ly, adv. In a desponding manner.

desponsage.c: Desponsage De*spon"sage (?), n. [From L. desponsus, p. p. See Despond.] Betrothal. [Obs.]

desponsate.c: Desponsate De*spon"sate (?), v. t. [L. desponsatus, p. p. of desponsare, intens. of despondere to betroth. See Despond.] To betroth. [Obs.] Johnson.

desponsation.c: Desponsation Des`pon*sa"tion (?), n. [L. desponsatio: cf. OF. desponsation.] A betrothing; betrothal. [Obs.]

desponsory.c: Desponsory De*spon"so*ry (?), n.; pl. Desponsories (?). A written pledge of marriage. Clarendon.

desport.c: Desport De*sport" (?), v. t. & i. See Disport.

despot.c: Despot Des"pot (?), n. [F. despote, LL. despotus, fr. Gr. despo`ths master, lord, the second part of which is akin to po`sis husband, and L. potens. See Potent.] 1. A master; a lord; especially, an absolute or irresponsible ruler or sovereign.

despotat.c: Despotat Des"po*tat (?), n. [Cf. F. despotat.] The station or government of a despot; also, the domain of a despot. Freeman.

despotical.c: Despotical Despotic { Des*pot"ic (?), Des*pot"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr. despotiko`s: cf. F. despotique.] Having the character of, or pertaining to, a despot; absolute in power; possessing and abusing unlimited power; evincing despotism; tyrannical; arbitrary. -- Des*pot"ic*al*ly, adv. -- Des*pot"ic*al*ness, n.

despotism.c: Despotism Des"po*tism (?), n. [Cf. F. despotisme.] 1. The power, spirit, or principles of a despot; absolute control over others; tyrannical sway; tyranny. “The despotism of vice.” Byron.

despotist.c: Despotist Des"po*tist, n. A supporter of despotism. [R.]

despotize.c: Despotize Des"po*tize (?), v. t. To act the despot.

despread.c: Despread De*spread" (?), v. t. & i. See Dispread.

despumate.c: Despumate Des"pu*mate (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Despumated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Despumating (?).] [L. despumatus, p. p. of despumare to despume; de- + spumare to foam, froth, spuma froth, scum.] To throw off impurities in spume; to work off in foam or scum; to foam.

despumation.c: Despumation Des`pu*ma"tion (?), n. [L. despumatio: cf. F. despumation.] The act of throwing up froth or scum; separation of the scum or impurities from liquids; scumming; clarification.

despume.c: Despume De*spume" (?), v. t. [Cf. F. despumer. See Despumate.] To free from spume or scum. [Obs.]

desquamate.c: Desquamate Des"qua*mate (?), v. i. [L. desquamatus, p. p. of desquamare to scale off; de- + squama scale.] (Med.) To peel off in the form of scales; to scale off, as the skin in certain diseases.

desquamation.c: Desquamation Des`qua*ma"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. desquamation.] (Med.) The separation or shedding of the cuticle or epidermis in the form of flakes or scales; exfoliation, as of bones.

desquamatory.c: Desquamatory Desquamative { De*squam"a*tive (?), De*squam"a*to*ry (?), } a. Of, pertaining to, or attended with, desquamation.
Desquamatory De*squam"a*to*ry, n. (Surg.) An instrument formerly used in removing the laminæ of exfoliated bones.

dessert.c: Dessert Des*sert" (?), n. [F., fr. desservir to remove from table, to clear the table; pref. des- (L. dis-) + servir to serve, to serve at table. See Serve.] A service of pastry, fruits, or sweetmeats, at the close of a feast or entertainment; pastry, fruits, etc., forming the last course at dinner.

destemper.c: Destemper Des*tem"per (?), n. [Cf. F. détrempe, fr. détremper.] A kind of painting. See Distemper.

destin.c: Destin Des"tin (?), n. [Cf. F. destin.] Destiny. [Obs.] Marston.

destinable.c: Destinable Des"ti*na*ble (?), a. [Cf. OF. destinable.] Determined by destiny; fated. Chaucer.

destinably.c: Destinably Des"ti*na*bly, adv. In a destinable manner.

destinal.c: Destinal Des"ti*nal (?), a. Determined by destiny; fated. [Obs.] “The order destinal.” Chaucer.

destinate.c: Destinate Des"ti*nate (?), a. [L. destinatus, p. p. of destinare. See Destine.] Destined. [Obs.] “Destinate to hell.” Foxe.
Destinate Des"ti*nate (?), v. t. To destine, design, or choose. [Obs.] “That name that God... did destinate.” Udall.

destination.c: Destination Des`ti*na"tion (?), n. [L. destinatio determination: cf. F. destination destination.] 1. The act of destining or appointing.

destine.c: Destine Des"tine (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Destined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Destining.] [F. destiner, L. destinare; de + the root of stare to stand. See Stand, and cf. Obstinate.] To determine the future condition or application of; to set apart by design for a future use or purpose; to fix, as by destiny or by an authoritative decree; to doom; to ordain or preordain; to appoint; -- often with the remoter object preceded by to or for.

destinist.c: Destinist Des"ti*nist (?), n. A believer in destiny; a fatalist. [R.]

destiny.c: Destiny Des"ti*ny (?), n.; pl. Destinies (#). [OE. destinee, destene, F. destinée, from destiner. See Destine.] 1. That to which any person or thing is destined; predetermined state; condition foreordained by the Divine or by human will; fate; lot; doom.

destituent.c: Destituent De*stit"u*ent (?; 135), a. [L. destituens, p. pr. of destituere.] Deficient; wanting; as, a destituent condition. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

destitute.c: Destitute Des"ti*tute (?), a. [L. destitutus, p. p. of destituere to set away, leave alone, forsake; de + statuere to set. See Statute.] 1. Forsaken; not having in possession (something necessary, or desirable); deficient; lacking; devoid; -- often followed by of.
Destitute Des"ti*tute, v. t. 1. To leave destitute; to forsake; to abandon. [Obs.]

destitution.c: Destitution Des`ti*tu"tion (?), n. [L. destitutio a forsaking.] The state of being deprived of anything; the state or condition of being destitute, needy, or without resources; deficiency; lack; extreme poverty; utter want; as, the inundation caused general destitution.

dextrer.c: Dextrer Destrer { Des*trer" (?), Dex"trer (?) }, n. [OF. destrier, fr. L. dextra on the right side. The squire led his master's horse beside him, on his right hand. Skeat.] A war horse. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Dextrer Dex*trer" (?), n. A war horse; a destrer. [Obs.] “By him baiteth his dextrer.” Chaucer.

destrie.c: Destrie De*strie" (?), v. t. To destroy. [Obs.] Chaucer.

destroy.c: Destroy De*stroy" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Destroyed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Destroying.] [OE. destroien, destruien, destrien, OF. destruire, F. détruire, fr. L. destruere, destructum; de + struere to pile up, build. See Structure.] 1. To unbuild; to pull or tear down; to separate virulently into its constituent parts; to break up the structure and organic existence of; to demolish.

destroyer.c: Destroyer De*stroy"er (?), n. [Cf. OF. destruior.] 1. One who destroys, ruins, kills, or desolates.

destruct.c: Destruct De*struct" (?), v. t. [L. destructus, p. p. of destruere. See Destroy.] To destroy. [Obs.] Mede.

destructibility.c: Destructibility De*struc`ti*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. destructibilité.] The quality of being capable of destruction; destructibleness.

destructible.c: Destructible De*struc"ti*ble (?), a. [L. destructibilis.] Liable to destruction; capable of being destroyed.

destructibleness.c: Destructibleness De*struc"ti*ble*ness, n. The quality of being destructible.

destruction.c: Destruction De*struc"tion (?), n. [L. destructio: cf. F. destruction. See Destroy.] 1. The act of destroying; a tearing down; a bringing to naught; subversion; demolition; ruin; slaying; devastation.

destructionist.c: Destructionist De*struc"tion*ist, n. 1. One who delights in destroying that which is valuable; one whose principles and influence tend to destroy existing institutions; a destructive.

destructive.c: Destructive De*struc"tive (?), a. [L. destructivus: cf. F. destructif.] Causing destruction; tending to bring about ruin, death, or devastation; ruinous; fatal; productive of serious evil; mischievous; pernicious; -- often with of or to; as, intemperance is destructive of health; evil examples are destructive to the morals of youth.
Destructive De*struc"tive, n. One who destroys; a radical reformer; a destructionist.

destructively.c: Destructively De*struc"tive*ly, adv. In a destructive manner.

destructiveness.c: Destructiveness De*struc"tive*ness (?), n. 1. The quality of destroying or ruining. Prynne.

destructor.c: Destructor De*struc"tor (?), n. [L., from destruere. See Destroy, and cf. Destroyer.] 1. A destroyer. [R.]

destruie.c: Destruie De*struie" (?), v. t. To destroy. [Obs.] Chaucer.

desudation.c: Desudation Des`u*da"tion (?), n. [L. desudatio, fr. desudare to sweat greatly; de + sudare to sweat.] (Med.) A sweating; a profuse or morbid sweating, often succeeded by an eruption of small pimples.

desuete.c: Desuete De*suete" (?), a. [L. desuetus, p. p. of desuescere to disuse.] Disused; out of use. [R.]

desuetude.c: Desuetude Des"ue*tude (?), n. [L. desuetudo, from desuescere, to grow out of use, disuse; de + suescere to become used or accustomed: cf. F. désuétude. See Custom.] The cessation of use; disuse; discontinuance of practice, custom, or fashion.

desulphurate.c: Desulphurate De*sul"phu*rate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Desulphurated; p. pr. & vb. n. Desulphurating.] To deprive of sulphur.

desulphuration.c: Desulphuration De*sul`phu*ra"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. désulfuration.] The act or process of depriving of sulphur.

desulphurize.c: Desulphurize De*sul"phur*ize (?), v. t. To desulphurate; to deprive of sulphur. -- De*sul`phur*i*za"tion (#), n.

desultorily.c: Desultorily Des"ul*to*ri*ly (?), adv. In a desultory manner; without method; loosely; immethodically.

desultoriness.c: Desultoriness Des"ul*to*ri*ness, n. The quality of being desultory or without order or method; unconnectedness.

desultory.c: Desultory Des"ul*to*ry (?), a. [L. desultorius, fr. desultor a leaper, fr. desilire, desultum, to leap down; de + salire to leap. See Saltation.] 1. Leaping or skipping about. [Obs.]

desume.c: Desume De*sume" (?), v. t. [L. desumere; de + sumere to take.] To select; to borrow. [Obs.] Sir. M. Hale.

desynonymization.c: Desynonymization De`syn*on`y*mi*za"tion (?), n. The act of desynonymizing.

desynonymize.c: Desynonymize De`syn*on"y*mize (?), v. t. To deprive of synonymous character; to discriminate in use; -- applied to words which have been employed as synonyms. Coleridge. Trench.

detach.c: Detach De*tach" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Detached (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Detaching.] [F. détacher (cf. It. distaccare, staccare); pref. dé (L. dis) + the root found also in E. attach. See Attach, and cf. Staccato.] 1. To part; to separate or disunite; to disengage; -- the opposite of attach; as, to detach the coats of a bulbous root from each other; to detach a man from a leader or from a party.
Detach De*tach", v. i. To push asunder; to come off or separate from anything; to disengage.

detachable.c: Detachable De*tach"a*ble (?), a. That can be detached.

detached.c: Detached De*tached" (?), a. Separate; unconnected, or imperfectly connected; as, detached parcels. “Extensive and detached empire.” Burke.

detachment.c: Detachment De*tach"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. détachement.] 1. The act of detaching or separating, or the state of being detached.

detail.c: Detail De"tail (dē"tāl or de*tāl"; 277), n. [F. détail, fr. détailler to cut in pieces, tell in detail; pref. dé- (L. de or dis-) + tailler to cut. See Tailor.] 1. A minute portion; one of the small parts; a particular; an item; -- used chiefly in the plural; as, the details of a scheme or transaction.

Detail De"tail (de*tāl"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Detailed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Detailing.] [Cf. F. détailler to cut up in pieces, tell in detail. See Detail, n.] 1. To relate in particulars; to particularize; to report minutely and distinctly; to enumerate; to specify; as, he detailed all the facts in due order.

detain.c: Detain De*tain" (de*tān"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Detained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Detaining.] [F. détenir, L. detinere, detentum; de + tenere to hold. See Tenable.] 1. To keep back or from; to withhold.

detainder.c: Detainder De*tain"der (-dẽr), n. (Law) A writ. See Detinue.

detainment.c: Detainment De*tain"ment (?), n. [Cf. OF. detenement.] Detention. [R.] Blackstone.

detect.c: Detect De*tect" (de*tĕkt"), a. [L. detectus, p. p. of detegere to uncover, detect; de + tegere to cover. See Tegument.] Detected. [Obs.] Fabyan.

Detect De*tect" (de*tĕkt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Detected; p. pr. & vb. n. Detecting.] 1. To uncover; to discover; to find out; to bring to light; as, to detect a crime or a criminal; to detect a mistake in an account.

detectible.c: Detectible Detectable { De*tect"a*ble (-ȧ*b'l), De*tect"i*ble (?), } a. Capable of being detected or found out; as, parties not detectable. “Errors detectible at a glance.” Latham.

detecter.c: Detecter De*tect"er (?), n. One who, or that which, detects or brings to light; one who finds out what another attempts to conceal; a detector.

detection.c: Detection De*tec"tion (?), n. [L. detectio an uncovering, revealing.] The act of detecting; the laying open what was concealed or hidden; discovery; as, the detection of a thief; the detection of fraud, forgery, or a plot.

detective.c: Detective De*tect"ive (?), a. Fitted for, or skilled in, detecting; employed in detecting crime or criminals; as, a detective officer.
Detective De*tect"ive, n. One who business it is so detect criminals or discover matters of secrecy.

detector.c: Detector De*tect"or (?), n. [L., a revealer.] One who, or that which, detects; a detecter. Shak.

Detector bar De*tect"or bar. (Railroads) A bar, connected with a switch, longer than the distance between any two consecutive wheels of a train (45 to 50 feet), laid inside a rail and operated by the wheels so that the switch cannot be thrown until all the train is past the switch.

detenebrate.c: Detenebrate De*ten"e*brate (?), v. t. [L. de + tenebrare to make dark, fr. tenebrae darkness.] To remove darkness from. [Obs.] Ash.

detent.c: Detent De*tent" (?), n. [F. détente, fr. détendre to unbend, relax; pref. dé- (L. dis- or de) + tendre to stretch. See Distend.] (Mech.) That which locks or unlocks a movement; a catch, pawl, or dog; especially, in clockwork, the catch which locks and unlocks the wheelwork in striking.

detention.c: Detention De*ten"tion (?), n. [L. detentio: cf. F. détention. See Detain.] 1. The act of detaining or keeping back; a withholding.

deter.c: Deter De*ter" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deterred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Deterring.] [L. deterrere; de + terrere to frighten, terrify. See Terror.] To prevent by fear; hence, to hinder or prevent from action by fear of consequences, or difficulty, risk, etc. Addison.

deterge.c: Deterge De*terge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deterged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Deterging.] [L. detergere, detersum; de + tergere to rub or wipe off: cf. F. déterger.] To cleanse; to purge away, as foul or offending matter from the body, or from an ulcer.

detergency.c: Detergency De*ter"gen*cy (?), n. A cleansing quality or power. De Foe.

detergent.c: Detergent De*ter"gent (?), a. [L. detergens, -entis, p. pr. of detergere: cf. F. détergent.] Cleansing; purging. -- n. A substance which cleanses the skin, as water or soap; a medicine to cleanse wounds, ulcers, etc.

deteriorate.c: Deteriorate De*te"ri*o*rate (de*tē"rĭ*o*rāt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deteriorated (de*tē"rĭ*o*rā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Deteriorating (de*tē"rĭ*o*rā`tĭng).] [L. deterioratus, p. p. of deteriorare to deteriorate, fr. deterior worse, prob. a comparative fr. de down, away.] To make worse; to make inferior in quality or value; to impair; as, to deteriorate the mind. Whately.
deteriorate de*te"ri*o*rate (de*tē"rĭ*o*rāt), v. i. To grow worse; to be impaired in quality; to degenerate.

deterioration.c: Deterioration De*te`ri*o*ra"tion (?), n. [LL. deterioratio: cf. F. détérioration.] The process of growing worse, or the state of having grown worse.

deteriority.c: deteriority de*te`ri*or"i*ty (?), n. [L. deterior worse. See Deteriorate.] Worse state or quality; inferiority. “The deteriority of the diet.” [R.] Ray.

determent.c: Determent De*ter"ment (?), n. [From Deter.] The act of deterring; also, that which deters. Boyle.

determinability.c: Determinability De*ter`mi*na*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being determinable; determinableness. Coleridge.

determinable.c: Determinable De*ter"mi*na*ble (?), a. [L. determinabilis finite. See Determine, v. t.] Capable of being determined, definitely ascertained, decided upon, or brought to a conclusion.

determinableness.c: Determinableness De*ter"mi*na*ble*ness, n. Capability of being determined; determinability.

determinant.c: Determinant De*ter"mi*nant (?), a. [L. determinans, p. pr. of determinare: cf. F. déterminant.] Serving to determine or limit; determinative.
Determinant De*ter"mi*nant, n. 1. That which serves to determine; that which causes determination.

determinate.c: Determinate De*ter"mi*nate (?), a. [L. determinatus, p. p. of determinare. See Determine.] 1. Having defined limits; not uncertain or arbitrary; fixed; established; definite.
Determinate De*ter"mi*nate (?), v. t. To bring to an end; to determine. See Determine. [Obs.]

determinately.c: Determinately De*ter"mi*nate*ly (?), adv. 1. In a determinate manner; definitely; ascertainably.

determinateness.c: Determinateness De*ter"mi*nate*ness, n. State of being determinate.

determination.c: Determination De*ter`mi*na"tion (?), n. [L. determinatio boundary, end: cf. F. détermination.] 1. The act of determining, or the state of being determined.

determinative.c: Determinative De*ter"mi*na*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. déterminatif.] Having power to determine; limiting; shaping; directing; conclusive.
Determinative De*ter"mi*na*tive (?), n. That which serves to determine.

determinator.c: Determinator De*ter"mi*na`tor (?), n. [L.] One who determines. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

determine.c: Determine De*ter"mine (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Determined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Determining.] [F. déterminer, L. determinare, determinatum; de + terminare limit, terminus limit. See Term.] 1. To fix the boundaries of; to mark off and separate.
Determine De*ter"mine, v. i. 1. To come to an end; to end; to terminate. [Obs.]

determined.c: Determined De*ter"mined (?), a. Decided; resolute. “Adetermined foe.” Sparks.

determinedly.c: Determinedly De*ter"min*ed*ly (?), adv. In a determined manner; with determination.

determiner.c: Determiner De*ter"min*er (?), n. One who, or that which, determines or decides.

determinism.c: Determinism De*ter"min*ism (?), n. (Metaph.) The doctrine that the will is not free, but is inevitably and invincibly determined by motives, preceding events, and natural laws.

determinist.c: Determinist De*ter"min*ist, n. (Metaph.) One who believes in determinism. Also adj.; as, determinist theories.

deterration.c: Deterration De`ter*ra"tion (?), n. [L. de + terra earth: cf. F. déterrer to unearth.] The uncovering of anything buried or covered with earth; a taking out of the earth or ground. Woodward.

deterrence.c: Deterrence De*ter"rence (?), n. That which deters; a deterrent; a hindrance. [R.]

deterrent.c: Deterrent De*ter"rent (?), a. [L. deterrens, p. pr. of deterrere. See Deter.] Serving to deter. “The deterrent principle.” E. Davis.
Deterrent De*ter"rent, n. That which deters or prevents.

detersion.c: Detersion De*ter"sion (?), n. [Cf. F. détersion. See Deterge.] The act of deterging or cleansing, as a sore.

detersive.c: Detersive De*ter"sive (?), a. [Cf. détersif.] Cleansing; detergent. -- n. A cleansing agent; a detergent.

detersively.c: Detersively De*ter"sive*ly, adv. In a way to cleanse.

detersiveness.c: Detersiveness De*ter"sive*ness, n. The quality of cleansing.

detest.c: Detest De*test" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Detested; p. pr. & vb. n. Detesting.] [L. detestare, detestatum, and detestari, to curse while calling a deity to witness, to execrate, detest; de + testari to be a witness, testify, testis a witness: cf. F. détester. See Testify.] 1. To witness against; to denounce; to condemn. [Obs.]

detestability.c: Detestability De*test`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. Capacity of being odious. [R.] Carlyle.

detestable.c: Detestable De*test"a*ble (?), a. [L. detestabilis: cf. F. détestable.] Worthy of being detested; abominable; extremely hateful; very odious; deserving abhorrence; as, detestable vices.

detestableness.c: Detestableness De*test"a*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being detestable.

detestably.c: Detestably De*test"a*bly, adv. In a detestable manner.

detestate.c: Detestate De*tes"tate (?), v. t. To detest. [Obs.] Udall.

detestation.c: Detestation Det`es*ta"tion (?; 277), n. [L. detestatio: cf. F. détestation.] The act of detesting; extreme hatred or dislike; abhorrence; loathing.

dethrone.c: dethrone de*throne" (de*thrōn"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dethroned (de*thrōnd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Dethroning.] [Pref. de- + throne: cf. F. détrôner; pref. dé- (L. dis-) + trône throne. See Throne.] To remove or drive from a throne; to depose; to divest of supreme authority and dignity. “The Protector was dethroned.” Hume.

dethronement.c: dethronement de*throne"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. détrônement.] Deposal from a throne; deposition from regal power.

dethronize.c: Dethronize De*thron"ize (?), v. t. [Cf. LL. dethronizare.] To dethrone or unthrone. [Obs.] Cotgrave.

detinue.c: Detinue Det"i*nue (?; 277), n. [OF. detinu, detenu, p. p. of detenir to detain. See Detain.] A person or thing detained; (Law) A form of action for the recovery of a personal chattel wrongfully detained.

detonate.c: Detonate Det"o*nate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Detonated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Detonating (?).] [L. detonare, v. i., to thunder down; de + tonare to thunder; akin to E. thunder. See Thunder, and cf. Detonize.] To explode with a sudden report; as, niter detonates with sulphur.
Detonate Det"o*nate, v. t. To cause to explode; to cause to burn or inflame with a sudden report.

detonation.c: Detonation Det`o*na"tion (dĕt`o*nā"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. détonation.] An explosion or sudden report made by the instantaneous decomposition or combustion of unstable substances; as, the detonation of gun cotton.

detonator.c: Detonator Det"o*na`tor (dĕt"o*nā`tẽr), n. One that detonates; specif.: (a) An explosive whose action is practically instantaneous. (b) Something used to detonate a charge, as a detonating fuse. (c) A case containing detonating powder, the explosion of which serves as a signal, as on railroads. (d) A gun fired by a percussion cap. [Obs.]

detonization.c: Detonization Det`o*ni*za"tion (dĕt`o*nĭ*zā"shŭn), n. The act of detonizing; detonation.

detonize.c: Detonize Det"o*nize (dĕt"o*nīz), v. t. & i. [See Detonate.] [imp. & p. p.Detonized (#); p. pr. & vb. n. Detonizing.] To explode, or cause to explode; to burn with an explosion; to detonate.

detort.c: Detort De*tort" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Detorted; p. pr. & vb. n. Detorting.] [L. detortus, p. p. of detorquere to turn away; de + torquere to turn about, twist: cf. F. détorquer, détordre.] To turn form the original or plain meaning; to pervert; to wrest. Hammond.

detortion.c: Detortion De*tor"tion (?), n. The act of detorting, or the state of being detorted; a twisting or warping.

detour.c: Detour De`tour" (?), n. [F. détour, fr. détourner to turn aside; pref. dé- (L. dis-) + tourner to turn. See Turn.] A turning; a circuitous route; a deviation from a direct course; as, the detours of the Mississippi.

detract.c: Detract De*tract" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Detracted; p. pr. & vb. n. Detracting.] [L. detractus, p. p. of detrahere to detract; de + trahere to draw: cf. F. détracter. See Trace.] 1. To take away; to withdraw.
Detract De*tract", v. i. To take away a part or something, especially from one's credit; to lessen reputation; to derogate; to defame; -- often with from.

detracter.c: Detracter De*tract"er (?), n. One who detracts; a detractor.

detractingly.c: Detractingly De*tract"ing*ly, adv. In a detracting manner.

detraction.c: Detraction De*trac"tion (?), n. [F. détraction, L. detractio.] 1. A taking away or withdrawing. [Obs.]

detractious.c: Detractious De*trac"tious (?), a. Containing detraction; detractory. [R.] Johnson.

detractive.c: Detractive De*tract"ive (?), a. 1. Tending to detractor draw. [R.]

detractiveness.c: Detractiveness De*tract"ive*ness, n. The quality of being detractive.

detractor.c: Detractor De*tract"or (?), n. [L.: cf. F. détracteur.] One who detracts; a derogator; a defamer.

detractory.c: Detractory De*tract"o*ry (?), a. Defamatory by denial of desert; derogatory; calumnious. Sir T. Browne.

detractress.c: Detractress De*tract"ress, n. A female detractor. Addison.

detrain.c: Detrain De*train" (?), v. i. & t. To alight, or to cause to alight, from a railway train. [Eng.] London Graphic.

detrect.c: Detrect De*trect" (?), v. t. [L. detrectare; de + tractare, intens. of trahere to draw.] To refuse; to decline. [Obs.] “To detrect the battle.” Holinshed.

detriment.c: Detriment Det"ri*ment (dĕt"rĭ*meint), n. [L. detrimentum, fr. deterere, detritum, to rub or wear away; de + terere to rub: cf. F. détriment. See Trite.] 1. That which injures or causes damage; mischief; harm; diminution; loss; damage; -- used very generically; as, detriments to property, religion, morals, etc.
Detriment Det"ri*ment (?), v. t. To do injury to; to hurt. [Archaic]

detrimental.c: Detrimental Det`ri*men"tal (?), a. Causing detriment; injurious; hurtful.

detrimentalness.c: Detrimentalness Det`ri*men"tal*ness, n. The quality of being detrimental; injuriousness.

detrital.c: Detrital De*tri"tal (?), a. (Geol.) Pertaining to, or composed of, detritus.

detrite.c: Detrite De*trite" (?), a. [L. detritus, p. p.] Worn out.

detrition.c: Detrition De*tri"tion (?), n. [LL. detritio. See Detriment.] A wearing off or away.

detritus.c: Detritus De*tri"tus (?), n. [F. détritus, fr. L. detritus, p. p. of deterere. See Detriment.] 1. (Geol.) A mass of substances worn off from solid bodies by attrition, and reduced to small portions; as, diluvial detritus.

detrude.c: Detrude De*trude" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Detruded; p. pr. & vb. n. Detruding.] [L. detrudere, detrusum; de + trudere to thrust, push.] To thrust down or out; to push down with force. Locke.

detruncate.c: Detruncate De*trun"cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Detruncated; p. pr. & vb. n. Detruncating.] [L. detruncatus, p. p. of detruncare to cut off; de + truncare to maim, shorten, cut off. See Truncate.] To shorten by cutting; to cut off; to lop off.

detruncation.c: Detruncation De`trun*ca"tion (?), n. [L. detruncatio: cf. F. détroncation.] The act of lopping or cutting off, as the head from the body.

detrusion.c: Detrusion De*tru"sion (?), n. [L. detrusio. See Detrude.] The act of thrusting or driving down or outward; outward thrust. -- De*tru"sive, a.

detteles.c: Detteles Dette"les (?), a. Free from debt. [Obs.] Chaucer.

detumescence.c: Detumescence De`tu*mes"cence (?), n. [L. detumescere to cease swelling; de + tumescere, tumere, to swell.] Diminution of swelling; subsidence of anything swollen. [R.] Cudworth.

detur.c: Detur ‖De"tur (?), n. [L. detur let it be given.] A present of books given to a meritorious undergraduate student as a prize. [Harvard Univ., U. S.]

deturb.c: Deturb De*turb" (?), v. t. [L. deturbare.] To throw down. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

deturbate.c: Deturbate De*tur"bate (?), v. t. [LL. deturbatus, p. p. of deturbare, fr. L. deturbare to thrust down.] To evict; to remove. [Obs.] Foxe.

deturbation.c: Deturbation Det`ur*ba"tion (?), n. The act of deturbating. [Obs.]

deturn.c: Deturn De*turn" (?), v. t. [Pref. de- + turn. Cf. Detour.] To turn away. [Obs.] Sir K. Digby.

deturpate.c: Deturpate De*tur"pate (?), v. t. [L. deturpare; de + turpare to make ugly, defile, turpis ugly, foul.] To defile; to disfigure. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

deturpation.c: Deturpation Det`ur*pa"tion (?), n. A making foul. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

deuce.c: Deuce Deuce (dūs), n. [F. deux two, OF. deus, fr. L. duo. See Two.] 1. (Gaming) Two; a card or a die with two spots; as, the deuce of hearts.

Deuce Deuce, n. [Cf. LL. dusius, Armor, dus, teûz, phantom, specter; Gael. taibhs, taibhse, apparition, ghost; or fr. OF. deus God, fr. L. deus (cf. Deity).] The devil; a demon. [A euphemism, written also deuse.] [Low]

deuced.c: Deuced Deu"ced (?), a. Devilish; excessive; extreme. [Low] -- Deu"ced*ly, adv.

deused.c: Deused Deuse Deuse (dūs), n.; Deu"sed (dū"sĕd), a. See Deuce, Deuced.

deuterocanonical.c: Deuterocanonical Deu`ter*o*ca*non"ic*al (?), a. [Gr.? second + E. canonical.] Pertaining to a second canon, or ecclesiastical writing of inferior authority; -- said of the Apocrypha, certain Epistles, etc.

deuterogamist.c: Deuterogamist Deu`ter*og"a*mist (?), n. [See Deuterogamy.] One who marries the second time.

deuterogamy.c: Deuterogamy Deu`ter*og"a*my (?), n. [Gr.?;? second +? wedding, marriage.] A second marriage, after the death of the first husband of wife; -- in distinction from bigamy, as defined in the old canon law. See Bigamy. Goldsmith.

deuterogenic.c: Deuterogenic Deu`ter*o*gen"ic (?), a. [Gr.? second + root of gi`gnesqai to be born.] (Geol.) Of secondary origin; -- said of certain rocks whose material has been derived from older rocks.

deuteronomist.c: Deuteronomist Deu`ter*on"o*mist (?), n. The writer of Deuteronomy.

deuteronomy.c: Deuteronomy Deu`ter*on"o*my (?), n. [Gr.?;? second +? law: cf. L. Deuteronomium.] (Bibl.) The fifth book of the Pentateuch, containing the second giving of the law by Moses.

deuteropathy.c: Deuteropathy Deuteropathia { ‖Deu`ter*o*pa*thi"a (?), Deu`ter*op"a*thy (?), } n. [NL. deuteropathia, fr. Gr.? second +? suffering, fr.?,?, to suffer: cf. F. deutéropathie.] (Med.) A sympathetic affection of any part of the body, as headache from an overloaded stomach.

deuteropathic.c: Deuteropathic Deu`ter*o*path"ic (?), a. Pertaining to deuteropathy; of the nature of deuteropathy.

deuterozooid.c: Deuterozooid Deu`ter*o*zo"oid (?), n. [Gr.? second + E. zooid.] (Zool.) One of the secondary, and usually sexual, zooids produced by budding or fission from the primary zooids, in animals having alternate generations. In the tapeworms, the joints are deuterozooids.

deut.c: Deut- Deuto- Deu"to- (?) or Deut- (dūt-) [Contr. from Gr. dey`teros second.] (Chem.) A prefix which formerly properly indicated the second in a regular series of compound in the series, and not to its composition, but which is now generally employed in the same sense as bi- or di-, although little used.

deutohydroguret.c: Deutohydroguret Deu`to*hy*drog"u*ret (?), n. [Pref. deut-, deuto- + hydroguret.] (Chem.) A compound containing in the molecule two atoms of hydrogen united with some other element or radical. [Obs.]

deutoplasm.c: Deutoplasm Deu"to*plasm (?), n. [Pref. deuto- + Gr.? form.] (Biol.) The lifeless food matter in the cytoplasm of an ovum or a cell, as distinguished from the active or true protoplasm; yolk substance; yolk.

deutoplastic.c: Deutoplastic Deu`to*plas"tic (?), a. [Pref. deuto- + Gr.? plastic.] (Biol.) Pertaining to, or composed of, deutoplasm.

deutosulphuret.c: Deutosulphuret Deu`to*sul"phu*ret (?), n. [Pref. deuto- + sulphuret.] (Chem.) A disulphide. [Obs.]

deutoxide.c: Deutoxide Deu*tox"ide (?; 104), n. [Pref. deut- + oxide.] (Chem.) A compound containing in the molecule two atoms of oxygen united with some other element or radical; -- usually called dioxide, or less frequently, binoxide.

deutzia.c: Deutzia ‖Deut"zi*a (?), n. [NL. Named after Jan Deutz of Holland.] (Bot.) A genus of shrubs with pretty white flowers, much cultivated.

deva.c: Deva Dev ‖Dev (?), or ‖De"va (?), n. [Skr. d?va. Cf. Deity.] (Hind. Myth.) A god; a deity; a divine being; an idol; a king.

devanagari.c: Devanagari ‖De`va*na"ga*ri (?), n. [Skr. dēvanāgarī; dēva god + nagara city, i. e., divine city.] The script or characters in which Sanskrit and Hindi are written.

devaporation.c: Devaporation De*vap`o*ra"tion (?), n. The change of vapor into water, as in the formation of rain.

devast.c: Devast De*vast" (?), v. t. [Cf. F. dévaster. See Devastate.] To devastate. [Obs.] Bolingbroke.

devastate.c: Devastate Dev"as*tate (?; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Devastated; p. pr. & vb. n. Devastating.] [L. devastatus, p. p. of devastare to devastate; de + vastare to lay waste, vastus waste. See Vast.] To lay waste; to ravage; to desolate.

devastation.c: Devastation Dev`as*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. dévastation.] 1. The act of devastating, or the state of being devastated; a laying waste.

devastator.c: Devastator Dev"as*ta`tor (?), n. [L.] One who, or that which, devastates. Emerson.

devastavit.c: Devastavit ‖Dev`as*ta"vit (?), n. [L., he has wasted.] (Law) Waste or misapplication of the assets of a deceased person by an executor or an administrator. Bouvier.

devata.c: Devata ‖De"va*ta (?), n. [Hind., fr. Skr. d?va god.] (Hind. Myth.) A deity; a divine being; a good spirit; an idol. [Written also dewata.]

develin.c: Develin Dev"el*in (?), n. (Zool.) The European swift. [Prov. Eng.]

develop.c: Develop De*vel"op (de*vĕl"ŏp), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Developed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Developing.] [F. déveloper; dé- (L. dis-) + OF. voluper, voleper, to envelop, perh. from L. volup agreeably, delightfully, and hence orig., to make agreeable or comfortable by enveloping, to keep snug (cf. Voluptuous); or. perh. fr. a derivative of volvere, volutum, to roll (cf. Devolve). Cf. Envelop.] [Written also develope.] 1. To free from that which infolds or envelops; to unfold; to lay open by degrees or in detail; to make visible or known; to disclose; to produce or give forth; as, to develop theories; a motor that develops 100 horse power.

Develop De*vel"op (?), v. i. 1. To go through a process of natural evolution or growth, by successive changes from a less perfect to a more perfect or more highly organized state; to advance from a simpler form of existence to one more complex either in structure or function; as, a blossom develops from a bud; the seed develops into a plant; the embryo develops into a well-formed animal; the mind develops year by year.

developable.c: Developable De*vel"op*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being developed. J. Peile.

developer.c: Developer De*vel"op*er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, develops.

development.c: Development De*vel"op*ment (?), n. [Cf. F. développement.] [Written also developement.] 1. The act of developing or disclosing that which is unknown; a gradual unfolding process by which anything is developed, as a plan or method, or an image upon a photographic plate; gradual advancement or growth through a series of progressive changes; also, the result of developing, or a developed state.

developmental.c: Developmental De*vel`op*men"tal (?), a. Pertaining to, or characteristic of, the process of development; as, the developmental power of a germ. Carpenter.

devenustate.c: Devenustate Dev`e*nus"tate (?), v. t. [L. devenustatus, p. p. of devenustare to disfigure; de + venustus lovely, graceful.] To deprive of beauty or grace. [Obs.]

devergency.c: Devergency Devergence { De*ver"gence (?), De*ver"gen*cy (?), } n. See Divergence. [Obs.]

devest.c: Devest De*vest" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Devested; p. pr. & vb. n. Devesting.] [L. devestire to undress; de + vestire to dress: cf. OF. devestir, F. dévêtir. Cf. Divest.] 1. To divest; to undress. Shak.
Devest De*vest", v. i. (Law) To be taken away, lost, or alienated, as a title or an estate.

devex.c: Devex De*vex" (?), a. [L. devexus, from devehere to carry down.] Bending down; sloping. [Obs.]

devexity.c: Devexity De*vex"i*ty (?), n. [L. devexitas, fr. devexus. See Devex, a.] A bending downward; a sloping; incurvation downward; declivity. [R.] Davies (Wit's Pilgr.)

devi.c: Devi ‖De"vi (?), n.; fem. of Deva. A goddess.

deviate.c: Deviate De"vi*ate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Deviated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Deviating (?).] [L. deviare to deviate; de + viare to go, travel, via way. See Viaduct.] To go out of the way; to turn aside from a course or a method; to stray or go astray; to err; to digress; to diverge; to vary.
Deviate De"vi*ate, v. t. To cause to deviate. [R.]

deviation.c: deviation de`vi*a"tion (?), n. [LL. deviatio: cf. F. déviation.] 1. The act of deviating; a wandering from the way; variation from the common way, from an established rule, etc.; departure, as from the right course or the path of duty.

deviator.c: Deviator De"vi*a`tor (?), n. [L., a forsaker.] One who, or that which, deviates.

deviatory.c: Deviatory De"vi*a*to*ry (?), a. Tending to deviate; devious; as, deviatory motion. [R.] Tully.

device.c: Device De*vice" (?), n. [OE. devis, devise, will, intention, opinion, invention, fr. F. devis architect's plan and estimates (in OF., division, plan, wish), devise device (in sense 3), in OF. also, division, wish, last will, fr. deviser. See Devise, v. t., and cf. Devise, n.] 1. That which is devised, or formed by design; a contrivance; an invention; a project; a scheme; often, a scheme to deceive; a stratagem; an artifice.

deviceful.c: Deviceful De*vice"ful (?), a. Full of devices; inventive. [R.]

devicefully.c: Devicefully De*vice"ful*ly, adv. In a deviceful manner. [R.]

devil.c: Devil Dev"il (?), n. [AS. deófol, deóful; akin to G.?eufel, Goth. diabaúlus; all fr. L. diabolus the devil, Gr.? the devil, the slanderer, fr.? to slander, calumniate, orig., to throw across;? across +? to throw, let fall, fall; cf. Skr. gal to fall. Cf. Diabolic.] 1. The Evil One; Satan, represented as the tempter and spiritual of mankind.
devil dev"il (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Deviled (?) or Devilled; p. pr. & vb. n. Deviling (?) or Devilling.] 1. To make like a devil; to invest with the character of a devil.
Devil bird Devil-diver Dev"il-div`er (?), Dev"il bird` (?), n.. (Zool.) A small water bird. See Dabchick.

devilet.c: Devilet Dev"il*et (?), n. A little devil. [R.] Barham.

devilfish.c: Devilfish Dev"il*fish` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) A huge ray (Manta birostris or Cephaloptera vampyrus) of the Gulf of Mexico and Southern Atlantic coasts. Several other related species take the same name. See Cephaloptera. (b) A large cephalopod, especially the very large species of Octopus and Architeuthis. See Octopus. (c) The gray whale of the Pacific coast. See Gray whale. (d) The goosefish or angler (Lophius), and other allied fishes. See Angler.

deviling.c: Deviling Dev"il*ing, n. A young devil. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

devilish.c: Devilish Dev"il*ish, a. 1. Resembling, characteristic of, or pertaining to, the devil; diabolical; wicked in the extreme. “Devilish wickedness.” Sir P. Sidney.

devilism.c: Devilism Dev"il*ism (?), n. The state of the devil or of devils; doctrine of the devil or of devils. Bp. Hall.

devilize.c: Devilize Dev"il*ize (?), v. t. To make a devil of. [R.]

devilkin.c: Devilkin Dev"il*kin (?), n. A little devil; a devilet.

devilry.c: Devilry Dev"il*ry (?), n.; pl. Devilries (?). 1. Conduct suitable to the devil; extreme wickedness; deviltry.

devils.c: Devil's darning-needle Dev"il's darn"ing-nee`dle. (Zool.) A dragon fly. See Darning needle, under Darn, v. t.

devilship.c: Devilship Dev"il*ship, n. The character or person of a devil or the devil. Cowley.

deviltry.c: Deviltry Dev"il*try (?), n.; pl. Deviltries (?). Diabolical conduct; malignant mischief; devilry. C. Reade.

devilwood.c: Devilwood Dev"il*wood` (?), n. (Bot.) A kind of tree (Osmanthus Americanus), allied to the European olive.

devious.c: Devious De"vi*ous (?), a. [L. devius; de + via way. See Viaduct.] 1. Out of a straight line; winding; varying from directness; as, a devious path or way.

devirginate.c: Devirginate De*vir"gin*ate (?), a. [L. devirginatus, p. p. of devirginare.] Deprived of virginity. [R.]
Devirginate De*vir"gin*ate (?), v. t. To deprive of virginity; to deflower. [R.] Sandys.

devirgination.c: Devirgination De*vir`gi*na"tion (?), n. [L. devirginatio.] A deflowering. [R.] Feltham.

devisable.c: Devisable De*vis"a*ble (?), a. [From Devise.] 1. Capable of being devised, invented, or contrived.

devise.c: Devise De*vise" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Devised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Devising.] [OF. deviser to distribute, regulate, direct, relate, F., to chat, fr. L. divisus divided, distributed, p. p. of dividere. See Divide, and cf. Device.] 1. To form in the mind by new combinations of ideas, new applications of principles, or new arrangement of parts; to formulate by thought; to contrive; to excogitate; to invent; to plan; to scheme; as, to devise an engine, a new mode of writing, a plan of defense, or an argument.
Devise De*vise", v. i. To form a scheme; to lay a plan; to contrive; to consider.

Devise De*vise" (?), n. [OF. devise division, deliberation, wish, will, testament. See Device.] 1. The act of giving or disposing of real estate by will; -- sometimes improperly applied to a bequest of personal estate.

devisee.c: Devisee Dev`i*see" (?), n. (Law) One to whom a devise is made, or real estate given by will.

devisor.c: Devisor De*vis"or (?), n. (Law) One who devises, or gives real estate by will; a testator; -- correlative to devisee.

devitable.c: Devitable Dev"i*ta*ble (?), a. [L. devitare to avoid; de + vitare to shun, avoid.] Avoidable. [Obs.]

devitalize.c: Devitalize De*vi"tal*ize (?), v. t. To deprive of life or vitality. -- De*vi`tal*i*za"tion (#), n.

devitation.c: Devitation Dev`i*ta"tion (?), n. [L. devitatio.] An avoiding or escaping; also, a warning. [Obs.] Bailey.

devitrification.c: Devitrification De*vit`ri*fi*ca"tion (?), n. The act or process of devitrifying, or the state of being devitrified. Specifically, the conversion of molten glassy matter into a stony mass by slow cooling, the result being the formation of crystallites, microbites, etc., in the glassy base, which are then called devitrification products.

devitrify.c: Devitrify De*vit"ri*fy (?), v. t. To deprive of glasslike character; to take away vitreous luster and transparency from.

devocalize.c: Devocalize De*vo"cal*ize (?), v. t. To make toneless; to deprive of vowel quality. -- De*vo`cal*i*za"tion, n.

devocation.c: Devocation Dev`o*ca"tion (?), n. [L. devocare to call off or away; de + vocare to call.] A calling off or away. [R.] Hallywell.

devoid.c: Devoid De*void" (?), v. t. [OE. devoiden to leave, OF. desvuidier, desvoidier, to empty out. See Void.] To empty out; to remove.
Devoid De*void", a. [See Devoid, v. t.] 1. Void; empty; vacant. [Obs.] Spenser.

devoir.c: Devoir ‖De*voir" (?), n. [F., fr. L. debere to owe. See Due.] Duty; service owed; hence, due act of civility or respect; -- now usually in the plural; as, they paid their devoirs to the ladies. “Do now your devoid, young knights!” Chaucer.

devolute.c: Devolute Dev"o*lute (?), v. t. [L. devolutus, p. p. of devolvere. See Devolve.] To devolve. [Obs.] Foxe.

devolution.c: Devolution Dev`o*lu"tion (?), n. [LL. devolutio: cf. F. dévolution.] 1. The act of rolling down. [R.]

devolve.c: Devolve De*volve" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Devolved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Devolving.] [L. devolvere, devolutum, to roll down; de + volvere to roll down; de + volvere to roll. See Voluble.] 1. To roll onward or downward; to pass on.

Devolve De*volve", v. i. To pass by transmission or succession; to be handed over or down; -- generally with on or upon, sometimes with to or into; as, after the general fell, the command devolved upon (or on) the next officer in rank.

devolvement.c: Devolvement De*volve"ment (?), n. The act or process of devolving;; devolution.

devon.c: Devon De"von (?), n. One of a breed of hardy cattle originating in the country of Devon, England. Those of pure blood have a deep red color. The small, longhorned variety, called North Devons, is distinguished by the superiority of its working oxen.

devonian.c: Devonian De*vo"ni*an (?), a. (Geol.) Of or pertaining to Devon or Devonshire in England; as, the Devonian rocks, period, or system.
Devonian De*vo"ni*an, n. The Devonian age or formation.

devoration.c: Devoration Dev`o*ra"tion (?), n. [L. devoratio. See Devour.] The act of devouring. [Obs.] Holinshed.

devotary.c: Devotary De*vo"ta*ry (?), n. [See Devote, Votary.] A votary. [Obs.] J. Gregory.

devote.c: Devote De*vote" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Devoted; p. pr. & vb. n. Devoting.] [L. devotus, p. p. of devovere; de + vovere to vow. See Vow, and cf. Devout, Devow.] 1. To appropriate by vow; to set apart or dedicate by a solemn act; to consecrate; also, to consign over; to doom; to evil; to devote one to destruction; the city was devoted to the flames.
Devote De*vote" (?), a. [L. devotus, p. p.] Devoted; addicted; devout. [Obs.] Milton.
Devote De*vote", n. A devotee. [Obs.] Sir E. Sandys.

devoted.c: Devoted De*vot"ed, a. Consecrated to a purpose; strongly attached; zealous; devout; as, a devoted admirer. -- De*vot"ed*ly, adv. -- De*vot"ed*ness, n.

devotee.c: Devotee Dev`o*tee" (?), n. One who is wholly devoted; esp., one given wholly to religion; one who is superstitiously given to religious duties and ceremonies; a bigot.

devotement.c: Devotement De*vote"ment (?), n. The state of being devoted, or set apart by a vow. [R.] Bp. Hurd.

devoter.c: Devoter De*vot"er (?), n. One who devotes; a worshiper.

devotion.c: Devotion De*vo"tion (?), n. [F. dévotion, L. devotio.] 1. The act of devoting; consecration.

devotional.c: Devotional De*vo"tion*al (?), a. [L. devotionalis.] Pertaining to, suited to, or used in, devotion; as, a devotional posture; devotional exercises; a devotional frame of mind.

devotionist.c: Devotionist Devotionalist { De*vo"tion*al*ist, De*vo"tion*ist, } n. One given to devotion, esp. to excessive formal devotion.

devotionality.c: Devotionality De*vo`tion*al"i*ty (?), n. The practice of a devotionalist. A. H. Clough.

devotionally.c: Devotionally De*vo"tion*al*ly (?), adv. In a devotional manner; toward devotion.

devoto.c: Devoto ‖De*vo"to (?), n. [It.] A devotee. Dr. J. Scott.

devotor.c: Devotor De*vo"tor (?), n. [L.] A worshiper; one given to devotion. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

devour.c: Devour De*vour" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Devoured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Devouring.] [F. dévorer, fr. L. devorare; de + vorare to eat greedily, swallow up. See Voracious.] 1. To eat up with greediness; to consume ravenously; to feast upon like a wild beast or a glutton; to prey upon.

devourable.c: Devourable De*vour"a*ble (?), a. That may be devoured.

devourer.c: Devourer De*vour"er (?), n. One who, or that which, devours.

devouringly.c: Devouringly De*vour"ing*ly, adv. In a devouring manner.

devout.c: Devout De*vout" (?), a. [OE. devot, devout, F. dévot, from L. devotus devoted, p. p. of devovere. See Devote, v. t.] 1. Devoted to religion or to religious feelings and duties; absorbed in religious exercises; given to devotion; pious; reverent; religious.

devoutless.c: Devoutless De*vout"less, a. Destitute of devotion. -- De*vout"less*ly, adv. -- De*vout"less*ness, n.

devoutly.c: Devoutly De*vout"ly, adv. 1. In a devout and reverent manner; with devout emotions; piously.

devoutness.c: Devoutness De*vout"ness, n. Quality or state of being devout.

devove.c: Devove De*vove" (?), v. t. [See Devote, v. t.] To devote. [Obs.] Cowley.

devow.c: Devow De*vow" (?), v. t. [F. dévouer, L. devovere. See Devote, v. t.] 1. To give up; to devote. [Obs.]

devulgarize.c: Devulgarize De*vul"gar*ize (?), v. t. To free from what is vulgar, common, or narrow.

dew.c: Dew Dew (dū), n. [AS. deáw; akin to D. dauw, G. thau, tau, Icel. dögg, Sw. dagg, Dan. dug; cf. Skr. dhav, dhāv, to flow. √72. Cf. Dag dew.] 1. Moisture from the atmosphere condensed by cool bodies upon their surfaces, particularly at night.
Dew Dew, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dewed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dewing.] To wet with dew or as with dew; to bedew; to moisten; as with dew.
Dew Dew, a. & n. Same as Due, or Duty. [Obs.] Spenser.

dewar.c: Dewar flask Dewar vessel Dewar Dew"ar (dū"ẽr), Dew"ar ves`sel, Dew"ar flask. [After Sir James Dewar, British physicist.] A double-walled glass vessel for holding liquid air, liquid nitrogen, etc., having the space between the walls exhausted so as to prevent conduction of heat, and sometimes having the glass silvered to prevent absorption of radiant heat; -- called also, according to the particular shape, Dewar bulb, Dewar tube, etc.

dewberry.c: Dewberry Dew"ber`ry (?), n. (Bot.) (a) The fruit of certain species of bramble (Rubus); in England, the fruit of Rubus cæsius, which has a glaucous bloom; in America, that of Rubus canadensis and Rubus hispidus, species of low blackberries. (b) The plant which bears the fruit.

dewclaw.c: Dewclaw Dew"claw` (?), n. In any animal, esp. of the Herbivora, a rudimentary claw or small hoof not reaching the ground.

dewdrop.c: Dewdrop Dew"drop` (?), n. A drop of dew. Shak.

dewfall.c: dewfall dew"fall` (?), n. The falling of dew; the time when dew begins to fall.

dewiness.c: dewiness dew"i*ness (?), n. State of being dewy.

dewlap.c: Dewlap Dew"lap` (?), n. [Dew + lap to lick.] 1. The pendulous skin under the neck of an ox, which laps or licks the dew in grazing.

dewlapped.c: Dewlapped Dew"lapped` (?), a. Furnished with a dewlap.

dewless.c: Dewless Dew"less, a. Having no dew. Tennyson.

dewpoint.c: Dew-point Dew"-point` (?), n. (Meteor.) The temperature at which dew begins to form. It varies with the humidity and temperature of the atmosphere.

dewret.c: Dewret Dew"ret` (?), v. t. [Dew + ret, v. t.] To ret or rot by the process called dewretting.

dewretting.c: Dewretting Dew"ret`ting, n. Dewrotting; the process of decomposing the gummy matter of flax and hemp and setting the fibrous part, by exposure on a sward to dew, rain, and sunshine.

dewrot.c: Dewrot Dew"rot` (?), v. t. To rot, as flax or hemp, by exposure to rain, dew, and sun. See Dewretting.

dewy.c: Dewy Dew"y (?), a. 1. Pertaining to dew; resembling, consisting of, or moist with, dew.

dexter.c: Dexter Dex"ter (dĕks"tẽr), a. [L.,; akin to Gr.?,?, Skr. dakshiṇa (cf. daksh to be strong, suit); Goth. taihswa, OHG. zeso. Cf. Dexterous.] 1. Pertaining to, or situated on, the right hand; right, as opposed to sinister, or left.

Dexter Dex"ter, n. [Prob. so named after the original breeder.] One of a breed of small hardy cattle originating from the Kerry breed of Ireland, valuable both for beef and milk. They are usually chiefly black, sometimes red, and somewhat resemble a small shorthorn in build. Called also Dexter Kerry.

dexterity.c: Dexterity Dex*ter"i*ty (?), n. [L. dexteritas, fr. dexter: cf. F. dextérité. See Dexter.] 1. Right-handedness.

dexterous.c: Dexterous Dex"ter*ous (?), a. [L. dexter. See Dexter.] [Written also dextrous.] 1. Ready and expert in the use of the body and limbs; skillful and active with the hands; handy; ready; as, a dexterous hand; a dexterous workman.

dexterously.c: Dexterously Dex"ter*ous*ly (?), adv. In a dexterous manner; skillfully.

dexterousness.c: Dexterousness Dex"ter*ous*ness, n. The quality of being dexterous; dexterity.

dextrad.c: Dextrad Dex"trad (?), adv. [L. dextra the right hand + ad to.] (Anat.) Toward the right side; dextrally.

dextral.c: Dextral Dex"tral (?), a. [From Dexter.] Right, as opposed to sinistral, or left.

dextrality.c: Dextrality Dex*tral"i*ty (?), n. The state of being on the right-hand side; also, the quality of being right-handed; right-handedness. Sir T. Browne.

dextrally.c: Dextrally Dex"tral*ly (?), adv. Towards the right; as, the hands of a watch rotate dextrally.

dextrin.c: Dextrin Dex"trin (?), n. [Cf. F. dextrine, G. dextrin. See Dexter.] (Chem.) A translucent, gummy, amorphous substance, nearly tasteless and odorless, used as a substitute for gum, for sizing, etc., and obtained from starch by the action of heat, acids, or diastase. It is of somewhat variable composition, containing several carbohydrates which change easily to their respective varieties of sugar.
