discal.c: Discal Disc"al (?), a. Pertaining to, or resembling, a disk; as, discal cells.

discalceate.c: Discalceate Dis*cal"ce*ate (?), v. t. [L. discalceatus unshod; dis- + calceus shoe.] To pull off shoes or sandals from. [Obs.] Cockeram.

discalceated.c: Discalceated Dis*cal"ce*at`ed (?), a. Deprived off shoes or sandals; unshod; discalced.

discalceation.c: Discalceation Dis*cal`ce*a"tion (?), n. The act of pulling off the shoes or sandals. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

discalced.c: Discalced Dis*calced" (?), a. Unshod; barefooted; -- in distinction from calced. “The foundation of houses of discalced friars.” Cardinal Manning's St. Teresa.

discamp.c: Discamp Dis*camp" (?), v. t. [See Decamp.] To drive from a camp. [Obs.] Holland.

discandy.c: Discandy Dis*can"dy (?), v. i. To melt; to dissolve; to thaw. [Obs.]

discapacitate.c: Discapacitate Dis*ca*pac"i*tate (?), v. t. To deprive of capacity; to incapacitate. [R.]

discard.c: Discard Dis*card" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discarded; p. pr. & vb. n. Discarding.] 1. (Card Playing) To throw out of one's hand, as superfluous cards; to lay aside (a card or cards).
Discard Dis*card", v. i. (Card Playing) To make a discard.
Discard Dis*card", n. (Card Playing) The act of discarding; also, the card or cards discarded.

discarnate.c: Discarnate Dis*car"nate (?), a. [L. dis- + carnatus fleshy, fr. caro, carnis, flesh.] Stripped of flesh. [Obs.] “Discarnate bones.” Glanvill.

discase.c: Discase Dis*case" (?), v. t. To strip; to undress. Shak.

discede.c: Discede Dis*cede" (?), v. i. [L. discedere; dis- + cedere to yield.] To yield or give up; to depart. [Obs.]

discept.c: Discept Dis*cept" (?), v. i. [L. disceptare.] To debate; to discuss. [R.]

disceptation.c: Disceptation Dis`cep*ta"tion (?), n. [L. disceptatio.] Controversy; disputation; discussion. [Archaic]

disceptator.c: Disceptator Dis`cep*ta"tor (?), n. [L.] One who arbitrates or decides. [R.] Cowley.

discern.c: Discern Dis*cern" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discerned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discerning.] [F. discerner, L. discernere, discretum; dis- + cernere to separate, distinguish. See Certain, and cf. Discreet.] 1. To see and identify by noting a difference or differences; to note the distinctive character of; to discriminate; to distinguish.
Discern Dis*cern", v. i. 1. To see or understand the difference; to make distinction; as, to discern between good and evil, truth and falsehood.

discerner.c: Discerner Dis*cern"er (?), n. One who, or that which, discerns, distinguishes, perceives, or judges; as, a discerner of truth, of right and wrong.

discernible.c: Discernible Dis*cern"i*ble (?), a. [L. discernibilis.] Capable of being discerned by the eye or the understanding; as, a star is discernible by the eye; the identity of difference of ideas is discernible by the understanding.

discernibleness.c: Discernibleness Dis*cern"i*ble*ness, n. The quality of being discernible.

discernibly.c: Discernibly Dis*cern"i*bly, adv. In a manner to be discerned; perceptibly; visibly. Hammond.

discerning.c: Discerning Dis*cern"ing, a. Acute; shrewd; sagacious; sharp-sighted. Macaulay.

discerningly.c: Discerningly Dis*cern"ing*ly, adv. In a discerning manner; with judgment; judiciously; acutely. Garth.

discernment.c: Discernment Dis*cern"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. discernement.] 1. The act of discerning.

discerp.c: Discerp Dis*cerp" (?), v. t. [L. discerpere, discerptum; dis- + carpere to pluck.] 1. To tear in pieces; to rend. [R.] Stukeley.

discerptibility.c: Discerptibility Discerpibility { Dis*cerp`i*bil"i*ty (?), Dis*cerp`ti*bil"i*ty (?) }, n. Capability or liableness to be discerped. [R.] Wollaston.

discerptible.c: Discerptible Discerpible { Dis*cerp"i*ble (?), Dis*cerp"ti*ble (?) }, a. [See Discerp.] Capable of being discerped. [R.]

discerption.c: Discerption Dis*cerp"tion (?), n. [L. discerptio.] The act of pulling to pieces, or of separating the parts. Bp. Hall.

discerptive.c: Discerptive Dis*cerp"tive (?), a. Tending to separate or disunite parts. Encys. Dict.

discession.c: Discession Dis*ces"sion (?), n. [L. discessio, fr. discedere, discessum. See Discede.] Departure. [Obs.]

discharge.c: Discharge Dis*charge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discharged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discharging.] [OE. deschargen, dischargen, OF. deschargier, F. décharger; pref. des- (L. dis) + chargier, F. charger. See Charge.] 1. To relieve of a charge, load, or burden; to empty of a load or cargo; to unburden; to unload; as, to discharge a vessel.
Discharge Dis*charge", v. i. To throw off or deliver a load, charge, or burden; to unload; to emit or give vent to fluid or other contents; as, the water pipe discharges freely.

Discharge Dis*charge", n. [Cf. F. décharge. See Discharge, v. t.] 1. The act of discharging; the act of relieving of a charge or load; removal of a load or burden; unloading; as, the discharge of a ship; discharge of a cargo.

discharger.c: Discharger Dis*char"ger (?), n. One who, or that which, discharges. Specifically, in electricity, an instrument for discharging a Leyden jar, or electrical battery, by making a connection between the two surfaces; a discharging rod.

dischurch.c: Dischurch Dis*church" (?), v. t. To deprive of status as a church, or of membership in a church. Bp. Hall.

discide.c: Discide Dis*cide" (?), v. t. [L. discidere; dis- + caedere to cut.] To divide; to cleave in two. [Obs.] Spenser.

disciflorous.c: Disciflorous Discifloral { Dis`ci*flo"ral (?), Dis`ci*flo"rous (?), } a. [See Disk, and Floral.] (Bot.) Bearing the stamens on a discoid outgrowth of the receptacle; -- said of a subclass of plants. Cf. Calycifloral.

discina.c: Discina ‖Dis*ci"na (?), n. [NL., fr. L. discus disk, Gr.?.] (Zool.) A genus of Branchiopoda, having a disklike shell, attached by one valve, which is perforated by the peduncle.

discinct.c: Discinct Dis*cinct (?), a. [L. discinctus, p. p. of discingere to ungird; dis- + cingere to gird.] Ungirded; loosely dressed. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

discind.c: Discind Dis*cind" (?), v. t. [L. discindere; dis- + scindere to cut, split.] To part; to divide. [Obs.] Boyle.

disciple.c: Disciple Dis*ci"ple (?), n. [OE. disciple, deciple, OF. disciple, fr. L. discipulus, fr. discere to learn (akin to docere to teach; see Docile) + prob. a root meaning to turn or drive, as in L. pellere to drive (see Pulse).] One who receives instruction from another; a scholar; a learner; especially, a follower who has learned to believe in the truth of the doctrine of his teacher; an adherent in doctrine; as, the disciples of Plato; the disciples of our Savior.
Disciple Dis*ci"ple, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discipled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discipling.] 1. To teach; to train. [Obs.]

discipleship.c: Discipleship Dis*ci"ple*ship, n. The state of being a disciple or follower in doctrines and precepts. Jer. Taylor.

disciplinable.c: Disciplinable Dis"ci*plin*a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. disciplinable. See Discipline.] 1. Capable of being disciplined or improved by instruction and training.

disciplinableness.c: Disciplinableness Dis"ci*plin*a*ble*ness, n. The quality of being improvable by discipline. Sir M. Hale.

disciplinal.c: Disciplinal Dis"ci*plin*al (?), a. Relating to discipline. Latham.

disciplinant.c: Disciplinant Dis"ci*plin*ant (?), n. [See Discipline.] (Eccl. Hist.) A flagellant. See Flagellant.

disciplinarian.c: Disciplinarian Dis`ci*plin*a"ri*an (?), a. Pertaining to discipline. “Displinarian system.” Milman.

Disciplinarian Dis`ci*plin*a"ri*an, n. 1. One who disciplines; one who excels in training, especially with training, especially with regard to order and obedience; one who enforces rigid discipline; a stickler for the observance of rules and methods of training; as, he is a better disciplinarian than scholar.

disciplinary.c: Disciplinary Dis"ci*plin*a*ry (?), a. [LL. disciplinarius flogging: cf. F. disciplinaire.] Pertaining to discipline; intended for discipline; corrective; belonging to a course of training.

discipline.c: Discipline Dis`ci*pline (?), n. [F. discipline, L. disciplina, from discipulus. See Disciple.] 1. The treatment suited to a disciple or learner; education; development of the faculties by instruction and exercise; training, whether physical, mental, or moral.

Discipline Dis"ci*pline (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disciplined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disciplining.] [Cf. LL. disciplinarian to flog, fr. L. disciplina discipline, and F. discipliner to discipline.] 1. To educate; to develop by instruction and exercise; to train.

disclaim.c: Disclaim Dis*claim" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disclaimed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disclaiming.] 1. To renounce all claim to deny; ownership of, or responsibility for; to disown; to disavow; to reject.
Disclaim Dis*claim", v. t. To disavow or renounce all part, claim, or share. Blackstone.

disclaimer.c: Disclaimer Dis*claim"er (?), n. 1. One who disclaims, disowns, or renounces.

disclamation.c: Disclamation Dis`cla*ma"tion (?), n. A disavowing or disowning. Bp. Hall.

disclame.c: Disclame Dis*clame" (?), v. t. To disclaim; to expel. [Obs.] “Money did love disclame.” Spenser.

disclaunder.c: Disclaunder Dis*claun"der (?), v. t. [From OE. disclaundre, n., for sclandre, esclandre, OF. esclandre. See Sclaundre, Slander.] To injure one's good name; to slander. [Obs.]

discloak.c: Discloak Dis*cloak" (?), v. t. To take off a cloak from; to uncloak. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

disclose.c: Disclose Dis*close" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disclosed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disclosing.] [OE. desclosen, disclosen, fr. disclos, desclos, not shut in, open, OF. desclos, p. p. of desclore to open, F. déclore; pref. des- (L. dis-) + clore to shut, fr. L. claudere to shut. See Close, and cf. Disclusion.] 1. To unclose; to open; -- applied esp. to eggs in the sense of to hatch.

disclosed.c: Disclosed Dis*closed" (?), p. a. (Her.) Represented with wings expanded; -- applied to doves and other birds not of prey. Cussans.

disclosure.c: Disclosure Dis*clo"sure (?; 135), n. [See Disclose, v. t., and cf. Closure.] 1. The act of disclosing, uncovering, or revealing; bringing to light; exposure.

discloud.c: Discloud Dis*cloud" (?), v. t. To clear from clouds. [Archaic] Fuller.

disclout.c: Disclout Dis*clout" (?), v. t. To divest of a clout. [R.]

disclusion.c: Disclusion Dis*clu"sion (?), n. [L. disclusio, fr. discludere, disclusum, to separate. See Disclose.] A shutting off; exclusion. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

discoast.c: Discoast Dis*coast" (?), v. i. [Pref. dis- + coast: cf. It. discostare.] To depart; to quit the coast (that is, the side or border) of anything; to be separated. [Obs.]

discoblastic.c: Discoblastic Dis`co*blas"tic (?), a. [Gr.? disk +? to grow.] (Biol.) Applied to a form of egg cleavage seen in osseous fishes, which occurs only in a small disk that separates from the rest of the egg.

discobolus.c: Discobolus ‖Dis*cob"o*lus (?), n.; pl. Discoboli (#). [L., fr. Gr.?;? a discu +? to throw.] (Fine Arts) (a) A thrower of the discus. (b) A statue of an athlete holding the discus, or about to throw it.

discodactyl.c: Discodactyl Dis`co*dac"tyl (?), n. [See Discodactylia.] (Zool.) One of the tree frogs.

discodactylia.c: Discodactylia ‖Dis`co*dac*tyl"i*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? disk +? finger.] (Zool.) A division of amphibians having suctorial disks on the toes, as the tree frogs.

discodactylous.c: Discodactylous Dis`co*dac"tyl*ous (?), a. (Zool.) Having sucking disks on the toes, as the tree frogs.

discoid.c: Discoid Dis"coid (?), a. [Gr.? quoit-shaped,? a round plate, quoit + e'i^dos form, shape: cf. F. discoïde. See Disk.] Having the form of a disk, as those univalve shells which have the whorls in one plane, so as to form a disk, as the pearly nautilus.
Discoid Dis"coid, n. Anything having the form of a discus or disk; particularly, a discoid shell.

discoidal.c: Discoidal Dis*coid"al (?), a. [Cf. F. discoïdal.] Disk-shaped; discoid.

discolith.c: Discolith Dis"co*lith (?), n. [Gr.? a round plate + -lith.] (Biol.) One of a species of coccoliths, having an oval discoidal body, with a thick strongly refracting rim, and a thinner central portion. One of them measures about of an inch in its longest diameter.

discolor.c: Discolor Dis*col"or (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discolored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discoloring.] [OE. descolouren, OF. descolorer, F. décolorer, fr. L. dis- + cololare, coloratum, to color, color color. See Color.] [Written also discolour.] 1. To alter the natural hue or color of; to change to a different color; to stain; to tinge; as, a drop of wine will discolor water; silver is discolored by sea water.

discolorate.c: Discolorate Dis*col"or*ate (?), v. t. To discolor. [R.] Fuller.

discoloration.c: Discoloration Dis*col`or*a"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. decoloration.] 1. The act of discoloring, or the state of being discolored; alteration of hue or appearance. Darwin.

discolored.c: discolored dis*col"ored (?), a. 1. Altered in color; stained; spotted or streaked with foreign matter.

discomfit.c: Discomfit Dis*com"fit (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discomfited; p. pr. & vb. n. Discomfiting.] [OF. desconfit, p. p. of desconfire, F. déconfire; fr. L. dis- + conficere to make ready, prepare, bring about. See Comfit, Fact.] 1. To scatter in fight; to put to rout; to defeat.

discomfiture.c: Discomfiture Dis*com"fi*ture (?; 135), n. [OF. desconfiture, F. déconfiture. See Discomfort, v. t., and cf. Comfiture.] The act of discomfiting, or the state of being discomfited; rout; overthrow; defeat; frustration; confusion and dejection.

discomfort.c: Discomfort Dis*com"fort (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discomforted; p. pr. & vb. n. Discomforting.] [OF. desconforter, F. déconforter, to discourage; pref. des- (L dis-) + conforter. See Comfort.] 1. To discourage; to deject.
Discomfort Dis*com"fort, n. [OF. desconfort, F. déconfort. See Discomfort, v. t.] 1. Discouragement. [Obs.] Shak.

discomfortable.c: Discomfortable Dis*com"fort*a*ble (?), a. [Cf. OF. desconfortable.] 1. Causing discomfort; occasioning uneasiness; making sad. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

discommend.c: Discommend Dis`com*mend" (?), v. t. 1. To mention with disapprobation; to blame; to disapprove. [R.] Spenser.

discommendable.c: Discommendable Dis`com*mend"a*ble (dĭs`kŏm*mĕnd"ȧ*b'l), a. Deserving, disapprobation or blame. -- Dis`com*mend"a*ble*ness, n.

discommendation.c: Discommendation Dis*com`men*da"tion (?), n. Blame; censure; reproach. [R.] Ayliffe.

discommender.c: Discommender Dis`com*mend"er (?), n. One who discommends; a dispraiser. Johnson.

discommission.c: Discommission Dis`com*mis"sion (?), v. t. To deprive of a commission or trust. [R.] Laud.

discommodate.c: Discommodate Dis*com"mo*date (?), v. t. [L. dis- + commodatus, p. p. of commodare to make fit or suitable, fr. commodus fit, commodious. See Commodious, and cf. Discommode.] To discommode. [Obs.] Howell.

discommode.c: Discommode Dis`com*mode" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discommoded; p. pr. & vb. n. Discommoding.] [See Discommodate.] To put inconvenience; to incommode; to trouble. [R.]

discommodious.c: Discommodious Dis`com*mo"di*ous (?), a. Inconvenient; troublesome; incommodious. [R.] Spenser.

discommon.c: Discommon Dis*com"mon (?), v. t. 1. To deprive of the right of common. [R.] Bp. Hall.

discommunity.c: Discommunity Dis`com*mu"ni*ty (?), n. A lack of common possessions, properties, or relationship.

discompany.c: Discompany Dis*com"pa*ny (?), v. t. To free from company; to dissociate. [R.]

discomplexion.c: Discomplexion Dis`com*plex"ion (?), v. t. To change the complexion or hue of. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

discompliance.c: Discompliance Dis`com*pli"ance (?), n. Failure or refusal to comply; noncompliance.

discompose.c: Discompose Dis`com*pose" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discomposed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discomposing.] [Pref. dis- + compose: cf. OF. decomposer, F. décomposer.] 1. To disarrange; to interfere with; to disturb; to disorder; to unsettle; to break up.

discomposed.c: Discomposed Dis`com*posed" (?), a. Disordered; disturbed; disquieted. -- Dis`com*pos"ed*ly (#), adv. -- Dis`com*pos"ed*ness, n.

discomposure.c: Discomposure Dis`com*po"sure (?; 135), n. 1. The state of being discomposed; disturbance; disorder; agitation; perturbation.

discompt.c: Discompt Dis*compt" (?), v. t. [See Discount.] To discount. See Discount. Hudibras.

disconcert.c: Disconcert Dis`con*cert" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disconcerted; p. pr. & vb. n. Disconcerting.] [Pref. dis- + concert: cf. OF. desconcerter, F. déconcerter.] 1. To break up the harmonious progress of; to throw into disorder or confusion; as, the emperor disconcerted the plans of his enemy.
Disconcert Dis`con*cert" (?), n. Want of concert; disagreement. Sir W. Temple.

disconcertion.c: Disconcertion Dis`con*cer"tion (?), n. The act of disconcerting, or state of being disconcerted; discomposure; perturbation. [R.] State Trials (1794).

disconducive.c: Disconducive Dis`con*du"cive (?), a. Not conductive; impeding; disadvantageous. [R.]

disconformity.c: Disconformity Dis`con*form"i*ty (?), n. Want of conformity or correspondence; inconsistency; disagreement.

discongruity.c: Discongruity Dis`con*gru"i*ty (?), n. Incongruity; disagreement; unsuitableness. Sir M. Hale.

disconnect.c: Disconnect Dis`con*nect" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disconnected; p. pr. & vb. n. Disconnecting.] To dissolve the union or connection of; to disunite; to sever; to separate; to disperse.

disconnection.c: Disconnection Dis`con*nec"tion (?), n. The act of disconnecting, or state of being disconnected; separation; want of union.

disconsecrate.c: Disconsecrate Dis*con"se*crate (?), v. t. To deprive of consecration or sacredness. [R.]

disconsent.c: Disconsent Dis`con*sent" (dĭs`kŏn*sĕnt"), v. i. To differ; to disagree; to dissent. [Obs.] Milton.

disconsolacy.c: Disconsolacy Dis*con"so*la`cy (?), n. The state of being disconsolate. [Obs.] Barrow.

disconsolate.c: Disconsolate Dis*con"so*late (?), a. [LL. disconsolatus; L. dis- + consolatus, p. p. of consolari to console. See Console, v. t.] 1. Destitute of consolation; deeply dejected and dispirited; hopelessly sad; comfortless; filled with grief; as, a bereaved and disconsolate parent.

disconsolation.c: Disconsolation Dis*con`so*la"tion (?), n. Dejection; grief. [R.] Bp. Hall.

discontent.c: Discontent Dis`con*tent" (dĭs`kŏn*tĕnt"), a. Not content; discontented; dissatisfied. Jer. Taylor.
Discontent Dis`con*tent", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discontented; p. pr. & vb. n. Discontenting.] To deprive of content; to make uneasy; to dissatisfy. Suckling.
Discontent Dis`con*tent", n. 1. Want of content; uneasiness and inquietude of mind; dissatisfaction; disquiet.

discontented.c: Discontented Dis`con*tent"ed (?), p. p. & a. Dissatisfied; uneasy in mind; malcontent.

discontentive.c: Discontentive Dis`con*tent"ive (?), a. Relating or tending to discontent. [R.] “Pride is ever discontentive.” Feltham.

discontentment.c: Discontentment Dis`con*tent"ment (?), n. The state of being discontented; uneasiness; inquietude. Bacon.

discontinuable.c: Discontinuable Dis`con*tin"u*a*ble (?), a. Admitting of being discontinued. [R.]

discontinuance.c: Discontinuance Dis`con*tin"u*ance (?), n. 1. The act of discontinuing, or the state of being discontinued; want of continued connection or continuity; breaking off; cessation; interruption; as, a discontinuance of conversation or intercourse; discontinuance of a highway or of travel.

discontinuation.c: Discontinuation Dis`con*tin`u*a"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. discontinuation.] Breach or interruption of continuity; separation of parts in a connected series; discontinuance.

discontinue.c: Discontinue Dis`con*tin"ue (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discontinued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discontinuing.] [Cf. F. discontinuer.] To interrupt the continuance of; to intermit, as a practice or habit; to put an end to; to cause to cease; to cease using, to stop; to leave off.
Discontinue Dis`con*tin"ue, v. i. 1. To lose continuity or cohesion of parts; to be disrupted or broken off. Bacon.

discontinuee.c: Discontinuee Dis`con*tin`u*ee" (?), n. (Law) One whose possession of an estate is broken off, or discontinued; one whose estate is subject to discontinuance.

discontinuer.c: Discontinuer Dis`con*tin"u*er (?), n. One who discontinues, or breaks off or away from; an absentee.

discontinuity.c: Discontinuity Dis*con`ti*nu"i*ty (?), n. Want of continuity or cohesion; disunion of parts. “Discontinuity of surface.” Boyle.

discontinuor.c: Discontinuor Dis`con*tin"u*or (?), n. (Law) One who deprives another of the possession of an estate by discontinuance. See Discontinuance, 2.

discontinuous.c: Discontinuous Dis`con*tin"u*ous (?), a. 1. Not continuous; interrupted; broken off.

disconvenient.c: Disconvenient Dis`con*ven"ient (?), a. Not convenient or congruous; unsuitable; ill-adapted. [Obs.] Bp. Reynolds.

discophora.c: Discophora ‖Dis*coph"o*ra (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? disk +? to bear.] (Zool.) A division of acalephs or jellyfishes, including most of the large disklike species. -- Dis*coph"o*rous (#), a.

discord.c: Discord Dis"cord` (?), n. [OE. discord, descord, OF. discorde, descorde, F. discorde, from L. discordia, fr. discors, -cordis, discordant, disagreeable; dis- + cor, cordis, heart; cf. F. discord, n., and OF. descorder, discorder, F. discorder, to discord, L. discordare, from discors. See Heart, and cf. Discord, v. i.] 1. Want of concord or agreement; absence of unity or harmony in sentiment or action; variance leading to contention and strife; disagreement; -- applied to persons or to things, and to thoughts, feelings, or purposes.
Discord Dis*cord" (?), v. i. [OE. discorden, descorden, from the French. See Discord, n.] To disagree; to be discordant; to jar; to clash; not to suit. [Obs.]

discordable.c: Discordable Dis*cord"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. OF. descordable.] That may produce discord; disagreeing; discordant. [R.] Halliwell.

discordancy.c: Discordancy Discordance { Dis*cord"ance (?), Dis*cord"an*cy (?), } n. [Cf. F. discordance.] State or quality of being discordant; disagreement; inconsistency.

discordant.c: Discordant Dis*cord"ant (?), a. [OE. discordant, descordaunt, OF. descordant, discordant, F. discordant, p. pr. of discorder, OF. also, descorder. See Discord, n.] 1. Disagreeing; incongruous; being at variance; clashing; opposing; not harmonious.

discordful.c: Discordful Dis*cord"ful (?), a. Full of discord; contentious. [Obs.] “His discordful dame.” Spenser.

discorporate.c: Discorporate Dis*cor"po*rate (?), a. Deprived of the privileges or form of a body corporate. [Obs.] Jas. II.

discost.c: Discost Dis*cost" (?), v. i. Same as Discoast. [Obs.]

discounsel.c: Discounsel Dis*coun"sel (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + counsel: cf. OF. desconseiller.] To dissuade. [Obs.] Spenser.

discount.c: Discount Dis"count` (?; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discounted; p. pr. & vb. n. Discounting.] [OF. desconter, descompter, to deduct, F. décompter to discount; pref. des- (L. dis-) + conter, compter. See Count, v.] 1. To deduct from an account, debt, charge, and the like; to make an abatement of; as, merchants sometimes discount five or six per cent for prompt payment of bills.
Discount Dis"count` (?; 277), v. i. To lend, or make a practice of lending, money, abating the discount; as, the discount for sixty or ninety days.

Discount Dis"count` (?), n. [Cf. F. décompte. See Discount, v. t.] 1. A counting off or deduction made from a gross sum on any account whatever; an allowance upon an account, debt, demand, price asked, and the like; something taken or deducted.

discountable.c: Discountable Dis*count"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being, or suitable to be, discounted; as, certain forms are necessary to render notes discountable at a bank.

discountenance.c: Discountenance Dis*coun"te*nance (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discountenanced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discountenancing (?).] [Pref. dis- + countenance: cf. OF. descontenancer, F. décontenancer.] 1. To ruffle or discompose the countenance of; to put of countenance; to put to shame; to abash.
Discountenance Dis*coun"te*nance, n. Unfavorable aspect; unfriendly regard; cold treatment; disapprobation; whatever tends to check or discourage.

discountenancer.c: Discountenancer Dis*coun"te*nan*cer (?), n. One who discountenances; one who disfavors. Bacon.

discounter.c: Discounter Dis"count`er (?), n. One who discounts; a discount broker. Burke.

discourage.c: Discourage Dis*cour"age (?; 48), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discouraged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discouraging (?).] [Pref. dis- + courage: cf. OF. descoragier, F. décourager: pref. des- (L. dis-) + corage, F. courage. See Courage.] 1. To extinguish the courage of; to dishearten; to depress the spirits of; to deprive of confidence; to deject; -- the opposite of encourage; as, he was discouraged in his undertaking; he need not be discouraged from a like attempt.
Discourage Dis*cour"age, n. Lack of courage; cowardliness.

discourageable.c: Discourageable Dis*cour"age*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being discouraged; easily disheartened. Bp. Hall.

discouragement.c: Discouragement Dis*cour"age*ment (?), n. [Cf. OF. descouragement, F. découragement.] 1. The act of discouraging, or the state of being discouraged; depression or weakening of confidence; dejection.

discouraging.c: Discouraging Dis*cour"a*ging (?), a. Causing or indicating discouragement. -- Dis*cour"a*ging*ly, adv.

discourse.c: Discourse Dis*course" (?), n. [L. discursus a running to and fro, discourse, fr. discurrere, discursum, to run to and fro, to discourse; dis- + currere to run: cf. F. discours. See Course.] 1. The power of the mind to reason or infer by running, as it were, from one fact or reason to another, and deriving a conclusion; an exercise or act of this power; reasoning; range of reasoning faculty. [Obs.]

Discourse Dis*course" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Discoursed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discoursing.] 1. To exercise reason; to employ the mind in judging and inferring; to reason. [Obs.] “Have sense or can discourse.” Dryden.
Discourse Dis*course", v. t. 1. To treat of; to expose or set forth in language. [Obs.]

discourser.c: Discourser Dis*cours"er (?), n. 1. One who discourse; a narrator; a speaker; an haranguer.

discoursive.c: Discoursive Dis*cours"ive (?), a. [See Discursive.] 1. Reasoning; characterized by reasoning; passing from premises to consequences; discursive. Milton.
Discoursive Dis*cours"ive, n. The state or quality of being discoursive or able to reason. [R.] Feltham.

discourteous.c: Discourteous Dis*cour"te*ous (?; see Courteous, 277), a. [Pref. dis- + courteous: cf. OF. discortois.] Uncivil; rude; wanting in courtesy or good manners; uncourteous. -- Dis*cour"te*ous*ly, adv. -- Dis*cour"te*ous*ness, n.

discourtesy.c: Discourtesy Dis*cour"te*sy (?), n. [Pref. dis- + courtesy: cf. OF. descourtoisie.] Rudeness of behavior or language; ill manners; manifestation of disrespect; incivility.

discourtship.c: Discourtship Dis*court"ship (?), n. Want of courtesy. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

discous.c: Discous Disc"ous (?), a. [L. discus disk. See Disk.] Disklike; discoid.

discovenant.c: Discovenant Dis*cov"e*nant (?), v. t. To dissolve covenant with.

discover.c: Discover Dis*cov"er (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discovered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discovering.] [OE. discoveren, discuren, descuren, OF. descovrir, descouvrir, F. découvrir; des- (L. dis-) + couvrir to cover. See Cover.] 1. To uncover. [Obs.]
Discover Dis*cov"er, v. i. To discover or show one's self. [Obs.]

discoverability.c: Discoverability Dis*cov`er*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being discoverable. [R.] Carlyle.

discoverable.c: Discoverable Dis*cov"er*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being discovered, found out, or perceived; as, many minute animals are discoverable only by the help of the microscope; truths discoverable by human industry.

discoverer.c: Discoverer Dis*cov"er*er (?), n. 1. One who discovers; one who first comes to the knowledge of something; one who discovers an unknown country, or a new principle, truth, or fact.

discovert.c: Discovert Dis*cov"ert (?), a. [Cf. F. découvert uncovered, OF. descovert. See Discover, Covert.] (Law) Not covert; not within the bonds of matrimony; unmarried; -- applied either to a woman who has never married or to a widow.
Discovert Dis*cov"ert, n. An uncovered place or part. [Obs.]

discoverture.c: Discoverture Dis*cov"er*ture (?; 135), n. [Pref. dis- + coverture: cf. OF. descoverture.] 1. Discovery. [Obs.]

discovery.c: Discovery Dis*cov"er*y (?), n.; pl. Discoveries (?). 1. The action of discovering; exposure to view; laying open; showing; as, the discovery of a plot.
Discovery Day Dis*cov"er*y Day. same as Columbus Day, above.

discradle.c: Discradle Dis*cra"dle (?), v. t. To take from a cradle. [R.]

discredit.c: Discredit Dis*cred"it (?), n. [Cf. F. discrédit.] 1. The act of discrediting or disbelieving, or the state of being discredited or disbelieved; as, later accounts have brought the story into discredit.

Discredit Dis*cred"it, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discredited; p. pr. & vb. n. Discrediting.] [Cf. F. discréditer.] 1. To refuse credence to; not to accept as true; to disbelieve; as, the report is discredited.

discreditable.c: discreditable dis*cred"it*a*ble (?), a. Not creditable; injurious to reputation; disgraceful; disreputable. -- Dis*cred"it*a*bly, adv.

discreet.c: Discreet Dis*creet" (?), a. [Compar. Discreeter (?); superl. Discreetest.] [F. discret, L. discretus separated (whence the meaning reserved, prudent), p. p. of discernere. See Discern, and cf. Discrete.] 1. Possessed of discernment, especially in avoiding error or evil, and in the adaptation of means to ends; prudent; sagacious; judicious; not rash or heedless; cautious.

discrepancy.c: Discrepancy Discrepance { Dis*crep"ance (?; 277), Dis*crep"an*cy (?), } n.; pl. -ances (#), -ancies (#). [L. disrepantia: cf. OF. discrepance. See Discrepant.] The state or quality of being discrepant; disagreement; variance; discordance; dissimilarity; contrariety.

discrepant.c: Discrepant Dis*crep"ant (?), a. [L. discrepans, -antis, p. pr. of discrepare to sound differently or discordantly; dis- + crepare to rattle, creak: cf. OF. discrepant. See Crepitate.] Discordant; at variance; disagreeing; contrary; different.
Discrepant Dis*crep"ant, n. A dissident. J. Taylor.

discrete.c: Discrete Dis*crete" (?), a. [L. discretus, p. p. of discernere. See Discreet.] 1. Separate; distinct; disjunct. Sir M. Hale.
Discrete Dis*crete", v. t. To separate. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

discretion.c: Discretion Dis*cre"tion (?), n. [F. discrétion, L. discretio separation, difference, discernment, fr. discernere, discretum. See Discreet, Discern.] 1. Disjunction; separation. [Obs.] Mede.

discretionary.c: Discretionary Discretional { Dis*cre"tion*al (?), Dis*cre"tion*a*ry (?), }[Cf. F. discrétionnaire.] Left to discretion; unrestrained except by discretion or judgment; as, an ambassador with discretionary powers.

discretionarily.c: Discretionarily Discretionally { Dis*cre"tion*al*ly (?), Dis*cre"tion*a*ri*ly (?), } adv. At discretion; according to one's discretion or judgment.

discretive.c: Discretive Dis*cre"tive (?), a. [L. discretivus. See Discrete.] Marking distinction or separation; disjunctive.

discretively.c: Discretively Dis*cre"tive*ly, adv. In a discretive manner.

discriminable.c: Discriminable Dis*crim"i*na*ble (?), a. Capable of being discriminated. [Obs.] Bailey.

discriminal.c: Discriminal Dis*crim"i*nal (?), a. [L. discriminalis serving to divide.] In palmistry, applied to the line which marks the separation between the hand and the arm.

discriminant.c: Discriminant Dis*crim"i*nant (?), n. [L. discriminans, p. pr. of discriminare.] (Math.) The eliminant of the n partial differentials of any homogenous function of n variables. See Eliminant.

discriminate.c: Discriminate Dis*crim"i*nate (?), a. [L. discriminatus, p. p. of discriminare to divide, separate, fr. discrimen division, distinction, decision, fr. discernere. See Discern, and cf. Criminate.] Having the difference marked; distinguished by certain tokens. Bacon.

Discriminate Dis*crim"i*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discriminated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discriminating (?).] To set apart as being different; to mark as different; to separate from another by discerning differences; to distinguish. Cowper.

Discriminate Dis*crim"i*nate (?), v. i. 1. To make a difference or distinction; to distinguish accurately; as, in judging of evidence, we should be careful to discriminate between probability and slight presumption.

discriminately.c: Discriminately Dis*crim"i*nate*ly (?), adv. In a discriminating manner; distinctly.

discriminateness.c: Discriminateness Dis*crim"i*nate*ness, n. The state of being discriminated; distinctness.

discriminating.c: Discriminating Dis*crim"i*na`ting (?), a. 1. Marking a difference; distinguishing. -- Dis*crim"i*na`ting*ly, adv.

discrimination.c: Discrimination Dis*crim`i*na"tion (?), n. [L. discriminatio the contrasting of opposite thoughts.] 1. The act of discriminating, distinguishing, or noting and marking differences.

discriminative.c: Discriminative Dis*crim"i*na*tive (?), a. 1. Marking a difference; distinguishing; distinctive; characteristic.

discriminatively.c: Discriminatively Dis*crim"i*na*tive*ly, adv. With discrimination or distinction. J. Foster.

discriminous.c: Discriminous Dis*crim"i*nous (?), a. [LL. discriminosus, fr. L. discrimen the dangerous, decisive moment. See Discriminate, a.] Hazardous; dangerous. [Obs.] Harvey.

discrive.c: Discrive Dis*crive" (?), v. t. [OF. descrivre. See Describe.] To describe. [Obs.] Chaucer.

discrown.c: Discrown Dis*crown" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discrowned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discrowning.] To deprive of a crown.

discruciate.c: Discruciate Dis*cru"ci*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discruciated; p. pr. & vb. n. Discruciating.] [L. discruciatus, p. p. of discruciare. See Cruciate.] To torture; to excruciate. [Obs.]

discubitory.c: Discubitory Dis*cu"bi*to*ry (?), a. [L. discumbere, discubitum, to lie down, recline at table; dis- + cumbere (in comp.) to lie down.] Leaning; fitted for a reclining posture. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

disculpate.c: Disculpate Dis*cul"pate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disculpated; p. pr. & vb. n. Disculpating.] [LL. disculpatus, p. p. of disculpare to disculpate; dis- + L. culpare to blame, culpa fault.] To free from blame or the imputation of a fault; to exculpate.

disculpation.c: Disculpation Dis`cul*pa"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. disculpation.] Exculpation. Burke.

disculpatory.c: Disculpatory Dis*cul"pa*to*ry (?), a. Tending to exculpate; exculpatory.

discumbency.c: Discumbency Dis*cum"ben*cy (?), n. [From L. discumbens, p. pr. of discumbere. See Discubitory.] The act of reclining at table according to the manner of the ancients at their meals. Sir T. Browne.

discumber.c: Discumber Dis*cum"ber (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + cumber: cf. OF. descombrer.] To free from that which cumbers or impedes; to disencumber. [Archaic] Pope.

discure.c: Discure Dis*cure" (?), v. t. [See Discover.] To discover; to reveal; to discoure. [Obs.]

discurrent.c: Discurrent Dis*cur"rent (?), a. Not current or free to circulate; not in use. [Obs.] Sir E. Sandys.

discursion.c: Discursion Dis*cur"sion (?), n. [LL. discursio a running different ways. See Discourse.] The act of discoursing or reasoning; range, as from thought to thought. Coleridge.

discursist.c: Discursist Dis*cur"sist, n. A discourser. [Obs.] L. Addison.

discursive.c: Discursive Dis*cur"sive (?), a. [Cf. F. discursif. See Discourse, and cf. Discoursive.] 1. Passing from one thing to another; ranging over a wide field; roving; digressive; desultory. “Discursive notices.” De Quincey.

discursory.c: Discursory Dis*cur`so*ry (?), a. Argumentative; discursive; reasoning. [R.] Bp. Hall.

discursus.c: Discursus Dis*cur"sus (?), n. [L.] (Logic) Argumentation; ratiocination; discursive reasoning.

discus.c: Discus Dis"cus (?), n.; pl. E. Discuses (#), L. Disci (#). [L. See Disk.] 1. (a) A quoit; a circular plate of some heavy material intended to be pitched or hurled as a trial of strength and skill. (b) The exercise with the discus.

discuss.c: Discuss Dis*cuss" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Discussed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Discussing.] [L. discussus, p. p. of discutere to strike asunder (hence came the sense to separate mentally, distinguish); dis- + quatere to shake, strike. See Quash.] 1. To break to pieces; to shatter. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

discusser.c: Discusser Dis*cuss"er (?), n. One who discusses; one who sifts or examines. Wood.

discussion.c: Discussion Dis*cus"sion (?), n. [L. discussio a shaking, examination, discussion: cf. F. discussion.] 1. The act or process of discussing by breaking up, or dispersing, as a tumor, or the like. [archaic]

discussive.c: discussive dis*cuss"ive (?), a. [Cf. F. discussif.] 1. (Med.) Able or tending to discuss or disperse tumors or coagulated matter; discutient.
Discussive Dis*cuss"ive, n. (Med.) A medicine that discusses or disperses morbid humors; a discutient.

discutient.c: Discutient Dis*cu"tient (?), a. [L. discutiens, p. pr. of discutere. See Discuss.] (Med.) Serving to disperse morbid matter; discussive; as, a discutient application. -- n. An agent (as a medicinal application) which serves to disperse morbid matter. “Foment with discutiens.” Wiseman.

disdain.c: Disdain Dis*dain" (?; 277), n. [OE. desdain, disdein, OF. desdein, desdaing, F. dédain, fr. the verb. See Disdain, v. t.] 1. A feeling of contempt and aversion; the regarding anything as unworthy of or beneath one; scorn.

Disdain Dis*dain" (?; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disdained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disdaining.] [OE. disdainen, desdainen, OF. desdeigner, desdaigner, F. dédaigner; des- (L. dis-) + daigner to deign, fr. L. dignari to deem worthy. See Deign.] 1. To think unworthy; to deem unsuitable or unbecoming; as, to disdain to do a mean act.
Disdain Dis*dain", v. i. To be filled with scorn; to feel contemptuous anger; to be haughty.

disdainful.c: Disdainful Dis*dain"ful (?), a. Full of disdain; expressing disdain; scornful; contemptuous; haughty.

disdainous.c: Disdainous Dis*dain"ous (?), a. [OF. desdeignos, desdaigneux, F. dédaigneux.] Disdainful. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

disdeify.c: Disdeify Dis*de"i*fy (?), v. t. To divest or deprive of deity or of a deific rank or condition. Feltham.

disdiaclast.c: Disdiaclast Dis*di"a*clast (?), n. [Gr. di`s- twice + diakla^n to break in twain; dia` through + kla^n to break.] (Physiol.) One of the dark particles forming the doubly refracting disks of muscle fibers.

disdiapason.c: Disdiapason Dis*di`a*pa"son (?), n. [Pref. dis- (Gr.?) + diapason.] (Anc. Mus.) An interval of two octaves, or a fifteenth; -- called also bisdiapason. Compare diapason{1}.

disease.c: Disease Dis*ease" (?), n. [OE. disese, OF. desaise; des- (L. dis-) + aise ease. See Ease.] 1. Lack of ease; uneasiness; trouble; vexation; disquiet. [Obs.]
Disease Dis*ease", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Diseased (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Diseasing.] 1. To deprive of ease; to disquiet; to trouble; to distress. [Obs.]

diseasedness.c: Diseasedness Dis*eas"ed*ness (?), n. The state of being diseased; a morbid state; sickness. [R.] T. Burnet.

diseasefulness.c: Diseasefulness Dis*ease"ful*ness, n. The quality of being diseaseful; trouble; trial. [R.] Sir P. Sidney.

disedge.c: Disedge Dis*edge" (?), v. t. To deprive of an edge; to blunt; to dull.

disedify.c: Disedify Dis*ed"i*fy (?), v. t. To fail of edifying; to injure. [R.]

diselder.c: Diselder Dis*eld"er (?), v. t. To deprive of an elder or elders, or of the office of an elder. [Obs.] Fuller.

diselenide.c: Diselenide Di*sel"e*nide (?; 104), n. [Pref. di- + selenide.] (Chem.) A selenide containing two atoms of selenium in each molecule.

disembark.c: Disembark Dis`em*bark" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disembarked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disembarking.] [Pref. dis- + embark: cf. F. désembarquer.] To remove from on board a vessel; to put on shore; to land; to debark; as, the general disembarked the troops.
Disembark Dis`em*bark" (?), v. i. To go ashore out of a ship or boat; to leave a ship; to debark.

disembarkation.c: Disembarkation Dis*em`bar*ka"tion (?), n. The act of disembarking.

disembarrass.c: Disembarrass Dis`em*bar"rass (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disembarrassed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disembarrassing.] [Pref. dis- + embarrass: cf. F. désembarasser.] To free from embarrassment, or perplexity; to clear; to extricate.

disembarrassment.c: Disembarrassment Dis`em*bar"rass*ment (?), n. Freedom or relief from impediment or perplexity.

disembay.c: Disembay Dis`em*bay" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disembayed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disembaying.] [Pref. dis- + embay.] To clear from a bay. Sherburne.

disembellish.c: Disembellish Dis`em*bel"lish (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + embellish: cf. F. désembellir.] To deprive of embellishment; to disadorn. Carlyle.

disembitter.c: Disembitter Dis`em*bit"ter (?), v. t. To free from

disembodied.c: Disembodied Dis`em*bod"ied (?), a. Divested of a body; ceased to be corporal; incorporeal.

disembodiment.c: Disembodiment Dis`em*bod"i*ment (?), n. The act of disembodying, or the state of being disembodied.

disembody.c: Disembody Dis`em*bod"y (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disembodied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disembodying.] 1. To divest of the body or corporeal existence.

disembogue.c: Disembogue Dis`em*bogue" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disembogued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disemboguing.] [Sp. desembocar; pref. des- (L. dis-) + embocar to put into the mouth, fr. en (L. in) + boca mouth, fr. L. bucca cheek. Cf. Debouch, Embogue.] 1. To pour out or discharge at the mouth, as a stream; to vent; to discharge into an ocean, a lake, etc.
Disembogue Dis`em*bogue", v. i. To become discharged; to flow out; to find vent; to pour out contents.

disemboguement.c: Disemboguement Dis`em*bogue"ment (?), n. The act of disemboguing; discharge. Mease.

disembossom.c: Disembossom Dis`em*bos"som (?), v. t. To separate from the bosom. [R.] Young.

disembowel.c: Disembowel Dis`em*bow"el (dĭs`ĕm*bou"ĕl), v. t. [See Embowel.] 1. To take or let out the bowels or interior parts of; to eviscerate.

disembowelment.c: Disembowelment Dis`em*bow"el*ment (?), n. The act of disemboweling, or state of being disemboweled; evisceration.

disembowered.c: Disembowered Dis`em*bow"ered (?), a. Deprived of, or removed from, a bower. [Poetic] Bryant.

disembrangle.c: Disembrangle Dis`em*bran"gle (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + em = en (L. in) + brangle.] To free from wrangling or litigation. [Obs.] Berkeley.

disembroil.c: Disembroil Dis`em*broil" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disembroiled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disembroiling.] [Pref. dis- + embroil.] To disentangle; to free from perplexity; to extricate from confusion.

disemploy.c: Disemploy Dis`em*ploy" (?), v. t. To throw out of employment. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

disemployment.c: Disemployment Dis`em*ploy"ment (?), n. The state of being disemployed, or deprived of employment.

disempower.c: Disempower Dis`em*pow"er (?), v. t. To deprive of power; to divest of strength. H. Bushnell.

disenable.c: Disenable Dis`en*a"ble (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + enable.] To disable; to disqualify.

disenamor.c: Disenamor Dis`en*am"or (?), v. t. To free from the captivity of love. Shelton.

disenchained.c: Disenchained Dis`en*chained" (?), a. Freed from restraint; unrestrained. [Archaic] E. A. Poe.

disenchant.c: Disenchant Dis`en*chant" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disenchanted; p. pr. & vb. n. Disenchanting.] [Pref. dis- + enchant: cf. F. désenchanter.] 1. To free from enchantment; to deliver from the power of charms or spells.

disenchanter.c: Disenchanter Dis`en*chant"er (?), n. One who, or that which, disenchants.

disenchantment.c: Disenchantment Dis`en*chant"ment (?), n. [Pref. dis- + enchantment: cf. F. désenchantement.] The act of disenchanting, or state of being disenchanted. Shelton.

disencharm.c: Disencharm Dis`en*charm" (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + en (L. in) + charm.] To free from the influence of a charm or spell; to disenchant. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

disencrese.c: Disencrese Dis`en*crese" (?), v. i. [Pref. dis- + OE. encrese, E. increase.] To decrease. [Obs.] Chaucer.

disencumber.c: Disencumber Dis`en*cum"ber (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disencumbered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disencumbering.] [Pref. dis- + encumber: cf. F. désencombrer.] To free from encumbrance, or from anything which clogs, impedes, or obstructs; to disburden. Owen.

disencumbrance.c: Disencumbrance Dis`en*cum"brance (?), n. Freedom or deliverance from encumbrance, or anything burdensome or troublesome. Spectator.

disendow.c: Disendow Dis`en*dow" (?), v. t. To deprive of an endowment, as a church. Gladstone.

disendowment.c: Disendowment Dis`en*dow"ment (?), n. The act of depriving of an endowment or endowments.

disenfranchise.c: Disenfranchise Dis`en*fran"chise (?), v. t. To disfranchise; to deprive of the rights of a citizen. -- Dis`en*fran"chise*ment (#), n.

disengage.c: Disengage Dis`en*gage" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disengaged (#); p. pr. & vb. n. Disengaging.] [Pref. dis- + engage: cf. F. désengager.] To release from that with which anything is engaged, engrossed, involved, or entangled; to extricate; to detach; to set free; to liberate; to clear; as, to disengage one from a party, from broils and controversies, from an oath, promise, or occupation; to disengage the affections a favorite pursuit, the mind from study.
Disengage Dis`en*gage", v. i. To release one's self; to become detached; to free one's self.

disengaged.c: Disengaged Dis`en*gaged" (?), a. Not engaged; free from engagement; at leisure; free from occupation or care; vacant. -- Dis`en*ga"ged*ness (#), n.

disengagement.c: Disengagement Dis`en*gage"ment (?), n. [Pref. dis- + engagement: cf. F. désengagement.] 1. The act of disengaging or setting free, or the state of being disengaged.

disengaging.c: Disengaging Dis`en*ga"ging (?), a. Loosing; setting free; detaching.

disennoble.c: Disennoble Dis`en*no"ble (?), v. t. To deprive of that which ennobles; to degrade.

disenroll.c: Disenroll Dis`en*roll" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Disenrolled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disenrolling.] To erase from a roll or list. [Written also disenrol.] Donne.

disensanity.c: Disensanity Dis`en*san"i*ty (?), n. [Pref. dis- + en (L. in) + sanity.] Insanity; folly. [Obs.]

disenshrouded.c: Disenshrouded Dis`en*shroud"ed (?), a. Freed from a shroudlike covering; unveiled.

disenslave.c: Disenslave Dis`en*slave" (?), v. t. To free from bondage or slavery; to disenthrall.

disentail.c: Disentail Dis`en*tail" (?), v. t. (Law) To free from entailment.

disentangle.c: disentangle dis`en*tan"gle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disentangled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disentangling (?).] 1. To free from entanglement; to release from a condition of being intricately and confusedly involved or interlaced; to reduce to orderly arrangement; to straighten out; as, to disentangle a skein of yarn.

disentanglement.c: Disentanglement Dis`en*tan"gle*ment (?), n. The act of disentangling or clearing from difficulties. Warton.

disenthrall.c: Disenthrall Dis`en*thrall" (?), v. t. [See Enthrall.] To release from thralldom or slavery; to give freedom to; to disinthrall. [Written also disenthral.] Milton.

disenthrallment.c: Disenthrallment Dis`en*thrall"ment (?), n. Liberation from bondage; emancipation; disinthrallment. [Written also disenthralment.]

disenthrone.c: Disenthrone Dis`en*throne" (?), v. t. To dethrone; to depose from sovereign authority. Milton.

disentitle.c: Disentitle Dis`en*ti"tle (?), v. t. To deprive of title or claim.

disentomb.c: Disentomb Dis`en*tomb" (?), v. t. To take out from a tomb; a disinter.

disentrail.c: Disentrail Dis`en*trail" (?), v. t. To disembowel; to let out or draw forth, as the entrails. [Obs.]

disentrance.c: Disentrance Dis`en*trance" (?), v. t. To awaken from a trance or an enchantment. Hudibras.

disentwine.c: Disentwine Dis`en*twine" (?), v. t. To free from being entwined or twisted. Shelley.

disepalous.c: Disepalous Di*sep"al*ous (?), a. [Pref. di- + sepalous.] (Bot.) Having two sepals; two-sepaled.

disert.c: Disert Dis*ert" (?), a. [L. disertus, for dissertus, p. p.: cf. F. disert. See Dissert.] Eloquent. [Obs.]

diserty.c: Diserty Dis*ert"y (?), adv. Expressly; clearly; eloquently. [Obs.] Holland.

disespouse.c: Disespouse Dis`es*pouse" (?), v. t. To release from espousal or plighted faith. [Poetic] Milton.

disestablish.c: Disestablish Dis`es*tab"lish (?), v. t. To unsettle; to break up (anything established); to deprive, as a church, of its connection with the state. M. Arnold.

disestablishment.c: Disestablishment Dis`es*tab"lish*ment (?), n. 1. The act or process of unsettling or breaking up that which has been established; specifically, the withdrawal of the support of the state from an established church; as, the disestablishment and disendowment of the Irish Church by Act of Parliament.

disesteem.c: Disesteem Dis`es*teem" (?), n. Want of esteem; low estimation, inclining to dislike; disfavor; disrepute.
Disesteem Dis`es*teem", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disesteemed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disesteeming.] 1. To feel an absence of esteem for; to regard with disfavor or slight contempt; to slight.

disesteemer.c: Disesteemer Dis`es*teem"er (?), n. One who disesteems. Boyle.

disexercise.c: Disexercise Dis*ex"er*cise (?), v. t. To deprive of exercise; to leave untrained. [Obs.]

disfashion.c: Disfashion Dis*fash"ion (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + fashion. See Fashion, and cf. Defeat.] To disfigure. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

disfavor.c: Disfavor Dis*fa"vor (?), n. [Pref. dis- + favor: cf. OF. disfaveur, F. défaveur.] [Written also disfavour.] 1. Want of favor of favorable regard; disesteem; disregard.
Disfavor Dis*fa"vor, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disfavored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disfavoring.] 1. To withhold or withdraw favor from; to regard with disesteem; to show disapprobation of; to discountenance.

disfavorable.c: Disfavorable Dis*fa"vor*a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. défavorable.] Unfavorable. [Obs.] Stow.

disfavorer.c: Disfavorer Dis*fa"vor*er (?), n. One who disfavors. Bacon.

disfeature.c: Disfeature Dis*fea"ture (?; 135), v. t. [Cf. Defeature.] To deprive of features; to mar the features of. [R.]

disfellowship.c: Disfellowship Dis*fel"low*ship (?), v. t. [See Fellowship, v. t.] To exclude from fellowship; to refuse intercourse with, as an associate.

disfiguration.c: Disfiguration Dis*fig`u*ra"tion (?), n. [See Disfigure, and cf. Defiguration.] The act of disfiguring, or the state of being disfigured; defacement; deformity; disfigurement. Gauden.

disfigure.c: Disfigure Dis*fig"ure (?; 135), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disfigured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disfiguring.] [OF. desfigurer, F. défigurer; pref. des- (L. dis-) + figurer to fashion, shape, fr. L. figurare, fr. figura figure. See Figure, and cf. Defiguration.] To mar the figure of; to render less complete, perfect, or beautiful in appearance; to deface; to deform.

disfigurement.c: Disfigurement Dis*fig"ure*ment (?), n. 1. Act of disfiguring, or state of being disfigured; deformity. Milton.

disflesh.c: Disflesh Dis*flesh" (?), v. t. To reduce the flesh or obesity of. [Obs.] Shelton.

disforest.c: Disforest Dis*for"est (?), v. t. 1. To disafforest. Fuller.

disforestation.c: Disforestation Dis*for`es*ta"tion (?), n. The act of clearing land of forests. Daniel.

disformity.c: Disformity Dis*form"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. Deformity.] Discordance or diversity of form; unlikeness in form.

disfranchise.c: Disfranchise Dis*fran"chise (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disfranchised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disfranchising.] [Cf. Diffranchise.] To deprive of a franchise or chartered right; to dispossess of the rights of a citizen, or of a particular privilege, as of voting, holding office, etc.

disfranchisement.c: Disfranchisement Dis*fran"chise*ment (?), n. The act of disfranchising, or the state of being disfranchised; deprivation of privileges of citizenship or of chartered immunities.

disfriar.c: Disfriar Dis*fri"ar (dĭs*frī"ẽr), v. t. To depose or withdraw from the condition of a friar. [Obs.]

disfurnish.c: Disfurnish Dis*fur"nish (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disfurnished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disfurnishing.] [Pref. dis- + furnish.] To deprive of that with which anything is furnished (furniture, equipments, etc.); to strip; to render destitute; to divest.

disfurnishment.c: Disfurnishment Dis*fur"nish*ment (?), n. The act of disfurnishing, or the state of being disfurnished. Daniel.

disfurniture.c: Disfurniture Dis*fur"ni*ture (?; 135), n. The act of disfurnishing, or the state of being disfurnished. [Obs.]
Disfurniture Dis*fur"ni*ture, v. t. To disfurnish. [R.] East.

disgage.c: Disgage Dis*gage" (?), v. t. To free from a gage or pledge; to disengage. [Obs.] Holland.

disgallant.c: Disgallant Dis*gal"lant (?), v. t. To deprive of gallantry. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

disgarland.c: Disgarland Dis*gar"land (?), v. t. To strip of a garland. [Poetic] “Thy locks disgarland.” Drummond.

disgarnish.c: Disgarnish Dis*gar"nish (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + garnish. See Degarnish.] To divest of garniture; to disfurnish; to dismantle. Bp. Hall.

disgarrison.c: Disgarrison Dis*gar"ri*son (?), v. t. To deprive of a garrison. Hewyt.

disgavel.c: Disgavel Dis*gav"el (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disgaveled (?) or Disgaveled; p. pr. & vb. n. Disgaveling.] [See Gavelkind.] (Eng. Law) To deprive of that principal quality of gavelkind tenure by which lands descend equally among all the sons of the tenant; -- said of lands. Burrill.

disgest.c: Disgest Dis*gest" (?), v. t. To digest. [Obs.] Bacon.

disglorify.c: Disglorify Dis*glo"ri*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disglorified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disglorifying.] To deprive of glory; to treat with indignity. [R.]

disgorge.c: Disgorge Dis*gorge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disgorged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disgorging.] [F. dégorger, earlier desgorger; pref. dé-, des- (L. dis-) + gorge. See Gorge.] 1. To eject or discharge by the throat and mouth; to vomit; to pour forth or throw out with violence, as if from the mouth; to discharge violently or in great quantities from a confined place.
Disgorge Dis*gorge", v. i. To vomit forth what anything contains; to discharge; to make restitution.

disgorgement.c: Disgorgement Dis*gorge"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. dégorgement.] The act of disgorging; a vomiting; that which is disgorged. Bp. Hall.

disgospel.c: Disgospel Dis*gos"pel (?), v. i. To be inconsistent with, or act contrary to, the precepts of the gospel; to pervert the gospel. [Obs.] Milton.

disgrace.c: Disgrace Dis*grace" (?; 277), n. [F. disgrâce; pref. dis- (L. dis-) + grâce. See Grace.] 1. The condition of being out of favor; loss of favor, regard, or respect.
Disgrace Dis*grace", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disgraced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disgracing (?).] [Cf. F. disgracier. See Disgrace, n.] 1. To put out of favor; to dismiss with dishonor.

disgraceful.c: Disgraceful Dis*grace"ful (?), a. Bringing disgrace; causing shame; shameful; dishonorable; unbecoming; as, profaneness is disgraceful to a man. -- Dis*grace"ful*ly, adv. -- Dis*grace"ful*ness, n.

disgracious.c: Disgracious Dis*gra"cious (?), a. [Cf. F. disgracieux.] Wanting grace; unpleasing; disagreeable. Shak.

disgradation.c: Disgradation Dis`gra*da"tion (?), n. (Scots Law) Degradation; a stripping of titles and honors.

disgrade.c: Disgrade Dis*grade" (?), v. t. To degrade. [Obs.] Foxe.

disgraduate.c: Disgraduate Dis*grad"u*ate (?; 135), v. t. To degrade; to reduce in rank. [Obs.] Tyndale.

disgregate.c: Disgregate Dis"gre*gate (?), v. t. [L. disgregare; dis- + gregare to collect, fr. grex, gregis, flock or herd.] To disperse; to scatter; -- opposite of congregate. [Obs.]

disgregation.c: Disgregation Dis`gre*ga"tion (?), n. (Physiol.) The process of separation, or the condition of being separate, as of the molecules of a body.

disgruntle.c: Disgruntle Dis*grun"tle (?), v. t. To dissatisfy; to disaffect; to anger. [Colloq.]

disguise.c: Disguise Dis*guise" (?; 232), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disguised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disguising.] [OE. desguisen, disgisen, degisen, OF. desguisier, F. déguiser; pref. des- (L. dis-) + guise. See Guise.] 1. To change the guise or appearance of; especially, to conceal by an unusual dress, or one intended to mislead or deceive.
Disguise Dis*guise", n. 1. A dress or exterior put on for purposes of concealment or of deception; as, persons doing unlawful acts in disguise are subject to heavy penalties.

disguisedness.c: Disguisedness Dis*guis"ed*ness, n. The state of being disguised.

disguiser.c: Disguiser Dis*guis"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, disguises. Shak.

disguising.c: Disguising Dis*guis"ing, n. A masque or masquerade. [Obs.]

disgust.c: Disgust Dis*gust" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disgusted; p. pr. & vb. n. Disgusting.] [OF. desgouster, F. dégoûter; pref. des- (L. dis-) + gouster to taste, F. goûter, fr. L. gustare, fr. gustus taste. See Gust to taste.] To provoke disgust or strong distaste in; to cause (any one) loathing, as of the stomach; to excite aversion in; to offend the moral taste of; -- often with at, with, or by.

Disgust Dis*gust", n. [Cf. OF. desgoust, F. dégoût. See Disgust, v. t.] Repugnance to what is offensive; aversion or displeasure produced by something loathsome; loathing; strong distaste; -- said primarily of the sickening opposition felt for anything which offends the physical organs of taste; now rather of the analogous repugnance excited by anything extremely unpleasant to the moral taste or higher sensibilities of our nature; as, an act of cruelty may excite disgust.

disgustful.c: Disgustful Dis*gust"ful (?), a. Provoking disgust; offensive to the taste; exciting aversion; disgusting.

disgustfulness.c: Disgustfulness Dis*gust"ful*ness, n. The state of being disgustful.

disgusting.c: Disgusting Dis*gust"ing, a. That causes disgust; sickening; offensive; revolting. -- Dis*gust"ing*ly, adv.

dish.c: Dish Dish (dĭsh), n. [AS. disc, L. discus dish, disc, quoit, fr. Gr. di`skos quoit, fr. dikei^n to throw. Cf. Dais, Desk, Disc, Discus.] 1. A vessel, as a platter, a plate, a bowl, used for serving up food at the table.
Dish Dish, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dishing.] 1. To put in a dish, ready for the table.

dishabilitate.c: Dishabilitate Dis`ha*bil"i*tate (?), v. t. [Cf. Disability.] To disqualify. [R.]

dishabille.c: Dishabille Dis`ha*bille" (?), n. [See Deshabille.] An undress; a loose, negligent dress; deshabille.

dishabit.c: Dishabit Dis*hab"it (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + habit to inhabit.] To dislodge. [Obs.]

dishabited.c: Dishabited Dis*hab"it*ed, p. a. Rendered uninhabited. “Dishabited towns.” R. Carew.

dishabituate.c: Dishabituate Dis`ha*bit"u*ate (?; 135), v. t. To render unaccustomed.

dishallow.c: Dishallow Dis*hal"low (?), v. t. To make unholy; to profane. Tennyson.

disharmony.c: Disharmony Dis*har"mo*ny (?), n. Want of harmony; discord; incongruity. [R.]

dishaunt.c: Dishaunt Dis*haunt" (?), v. t. To leave; to quit; to cease to haunt. Halliwell.

dishcloth.c: Dishcloth Dish"cloth` (?; 115), n. A cloth used for washing dishes.

dishearten.c: Dishearten Dis*heart"en (dĭs*härt"'n), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disheartened (dĭs*härt"'nd); p. pr. & vb. n. Disheartening.] [Pref. dis- + hearten.] To discourage; to deprive of courage and hope; to depress the spirits of; to deject.

disheartenment.c: disheartenment dis*heart"en*ment (dĭs*härt"'n*meint), n. Discouragement; dejection; depression of spirits.

disheir.c: disheir dis*heir" (dĭz*âr"), v. t. [Cf. Disherit.] To disinherit. [Obs.] Dryden.

dishelm.c: dishelm dis*helm" (dĭs*hĕlm"), v. t. [Pref. dis- + helm helmet.] To deprive of the helmet. [Poetic]

disherison.c: disherison dis*her"i*son (dĭs*hĕr"ĭz'n), n. [See Disherit.] The act of disheriting, or debarring from inheritance; disinherison. Bp. Hall.

disherit.c: disherit dis*her"it (dĭs*hĕr"ĭt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disherited; p. pr. & vb. n. Disheriting.] [F. déshériter; pref. dés- (L. dis-) + hériter to inherit. See Inherit, and cf. Dusheir, Disinherit.] To disinherit; to cut off, or detain, from the possession or enjoyment of an inheritance. [Obs.] Spenser.

disheritance.c: Disheritance Dis*her"it*ance (dĭs*hĕr"ĭt*ains), n. [Cf. OF. desheritance.] The act of disinheriting or state of being disinherited; disinheritance. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

disheritor.c: Disheritor Dis*her"it*or (dĭs*hĕr"ĭt*ẽr), n. (Law) One who puts another out of his inheritance.

dishevel.c: Dishevel Di*shev"el (dĭ*shĕv"'l or -ĕl), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disheveled (?) or Dishevelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Disheveling or Dishevelling.] [OF. descheveler, F. décheveler, LL. discapillare; dis- + L. capillus the hair of the head. See Capillary.] 1. To suffer (the hair) to hang loosely or disorderly; to spread or throw (the hair) in disorder; -- used chiefly in the passive participle.
Dishevel Di*shev"el, v. i. To be spread in disorder or hang negligently, as the hair. [R.] Sir T. Herbert.

dishevelled.c: dishevelled disheveled di*shev"eled, di*shev"elled (?), a. 1. Hanging in loose disorder; disarranged; in disarray; not made neat; -- used especially of hair or clothing; as, disheveled hair.

dishful.c: Dishful Dish"ful (?), n.; pl. Dishfuls (?). As much as a dish holds when full.

dishonest.c: Dishonest Dis*hon"est (?), a. [Pref. dis- + honest: cf. F. déshonnête, OF. deshoneste.] 1. Dishonorable; shameful; indecent; unchaste; lewd. [Obs.]
Dishonest Dis*hon"est, v. t. [Cf. OF. deshonester.] To disgrace; to dishonor; as, to dishonest a maid. [Obs.]

dishonestly.c: Dishonestly Dis*hon"est*ly, adv. In a dishonest manner.

dishonesty.c: Dishonesty Dis*hon"es*ty (?), n. [Cf. OF. deshonesté, F. déshonnêteté.] 1. Dishonor; dishonorableness; shame. [Obs.] “The hidden things of dishonesty.” 2 Cor. iv. 2.

dishonor.c: Dishonor Dis*hon"or (dĭs*ŏn"ẽr or dĭz*ŏn"ẽr), n. [OE. deshonour, dishonour, OF. deshonor, deshonur, F. déshonneur; pref. des- (L. dis-) + honor, honur, F. honneur, fr. L. honor. See Honor.] [Written also dishonour.]

Dishonor Dis*hon"or (dĭs*ŏn"ẽr or dĭz*ŏn"ẽr), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dishonored (dĭs*ŏn"ẽrd or dĭz*ŏn"ẽrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Dishonoring.] [OE. deshonouren, F. déshonorer; pref. dés- (L. dis-) + honorer to honor, fr. L. honorare. See Honor, v. t.] [Written also dishonour.] 1. To deprive of honor; to disgrace; to bring reproach or shame on; to treat with indignity, or as unworthy in the sight of others; to stain the character of; to lessen the reputation of; as, the duelist dishonors himself to maintain his honor.

dishonorable.c: Dishonorable Dis*hon"or*a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. déshonorable.] 1. Wanting in honor; not honorable; bringing or deserving dishonor; staining the character, and lessening the reputation; shameful; disgraceful; base.

dishonorary.c: Dishonorary Dis*hon"or*a*ry (?), a. Bringing dishonor on; tending to disgrace; lessening reputation. Holmes.

dishonorer.c: Dishonorer Dis*hon"or*er (?), n. One who dishonors or disgraces; one who treats another indignity. Milton.

dishorn.c: Dishorn Dis*horn" (?), v. t. To deprive of horns; as, to dishorn cattle. “Dishorn the spirit.” Shak.

dishorse.c: Dishorse Dis*horse" (?), v. t. To dismount; to knock (a person) from a horse. Tennyson.

dishouse.c: Dishouse Dis*house" (?), v. t. To deprive of house or home. “Dishoused villagers.” James White.

dishumor.c: Dishumor Dis*hu"mor, v. t. To deprive of humor or desire; to put out of humor. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

dishwasher.c: Dishwasher Dish"wash`er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, washes dishes.

dishwater.c: Dishwater Dish"wa`ter (?), n. Water in which dishes have been washed. “Suds and dishwater.” Beau. & Fl.

disillusion.c: Disillusion Dis`il*lu"sion (?), n. The act or process of freeing from an illusion, or the state of being freed therefrom. Lowell.
Disillusion Dis`il*lu"sion, v. t. To free from an illusion; to disillusionize.

disillusionize.c: Disillusionize Dis`il*lu"sion*ize (?), v. t. To disenchant; to free from illusion. “The bitter disillusionizing experience of postnuptial life.” W. Black.

disillusionment.c: Disillusionment Dis`il*lu"sion*ment (?), n. The act of freeing from an illusion, or the state of being freed therefrom.

disimbitter.c: Disimbitter Dis`im*bit"ter (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + imbitter. Cf. Disembitter.] To free from bitterness.

disimpark.c: Disimpark Dis`im*park" (?), v. t. To free from the barriers or restrictions of a park. [R.] Spectator.

disimpassioned.c: Disimpassioned Dis`im*pas"sioned (?), a. Free from warmth of passion or feeling.

disimprove.c: Disimprove Dis`im*prove" (?), v. t. To make worse; -- the opposite of improve. [R.] Jer. Taylor.
Disimprove Dis`im*prove", v. i. To grow worse; to deteriorate.

disimprovement.c: Disimprovement Dis`im*prove"ment (?), n. Reduction from a better to a worse state; as, disimprovement of the earth; specific features which are worse than former features; disimprovements in the new Windows operating system.

disincarcerate.c: Disincarcerate Dis`in*car"cer*ate (?), v. t. To liberate from prison. [R.] Harvey.

disinclination.c: Disinclination Dis*in`cli*na"tion (?), n. The state of being disinclined; want of propensity, desire, or affection; slight aversion or dislike; indisposition.

disincline.c: Disincline Dis`in*cline" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disinclined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disinclining.] To incline away the affections of; to excite a slight aversion in; to indispose; to make unwilling; to alienate.

disinclose.c: Disinclose Dis`in*close" (?), v. t. [Cf. Disenclose.] To free from being inclosed.

disincorporate.c: Disincorporate Dis`in*cor"po*rate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disincorporated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disincorporating (?).] 1. To deprive of corporate powers, rights, or privileges; to divest of the condition of a corporate body.
Disincorporate Dis`in*cor"po*rate (?), a. Separated from, or not included in, a corporation; disincorporated. Bacon.

disincorporation.c: Disincorporation Dis`in*cor`po*ra"tion (?), n. Deprivation of the rights and privileges of a corporation. T. Warton.

disinfect.c: Disinfect Dis`in*fect" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disinfected; p. pr. & vb. n. Disinfecting.] To free from infectious or contagious matter; to destroy putrefaction; to purify; to make innocuous.

disinfectant.c: disinfectant dis`in*fect"ant (?), n. That which disinfects, especially an agent for killing or removing the microorganisms which cause infection. Commonly used disinfectants are chlorine, sodium hypochlorite solution, hydrogen peroxide, and alcohol.

disinfection.c: disinfection dis`in*fec"tion (?), n. The act of disinfecting; purification from infecting matter.

disinfector.c: disinfector dis`in*fect"or (?), n. One who, or that which, disinfects; an apparatus for applying disinfectants.

disinflame.c: Disinflame Dis`in*flame" (?), v. t. To divest of flame or ardor. Chapman.

disingenuous.c: Disingenuous Dis`in*gen"u*ous (?), a. 1. Not noble; unbecoming true honor or dignity; mean; unworthy; as, disingenuous conduct or schemes.

disinherison.c: Disinherison Dis`in*her"i*son (?), n. [See Disinherit, v. t., and cf. Disherison.] Same as Disherison. Bacon.

disinherit.c: Disinherit Dis`in*her"it (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disinherited; p. pr. & vb. n. Disinheriting.] [Cf. Disherit, Disheir.] 1. To cut off from an inheritance or from hereditary succession; to prevent, as an heir, from coming into possession of any property or right, which, by law or custom, would devolve on him in the course of descent.

disinheritance.c: Disinheritance Dis`in*her"it*ance (?), n. The act of disinheriting, or the condition of being; disinherited; disherison.

disinsure.c: Disinsure Dis`in*sure" (?), v. t. To render insecure; to put in danger. [Obs.] Fanshawe.

disintegrable.c: Disintegrable Dis*in"te*gra*ble (?), a. Capable of being disintegrated, or reduced to fragments or powder.

disintegrate.c: Disintegrate Dis*in"te*grate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disintegrated; p. pr. & vb. n. Disintegrating.] [L. dis- + integratus, p. p. of integrare to renew, repair, fr. integer entire, whole. See Integer.] To separate into integrant parts; to reduce to fragments or to powder; to break up, or cause to fall to pieces, as a rock, by blows of a hammer, frost, rain, and other mechanical or atmospheric influences.
Disintegrate Dis*in"te*grate, v. i. To decompose into integrant parts; as, chalk rapidly disintegrates.

disintegration.c: Disintegration Dis*in`te*gra"tion (?), n. (a) The process by which anything is disintegrated; the condition of anything which is disintegrated. Specifically (b) (Geol.) The wearing away or falling to pieces of rocks or strata, produced by atmospheric action, frost, ice, etc.

disintegrator.c: Disintegrator Dis*in"te*gra`tor (?), n. (Mech.) A machine for grinding or pulverizing by percussion.

disinter.c: Disinter Dis`in*ter" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disinterred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disinterring.] 1. To take out of the grave or tomb; to unbury; to exhume; to dig up.

disinteress.c: Disinteress Dis*in"ter*ess (?), v. t. [F. désintéresser to deprive of interest in; pref. dés- (L. dis-) + intéresser to interest, fr. L. interesse to import, concern. See Interest, and cf. Disinterest.] To deprive or rid of interest in, or regard for; to disengage. [Obs.]

disinteressment.c: Disinteressment Dis*in"ter*ess*ment (?), n. [Cf. F. désintéressement.] Disinterestedness; impartiality; fairness. [Obs.] Prior.

disinterest.c: Disinterest Dis*in"ter*est, n. 1. What is contrary to interest or advantage; disadvantage. [Obs.] Glanvill.
Disinterest Dis*in"ter*est, v. t. To divest of interest or interested motives. [Obs.] Feltham.

disinterested.c: Disinterested Dis*in"ter*est*ed, a. [Cf. Disinteressed.] Not influenced by regard to personal interest or advantage; free from selfish motive; having no relation of interest or feeling; not biased or prejudiced; as, a disinterested decision or judge.

disinterestedly.c: Disinterestedly Dis*in"ter*est*ed*ly, adv. In a disinterested manner; without bias or prejudice.

disinterestedness.c: Disinterestedness Dis*in"ter*est*ed*ness, n. The state or quality of being disinterested; impartiality.

disinteresting.c: Disinteresting Dis*in"ter*est*ing, a. Uninteresting. [Obs.] “Disinteresting passages.” Bp. Warburton.

disinterment.c: Disinterment Dis`in*ter"ment (?), n. The act of disinterring, or taking out of the earth; exhumation.

disinthrall.c: Disinthrall Dis`in*thrall" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disinthralled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disinthralling.] [Pref. dis- + inthrall. Cf. Disenthrall.] To free from thralldom; to disenthrall. [Written also disinthral.]

disinthrallment.c: Disinthrallment Dis`in*thrall"ment (?), n. A releasing from thralldom or slavery; disenthrallment. [Written also disinthralment.]

disintricate.c: Disintricate Dis*in"tri*cate (?), v. t. To disentangle. [R.] “To disintricate the question.” Sir W. Hamilton.

disinure.c: Disinure Dis`in*ure" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disinured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disinuring.] [Pref. dis- + inure.] To render unaccustomed or unfamiliar.

disinvestiture.c: Disinvestiture Dis`in*ves"ti*ture (?; 135), n. The act of depriving of investiture. [Obs.] Ogilvie.

disinvigorate.c: Disinvigorate Dis`in*vig"or*ate (?), v. t. To enervate; to weaken. [R.] Sydney Smith.

disinvolve.c: Disinvolve Dis`in*volve" (?), v. t. To uncover; to unfold or unroll; to disentangle. [R.] Dr. H. More.

disjection.c: Disjection Dis*jec"tion (?), n. [L. disjicere, disjectum, to throw asunder, disperse; dis- + jacere to throw.] Destruction; dispersion. Bp. Horsley.

disjoin.c: Disjoin Dis*join" (dĭs*join"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disjoined (dĭs*joind"); p. pr. & vb. n. Disjoining.] [OF. desjoindre, F. disjoindre, déjoindre, fr. L. disjungere; dis- + jungere to join. See Join, and cf. Disjoint, Disjunct.] To part; to disunite; to separate; to sunder.
Disjoin Dis*join", v. i. To become separated; to part.

disjoint.c: Disjoint Dis*joint" (?), a. [OF. desjoint, p. p. of desjoindre. See Disjoin.] Disjointed; unconnected; -- opposed to conjoint. Milton.
Disjoint Dis*joint", n. [From OF. desjoint, p. p. of desjoindre. See Disjoint, v. t.] Difficult situation; dilemma; strait. [Obs.] “I stand in such disjoint.” Chaucer.

Disjoint Dis*joint", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disjointed; p. pr. & vb. n. Disjointing.] 1. To separate the joints of; to separate, as parts united by joints; to put out of joint; to force out of its socket; to dislocate; as, to disjoint limbs; to disjoint bones; to disjoint a fowl in carving.
Disjoint Dis*joint", v. i. To fall in pieces. Shak.

disjointed.c: Disjointed Dis*joint"ed, a. Separated at the joints; disconnected; incoherent. -- Dis*joint"ed*ly, adv. -- Dis*joint"ed*ness, n.

disjointly.c: Disjointly Dis*joint"ly, adv. In a disjointed state. Sandys.

disjudication.c: Disjudication Dis*ju`di*ca"tion (?), n. Judgment; discrimination. See Dijudication. [Obs.] Boyle.

disjunct.c: Disjunct Dis*junct" (dĭs*jŭṉkt"), a. [L. disjunctus, p. p. of disjungere to disjoin. See Disjoin, and cf. Disjoint.] 1. Disjoined; separated. [R.]

disjunction.c: Disjunction Dis*junc"tion (?), n. [L. disjunctio.] 1. The act of disjoining; disunion; separation; a parting; as, the disjunction of soul and body.

disjunctive.c: Disjunctive Dis*junc"tive (?), a. [L. disjunctivus: cf. F. disjonctif.] 1. Tending to disjoin; separating; disjoining.
Disjunctive Dis*junc"tive, n. (a) (Gram.) A disjunctive conjunction. (b) (Logic) A disjunctive proposition.

disjunctively.c: Disjunctively Dis*junc"tive*ly, adv. In a disjunctive manner; separately. Dr. H. More.

disjuncture.c: Disjuncture Dis*junc"ture (?; 135), n. The act of disjoining, or state of being disjoined; separation. Fuller.

disk.c: Disk Disk (dĭsk), n. [L. discus, Gr. di`skos. See Dish.] [Written also disc.] 1. A discus; a quoit.
Disk clutch Disk clutch. (Engin.) A friction clutch in which the gripping surfaces are disks or more or less resemble disks.

diskindness.c: diskindness dis*kind"ness (?), n. Unkindness; disservice. [R.] A. Tucker.

diskless.c: Diskless Disk"less (?), a. Having no disk; appearing as a point and not expanded into a disk, as the image of a faint star in a telescope.

dislade.c: Dislade Dis*lade" (?), v. t. To unlade. [Obs.] Heywood.

disleal.c: Disleal Dis*leal" (?), a. [See Disloyal, Leal.] Disloyal; perfidious. [Obs.] “Disleal knight.” Spenser.

disleave.c: Disleave Dis*leave" (?), v. t. To deprive of leaves. [R.]

dislike.c: Dislike Dis*like" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Disliked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Disliking.] 1. To regard with dislike or aversion; to disapprove; to disrelish.

dislike dis*like", n. 1. A feeling of positive and usually permanent aversion to something unpleasant, uncongenial, or offensive; disapprobation; repugnance; displeasure; disfavor; -- the opposite of liking or fondness.

dislikeful.c: dislikeful dis*like"ful (?), a. Full of dislike; disaffected; malign; disagreeable. [Obs.] Spenser.

dislikelihood.c: dislikelihood dis*like"li*hood (?), n. The want of likelihood; improbability. Sir W. Scott.

disliken.c: Disliken Dis*lik"en (?), v. t. To make unlike; to disguise. [Obs.] Shak.

disliker.c: Disliker Dis*lik"er (?), n. One who dislikes or disrelishes.

dislimb.c: Dislimb Dis*limb" (?), v. t. To tear limb from limb; to dismember. [Obs.] Bailey.

dislimn.c: Dislimn Dis*limn" (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + limn.] To efface, as a picture. [Obs.] Shak.

dislink.c: Dislink Dis*link" (?), v. t. To unlink; to disunite; to separate. [R.] Tennyson.

dislive.c: Dislive Dis*live" (?), v. t. To deprive of life. [Obs.]

dislocate.c: Dislocate Dis"lo*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dislocated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dislocating (?).] [LL. dislocatus, p. p. of dislocare; dis- + locare to place, fr. locus place. See Locus.] To displace; to put out of its proper place. Especially, of a bone: To remove from its normal connections with a neighboring bone; to put out of joint; to move from its socket; to disjoint; as, to dislocate your bones. Shak.
Dislocate Dis"lo*cate (?), a. [LL. dislocatus, p. p.] Dislocated. Montgomery.

dislocation.c: Dislocation Dis`lo*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. dislocation.] 1. The act of displacing, or the state of being displaced. T. Burnet.

dislodge.c: Dislodge Dis*lodge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dislodged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dislodging.] [OF. deslogier, F. déloger; pref. des- (L. dis-) + OF. logier, F. loger. See Lodge.] 1. To drive from a lodge or place of rest; to remove from a place of quiet or repose; as, shells resting in the sea at a considerate depth are not dislodged by storms.
Dislodge Dis*lodge", v. i. To go from a place of rest. [R.]

dislodgment.c: Dislodgment Dis*lodg"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. délogement, OF. deslogement.] The act or process of dislodging, or the state of being dislodged.

disloign.c: Disloign Dis*loign" (?), v. t. [OF. desloignier. See Eloign.] To put at a distance; to remove. [Obs.]

disloyal.c: Disloyal Dis*loy"al (?), a. [Pref. dis- + loyal: cf. OF. desloial, desleal, F. déloyal. See Loyal.] Not loyal; not true to a sovereign or lawful superior, or to the government under which one lives; false where allegiance is due; faithless; as, a subject disloyal to the king; a husband disloyal to his wife.

disloyally.c: Disloyally Dis*loy"al*ly, adv. In a disloyal manner.

disloyalty.c: Disloyalty Dis*loy"al*ty (?), n. [Pref. dis- + loyalty: cf. OF. desloiauté, deslealté, F. déloyauté.] Want of loyalty; lack of fidelity; violation of allegiance.

dismail.c: Dismail Dis*mail" (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + mail: cf. OF. desmaillier.] To divest of coat of mail. Spenser.

dismal.c: Dismal Dis"mal (?), a. [Formerly a noun; e. g., “I trow it was in the dismalle.” Chaucer. Of uncertain origin; but perh. (as suggested by Skeat) from OF. disme, F. dîme, tithe, the phrase dismal day properly meaning, the day when tithes must be paid. See Dime.] 1. Fatal; ill-omened; unlucky. [Obs.]

dismally.c: Dismally Dis"mal*ly, adv. In a dismal manner; gloomily; sorrowfully; uncomfortably.

dismalness.c: Dismalness Dis"mal*ness, n. The quality of being dismal; gloominess.

disman.c: Disman Dis*man" (?), v. t. To unman. [Obs.] Feltham.

dismantle.c: Dismantle Dis*man"tle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dismantled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dismantling (?).] [F. démanteler, OF. desmanteler; pref: des- (L. dis-) + manteler to cover with a cloak, defend, fr. mantel, F. manteau, cloak. See Mantle.] 1. To strip or deprive of dress; to divest.

dismarch.c: Dismarch Dis*march" (?), v. i. To march away. [Obs.]

dismarry.c: Dismarry Dis*mar"ry (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + marry: cf. OF. desmarier, F. démarier.] To free from the bonds of marriage; to divorce. [Obs.] Ld. Berners.

dismarshal.c: Dismarshal Dis*mar"shal (?), v. t. To disarrange; to derange; to put in disorder. [R.] Drummond.

dismask.c: Dismask Dis*mask" (?), v. t. [Pref. dis- + mask: cf. F. démasquer.] To divest of a mask. Shak.

dismast.c: Dismast Dis*mast" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dismasted; p. pr. & vb. n. Dismasting.] [Pref. dis- + mast: cf. F. démâter.] To deprive of a mast of masts; to break and carry away the masts from; as, a storm dismasted the ship.

dismastment.c: Dismastment Dis*mast"ment (?), n. The act of dismasting; the state of being dismasted. [R.] Marshall.

dismaw.c: Dismaw Dis*maw" (?), v. t. To eject from the maw; to disgorge. [R.] Shelton.

dismay.c: Dismay Dis*may" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dismayed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dismaying.] [OE. desmaien, dismaien, OF. esmaier; pref. es- (L. ex) + OHG. magan to be strong or able; akin to E. may. In English the pref. es- was changed to dis- (L. dis-). See May, v. i.] 1. To disable with alarm or apprehensions; to depress the spirits or courage of; to deprive or firmness and energy through fear; to daunt; to appall; to terrify.
Dismay Dis*may", v. i. To take dismay or fright; to be filled with dismay. [Obs.] Shak.
Dismay Dis*may", n. [Cf. OF. esmai, F. émoi. See Dismay, v. t.] 1. Loss of courage and firmness through fear; overwhelming and disabling terror; a sinking of the spirits; consternation.
