dooly.c: Dooly Doo"ly (?), n.; pl. Doolies (#). [Skr. dōla.] A kind of litter suspended from men's shoulders, for carrying persons or things; a palanquin. [Written also doolee and doolie.] [East Indies]

doom.c: Doom Doom (dōom), n. [As. dōm; akin to OS. dōm, OHG. tuom, Dan. & Sw. dom, Icel. dōmr, Goth. dōms, Gr. qe`mis law; fr. the root of E. do, v. t. √65. See Do, v. t., and cf. Deem, -dom.] 1. Judgment; judicial sentence; penal decree; condemnation.
Doom Doom, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Doomed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dooming.] 1. To judge; to estimate or determine as a judge. [Obs.] Milton.

Doom palm Doom" palm` (?). [Ar. daum, dūm: cf. F. doume.] (Bot.) A species of palm tree (Hyphæne Thebaica), highly valued for the fibrous pulp of its fruit, which has the flavor of gingerbread, and is largely eaten in Egypt and Abyssinia. [Written also doum palm.]

doomage.c: Doomage Doom"age (?), n. A penalty or fine for neglect. [Local, New England]

doomful.c: Doomful Doom"ful (?), a. Full of condemnation or destructive power. [R.] “That doomful deluge.” Drayton.

doomsday.c: Doomsday Dooms"day` (?), n. [AS. d?mes dāg. See Doom, and Day.] 1. A day of sentence or condemnation; day of death. “My body's doomsday.” Shak.

doomsman.c: Doomsman Dooms"man, n. [Doom + man.] A judge; an umpire. [Obs.] Hampole.

door.c: Door Door (?), n. [OE. dore, dure, AS. duru; akin to OS. dura, dor, D. deur, OHG. turi, door, tor gate, G. thür, thor, Icel. dyrr, Dan. dör, Sw. dörr, Goth. daur, Lith. durys, Russ. dvere, Olr. dorus, L. fores, Gr.?; cf. Skr. dur, dvāra. √246. Cf. Foreign.] 1. An opening in the wall of a house or of an apartment, by which to go in and out; an entrance way.

doorcase.c: Doorcase Door"case` (?), n. The surrounding frame into which a door shuts.

doorcheek.c: Doorcheek Door"cheek` (?), n. The jamb or sidepiece of a door. Ex. xii. 22 (Douay version).

doorga.c: Doorga ‖Door"ga (?), n. [Skr. Durgā.] (Myth.) A Hindoo divinity, the consort of Siva, represented with ten arms. [Written also Durga.] Malcom.

dooring.c: Dooring Door"ing (?), n. The frame of a door. Milton.

doorkeeper.c: Doorkeeper Door"keep`er (?), n. One who guards the entrance of a house or apartment; a porter; a janitor.

doornail.c: Doornail Door"nail` (dōr"nāl`), n. The nail or knob on which in ancient doors the knocker struck; -- hence the old saying, “As dead as a doornail.”

doorplane.c: Doorplane Door"plane` (?), n. A plane on a door, giving the name, and sometimes the employment, of the occupant.

doorpost.c: Doorpost Door"post` (?), n. The jamb or sidepiece of a doorway.

doorsill.c: Doorsill Door"sill` (?), n. The sill or threshold of a door.

doorstead.c: Doorstead Door"stead (?), n. Entrance or place of a door. [Obs. or Local] Bp. Warburton.

doorstep.c: Doorstep Door"step` (?), n. The stone or plank forming a step before an outer door.

doorstone.c: Doorstone Door"stone` (?), n. The stone forming a threshold.

doorstop.c: doorstop door"stop` (?), n. (Carp.) The block or strip of wood or similar material which stops, at the right place, the shutting of a door; any object used to stop open doors from moving.

doorway.c: Doorway Door"way` (?), n. The passage of a door; entrance way into a house or a room.

dooryard.c: Dooryard Door"yard` (?), n. A yard in front of a house or around the door of a house.

doop.c: Doop Dop { Dop, Doop } (?), n. A little copper cup in which a diamond is held while being cut.

dop.c: Dop Dop, v. i. [Cf. Dap, Dip.] To dip. [Obs.] Walton.
Dop Dop, n. A dip; a low courtesy. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

dope.c: Dope Dope (dōp), n. [D. doop a dipping, fr. doopen to dip. Cf. Dip.] 1. Any thick liquid or pasty preparation, as of opium for medicinal purposes, of grease for a lubricant, etc.

Dope Dope, v. t. 1. To treat or affect with dope; as, to dope nitroglycerin; specif.: (a) To give stupefying drugs to; to drug. [Slang] (b) To administer a stimulant to (a horse) to increase his speed. It is a serious offense against the laws of racing. [Race-track Slang]

dopebook.c: Dope-book Dope"-book`, n. A chart of previous performances, etc., of race horses; a racing form. [Race-track Slang]

doppelganger.c: Doppelganger ‖Dop"pel*gäng`er (?), n. [G.] A spiritual or ghostly double or counterpart; esp., an apparitional double of a living person; a cowalker.

dopper.c: Dopper Dop"per (?), n. [D. dooper.] [Written also doper.] An Anabaptist or Baptist. [Contemptuous] B. Jonson.

dopplerite.c: Dopplerite Dop"pler*ite (?), n. [Named after the physicist and mathematician Christian Doppler.] (Min.) A brownish black native hydrocarbon occurring in elastic or jellylike masses.

doquet.c: Doquet Doq"uet (?), n. A warrant. See Docket.

dor.c: Dor Dor (?), n. [Cf. AS. dora drone, locust, D. tor beetle, L. taurus a kind of beetle. Cf. Dormouse.] (Zool.) A large European scaraboid beetle (Geotrupes stercorarius), which makes a droning noise while flying. The name is also applied to allied American species, as the June bug. Called also dorr, dorbeetle, or dorrbeetle, dorbug, dorrfly, and buzzard clock.
Dor Dor, n. [Cf. Dor a beetle, and Hum, Humbug.] A trick, joke, or deception. Beau. & Fl.
Dor Dor, v. t. To make a fool of; to deceive. [Obs.] [Written also dorr.] B. Jonson.

dorado.c: Dorado Do*ra"do (?), n. [Sp. dorado gilt, fr. dorar to gild, fr. L. deaurare. See 1st Dory, and cf. Fl Dorado.] 1. (Astron.) A southern constellation, within which is the south pole of the ecliptic; -- called also sometimes Xiphias, or the Swordfish.

doree.c: Doree Do"ree (?), n. [See Dory.] (Zool.) A European marine fish (Zeus faber), of a yellow color. See Illust. of John Doree.

doretree.c: Doretree Dore"tree` (?), n. A doorpost. [Obs.] “As dead as a doretree.” Piers Plowman.

dorhawk.c: Dorhawk Dor"hawk` (?), n. (Zool.) The European goatsucker; -- so called because it eats the dor beetle. See Goatsucker. [Written also dorrhawk.] Booth.

dorian.c: Dorian Do"ri*an (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to the ancient Greeks of Doris; Doric; as, a Dorian fashion.
Dorian Do"ri*an, n. A native or inhabitant of Doris in Greece.

doric.c: Doric Dor"ic (?), a. [L. Doricus, Gr.?, fr.? the Dorians.] 1. Pertaining to Doris, in ancient Greece, or to the Dorians; as, the Doric dialect.

doricism.c: Doricism Dor"i*cism (?), n. A Doric phrase or idiom.

doris.c: Doris ‖Do"ris (?), n. [L. Doris, the daughter of Oceanus, and wife of Nereus, Gr.?.] (Zool.) A genus of nudibranchiate mollusks having a wreath of branchiæ on the back.

dorism.c: Dorism Do"rism (?), n. [Gr.?.] A Doric phrase or idiom.

dorking.c: Dorking fowl Dor"king fowl` (dôr"kĭng foul`). [From the town of Dorking in England.] (Zool.) One of a breed of large-bodied domestic fowls, having five toes, or the hind toe double. There are several strains, as the white, gray, and silver-gray. They are highly esteemed for the table.

dormancy.c: Dormancy Dor"man*cy (?), n. [From Dormant.] The state of being dormant; quiescence; abeyance.
Dormancy Dor"man*cy (?), n. [From Dormant.] The state of being dormant; quiescence; abeyance.

dormant.c: Dormant Dor"mant (?), n. [See Dormant, a.] (Arch.) A large beam in the roof of a house upon which portions of the other timbers rest or “ sleep.” Arch. Pub. Soc. -- Called also dormant tree, dorman tree, dormond, and dormer. Halliwell.

dormer.c: Dormer window Dormer Dor"mer (?), or Dor"mer win"dow (?), n. [Literally, the window of a sleeping apartment. F. dormir to sleep. See Dormant, a. & n.] (Arch.) A window pierced in a roof, and so set as to be vertical while the roof slopes away from it. Also, the gablet, or houselike structure, in which it is contained.

dormitive.c: Dormitive Dor"mi*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. dormitif, fr. dormire to sleep.] Causing sleep; as, the dormitive properties of opium. Clarke. -- n. (Med.) A medicine to promote sleep; a soporific; an opiate.

dormitory.c: Dormitory Dor"mi*to*ry (?), n.; pl. Dormitories (#). [L. dormitorium, fr. dormitorius of or for sleeping, fr. dormire to sleep. See Dormant.] 1. A sleeping room, or a building containing a series of sleeping rooms; a sleeping apartment capable of containing many beds; esp., one connected with a college or boarding school. Thackeray.

dormouse.c: Dormouse Dor"mouse (?), n.; pl. Dormice (#). [Perh. fr. F. dormir to sleep (Prov. E. dorm to doze) + E. mouse; or perh. changed fr. F. dormeuse, fem., a sleeper, though not found in the sense of a dormouse.] (Zool.) A small European rodent of the genus Myoxus, of several species. They live in trees and feed on nuts, acorns, etc.; -- so called because they are usually torpid in winter.

dormy.c: Dormy Dor"my (?), a. [Origin uncertain.] (Golf) Up, or ahead, as many holes as remain to be played; -- said of a player or side.

dorn.c: Dorn Dorn (?), n. [Cf. G. dorn thorn, D. doorn, and G. dornfisch stickleback.] (Zool.) A British ray; the thornback.

dornock.c: Dornock Dornick { Dor"nick (?), or Dor"nock (?) }, n. A coarse sort of damask, originally made at Tournay (in Flemish, Doornick), Belgium, and used for hangings, carpets, etc. Also, a stout figured linen manufactured in Scotland. [Formerly written also darnex, dornic, dorneck, etc.] Halliwell. Jamieson.

dorp.c: Dorp Dorp (?), n. [LG. & D. dorp. See Thorpe.] A hamlet. “A mean fishing dorp.” Howell.

dorr.c: Dorr Dorr (?), n. The dorbeetle; also, a drone or an idler. See 1st Dor. Robynson (More's Utopia).
Dorr Dorr, v. t. 1. To deceive. [Obs.] See Dor, v. t.

dorsad.c: Dorsad Dor"sad (?), adv. [Dorsum +L. ad towards.] (Anat.) Toward the dorsum or back; on the dorsal side; dorsally.

dorsal.c: Dorsal Dor"sal (?), a. [F. dorsal, LL. dorsalis, fr. L. dorsualis, fr. dorsum back; cf. Gr.?,?, mountain ridge. Cf. Dorse, Dorsel, Dosel.] 1. (Anat.) Pertaining to, or situated near, the back, or dorsum, of an animal or of one of its parts; notal; tergal; neural; as, the dorsal fin of a fish; the dorsal artery of the tongue; -- opposed to ventral.
Dorsal Dor"sal, n. [LL. dorsale, neut. fr. dorsalis. See Dorsal, a.] (Fine Arts) A hanging, usually of rich stuff, at the back of a throne, or of an altar, or in any similar position.

dorsale.c: Dorsale Dor"sale (?), n. Same as Dorsal, n.

dorsally.c: Dorsally Dor"sal*ly (?), adv. (Anat.) On, or toward, the dorsum, or back; on the dorsal side of; dorsad.

dorse.c: Dorse Dorse (?), n. [Cf. L. dorsum the back. See Dorsel, Dosel.] 1. Same as dorsal, n. [Obs.]
Dorse Dorse, n. (Zool.) The Baltic or variable cod (Gadus callarias), by some believed to be the young of the common codfish.

dorsibranchiata.c: dorsibranchiata ‖dor`si*bran`chi*a"ta (?), n. pl. [NL., from L. dorsum back + branchiae gills.] (Zool.) A division of chætopod annelids in which the branchiæ are along the back, on each side, or on the parapodia. [See Illusts. under Annelida and Chætopoda.]

dorsibranchiate.c: Dorsibranchiate Dor`si*bran"chi*ate (?), a. (Zool.) Having branchiæ along the back; belonging to the Dorsibranchiata. -- n. One of the Dorsibranchiata.

dorsiferous.c: Dorsiferous Dor*sif"er*ous (?),. [Dorsum + -ferous; cf. F. dorsifère.] (Biol.) Bearing, or producing, on the back; -- applied to ferns which produce seeds on the back of the leaf, and to certain Batrachia, the ova of which become attached to the skin of the back of the parent, where they develop; dorsiparous.

dorsiparous.c: Dorsiparous Dor*sip"a*rous (?), a. [Dorsum + L. parere to bring forth.] (Biol.) Same as Dorsiferous.

dorsiventral.c: Dorsiventral Dor`si*ven"tral (?), a. [Dorsum + ventral.] 1. (Biol.) Having distinct upper and lower surfaces, as most common leaves. The leaves of the iris are not dorsiventral.

dorsoventral.c: Dorsoventral Dor`so*ven"tral (?), a. [dorsum + ventral.] (Anat.) From the dorsal to the ventral side of an animal; as, the dorsoventral axis.

dorsum.c: Dorsum ‖Dor"sum (?), n. [L.] 1. The ridge of a hill.

dorture.c: Dorture Dortour { Dor"tour (?), Dor"ture (?), } n. [F. dortoir, fr. L. dormitorium.] A dormitory. [Obs.] Bacon.

dory.c: Dory Do"ry (?), n.; pl. Dories (#). [Named from 1st color, fr. F. dorée gilded, fr. dorer to gild, L. deaurare. See Deaurate, and cf. Aureole.] 1. (Zool.) A European fish. See Doree, and John Doree.
Dory Do"ry, n.; pl. Dories (?). A small, strong, flat-bottomed rowboat, with sharp prow and flaring sides.

doryphora.c: Doryphora ‖Do*ryph"o*ra (?), n. [NL. See Doryphoros.] (Zool.) A genus of plant-eating beetles, including the potato beetle. See Potato beetle.

doryphoros.c: Doryphoros ‖Do*ryph"o*ros (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, lit., spear bearing;? a spear + fe`rein to bear.] (Fine Arts) A spear bearer; a statue of a man holding a spear or in the attitude of a spear bearer. Several important sculptures of this subject existed in antiquity, copies of which remain to us.

dosados.c: Dos-a-dos ‖Dos`-à-dos" (?), adv. [F.] Back to back; as, to sit dos-à-dos in a dogcart; to dance dos-à-dos, or so that two dancers move forward and pass back to back.
Dos-a-dos ‖Dos`-à-dos", n. A sofa, open carriage, or the like, so constructed that the occupants sit back to back.

dosage.c: Dosage Dos"age (dōs"aj), n. [Cf. F. dosage. See Dose, v.] 1. (Med.) The administration of medicine in doses; specif., a scheme or system of grading doses of medicine according to age, etc.

dose.c: Dose Dose (dōs), n. [F. dose, Gr. do`sis a giving, a dose, fr. dido`nai to give; akin to L. dare to give. See Date point of time.] 1. The quantity of medicine given, or prescribed to be taken, at one time.

Dose Dose, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dosed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. dosing.] [Cf. F. doser. See Dose, n.] 1. To proportion properly (a medicine), with reference to the patient or the disease; to form into suitable doses.

dosel.c: Dosel Dos"el (?), n. [OF. dossel; cf. LL. dorsale. See Dorsal, and cf. Dorse, Dorsel.] Same as Dorsal, n. [R.]

dosimetry.c: dosimetry do*sim"e*try (?), n. [NL. dosis dose + -metry.] (Med.) Measurement of doses; specif., a system of therapeutics which uses but few remedies, mostly alkaloids, and gives them in doses fixed by certain rules. -- Do`si*met"ric (#), a. -- Do*sim"e*trist (#), n.

doss.c: Doss Doss (dŏs), n. [Etym. uncertain.] A place to sleep in; a bed; hence, sleep. [Slang]
Doss house Doss house. A cheap lodging house.

dossel.c: Dossel Dos"sel (?), n. [See Dosel, n.] Same as Dorsal, n.

dosser.c: Dosser Dos"ser (?), n. [LL. dosserum, or F.dossier bundle of papers, part of a basket resting on the back, fr. L. dorsum back. See Dorsal, and cf. Dosel.] [Written also dorser and dorsel.] 1. A pannier, or basket.

dossier.c: Dossier ‖Dos`sier" (dos`sya"; E. dŏs"sĭ*ẽr), n. [F., back of a thing, bulging bundle of papers, fr. dos back.] A bundle containing the papers in reference to some matter.

dossil.c: Dossil Dos"sil (?), n. [OE. dosil faucet of a barrel, OF. dosil, duisil, spigot, LL. diciculus, ducillus, fr. L. ducere to lead, draw. See Duct, Duke.] 1. (Surg.) A small ovoid or cylindrical roil or pledget of lint, for keeping a sore, wound, etc., open; a tent.

dost.c: Dost Dost (?), 2d pers. sing. pres. of Do.

dot.c: Dot Dot (dŏt), n. [F., fr. L. dos, dotis, dowry. See Dower, and cf. Dote dowry.] (Law) A marriage portion; dowry. [Louisiana]
Dot Dot, n. [Cf. AS. dott small spot, speck; of uncertain origin.] 1. A small point or spot, made with a pen or other pointed instrument; a speck, or small mark.
Dot Dot, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dotted; p. pr. & vb. n. Dotting.] 1. To mark with dots or small spots; as, to dot a line.
Dot Dot, v. i. To make dots or specks.
D.O.T DOT DoT DoT, DOT, D.O.T. (dē"ō*tē`), prop. n. The United States Department of Transportation. [acronym]

dotage.c: Dotage Do"tage (?), n. [From Dote, v. i.] 1. Feebleness or imbecility of understanding or mind, particularly in old age; the childishness of old age; senility; as, a venerable man, now in his dotage.

dotal.c: Dotal Do"tal (?), a. [L. dotalis, fr. dos, dotis, dowry: cf. F. dotal. See Dot dowry.] Pertaining to dower, or a woman's marriage portion; constituting dower, or comprised in it. Garth.

dotard.c: Dotard Do"tard (?), n. [Dote, v. i.] One whose mind is impaired by age; one in second childhood.

dotardly.c: Dotardly Do"tard*ly, a. Foolish; weak. Dr. H. More.

dotary.c: Dotary Do"ta*ry (?), n. A dotard's weakness; dotage. [Obs.] Drayton.

dotation.c: Dotation Do*ta"tion (?), n. [LL. dotatio, fr. L. dotare to endow, fr. dos, dotis, dower: cf. F. dotation. See Dot dowry.] 1. The act of endowing, or bestowing a marriage portion on a woman.

dote.c: Dote Dote (?), n. [See Dot dowry.] 1. A marriage portion. [Obs.] See 1st Dot, n. Wyatt.

Dote Dote, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Doted; p. pr. & vb. n. Doting.] [OE. doten; akin to OD. doten, D. dutten, to doze, Icel. dotta to nod from sleep, MHG. t?zen to keep still: cf. F. doter, OF. radoter (to dote, rave, talk idly or senselessly), which are from the same source.] [Written also doat.] 1. To act foolishly. [Obs.]
Dote Dote, n. An imbecile; a dotard. Halliwell.

doter.c: Doter Dot"er (?), n. 1. One who dotes; a man whose understanding is enfeebled by age; a dotard. Burton.

dotery.c: Dotery Dot"er*y (?), n. The acts or speech of a dotard; drivel. [R.]

doth.c: Doth Doth (?), 3d pers. sing. pres. of Do.

doting.c: Doting Dot"ing (?), a. That dotes; silly; excessively fond. -- Dot"ing*ly, adv. -- Dot"ing*ness, n.

dotish.c: Dotish Dot"ish, a. Foolish; weak; imbecile. Sir W. Scott.

dottard.c: Dottard Dot"tard (?), n. [For Dotard?] An old, decayed tree. [R.] Bacon.

dotted.c: Dotted Dot"ted (?), a. Marked with, or made of, dots or small spots; diversified with small, detached objects.

dotterel.c: Dotterel Dot"ter*el (?), a. [Cf. Dottard.] Decayed. “Some old dotterel trees.” [Obs.] Ascham.

Dotterel Dot"ter*el, n. [From Dote, v. i.] 1. (Zool.) A European bird of the Plover family (Eudromias morinellus, syn. Charadrius morinellus). It is tame and easily taken, and is popularly believed to imitate the movements of the fowler.

dotting.c: Dotting pen Dot"ting pen` (?). See under Pun.

dotty.c: Dotty Dot"ty (?), a. [From 2d Dot.] 1. Composed of, or characterized by, dots.

doty.c: Doty Do"ty (?), a. [See Dottard.] Half-rotten; as, doty timber. [Local, U. S.]

douanier.c: Douanier ‖Dou`a"nier" (?), n. [F.] An officer of the French customs. [Anglicized form douaneer.]

douar.c: Douar Dou"ar (?), n. [F., fr. Ar. d?ār.] A village composed of Arab tents arranged in streets.

douay.c: Douay Bible Dou"ay Bi"ble (?). [From Douay, or Douai, a town in France.] A translation of the Scriptures into the English language for the use of English-speaking Roman Catholics; -- done from the Latin Vulgate by English scholars resident in France. The New Testament portion was published at Rheims, A. D. 1582, the Old Testament at Douai, A. D. 1609-10. Various revised editions have since been published. [Written also Doway Bible. Called also the Rheims and Douay version.]

doub.c: Doub grass Doub" grass` (dōob" grȧs).(Bot.) Doob grass.

double.c: Double Dou"ble (dŭb"'l), a. [OE. doble, duble, double, OF. doble, duble, double, F. double, fr. L. duplus, fr. the root of duo two, and perh. that of plenus full; akin to Gr. diplo`os double. See Two, and Full, and cf. Diploma, Duple.] 1. Twofold; multiplied by two; increased by its equivalent; made twice as large or as much, etc.

Double Dou"ble, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Doubled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Doubling (?).] [OE. doblen, dublen, doublen, F. doubler, fr. L. duplare, fr. duplus. See Double, a.] 1. To increase by adding an equal number, quantity, length, value, or the like; multiply by two; as, to double a sum of money; to double a number, or length.
Double Dou"ble, v. i. 1. To be increased to twice the sum, number, quantity, length, or value; to increase or grow to twice as much.
Double Dou"ble, n. 1. Twice as much; twice the number, sum, quantity, length, value, and the like.

Double first Dou"ble first` (?). (Eng. Universities) (a) A degree of the first class both in classics and mathematics. (b) One who gains at examinations the highest honor both in the classics and the mathematics. Beaconsfield.

doubleacting.c: Double-acting Dou"ble-act`ing (?), a. Acting or operating in two directions or with both motions; producing a twofold result; as, a double-acting engine or pump.

doublebank.c: Double-bank Dou"ble-bank" (?), v. t. (Naut.) To row by rowers sitting side by side in twos on a bank or thwart.

doublebanked.c: Double-banked Dou"ble-banked` (?), a. Applied to a kind of rowing in which the rowers sit side by side in twos, a pair of oars being worked from each bank or thwart.

doublebeat.c: Double-beat valve Dou"ble-beat` valve" (?). See under Valve.

doublebreasted.c: Double-breasted Dou"ble-breast`ed (?), a. Folding or lapping over on the breast, with a row of buttons and buttonholes on each side; as, a double-breasted coat.

doublecharge.c: Double-charge Dou"ble-charge` (?), v. t. 1. To load with a double charge, as of gunpowder.

doubledealer.c: double-dealer Double dealer Dou"ble deal"er, dou"ble-deal"er (?). One who practices double dealing; a deceitful, trickish person; a person who says one thing and does another. L'Estrange.

doubledealing.c: double-dealing Double dealing Dou"ble deal"ing, dou"ble-deal"ing (?). False or deceitful dealing; acting in bad faith; deception by pretending to entertain one set of intentions while acting under the influence of another. See Double dealing, under Dealing. Shak.

doubledecker.c: Double-decker Dou"ble-deck"er (?), n. 1. (Naut.) 1. A man-of-war having two gun decks.

doubledye.c: Double-dye Dou"ble-dye` (?), v. t. To dye again or twice over.

doubledyed.c: Double-dyed Dou"ble-dyed` (?), a. Dyed twice; thoroughly or intensely colored; hence; firmly fixed in opinions or habits; as, a double-dyed villain.

doubleender.c: Double-ender Dou"ble-end"er (?), n. (a) (Naut.) A vessel capable of moving in either direction, having bow and rudder at each end. (b) (Railroad) A locomotive with pilot at each end. Knight.

doubleentendre.c: Double-entendre ‖Dou"ble-en*ten"dre (?), n. [F. double double + entendre to mean. This is a barbarous compound of French words. The true French equivalent is double entente.] A word or expression admitting of a double interpretation, one of which is often obscure or indelicate.

doubleeyed.c: Double-eyed Dou"ble-eyed` (?), a. Having a deceitful look. [R.] “Deceitful meanings is double-eyed.” Spenser.

doubleganger.c: Doubleganger Dou"ble*gang`er (?), n. [G. doppelgänger; doppel double + gänger walker.] An apparition or double of a living person; a doppelgänger.

doublefaced.c: Double-faced Dou"ble-faced` (?), a. 1. Having two faces designed for use; as, a double-faced hammer.

doubleheaded.c: Double-headed Dou"ble-head"ed (?), a. Having two heads; bicipital.

doublehearted.c: Double-hearted Dou"ble-heart"ed (?), a. Having a false heart; deceitful; treacherous. Sandys.

doublehung.c: Double-hung Dou"ble-hung` (?), a. Having both sashes hung with weights and cords; -- said of a window.

doublelock.c: Double-lock Dou"ble-lock` (?), v. t. To lock with two bolts; to fasten with double security. Tatler.

doublemilled.c: Double-milled Dou"ble-milled` (?), a. Twice milled or fulled, to render more compact or fine; -- said of cloth; as, double-milled kerseymere.

doubleminded.c: Double-minded Dou"ble-mind"ed (?), a. Having different minds at different times; unsettled; undetermined.

doubleness.c: Doubleness Dou"ble*ness (?), n. 1. The state of being double or doubled.

doublequick.c: Double-quick Dou"ble-quick` (?), a. (Mil.) Of, or performed in, the fastest time or step in marching, next to the run; as, a double-quick step or march.
Double-quick Dou"ble-quick`, n. Double-quick time, step, or march.
Double-quick Dou"ble-quick`, v. i. & t. (Mil.) To move, or cause to move, in double-quick time.

doubler.c: Doubler Dou"bler (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, doubles.

doubleripper.c: Double-ripper Dou"ble-rip"per (?), n. A kind of coasting sled, made of two sleds fastened together with a board, one before the other. [Local, U. S.]

doubleshade.c: double-shade dou"ble-shade` (?), v. t. To double the natural darkness of (a place). Milton.

doublesurfaced.c: Double-surfaced Dou"ble-sur"faced (?), a. Having two surfaces; -- said specif. of aëroplane wings or aërocurves which are covered on both sides with fabric, etc., thus completely inclosing their frames.

doublet.c: Doublet Doub"let (?), n. [In sense 3, OF. doublet; in sense 4, F. doublet, dim. of double double. See Double, a.] 1. Two of the same kind; a pair; a couple.

doublethreaded.c: Double-threaded Dou"ble-thread`ed (?), a. 1. Consisting of two threads twisted together; using two threads.

doubletongued.c: Double-tongued Dou"ble-tongued` (?), a. Making contrary declarations on the same subject; deceitful.

doubletonguing.c: Double-tonguing Dou"ble-tongu`ing (?), n. (Mus.) A peculiar action of the tongue by flute players in articulating staccato notes; also, the rapid repetition of notes in cornet playing.

doubletree.c: Doubletree Dou"ble*tree` (?), n. The bar, or crosspiece, of a carriage, to which the singletrees are attached.

doublets.c: Doublets Doub"lets (?), n. pl. See Doublet, 6 and 7.

doubling.c: Doubling Dou"bling (?), n. 1. The act of one that doubles; a making double; reduplication; also, that which is doubled.

doubloon.c: Doubloon Doub*loon" (?), n. [F. doublon, Sp. doblon. See Double, a., and cf. Dupion.] A Spanish gold coin, no longer issued, varying in value at different times from over fifteen dollars to about five. See Doblon in Sup.

doublure.c: Doublure ‖Dou`blure" (?), n. [F.] 1. (Bookbinding) The lining of a book cover, esp. one of unusual sort, as of tooled leather, painted vellum, rich brocade, or the like.

doubly.c: Doubly Dou"bly (dŭb"ly̆), adv. 1. In twice the quantity; to twice the degree; as, doubly wise or good; to be doubly sensible of an obligation. Dryden.

doubt.c: Doubt Doubt (dout), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Doubted; p. pr. & vb. n. Doubting.] [OE. duten, douten, OF. duter, doter, douter, F. douter, fr. L. dubitare; akin to dubius doubtful. See Dubious.] 1. To waver in opinion or judgment; to be in uncertainty as to belief respecting anything; to hesitate in belief; to be undecided as to the truth of the negative or the affirmative proposition; to b e undetermined.

Doubt Doubt, v. t. 1. To question or hold questionable; to withhold assent to; to hesitate to believe, or to be inclined not to believe; to withhold confidence from; to distrust; as, I have heard the story, but I doubt the truth of it.

Doubt Doubt, n. [OE. dute, doute, F. doute, fr. douter to doubt. See Doubt, v. i.] 1. A fluctuation of mind arising from defect of knowledge or evidence; uncertainty of judgment or mind; unsettled state of opinion concerning the reality of an event, or the truth of an assertion, etc.; hesitation.

doubtable.c: Doubtable Doubt"a*ble (?), a. [OF. doutable, L. dubitabilis, from dubitare. Cf. Dubitable.] 1. Capable of being doubted; questionable.

doubtance.c: Doubtance Doubt"ance (?), n. [OF. doutance. Cf. Dubitancy.] State of being in doubt; uncertainty; doubt. [Obs.] Chaucer.

doubter.c: Doubter Doubt"er (?), n. One who doubts; one whose opinion is unsettled; one who scruples.

doubtful.c: Doubtful Doubt"ful (?), a. 1. Not settled in opinion; undetermined; wavering; hesitating in belief; also used, metaphorically, of the body when its action is affected by such a state of mind; as, we are doubtful of a fact, or of the propriety of a measure.

doubtfully.c: Doubtfully Doubt"ful*ly (?), adv. In a doubtful manner.

doubtfulness.c: Doubtfulness Doubt"ful*ness, n. 1. State of being doubtful.

doubting.c: Doubting Doubt"ing, a. That is uncertain; that distrusts or hesitates; having doubts. -- Doubt"ing*ly, adv.

doubtless.c: Doubtless Doubt"less, a. Free from fear or suspicion. [Obs.]

doubtous.c: Doubtous Doubt"ous (?), a. [OF. dotos, douteus, F. douteux.] Doubtful. [Obs.] Chaucer.

douc.c: Douc Douc (?), n. (Zool.) A monkey (Semnopithecus nemæus), remarkable for its varied and brilliant colors. It is a native of Cochin China.

douce.c: Douce Douce (?), a. [F. doux, masc., douce, fem., sweet, fr. L. duleis sweet.] 1. Sweet; pleasant. [Obs.]

doucepere.c: Doucepere Douce"pere` (?), n. [F. les douze pairs the twelve peers of France, renowned in romantic fiction.] One of the twelve peers of France, companions of Charlemagne in war. [Written also douzepere.] [Obs.]

dowset.c: Dowset Doucet { Dou"cet (?), Dow"set (?) }, n. [F. doucet sweet, dim. of doux. See Douce.] 1. A custard. [Obs.]

douceur.c: Douceur ‖Dou`ceur" (?), n. [F., fr. doux sweet. See Douce.] 1. Gentleness and sweetness of manner; agreeableness. Chesterfield.

douche.c: Douche Douche (?), n. [F., fr. It. doccia, fr. docciare to flow, pour, fr. an assumed LL. ductiare, fr. L. ducere, ductum, to lead, conduct (water). See Duct.] 1. A jet or current of water or vapor directed upon some part of the body to benefit it medicinally; a douche bath.

doucine.c: Doucine Dou"cine (?), n. [F.] (Arch.) Same as Cyma?recta, under Cyma.

doucker.c: Doucker Douck"er (?), n. [From aouck, for duck. See Duck, v. t.] (Zool.) A grebe or diver; -- applied also to the golden-eye, pochard, scoter, and other ducks. [Written also ducker.] [Prov. Eng.]

dough.c: Dough Dough (?), n. [OE. dagh, dogh, dow, AS. dāh; akin to D. deeg, G. teig, Icel. deig, Sw. deg, Dan. deig, Goth. daigs; also, to Goth. deigan to knead, L. fingere to form, shape, Skr. dih to smear; cf. Gr.? wall,? to touch, handle.?. Cf. Feign, Figure, Dairy, Duff.] 1. Paste of bread; a soft mass of moistened flour or meal, kneaded or unkneaded, but not yet baked; as, to knead dough.

doughbaked.c: Dough-baked Dough"-baked` (?), a. Imperfectly baked; hence, not brought to perfection; unfinished; also, of weak or dull understanding. [Colloq.] Halliwell.

doughbird.c: Doughbird Dough"bird` (?), n. (Zool.) The Eskimo curlew (Numenius borealis). See Curlew.

doughface.c: Doughface Dough"face` (?), n. A contemptuous nickname for a timid, yielding politician, or one who is easily molded. [Political cant, U. S.]

doughfaceism.c: Doughfaceism Dough"face`ism (?), n. The character of a doughface; truckling pliability.

doughiness.c: Doughiness Dough"i*ness, n. The quality or state of being doughy.

doughnut.c: Doughnut Dough"nut (?), n. A small cake (usually sweetened) fried in a kettle of boiling lard.

doughtily.c: Doughtily Dough"ti*ly (?), adv. In a doughty manner.

doughtiness.c: Doughtiness Dough"ti*ness, n. The quality of being doughty; valor; bravery.

doughtren.c: Doughtren Dough"tren (?), n. pl. [See Daughter.] Daughters. [Obs.] Chaucer.

doughty.c: Doughty Dough"ty (dou"ty̆), a. [Compar. Doughtier (dou"tĭ*ẽr); superl. Doughtiest.] [OE. duhti, dohti, douhti, brave, valiant, fit, useful, AS. dyhtig; akin to G. tüchtig, Dan. dygtig, Sw. dygdig virtuous, and fr. AS. dugan to avail, be of use, be strong, akin to D. deugen, OHG. tugan, G. taugen, Icel. & Sw. duga, Dan. due, Goth. dugan, but of uncertain origin; cf. Skr. duh to milk, give milk, draw out, or Gr. ty`chh fortune. √68.] Able; strong; valiant; redoubtable; as, a doughty hero.

doughy.c: Doughy Dough"y (dō"y̆), a. Like dough; soft and heavy; pasty; crude; flabby and pale; as, a doughy complexion.

doulocracy.c: Doulocracy Dou*loc"ra*cy (?), n. [Gr. doy^los slave + kratei^n to rule.] A government by slaves. [Written also dulocracy.] Hare.

doum.c: Doum palm Doum" palm` (dōom" päm`). See Doom palm.

doupe.c: Doupe Doupe (?), n. (Zool.) The carrion crow. [Written also dob.] [Prov. Eng.]

dour.c: Dour Dour (?), a. [Cf. F. dur, L. durus.] Hard; inflexible; obstinate; sour in aspect; hardy; bold. [Scot.]

dourah.c: dourah Doura Dou"ra, dourah (?), n. sorghums of dry regions of Asia and North Africa; A kind of millet. See Durra.

douroucouli.c: Douroucouli ‖Dou`rou*cou"li (?), n. (Zool.) A small, nocturnal, South American monkey of the genus Aotus (formerly Nyctipithecus trivirgatus), with large owl-like eyes; hence, the common name owl monkey. [Written also Durukuli and dourikuli.]

douse.c: Douse Douse (dous), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Doused (doust); p. pr. & vb. n. Dousing.] [Cf. Dowse, and OD. donsen to strike with the fist on the back, Sw. dunsa to fall down violently and noisily; perh. akin to E. din.] 1. To plunge suddenly into water; to duck; to immerse; to dowse. Bp. Stillingfleet.
Douse Douse, v. i. To fall suddenly into water. Hudibras.
Douse Douse, v. t. [AS. dwæscan. (Skeat.)] To put out; to extinguish; as, douse the lights. [Slang] “ To douse the glim.” Sir W. Scott.

dousingchock.c: Dousing-chock Dous"ing-chock` (?), n. (Shipbuilding) One of several pieces fayed across the apron and lapped in the knightheads, or inside planking above the upper deck. Ham. Nav. Encyc.

dout.c: Dout Dout (?), v. t. [Do + out. Cf. Doff.] To put out. [Obs.] “It douts the light.” Sylvester.

douter.c: Douter Dout"er (?), n. An extinguisher for candles. [Obs.]

dove.c: Dove Dove (dŭv), n. [OE. dove, duve, douve, AS. dūfe; akin to OS. dūba, D. duif, OHG. tūba, G. taube, Icel. dūfa, Sw. dufva, Dan. due, Goth. dūbō; perh. from the root of E. dive.] 1. (Zool.) A pigeon of the genus Columba and various related genera. The species are numerous.

Dove plant Dove" plant` (?). (Bot.) A Central American orchid (Peristeria elata), having a flower stem five or six feet high, with numerous globose white fragrant flowers. The column in the center of the flower resembles a dove; -- called also Holy Spirit plant.

dovecote.c: Dovecote Dovecot { Dove"cot` (?), Dove"cote` (?), } n. A small house or box, raised to a considerable height above the ground, and having compartments, in which domestic pigeons breed; a dove house.

doveeyed.c: Dove-eyed Dove"-eyed` (?), a. Having eyes like a dove; meekeyed; as, dove-eyed Peace.

dovekie.c: Dovekie Dove"kie (?), n. (Zool.) A guillemot (Uria grylle), of the arctic regions. Also applied to the little auk or sea dove. See under Dove.

dovelet.c: Dovelet Dove"let (?), n. A young or small dove. Booth.

dovelike.c: Dovelike Dove"like` (?), a. Mild as a dove; gentle; pure and lovable. Longfellow.

dovers.c: Dover's Powder Do"ver's Pow"der (?). [From Dr. Dover, an English physician.] (Med.) A powder of ipecac and opium, compounded, in the United States, with sugar of milk, but in England (as formerly in the United States) with sulphate of potash, and in France (as in Dr. Dover's original prescription) with nitrate and sulphate of potash and licorice. It is an anodyne diaphoretic.

dovesfoot.c: Dove's-foot Dove's"-foot` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) A small annual species of Geranium, native in England; -- so called from the shape of the leaf. (b) The columbine. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

doveship.c: Doveship Dove"ship (?), n. The possession of dovelike qualities, harmlessness and innocence. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

dovetail.c: Dovetail Dove"tail` (?), n. (Carp.) A flaring tenon, or tongue (shaped like a bird's tail spread), and a mortise, or socket, into which it fits tightly, making an interlocking joint between two pieces which resists pulling a part in all directions except one.
Dovetail Dove"tail`, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dovetailed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dovetailing.] 1. (Carp.) (a) To cut to a dovetail. (b) To join by means of dovetails.

dovish.c: Dovish Dov"ish (?), a. 1. Like a dove; harmless; innocent. “Joined with dovish simplicity.” Latimer.

dow.c: Dow Dow (?), n. A kind of vessel. See Dhow.
Dow Dow, v. t. [F. douer. See Dower.] To furnish with a dower; to endow. [Obs.] Wyclif.

dowable.c: Dowable Dow"a*ble (?), a. [From Dow, v. t.] Capable of being endowed; entitled to dower. Blackstone.

dowager.c: Dowager Dow"a*ger (?), n. [OF. douagiere, fr. douage dower. See Dower.] 1. (Eng. Law) A widow endowed, or having a jointure; a widow who either enjoys a dower from her deceased husband, or has property of her own brought by her to her husband on marriage, and settled on her after his decease. Blount. Burrill.

dowagerism.c: Dowagerism Dow"a*ger*ism (?), n. The rank or condition of a dowager; formality, as that of a dowager. Also used figuratively.

dowcet.c: Dowcet Dow"cet (?), n. [See Doucet.] One of the testicles of a hart or stag. [Spelt also doucet.] B. Jonson.

dowdy.c: Dowdy Dow"dy (?), a. [Compar. Dowdier (?); superl. Dowdiest.] [Scot. dawdie slovenly, daw, da sluggard, drab, Prov. E. dowd flat, dead.] Showing a vulgar taste in dress; awkward and slovenly in dress; vulgar-looking. -- Dow"di*ly (#), adv. -- Dow"di*ness, n.
Dowdy Dow"dy, n.; pl. Dowdies (?). An awkward, vulgarly dressed, inelegant woman. Shak. Dryden.

dowel.c: Dowel Dow"el (?), n. [Cf. G. döbel peg, F. douelle state of a cask, surface of an arch, douille socket, little pipe, cartridge.] (Mech.) 1. A pin, or block, of wood or metal, fitting into holes in the abutting portions of two pieces, and being partly in one piece and partly in the other, to keep them in their proper relative position.

Dowel Dow"el, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Doweled (?) or Dowelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Doweling or Dowelling.] To fasten together by dowels; to furnish with dowels; as, a cooper dowels pieces for the head of a cask.

dower.c: Dower Dow"er (?), n. [F. douaire, LL. dotarium, from L. dotare to endow, portion, fr. dos dower; akin to Gr.? gift, and to L. dare to give. See 1st Date, and cf. Dot dowry, Dotation.] 1. That with which one is gifted or endowed; endowment; gift.

dowered.c: Dowered Dow"ered (?), p. a. Furnished with, or as with, dower or a marriage portion. Shak.

dowerless.c: Dowerless Dow"er*less, a. Destitute of dower; having no marriage portion. Shak.

dowitcher.c: Dowitcher Dow"itch*er (?), n. (Zool.) The red-breasted or gray snipe (Macrorhamphus griseus); -- called also brownback, and grayback.

dowlas.c: Dowlas Dow"las (?), n. [Prob. fr. Doullens, a town of Picardy, in France, formerly celebrated for this manufacture.] A coarse linen cloth made in the north of England and in Scotland, now nearly replaced by calico. Shak.

dowle.c: Dowle Dowle (?), n. [Cf. OF. douille soft. Cf. Ductile.] Feathery or wool-like down; filament of a feather. Shak.

down.c: Down Down (?), n. [Akin to LG. dune, dun, Icel. d?nn, Sw. dun, Dan. duun, G. daune, cf. D. dons; perh. akin to E. dust.] 1. Fine, soft, hairy outgrowth from the skin or surface of animals or plants, not matted and fleecy like wool; esp.: (a) (Zool.) The soft under feathers of birds. They have short stems with soft rachis and bards and long threadlike barbules, without hooklets. (b) (Bot.) The pubescence of plants; the hairy crown or envelope of the seeds of certain plants, as of the thistle. (c) The soft hair of the face when beginning to appear.
Down Down (doun), v. t. To cover, ornament, line, or stuff with down. [R.] Young.

Down Down, n. [OE. dun, doun, AS. dūn; of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. dūn hill, fortified hill, Gael. dun heap, hillock, hill, W. din a fortified hill or mount; akin to E. town. See Town, and cf. Down, adv. & prep., Dune.] 1. A bank or rounded hillock of sand thrown up by the wind along or near the shore; a flattish-topped hill; -- usually in the plural.

Down Down, adv. [For older adown, AS. adūn, adūne, prop., from or off the hill. See 3d Down, and cf. Adown, and cf. Adown.] 1. In the direction of gravity or toward the center of the earth; toward or in a lower place or position; below; -- the opposite of up.
Down Down, prep. [From Down, adv.] 1. In a descending direction along; from a higher to a lower place upon or within; at a lower place in or on; as, down a hill; down a well.

Down Down, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Downed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Downing.] To cause to go down; to make descend; to put down; to overthrow, as in wrestling; hence, to subdue; to bring down. [Archaic or Colloq.] “To down proud hearts.” Sir P. Sidney.
Down Down, v. i. To go down; to descend. Locke.
Down Down, a. 1. Downcast; as, a down look. [R.]

downbear.c: Downbear Down"bear` (?), v. t. To bear down; to depress.

downcast.c: downcast down"cast` (?), a. Cast downward; directed to the ground, from bashfulness, modesty, dejection, or guilt.
Downcast Down"cast`, n. 1. Downcast or melancholy look.

downcome.c: Downcome Down"come` (doun"kŭm`), n. 1. Sudden fall; downfall; overthrow. Milton.

downcomer.c: Downcomer Down"com`er (?), n. A pipe to conduct something downwards; specif.: (a) (Iron Manuf.) A pipe for leading the hot gases from the top of a blast furnace downward to the regenerators, boilers, etc. (b) (Steam Engin.) In some water-tube boilers, a tube larger in diameter than the water tubes to conduct the water from each top drum to a bottom drum, thus completing the circulation.

downfall.c: Downfall Down"fall` (doun"fäl`), n. 1. A sudden fall; a body of things falling.

downgyved.c: Downgyved Down"gyved` (?), a. Hanging down like gyves or fetters. [Poetic & Rare] Shak.

downhaul.c: Downhaul Down"haul` (doun"häl`), n. (Naut.) A rope to haul down, or to assist in hauling down, a sail; as, a staysail downhaul; a trysail downhaul.

downhill.c: Downhill Down"hill` (?), adv. Towards the bottom of a hill; as, water runs downhill.
Downhill Down"hill`, a. Declivous; descending; sloping. “A downhill greensward.” Congrewe.

downiness.c: Downiness Down"i*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being downy.

downlooked.c: Downlooked Down"looked` (?), a. Having a downcast countenance; dejected; gloomy; sullen. [R.] Dryden.

downlying.c: Downlying Down"ly`ing (?), n. The time of retiring to rest; time of repose. Cavendish.

downpour.c: Downpour Down"pour` (?), n. A pouring or streaming downwards; esp., a heavy or continuous shower.

downright.c: Downright Down"right`, a. 1. Plain; direct; forthright; unceremonious; blunt; positive; as, he spoke in his downright way.

downshare.c: Down-share Down"-share` (?), n. A breastplow used in paring off turf on downs. [Eng.] Knight.

downsitting.c: Downsitting Down"sit`ting (?), n. The act of sitting down; repose; a resting.

downstairs.c: downstairs down"stairs (?), adv. Down the stairs; to a lower floor; as, she headed downstairs as soon as she heard the horn.

downstream.c: Downstream Down"stream` (?), adv. Down the stream; as, floating downstream.

downstroke.c: Downstroke Down"stroke` (?), n. (Penmanship) A stroke made with a downward motion of the pen or pencil.

downthrow.c: Downthrow Down"throw` (?), n. (Geol.) The sudden drop or depression of the strata of rocks on one side of a fault. See Throw, n.

downtrodden.c: Downtrodden Downtrod { Down"trod` (?), Down"trod`den (?), } a. Trodden down; trampled down; abused by superior power. Shak.

downwards.c: Downwards Downward { Down"ward (?), Down"wards (?), } adv. [AS. ad?nweard. See Down, adv., and -ward.] 1. From a higher place to a lower; in a descending course; as, to tend, move, roll, look, or take root, downward or downwards. “Looking downwards.” Pope.

downward.c: Downward Down"ward, a. 1. Moving or extending from a higher to a lower place; tending toward the earth or its center, or toward a lower level; declivous.

downweed.c: Downweed Down"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) Cudweed, a species of Gnaphalium.

downweigh.c: Downweigh Down`weigh" (-wā"), v. t. To weigh or press down.

downy.c: Downy Down"y (-y̆), a. 1. Covered with down, or with pubescence or soft hairs. “A downy feather.” Shak.

dowral.c: Dowral Dow"ral (dou"rail), a. Of or relating to a dower. [R.]

dowress.c: Dowress Dow"ress, n. A woman entitled to dower. Bouvier.

dowry.c: Dowry Dow"ry (dou"ry̆), n.; pl. Dowries (dou"rĭz). [Contr. from dowery; cf. LL. dotarium. See Dower.] 1. A gift; endowment. [Obs.] Spenser.

dowse.c: Dowse Dowse (?), v. t. [Cf. 1st Douse.] 1. To plunge, or duck into water; to immerse; to douse.
Dowse Dowse, v. i. To use the dipping or divining rod, as in search of water, ore, etc.
Dowse Dowse, n. A blow on the face. [Low] Colman.

dowser.c: Dowser Dows"er (?), n. 1. A divining rod used in searching for water, ore, etc., a dowsing rod. [Colloq.]

dowst.c: Dowst Dowst (?), n. A dowse. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

doxological.c: Doxological Dox`o*log"ic*al (?), a. Pertaining to doxology; giving praise to God. Howell.

doxologize.c: Doxologize Dox*ol"o*gize (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Doxologized; p. pr. & vb. n. Doxologizing.] To give glory to God, as in a doxology; to praise God with doxologies.

doxology.c: Doxology Dox*ol"o*gy (?), n.; pl. Doxologies (#). [LL. doxologia, Gr.?, fr.? praising, giving glory;? opinion, estimation, glory, praise (from? to think, imagine) +? to speak: cf. F. doxologie. See Dogma, and Legend.] In Christian worship: A hymn expressing praise and honor to God; a form of praise to God designed to be sung or chanted by the choir or the congregation.

doxy.c: Doxy Dox"y (?), n.; pl. Doxies (#). [See Duck a pet.] A loose wench; a disreputable sweetheart. Shak.

doyen.c: Doyen ‖Doy`en" (dwä`yäN"), n. [F. See Dean.] Lit., a dean; the senior member of a body or group; as, the doyen of French physicians. “This doyen of newspapers.” A. R. Colquhoun.

doze.c: Doze Doze (dōz), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Dozed (dōzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Dozing.] [Prob. akin to daze, dizzy: cf. Icel. dūsa to doze, Dan. döse to make dull, heavy, or drowsy, dös dullness, drowsiness, dösig drowsy, AS. dwǣs dull, stupid, foolish. √71. Cf. Dizzy.] To slumber; to sleep lightly; to be in a dull or stupefied condition, as if half asleep; to be drowsy.
Doze Doze, v. t. 1. To pass or spend in drowsiness; as, to doze away one's time.
Doze Doze, n. A light sleep; a drowse. Tennyson.

dozen.c: Dozen Doz"en (dŭz"'n), n.; pl. Dozen (before another noun), Dozens (dŭz"'nz). [OE. doseine, dosein, OF. doseine, F. douzaine, fr. douze twelve, fr. L. duodecim; duo two + decem ten. See Two, Ten, and cf. Duodecimal.] 1. A collection of twelve objects; a tale or set of twelve; with or without of before the substantive which follows. “Some six or seven dozen of Scots.” “A dozen of shirts to your back.” “A dozen sons.” “Half a dozen friends.” Shak.

dozer.c: Dozer Doz"er (?), n. One who dozes or drowses.

doziness.c: Doziness Doz"i*ness (?), n. The state of being dozy; drowsiness; inclination to sleep.

dozy.c: Dozy Doz"y (?), a. Drowsy; inclined to doze; sleepy; sluggish; as, a dozy head. Dryden.

dozzled.c: Dozzled Doz"zled (?), a. [√71.] Stupid; heavy. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

drab.c: Drab Drab (drăb), n. [AS. drabbe dregs, lees; akin to D. drab, drabbe, dregs, G. treber; for sense 1, cf. also Gael. drabag a slattern, drabach slovenly. Cf. Draff.] 1. A low, sluttish woman. King.
Drab Drab, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drabbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drabbing.] To associate with strumpets; to wench. Beau. & Fl.

Drab Drab, n. [F. drap cloth: LL. drappus, trapus, perh. orig., a firm, solid stuff, cf. F. draper to drape, also to full cloth; prob. of German origin; cf. Icel. drepa to beat, strike, AS. drepan, G. treffen; perh. akin to E. drub. Cf. Drape, Trappings.] 1. A kind of thick woolen cloth of a dun, or dull brownish yellow, or dull gray, color; -- called also drabcloth.
Drab Drab, a. Of a color between gray and brown. -- n. A drab color.

drabber.c: Drabber Drab"ber (?), n. One who associates with drabs; a wencher. Massinger.

drabbet.c: Drabbet Drab"bet (?), n. A coarse linen fabric, or duck.

drabbish.c: Drabbish Drab"bish, a. Somewhat drab in color.
Drabbish Drab"bish (?), a. Having the character of a drab or low wench. “The drabbish sorceress.” Drant.

drabble.c: Drabble Drab"ble (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Drabbled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drabbling (?).] [???.See Drab, Draff.] To draggle; to wet and befoul by draggling; as, to drabble a gown or cloak. Halliwell.
Drabble Drab"ble (?), v. i. To fish with a long line and rod; as, to drabble for barbels.

drabbler.c: Drabbler Drab"bler (?), n. (Naut.) A piece of canvas fastened by lacing to the bonnet of a sail, to give it a greater depth, or more drop.

drabbletail.c: Drabble-tail Drab"ble-tail` (?), n. A draggle-tail; a slattern. Halliwell.

dracaena.c: Dracaena ‖Dra*cæ"na (?), prop. n. [NL., fr. Gr.? she-dragon.] (Bot.) A genus of liliaceous plants with woody stems and funnel-shaped flowers.

dracanth.c: Dracanth Dra"canth (?), n. A kind of gum; -- called also gum tragacanth, or tragacanth. See Tragacanth.

drachma.c: Drachma ‖Drach"ma (?), n.; pl. E. Drachmas (#), L. Drachmæ (#). [L., fr. Gr.?. See Dram.] 1. A silver coin among the ancient Greeks, having a different value in different States and at different periods. The average value of the Attic drachma is computed to have been about 19 cents (U. S. currency, ca. 1913).

dracin.c: Dracin Dra"cin (?), n. [Cf. F. dracine.] (Chem.) See Draconin.

draco.c: Draco ‖Dra"co (?), n. [L. See Dragon.] 1. (Astron.) The Dragon, a northern constellation within which is the north pole of the ecliptic.

draconian.c: Draconian Dra*co"ni*an (?), a. Pertaining to Draco, a famous lawgiver of Athens, 621 b. c. Used especially in the phrase Draconian punishment.

draconic.c: Draconic Dra*con"ic (?), a. Relating to Draco, the Athenian lawgiver; or to the constellation Draco; or to dragon's blood.

draconin.c: Draconin Dra*co"nin (?), n. [Cf. F. draconine. See Draco.] (Chem.) A red resin forming the essential basis of dragon's blood; -- called also dracin.

dracontic.c: Dracontic Dra*con"tic (?), a. [From L. draco dragon, in allusion to the terms dragon's head and dragon's tail.] (Astron.) Belonging to that space of time in which the moon performs one revolution, from ascending node to ascending node. See Dragon's head, under Dragon. [Obs.] “Dracontic month.” Crabb.

dracontine.c: Dracontine Dra*con"tine (?), a. [L. draco dragon.] Belonging to a dragon. Southey.

dracunculus.c: Dracunculus ‖Dra*cun"cu*lus (?), n.; pl. Dracunculi (#). [L., dim. of draco dragon.] (Zool.) (a) A fish; the dragonet. (b) The Guinea worm (Filaria medinensis).

drad.c: Drad Drad (?), p. p. & a. Dreaded. [Obs.] Chaucer.

dradge.c: Dradge Dradge (?), n. (Min.) Inferior ore, separated from the better by cobbing. Raymond.

draff.c: Draff Draff (?), n. [Cf. D. draf the sediment of ale, Icel. draf draff, husks. Cf. 1st Drab.] Refuse; lees; dregs; the wash given to swine or cows; hogwash; waste matter.

draft.c: Draft Draft (drȧft), n. [The same word as draught. OE. draught, draht, fr. AS. dragan to draw. See Draw, and cf. Draught.] 1. The act of drawing; also, the thing drawn. Same as Draught.
Draft Draft, a. 1. Pertaining to, or used for, drawing or pulling (as vehicles, loads, etc.). Same as Draught; as, a draft horse.
Draft Draft (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Drafted; p. pr. & vb. n. Drafting.] 1. To draw the outline of; to delineate.

drag.c: Drag Drag (?), n. [See 3d Dredge.] A confection; a comfit; a drug. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Drag Drag, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dragged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dragging (?).] [OE. draggen; akin to Sw. dragga to search with a grapnel, fr. dragg grapnel, fr. draga to draw, the same word as E. draw.? See Draw.] 1. To draw slowly or heavily onward; to pull along the ground by main force; to haul; to trail; -- applied to drawing heavy or resisting bodies or those inapt for drawing, with labor, along the ground or other surface; as, to drag stone or timber; to drag a net in fishing.
Drag Drag, v. i. 1. To be drawn along, as a rope or dress, on the ground; to trail; to be moved onward along the ground, or along the bottom of the sea, as an anchor that does not hold.
Drag Drag, n. [See Drag, v. t., and cf. Dray a cart, and 1st Dredge.] 1. The act of dragging; anything which is dragged.
Drag rope Drag line { Drag line or Drag rope }. (Aëronautics) A guide rope.

dragantine.c: Dragantine Dra*gan"tine (?), n. [See Dracanth.] A mucilage obtained from, or containing, gum tragacanth.

dragbar.c: Dragbar Drag"bar` (?), n. Same as Drawbar (b). Called also draglink, and drawlink. [U. S.]

dragbolt.c: Dragbolt Drag"bolt` (?), n. A coupling pin. See under Coupling. [U. S.]

dragees.c: Dragees ‖Dra`gées" (?), n. pl. [F. See 3d Dredge.] (Pharmacy) Sugar-coated medicines.

draggle.c: Draggle Drag"gle (drăg"g'l), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Draggled (drăg"g'ld); p. pr. & vb. n. Draggling (drăg"glĭng).] [Freq. of drag. √73. Cf. Drawl.] To wet and soil by dragging on the ground, mud, or wet grass; to drabble; to trail. Gray.
Draggle Drag"gle, v. i. To be dragged on the ground; to become wet or dirty by being dragged or trailed in the mud or wet grass. Hudibras.

draggletail.c: Draggle-tail Drag"gle-tail` (?), n. A slattern who suffers her gown to trail in the mire; a drabble-tail.

draggletailed.c: Draggle-tailed Drag"gle-tailed` (?), a. Untidy; sluttish; slatternly. W. Irving.

draglink.c: Draglink Drag"link` (?), n. (Mach.) (a) A link connecting the cranks of two shafts. (b) A drawbar.

dragman.c: Dragman Drag"man (?), n.; pl. Dragmen (?). A fisherman who uses a dragnet. Sir M. Hale.

dragnet.c: Dragnet Drag"net` (?), n. [Cf. AS. drægnet.] A net to be drawn along the bottom of a body of water, as in fishing.

dragoman.c: Dragoman Drag"o*man (?), n.; pl. Dragomans (#). [From F. dragoman, or Sp. dragoman, or It. dragomanno; all fr. LGr.?, Ar. tarjumān, from the same source as E. targum. Cf. Drogman, Truchman.] An interpreter; -- so called in the Levant and other parts of the East.

dragon.c: dragon drag"on (drăg"ŭn), n. [F. dragon, L. draco, fr. Gr. dra`kwn, prob. fr. de`rkesqai, dra`kein, to look (akin to Skr. darç to see), and so called from its terrible eyes. Cf. Drake a dragon, Dragoon.] 1. (Myth.) A fabulous animal, generally represented as a monstrous winged serpent or lizard, with a crested head and enormous claws, and regarded as very powerful and ferocious.

dragonet.c: Dragonet Drag"on*et (?), n. 1. A little dragon. Spenser.

dragonish.c: Dragonish Drag"on*ish, a. resembling a dragon. Shak.

dragonlike.c: Dragonlike Drag"on*like` (-līk`), a. Like a dragon. Shak.

dragonnade.c: Dragonnade Drag`on*nade" (drăg`ŏn*nād"), n. [F., fr. dragon dragoon, because Louis XIV., in persecuting the Protestants of his kingdom, quartered dragoons upon them.] The severe persecution of French Protestants under Louis XIV., by an armed force, usually of dragoons; hence, a rapid and devastating incursion; dragoonade.

dragons.c: Dragon's tail Dragon's head Dragon's blood { Drag"on's blood, Drag"on's head, Drag"on's tail }. See Dragon's blood, Dragon's head, etc., under Dragon.

dragoon.c: Dragoon Dra*goon" (drȧ*gōon"), n. [F. dragon dragon, dragoon, fr. L. draco dragon, also, a cohort's standard (with a dragon on it). The name was given from the sense standard. See Dragon.] 1. ((Mil.) Formerly, a soldier who was taught and armed to serve either on horseback or on foot; now, a mounted soldier; a cavalry man.
Dragoon Dra*goon", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dragooned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dragooning.] 1. To harass or reduce to subjection by dragoons; to persecute by abandoning a place to the rage of soldiers.

drail.c: Drail Drail (drāl), v. t. & i. [√73.] To trail; to draggle. [Obs.] South.

drain.c: Drain Drain (drān), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Drained (drānd); p. pr. & vb. n. Draining.] [AS. drehnigean to drain, strain; perh. akin to E. draw.] 1. To draw off by degrees; to cause to flow gradually out or off; hence, to cause the exhaustion of.
Drain Drain, v. i. 1. To flow gradually; as, the water of low ground drains off.
Drain Drain, n. 1. The act of draining, or of drawing off; gradual and continuous outflow or withdrawal; as, the drain of specie from a country; the project is a drain on resources.

drainable.c: Drainable Drain"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being drained.

drainage.c: Drainage Drain"age (?), n. 1. A draining; a gradual flowing off of any liquid; also, that which flows out of a drain.

drainer.c: Drainer Drain"er (?), n. One who, or that which, drains.

draining.c: Draining Drain"ing, vb. n. of Drain, v. t. (Agric.) The art of carrying off surplus water, as from land.

drainpipe.c: Drainpipe Drain"pipe` (?), n. A pipe used for carrying off surplus water.

draintile.c: Draintile Drain"tile` (?), n. A hollow tile used in making drains; -- called also draining tile.

drake.c: Drake Drake (drāk), n. [Akin to LG. drake, OHG. antrache, anetrecho, G. enterich, Icel. andriki, Dan. andrik, OSw. andrak, andrage, masc., and fr. AS. ened, fem., duck; akin to D. eend, G. ente, Icel. önd, Dan. and, Sw. and, Lith. antis, L. anas, Gr.? (for?), and perh. Skr. āti a water fowl. √207. In English the first part of the word was lost. The ending is akin to E. rich. Cf. Gulaund.] 1. The male of the duck kind.
Drake Drake, n. [AS. draca dragon, L. draco. See Dragon.] 1. A dragon. [Obs.]
Drake Drake, n. [Cf. F. dravik, W. drewg, darnel, cockle, etc.] Wild oats, brome grass, or darnel grass; -- called also drawk, dravick, and drank. [Prov. Eng.] Dr. Prior.

drakestone.c: Drakestone Drake"stone (?), n. A flat stone so thrown along the surface of water as to skip from point to point before it sinks; also, the sport of so throwing stones; -- sometimes called ducks and drakes.

dram.c: Dram Dram (drăm), n. [OF. drame, F. drachme, L. drachma, drachm, drachma, fr. Gr. drachmh`, prop., a handful, fr. dra`ssesqai to grasp. Cf. Drachm, Drachma.] 1. A weight; in Apothecaries' weight, one eighth part of an ounce, or sixty grains; in Avoirdupois weight, one sixteenth part of an ounce, or 27.34375 grains.
Dram Dram, v. i. & t. To drink drams; to ply with drams. [Low] Johnson. Thackeray.

drama.c: Drama Dra"ma (drä"mȧ or drā"mȧ; 277), n. [L. drama, Gr. dra^ma, fr. dra^n to do, act; cf. Lith. daryti.] 1. A composition, in prose or poetry, accommodated to action, and intended to exhibit a picture of human life, or to depict a series of grave or humorous actions of more than ordinary interest, tending toward some striking result. It is commonly designed to be spoken and represented by actors on the stage.

dramatical.c: Dramatical Dramatic { Dra*mat"ic (drȧ*măt"ĭk), Dra*mat"ic*al (drȧ*măt"ĭ*kail), } a. [Gr. dramatiko`s, fr. dra^ma: cf. F. dramatique.] Of or pertaining to the drama; as, dramatic arts. [wns=3]

dramatically.c: Dramatically Dra*mat"ic*al*ly, adv. In a dramatic manner; theatrically; vividly.

dramatis.c: Dramatis personae ‖Dram"a*tis per*so"næ (?). [L.] The actors in a drama or play.

dramatist.c: Dramatist Dram"a*tist (?), n. [Cf. F. dramatiste.] The author of a dramatic composition; a writer of plays.

dramatizable.c: Dramatizable Dram"a*ti`za*ble (?), a. Capable of being dramatized.

dramatization.c: dramatization dram`a*ti*za"tion (?), n. Act of dramatizing; a dramatic representation.

dramatize.c: Dramatize Dram"a*tize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dramatized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dramatizing (?).] [Cf. F. dramatiser.] To compose in the form of the drama; to represent in a drama; to adapt to dramatic representation; as, to dramatize a novel, or an historical episode.

dramaturgist.c: Dramaturgist Dram"a*tur`gist (?), n. One versed in dramaturgy. Carlyle.

dramaturgy.c: Dramaturgy Dram"a*tur`gy (?), n. [Gr.? dramatic composition;? drama + a root akin to E. work: cf. F. dramaturgie.] The art of dramatic composition and representation.

dramming.c: Dramming Dram"ming (?), n. The practice of drinking drams.

dramseller.c: Dramseller Dram"sell`er (?), n. One who sells distilled liquors by the dram or glass.

dramshop.c: Dramshop Dram"shop` (?), n. A shop or barroom where spirits are sold by the dram.

drank.c: Drank Drank, n. [Cf. 3d Drake.] Wild oats, or darnel grass. See Drake a plant. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

drap.c: Drap d'ete ‖Drap` d'é*té" (?). [F., clot of summer.] A thin woolen fabric, twilled like merino.

drape.c: Drape Drape (drāp), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Draped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Draping (?).] [F. draper, fr. drap cloth. See 3d Drab.] 1. To cover or adorn with drapery or folds of cloth, or as with drapery; as, to drape a bust, a building, etc.
Drape Drape, v. i. 1. To make cloth. [Obs.] Bacon.

draper.c: Draper Dra"per (?), n. [F. drapier.] One who sells cloths; a dealer in cloths; as, a draper and tailor.

draperied.c: Draperied Dra"per*ied (?), a. Covered or supplied with drapery. [R.] Byron.

drapery.c: Drapery Dra"per*y (?), n.; pl. Draperies (#). [F. draperie.] 1. The occupation of a draper; cloth-making, or dealing in cloth. Bacon.

drapet.c: Drapet Dra"pet (?), n. [Dim. of drap.] Cloth. [Obs.] Spenser.

drastic.c: Drastic Dras"tic (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? to do, act: cf. F. drastique. See Drama.] (Med.) Acting rapidly and violently; efficacious; powerful; -- opposed to bland; as, drastic purgatives. -- n. (Med.) A violent purgative. See Cathartic.

drasty.c: Drasty Dras"ty (?), a. [AS. dærstan, dresten, dregs.] Filthy; worthless. [Obs.] “Drasty ryming.” Chaucer.

draught.c: Draught Draught (?), n. [The same as draft, the spelling with gh indicating an older pronunciation. See Draft, n., Draw.] 1. The act of drawing or pulling; as: (a) The act of moving loads by drawing, as by beasts of burden, and the like.
Draught Draught, a. 1. Used for drawing vehicles, loads, etc.; as, a draught beast; draught hooks.
Draught Draught (drȧft), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Draughted; p. pr. & vb. n. Draughting.] 1. To draw out; to call forth. See Draft. Addison.

draughtboard.c: Draughtboard Draught"board` (-bōrd`), n. A checkered board on which draughts are played. See Checkerboard.

draughthouse.c: Draughthouse Draught"house` (-hous`), n. A house for the reception of waste matter; a privy. [Obs.] 2 Kings x. 27.

draughts.c: Draughts Draughts (?), n. pl. A mild vesicatory. See Draught, n., 3 (c).
Draughts Draughts, n. pl. A game, now more commonly called checkers. See Checkers.

draughtsman.c: Draughtsman Draughts"man (?), n.; pl. Draughtsmen (?). 1. One who draws pleadings or other writings.

draughtsmanship.c: Draughtsmanship Draughts"man*ship, n. The office, art, or work of a draughtsman.

draughty.c: Draughty Draught"y (?), a. Pertaining to a draught, or current of air; as, a draughtly, comfortless room.

dravida.c: Dravida Dra"vi*da (?), n. pl. [Skr. Drāviḍa, prob. meaning, Tamil.] (Ethnol.) A race of Hindustan, believed to be the original people who occupied the land before the Hindu or Aryan invasion.

dravidian.c: Dravidian Dra*vid"i*an (?), prop. a. [From Skr. Drāviḍa, the name of the southern portion of the peninsula of India.] (Ethnol.) Of or pertaining to the Dravida.

draw.c: draw draw (drä), v. t. [imp. Drew (drü); p. p. Drawn (drän); p. pr. & vb. n. Drawing.] [OE. draȝen, drahen, draien, drawen, AS. dragan; akin to Icel. & Sw. draga, Dan. drage to draw, carry, and prob. to OS. dragan to bear, carry, D. dragen, G. tragen, Goth. dragan; cf. Skr. dhraj to move along, glide; and perh. akin to Skr. dhar to hold, bear. √73. Cf. 2d Drag, Dray a cart, 1st Dredge.] 1. To cause to move continuously by force applied in advance of the thing moved; to pull along; to haul; to drag; to cause to follow.
Draw Draw (?), v. i. 1. To pull; to exert strength in drawing anything; to have force to move anything by pulling; as, a horse draws well; the sails of a ship draw well.
Draw Draw, n. 1. The act of drawing; draught.

drawable.c: Drawable Draw"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being drawn.

drawback.c: Drawback Draw"back` (?), n. 1. A loss of advantage, or deduction from profit, value, success, etc.; a discouragement or hindrance; objectionable feature.

drawbar.c: Drawbar Draw"bar` (?), n. (Railroad) (a) An openmouthed bar at the end of a car, which receives a coupling link and pin by which the car is drawn. It is usually provided with a spring to give elasticity to the connection between the cars of a train. (b) A bar of iron with an eye at each end, or a heavy link, for coupling a locomotive to a tender or car.

drawbench.c: Drawbench Draw"bench` (?), n. (Med.) A machine in which strips of metal are drawn through a drawplate; especially, one in which wire is thus made; -- also called drawing bench.

drawbolt.c: Drawbolt Draw"bolt` (?), n. (Engin.) A coupling pin. See under Coupling.

drawbore.c: Drawbore Draw"bore` (?), n. (Joinery) A hole bored through a tenon nearer to the shoulder than the holes through the cheeks are to the edge or abutment against which the shoulder is to rest, so that a pin or bolt, when driven into it, will draw these parts together. Weale.
Drawbore Draw"bore`, v. t. 1. To make a drawbore in; as, to drawbore a tenon.

drawboy.c: Drawboy Draw"boy` (?), n. (Weaving) A boy who operates the harness cords of a hand loom; also, a part of power loom that performs the same office.

drawbridge.c: Drawbridge Draw"bridge` (?), n. A bridge of which either the whole or a part is made to be raised up, let down, or drawn or turned aside, to admit or hinder communication at pleasure, as before the gate of a town or castle, or over a navigable river or canal.

drawcansir.c: Drawcansir Draw"can*sir (?), n. [From the name of a bullying braggart character in the play by George Villiers called “The Rehearsal.”] A blustering, bullying fellow; a pot-valiant braggart; a bully.

drawcut.c: Draw-cut Draw"-cut` (?), n. A single cut with a knife.

drawee.c: drawee draw*ee" (?), n. (Law) The person on whom an order or bill of exchange is drawn; -- the correlative of drawer.

drawer.c: drawer draw"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, draws; as: (a) One who draws liquor for guests; a waiter in a taproom. Shak. (b) One who delineates or depicts; a draughtsman; as, a good drawer. (c) (Law) One who draws a bill of exchange or order for payment; -- the correlative of drawee.

drawfiling.c: Drawfiling Draw"fil`ing (?), n. The process of smooth filing by working the file sidewise instead of lengthwise.

drawgear.c: Drawgear Draw"gear` (?), n. 1. A harness for draught horses.

drawgloves.c: Drawgloves Draw"gloves` (?), n. pl. An old game, played by holding up the fingers. Herrick.

drawhead.c: Drawhead Draw"head` (?), n. (Railroad) The flanged outer end of a drawbar; also, a name applied to the drawgear.

drawing.c: Drawing Draw"ing, n. 1. The act of pulling, or attracting.

drawknife.c: Drawknife Drawing knife { Draw"ing knife" (?), Draw"knife` (?) }, n. 1. A woodworker`s and joiner's tool having a blade with a handle at each end, used to shave off surfaces, by drawing it toward one; a shave; -- called also drawshave, and drawing shave.

drawingroom.c: Drawing-room Draw"ing-room` (?), n. [Abbrev. fr. withdraw-ing-room.] 1. A room appropriated for the reception of company; a room to which company withdraws from the dining room.

drawl.c: Drawl Drawl (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Drawled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drawling.] [Prob. fr. draw: cf. D. dralen to linger, tarry, Icel. dralla to loiter. See Draw, and cf. Draggle.] To utter in a slow, lengthened tone.
Drawl Drawl, v. i. To speak with slow and lingering utterance, from laziness, lack of spirit, affectation, etc.
Drawl Drawl, n. A lengthened, slow monotonous utterance.

drawlatch.c: Drawlatch Draw"latch` (?), n. A housebreaker or thief. [Obs.] Old Play (1631).

drawling.c: Drawling Drawl"ing (?), n. The act of speaking with a drawl; a drawl. -- Drawl"ing*ly, adv. Bacon.

drawloom.c: Drawloom Draw"loom` (?), n. 1. A kind of loom used in weaving figured patterns; -- called also drawboy.

drawn.c: Drawn Drawn (?), p. p. & a. See Draw, v. t. & i.

drawnet.c: Drawnet Draw"net` (?), n. A net for catching the larger sorts of birds; also, a dragnet. Crabb.

drawplate.c: Drawplate Draw"plate` (?), n. A hardened steel plate having a hole, or a gradation of conical holes, through which wires are drawn to be reduced and elongated.

drawrod.c: Drawrod Draw"rod` (?), n. (Railroad) A rod which unites the drawgear at opposite ends of the car, and bears the pull required to draw the train.

drawspring.c: Drawspring Draw"spring` (?), n. (Railroad) The spring to which a drawbar is attached.

dray.c: Dray Dray (?), n. A squirrel's nest. Cowper.
Dray Dray, n. [AS. dræge a dragnet, fr. dragan.????. See Draw, and cf. 2d Drag, 1st Dredge.] 1. A strong low cart or carriage used for heavy burdens. Addison.

drayage.c: Drayage Dray"age (?), n. 1. Use of a dray.

drayman.c: Drayman Dray"man (?), n.; pl. Draymen (?). A man who attends a dray.

drazel.c: Drazel Draz"el (?), n. [Cf. Dross, Drossel.] A slut; a vagabond wench. Same as Drossel. [Obs.] Hudibras.

dread.c: Dread Dread (drĕd), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dreaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Dreading.] [AS. drǣdan, in comp.; akin to OS. drādan, OHG. trātan, both only in comp.] To fear in a great degree; to regard, or look forward to, with terrific apprehension.
Dread Dread, v. i. To be in dread, or great fear.
Dread Dread, n. 1. Great fear in view of impending evil; fearful apprehension of danger; anticipatory terror.
Dread Dread, a. 1. Exciting great fear or apprehension; causing terror; frightful; dreadful.

dreadable.c: Dreadable Dread"a*ble (?), a. Worthy of being dreaded.

dreadbolted.c: Dread-bolted Dread"-bolt`ed (?), a. Armed with dreaded bolts. “Dread-bolted thunder.” [Poetic] Shak.

dreader.c: Dreader Dread"er (?), n. One who fears, or lives in fear.

dreadful.c: Dreadful Dread"ful (?), a. 1. Full of dread or terror; fearful. [Obs.] “With dreadful heart.” Chaucer.

dreadfully.c: Dreadfully Dread"ful*ly (?), adv. In a dreadful manner; terribly. Dryden.

dreadfulness.c: Dreadfulness Dread"ful*ness, n. The quality of being dreadful.

dreadless.c: Dreadless Dread"less, a. 1. Free from dread; fearless; intrepid; dauntless; as, dreadless heart. “The dreadless angel.” Milton.

dreadly.c: Dreadly Dread"ly, a. Dreadful. [Obs.] “Dreadly spectacle.” Spenser. -- adv. With dread. [Obs.] “Dreadly to shake.” Sylvester (Du Bartas).

dreadnought.c: Dreadnought Dread"nought` (?), n. 1. (Capitalized) A British battleship, completed in 1906 -- 1907, having an armament consisting of ten 12-inch guns mounted in turrets, and of twenty-four 12-pound quick-fire guns for protection against torpedo boats. This was the first battleship of the type characterized by a main armament of big guns all of the same caliber. She had a displacement of 17,900 tons at load draft, and a speed of 21 knots per hour.

dream.c: Dream Dream (drēm), n. [Akin to OS. drōm, D. droom, G. traum, Icel. draumr, Dan. & Sw. dröm; cf. G. trügen to deceive, Skr. druh to harm, hurt, try to hurt. AS. dreám joy, gladness, and OS. drōm joy are, perh., different words; cf. Gr. qry^los noise.] 1. The thoughts, or series of thoughts, or imaginary transactions, which occupy the mind during sleep; a sleeping vision.

Dream Dream, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Dreamed (drēmd) or Dreamt (drĕmt); p. pr. & vb. n. Dreaming.] [Cf. AS. drēman, drȳman, to rejoice. See Dream, n.] 1. To have ideas or images in the mind while in the state of sleep; to experience sleeping visions; -- often with of; as, to dream of a battle, or of an absent friend.
Dream Dream, v. t. To have a dream of; to see, or have a vision of, in sleep, or in idle fancy; -- often followed by an objective clause.

dreamful.c: Dreamful Dream"ful (drēm"fụl), a. Full of dreams. “ Dreamful ease.” Tennyson. -- Dream"ful*ly, adv.

dreamily.c: Dreamily Dream"i*ly (drēm"ĭ*ly̆), adv. As if in a dream; softly; slowly; languidly. Longfellow.

dreaminess.c: Dreaminess Dream"i*ness, n. The state of being dreamy.

dreamingly.c: Dreamingly Dream"ing*ly, adv. In a dreamy manner.

dreamland.c: Dreamland Dream"land` (?), n. An unreal, delightful country such as in sometimes pictured in dreams; region of fancies; fairyland.

dreamless.c: Dreamless Dream"less, a. Free from, or without, dreams. Camden. -- Dream"less*ly, adv.

dreamy.c: dreamy dream"y (drēm"y̆), a. [Compar. Dreamier (drēm"ĭ*ẽr); superl. Dreamiest (?).] 1. Abounding in dreams or given to dreaming; appropriate to, or like, dreams; visionary. “The dreamy dells.” Tennyson.

drear.c: Drear Drear (drēr), a. [See Dreary.] Dismal; gloomy with solitude. “A drear and dying sound.” Milton.

drearihood.c: Drearihood Drearihead { Drear"i*head (drēr"ĭ*hĕd), Drear"i*hood (drēr"ĭ*hŏod), } n. Affliction; dreariness. [Obs.] Spenser.

dreary.c: Dreary Drear"y (drēr"y̆), a. [Compar. Drearier (?); superl. Dreariest.] [OE. dreori, dreri, AS. dreórig, sad; akin to G. traurig, and prob. to AS. dreósan to fall, Goth. driusan. Cf. Dross, Drear, Drizzle, Drowse.] 1. Sorrowful; distressful. [Obs.] “ Dreary shrieks.” Spenser.

drecche.c: Drecche Drec"che (drĕch"ei), v. t. [AS. dreccan, dreccean.] 1. To vex; to torment; to trouble. [Obs.]
Drecche Drec"che, v. i. To delay. [Obs.] Gower.

dredge.c: Dredge Dredge (drĕj), n. [F. drège, dreige, fish net, from a word akin to E. draw; cf. D. dreg, dregge, small anchor, dregnet dragnet. √73. See Draw.] 1. Any instrument used to gather or take by dragging; as: (a) A dragnet for taking up oysters, etc., from their beds. (b) A dredging machine. (c) An iron frame, with a fine net attached, used in collecting animals living at the bottom of the sea.
Dredge Dredge (drĕj), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dredged (drĕjd); p. pr. & vb. n. Dredging.] To catch or gather with a dredge; to deepen with a dredging machine. R. Carew.

Dredge Dredge, n. [OE. dragge, F. dragée, dredge, also, sugar plum; cf. Prov. dragea, It. treggea; corrupted fr. LL. tragemata, pl., sweetmeats, Gr. tragh`mata, fr. trw`gein to gnaw.] A mixture of oats and barley. [Obs.] Kersey.
Dredge Dredge, v. t. To sift or sprinkle flour, etc., on, as on roasting meat. Beau. & Fl.

dredger.c: Dredger Dredg"er (drĕj"ẽr), n. 1. One who fishes with a dredge.
Dredger Dredg"er, n. (Cookery) A box with holes in its lid; -- used for sprinkling flour, as on meat or a breadboard; -- called also dredging box, drudger, and drudging box.

dree.c: Dree Dree (drē), v. t. [AS. dreógan to bear, endure, complete.] To endure; to suffer. [Scot.]
Dree Dree, v. i. To be able to do or endure. [Obs.]

dreg.c: Dreg Dreg (drĕg), n. [Prob. from Icel. dregg; akin to Sw. drägg, cf. Icel. & Sw. draga to draw. Cf. Draw.] Corrupt or defiling matter contained in a liquid, or precipitated from it; refuse; feculence; lees; grounds; sediment; hence, the vilest and most worthless part of anything; as, the dregs of society.

dregginess.c: Dregginess Dreg"gi*ness (drĕg"gĭ*nĕs), n. Fullness of dregs or lees; foulness; feculence.

dreggish.c: Dreggish Dreg"gish (drĕg"gĭsh), a. Foul with lees; feculent. Harvey.

dreggy.c: Dreggy Dreg"gy (drĕg"gy̆), a. Containing dregs or lees; muddy; foul; feculent. Boyle.

dreibund.c: Dreibund ‖Drei"bund` (?), n. [G., fr. drei three + bund league.] A triple alliance; specif., the alliance of Germany, Austria, and Italy, formed in 1882.

drein.c: Drein Drein (?), v. i. To drain. [Obs.] Congreve.

dreint.c: Dreint Dreinte Drein"te (?), imp., Dreint (?), p. p. of Drench to drown. [Obs.] Chaucer.

dreissena.c: Dreissena ‖Dreis"se*na (?), prop. n. [NL. Named after Dreyssen, a Belgian physician.] (Zool.) A genus of bivalve shells of which one species (Dreissena polymorpha) is often so abundant as to be very troublesome in the fresh waters of Europe.

drench.c: Drench Drench (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Drenched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drenching.] [AS. drencan to give to drink, to drench, the causal of drincan to drink; akin to D. drenken, Sw. dränka, G. tränken. See Drink.] 1. To cause to drink; especially, to dose by force; to put a potion down the throat of, as of a horse; hence. to purge violently by physic.

Drench Drench, n. [AS. drenc. See Drench, v. t.] A drink; a draught; specifically, a potion of medicine poured or forced down the throat; also, a potion that causes purging. “A drench of wine.” Dryden.
Drench Drench, n. [AS. dreng warrior, soldier, akin to Icel. drengr.] (O. Eng. Law) A military vassal mentioned in Domesday Book. [Obs.] Burrill.

drenche.c: Drenche Drench"e (?), v. t. & i. To drown. [Obs.]

drencher.c: Drencher Drench"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, west or steeps.

drengage.c: Drengage Dren"gage (?), n. (O. Eng. Law) The tenure by which a drench held land. [Obs.] Burrill.

drent.c: Drent Drent (?), p. p. [See Dreinte.] Drenched; drowned. [Obs.] “Condemned to be drent.” Spenser.

dresden.c: Dresden ware Dres"den ware` (?). A superior kind of decorated porcelain made near Dresden in Saxony.

dress.c: Dress Dress (drĕs), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dressed (drĕst) or Drest; p. pr. & vb. n. Dressing.] [OF. drecier to make straight, raise, set up, prepare, arrange, F. dresser, (assumed) LL. directiare, fr. L. dirigere, directum, to direct; dis- + regere to rule. See Right, and cf. Address, Adroit, Direct, Dirge.] 1. To direct; to put right or straight; to regulate; to order. [Obs.]
Dress Dress, v. i. 1. (Mil.) To arrange one's self in due position in a line of soldiers; -- the word of command to form alignment in ranks; as, Dress right, dress!
Dress Dress, n. 1. That which is used as the covering or ornament of the body; clothes; garments; habit; apparel. “In your soldier's dress.” Shak.
Dress circle Dress circle. A gallery or balcony in a theater, generally the first above the floor, in which originally dress clothes were customarily worn.

Dress coat Dress" coat` (?). A coat with skirts behind only, as distinct from the frock coat, of which the skirts surround the body. It is worn on occasions of ceremony. The dress coat of officers of the United States army is a full-skirted frock coat.
Dress goods Dress" goods" (?). A term applied to fabrics for the gowns of women and girls; -- most commonly to fabrics of mixed materials, but also applicable to silks, printed linens, and calicoes.

dresser.c: dresser dress"er (?), n. 1. One who dresses; one who put in order or makes ready for use; one who on clothes or ornaments.
Dresser Dress"er, n. [F. dressoir. See Dress, v. t.] A piece of chamber furniture consisting of a chest of drawers, or bureau, with a mirror. [U. S.]

dressiness.c: Dressiness Dress"i*ness (?), n. The state of being dressy.

dressing.c: Dressing Dress"ing, n. 1. Dress; raiment; especially, ornamental habiliment or attire. B. Jonson.

dressmaker.c: Dressmaker Dress"mak`er (?), n. A maker of gowns, or similar garments; a mantuamaker.

dressmaking.c: Dressmaking Dress"mak`ing, n. The art, process, or occupation, of making dresses.

dressy.c: Dressy Dress"y (?), a. Showy in dress; attentive to dress.

dretch.c: Dretch Dretch (?), v. t. & i. See Drecche. [Obs.]

drevil.c: Drevil Drev"il (?), n. A fool; a drudge. See Drivel.

drey.c: Drey Drey (?), n. A squirrel's nest. See Dray. [Obs.]

dreynt.c: Dreynt Dreynte Dreyn"te (?), imp., Dreynt (?), p. p., of Drench to drown. [Obs.] Chaucer.

drib.c: Drib Drib (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dribbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dribbing.] [Cf. Drip.] To do by little and little; as: (a) To cut off by a little at a time; to crop. (b) To appropriate unlawfully; to filch; to defalcate.
Drib Drib (?), v. t. & i. (Archery) To shoot (a shaft) so as to pierce on the descent. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

dribber.c: Dribber Drib"ber (?), n. One who dribs; one who shoots weakly or badly. [Obs.] Ascham.

dribble.c: Dribble Drib"ble (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Dribbled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dribbing (?).] [Freq. of drib, which is a variant of drip.] 1. To fall in drops or small drops, or in a quick succession of drops; as, water dribbles from the eaves.
Dribble Drib"ble, v. t. 1. To let fall in drops.
Dribble Drib"ble, n. 1. A drizzling shower; a falling or leaking in drops. [Colloq.]

driblet.c: Driblet Dribblet { Drib"blet (?), Drib"let (?), } n. [From Dribble.] A small piece or part; a small sum; a small quantity of money in making up a sum; as, the money was paid in dribblets.

drie.c: Drie Drie (?), v. t. [See Dree.] To endure. [Obs.]

dried.c: Dried Dried (drīd), imp. & p. p. of Dry. Also adj.; as, dried apples.

drier.c: Drier Dri"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, dries; that which may expel or absorb moisture; a desiccative; as, the sun and a northwesterly wind are great driers of the earth.

driest.c: Driest Drier Dri"er, compar., Dri"est, superl., of Dry, a.

drift.c: Drift Drift (?), n. [From drive; akin to LG. & D. drift a driving, Icel. drift snowdrift, Dan. drift, impulse, drove, herd, pasture, common, G. trift pasturage, drove. See Drive.] 1. A driving; a violent movement.

Drift Drift, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drifted; p. pr. & vb. n. Drifting.] 1. To float or be driven along by, or as by, a current of water or air; as, the ship drifted astern; a raft drifted ashore; the balloon drifts slowly east.
