Drift Drift (?), v. t. 1. To drive or carry, as currents do a floating body. J. H. Newman.
Drift Drift, a. That causes drifting or that is drifted; movable by wind or currents; as, drift currents; drift ice; drift mud. Kane.

driftage.c: Driftage Drift"age (?), n. 1. Deviation from a ship's course due to leeway.

driftbolt.c: Driftbolt Drift"bolt` (?), n. A bolt for driving out other bolts.

driftless.c: Driftless Drift"less, a. Having no drift or direction; without aim; purposeless.

driftpiece.c: Driftpiece Drift"piece" (?), n. (Shipbuilding) An upright or curved piece of timber connecting the plank sheer with the gunwale; also, a scroll terminating a rail.

driftpin.c: Driftpin Drift"pin` (?), n. (Mech.) A smooth drift. See Drift, n., 9.

driftway.c: Driftway Drift"way` (?), n. 1. A common way, road, or path, for driving cattle. Cowell. Burrill.

driftweed.c: Driftweed Drift"weed` (?), n. Seaweed drifted to the shore by the wind. Darwin.

driftwind.c: Driftwind Drift"wind` (?), n. A driving wind; a wind that drives snow, sand, etc., into heaps. Beau. & Fl.

driftwood.c: Driftwood Drift"wood` (?), n. 1. Wood drifted or floated by water.

drifty.c: Drifty Drift"y (?), a. Full of drifts; tending to form drifts, as snow, and the like.

drill.c: Drill Drill (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Drilled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drilling.] [D. drillen to bore, drill (soldiers); probably akin to AS. pyrlian, pyrelian, to pierce. See Thrill.] 1. To pierce or bore with a drill, or a with a drill; to perforate; as, to drill a hole into a rock; to drill a piece of metal.
Drill Drill, v. i. To practice an exercise or exercises; to train one's self.

Drill Drill, n. 1. An instrument with an edged or pointed end used for making holes in hard substances; strictly, a tool that cuts with its end, by revolving, as in drilling metals, or by a succession of blows, as in drilling stone; also, a drill press.

Drill Drill, v. t. [Cf. Trill to trickle, Trickle, Dribble, and W. rhillio to put in a row, drill.] 1. To cause to flow in drills or rills or by trickling; to drain by trickling; as, waters drilled through a sandy stratum. [R.] Thomson.
Drill Drill, v. i. 1. To trickle. [Obs. or R.] Sandys.
Drill Drill, n. 1. A small trickling stream; a rill. [Obs.]
Drill Drill (?), n. [Cf. Mandrill.] (Zool.) A large African baboon (Cynocephalus leucophæus).
Drill Drill, n. [Usually in pl.] (Manuf.) Same as Drilling.
Drill press Drill" press`. A machine for drilling holes in metal, the drill being pressed to the metal by the action of a screw.

driller.c: Driller Drill"er (?), n. One who, or that which, drills.

drilling.c: Drilling Drill"ing, n. 1. The act of piercing with a drill.
Drilling Drill"ing, n. The act of using a drill in sowing seeds.

Drilling Drill"ing, n. [G. drillich, fr. L. trilix having three threads, fr. the of tres three + licium a thread of the warm. See Three, and cf. Twill.] (Manuf.) A heavy, twilled fabric of linen or cotton.

drillmaster.c: Drillmaster Drill"mas`ter (?), n. One who teaches drill, especially in the way of gymnastics. Macaulay.

drillstock.c: Drillstock Drill"stock` (?), n. (Mech.) A contrivance for holding and turning a drill. Knight.

drimys.c: Drimys ‖Dri"mys (drī"mĭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. drimy`s sharp, acrid.] (Bot.) A genus of magnoliaceous trees. Drimys aromatica furnishes Winter's bark.

drink.c: Drink Drink (drĭṉk), v. i. [imp. Drank (drăṉk), formerly Drunk (drŭṉk); & p. p. Drunk, Drunken (-'n); p. pr. & vb. n. Drinking. Drunken is now rarely used, except as a verbal adj. in sense of habitually intoxicated; the form drank, not infrequently used as a p. p., is not so analogical.] [AS. drincan; akin to OS. drinkan, D. drinken, G. trinken, Icel. drekka, Sw. dricka, Dan. drikke, Goth. drigkan. Cf. Drench, Drunken, Drown.] 1. To swallow anything liquid, for quenching thirst or other purpose; to imbibe; to receive or partake of, as if in satisfaction of thirst; as, to drink from a spring.
Drink Drink, v. t. 1. To swallow (a liquid); to receive, as a fluid, into the stomach; to imbibe; as, to drink milk or water.
Drink Drink, n. 1. Liquid to be swallowed; any fluid to be taken into the stomach for quenching thirst or for other purposes, as water, coffee, or decoctions.

drinkable.c: Drinkable Drink"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being drunk; suitable for drink; potable. Macaulay. Also used substantively, esp. in the plural. Steele.

drinkableness.c: Drinkableness Drink"a*ble*ness, n. State of being drinkable.

drinker.c: Drinker Drink"er (?), n. One who drinks; as, the effects of tea on the drinker; also, one who drinks spirituous liquors to excess; a drunkard.

drinking.c: Drinking Drink"ing, n. 1. The act of one who drinks; the act of imbibing.

drinkless.c: Drinkless Drink"less, a. Destitute of drink. Chaucer.

drip.c: Drip Drip (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Dripped (?) or Dript; p. pr. & vb. n. Dripping.] [Akin to LG. drippen, Dan. dryppe, from a noun. See Drop.] 1. To fall in drops; as, water drips from the eaves.
Drip Drip, v. t. To let fall in drops.
Drip Drip, n. 1. A falling or letting fall in drops; a dripping; that which drips, or falls in drops.

dripping.c: Dripping Drip"ping, n. 1. A falling in drops, or the sound so made.

dripple.c: Dripple Drip"ple (?), a. [From Drip, cf. Dribble.] Weak or rare. [Obs.]

dripstone.c: Dripstone Drip"stone` (?), n. (Arch.) A drip, when made of stone. See Drip, 2.

drive.c: Drive Drive (drīv), v. t. [imp. Drove (drōv), formerly Drave (drāv); p. p. Driven (drĭv'n); p. pr. & vb. n. Driving.] [AS. drīfan; akin to OS. drīban, D. drijven, OHG. trīban, G. treiben, Icel. drīfa, Goth. dreiban. Cf. Drift, Drove.] 1. To impel or urge onward by force in a direction away from one, or along before one; to push forward; to compel to move on; to communicate motion to; as, to drive cattle; to drive a nail; smoke drives persons from a room.
Drive Drive, n. 1. In various games, as tennis, cricket, etc., the act of player who drives the ball; the stroke or blow; the flight of the ball, etc., so driven.
Drive Drive, v. i. 1. To rush and press with violence; to move furiously.
Drive Drive (drīv), n. 1. The act of driving; a trip or an excursion in a carriage, as for exercise or pleasure; -- distinguished from a ride taken on horseback.

drivebolt.c: Drivebolt Drive"bolt` (?), n. A drift; a tool for setting bolts home.

drivel.c: Drivel Driv"el (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Driveled (?) or Drivelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Driveling or Drivelling.] [Cf. OE. dravelen, drabelen, drevelen, drivelen, to slaver, and E. drabble. Cf. Drool.] 1. To slaver; to let spittle drop or flow from the mouth, like a child, idiot, or dotard.
Drivel Driv"el, n. 1. Slaver; saliva flowing from the mouth.

driveler.c: Driveler Driv"el*er (?), n. A slaverer; a slabberer; an idiot; a fool. [Written also driveller.]

driven.c: Driven Driv"en (?), p. p. of Drive. Also adj.

drivepipe.c: Drivepipe Drive"pipe` (?), n. A pipe for forcing into the earth.

driver.c: Driver Driv"er (?), n. [From Drive.] 1. One who, or that which, drives; the person or thing that urges or compels anything else to move onward.

driveway.c: Driveway Drive"way` (?), n. A passage or way along or through which a carriage may be driven.

driving.c: Driving Driv"ing, a. 1. Having great force of impulse; as, a driving wind or storm.
Driving Driv"ing, n. 1. The act of forcing or urging something along; the act of pressing or moving on furiously.

drizzle.c: Drizzle Driz"zle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drizzled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drizzling (?).] [Prop. freq. of AS. dreósan to fall. See Dreary.] To rain slightly in very small drops; to fall, as water from the clouds, slowly and in fine particles; as, it drizzles; drizzling drops or rain. “Drizzling tears.” Spenser.
Drizzle Driz"zle, v. t. To shed slowly in minute drops or particles. “The air doth drizzle dew.” Shak.
Drizzle Driz"zle, n. A fine rain or mist. Halliwell.

drizzly.c: Drizzly Driz"zly (?), a. Characterized by small rain, or snow; moist and disagreeable. “Winter's drizzly reign.” Dryden.

drock.c: Drock Drock (?), n. A water course. [Prov. Eng.]

dryfland.c: Dryfland Drofland { Drof"land (?), Dryf"land (?) }, n. [See Drove.] (Law) An ancient yearly payment made by some tenants to the king, or to their landlords, for the privilege of driving their cattle through a manor to fairs or markets. Cowell.

drogher.c: Drogher Dro"gher (?), n. [Cf. Drag.] A small craft used in the West India Islands to take off sugars, rum, etc., to the merchantmen; also, a vessel for transporting lumber, cotton, etc., coastwise; as, a lumber drogher. [Written also droger.] Ham. Nar. Encyc.

drogoman.c: Drogoman Drogman { Drog"man (?), Drog"o*man (?) }, n. See Dragoman.

drogue.c: Drogue Drogue (drōg), n. 1. (Naut.) See Drag, n., 6, and Drag sail, under Drag, n.

droil.c: Droil Droil (droil), v. i. [D. druilen to mope.] To work sluggishly or slowly; to plod. [Obs.]
Droil Droil, n. [D. druil sluggard. Cf. Droll.] 1. A drudge. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

droit.c: Droit Droit (droit), n. [F. See Direct.] A right; law in its aspect of the foundation of rights; also, in old law, the writ of right. Abbott.

droitural.c: Droitural Droi"tu*ral (?), a. (O. Eng. Law) relating to the mere right of property, as distinguished from the right of possession; as, droitural actions. [Obs.] Burrill.

droll.c: Droll Droll (drōl), a. [Compar. Droller (?); superl. Drollest (?).] [F. drôle; cf. G. & D. drollig, LG. drullig, D. drol a thick and short person, a droll, Sw. troll a magical appearance, demon, trolla to use magic arts, enchant, Dan. trold elf, imp, Icel. tröll giant, magician, evil spirit, monster. If this is the origin, cf. Trull.] Queer, and fitted to provoke laughter; ludicrous from oddity; amusing and strange.
Droll Droll, n. 1. One whose practice it is to raise mirth by odd tricks; a jester; a buffoon; a merry-andrew. Prior.
Droll Droll, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drolled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drolling.] To jest; to play the buffoon. [R.]
Droll Droll, v. t. 1. To lead or influence by jest or trick; to banter or jest; to cajole.

droller.c: Droller Droll"er, n. A jester; a droll. [Obs.] Glanvill.

drollery.c: Drollery Droll"er*y (?), n.; pl. Drolleries (#). [F. drôlerie. See Droll.] 1. The quality of being droll; sportive tricks; buffoonery; droll stories; comical gestures or manners.

drollingly.c: Drollingly Droll"ing*ly, adv. In a jesting manner.

dromaeognathous.c: Dromaeognathous Dro`mæ*og"na*thous (?), a. [NL. dromaius emu + Gr. gna`qos jaw.] (Zool.) Having the structure of the palate like that of the ostrich and emu.

dromatherium.c: Dromatherium ‖Drom`a*the"ri*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. droma`s running + qhri`on beast. See Dromedary.] (Paleon.) A small extinct triassic mammal from North Carolina, the earliest yet found in America.

drome.c: Drome Drome (drōm), n. [F., fr. Gr. droma`s running. See Dromedary.] (Zool.) The crab plover (Dromas ardeola), a peculiar North African bird, allied to the oyster catcher.

dromedary.c: Dromedary Drom"e*da*ry (drŭm"e*da*ry̆), n.; pl. Dromedaries (-rĭz). [F. dromadaire, LL. dromedarius, fr. L. dromas (sc. camelus), fr. Gr. droma`s running, from dramei^n, used as aor. of tre`chein to run; cf. Skr. dram to run.] (Zool.) The Arabian camel (Camelus dromedarius), having one hump or protuberance on the back, in distinction from the Bactrian camel, which has two humps.

dromon.c: Dromon Dromond { Drom"ond (?), or Drom"on (?) }. [OF. dromont, L. dromo, fr. Gr. dro`mwn light vessel, prob. fr. dramei^n to run. See Dromedary.] In the Middle Ages, a large, fast-sailing galley, or cutter; a large, swift war vessel. [Hist. or Archaic] Fuller.

drone.c: Drone Drone (?), n. [OE. drane a dronebee, AS. drān; akin to OS. drān, OHG. treno, G. drohne, Dan. drone, cf. Gr.? a kind of wasp, dial. Gr.? drone. Prob. named fr. the droning sound. See Drone, v. i.] 1. (Zool.) The male of bees, esp. of the honeybee. It gathers no honey. See Honeybee.

Drone Drone (drōn), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Droned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Droning.] [Cf. (for sense 1) D. dreunen, G. dröhnen, Icel. drynja to roar, drynr a roaring, Sw. dröna to bellow, drone, Dan. dröne, Goth. drunjus sound, Gr.? dirge,? to cry aloud, Skr. dhran to sound. Cf. Drone, n.] 1. To utter or make a low, dull, monotonous, humming or murmuring sound.
Drone bee Drone" bee` (?). (Zool.) The male of the honeybee; a drone.
Drone fly Drone" fly` (?). (Zool.) A dipterous insect (Eristalis tenax), resembling the drone bee. See Eristalis.

dronepipe.c: Dronepipe Drone"pipe`, n. One of the low-toned tubes of a bagpipe.

drongo.c: Drongo Dron"go (?), n.; pl. Drongos (?). (Zool.) A passerine bird of the family Dicruridæ. They are usually black with a deeply forked tail. They are natives of Asia, Africa, and Australia; -- called also drongo shrikes.

dronish.c: Dronish Dron"ish (?), a. Like a drone; indolent; slow. Burke. -- Dron"ish*ly, adv. -- Dron"ish*ness, n.

dronkelewe.c: Dronkelewe Dron"ke*lewe (?), a. [See Drink.] Given to drink; drunken. [Obs.] Chaucer.

drony.c: Drony Dron"y (?), a. Like a drone; sluggish; lazy.

drool.c: Drool Drool (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drooled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drooling.] [Contr. fr. drivel.] To drivel, or drop saliva; as, the child drools.

droop.c: Droop Droop (drōop), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drooped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drooping.] [Icel. drūpa; akin to E. drop. See Drop.] 1. To hang bending downward; to sink or hang down, as an animal, plant, etc., from physical inability or exhaustion, want of nourishment, or the like. “The purple flowers droop.” “Above her drooped a lamp.” Tennyson.
Droop Droop, v. t. To let droop or sink. [R.] M. Arnold.
Droop Droop, n. A drooping; as, a droop of the eye.

drooper.c: Drooper Droop"er (?), n. One who, or that which, droops.

droopingly.c: Droopingly Droop"ing*ly, adv. In a drooping manner.

drop.c: Drop Drop (drŏp), n. [OE. drope, AS. dropa; akin to OS. dropo, D. drop, OHG. tropo, G. tropfen, Icel. dropi, Sw. droppe; and Fr. AS. dreópan to drip, drop; akin to OS. driopan, D. druipen, OHG. triofan, G. triefen, Icel. drjūpa. Cf. Drip, Droop.] 1. The quantity of fluid which falls in one small spherical mass; a liquid globule; a minim; hence, also, the smallest easily measured portion of a fluid; a small quantity; as, a drop of water.

Drop Drop (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dropped (?) or Dropt; p. pr. & vb. n. Dropping.] [OE. droppen, AS. dropan, v. i. See Drop, n.] 1. To pour or let fall in drops; to pour in small globules; to distill. “The trees drop balsam.” Creech.
Drop Drop, v. i. 1. To fall in drops.

droplet.c: droplet drop"let (?), n. A little drop; a tear. Shak.

droplight.c: droplight drop"light` (?), n. An electric or gas light suspended from the ceiling by a flexible cord or tube, allowing artificial light to be brought down from a chandelier nearer to a table or desk; a pendant; also, an electric light bulb in a small holder, which can be held in the hand or hung from a hook, and attached to a long electric cord, allowing light to be brought close to work in dark areas of a room.

dropmele.c: Dropmele Dropmeal { Drop"meal`, Drop"mele` } (?), adv. [AS. drop-mǣlum; dropa drop + mǣl portion. Cf. Piecemeal.] By drops or small portions. [Obs.]

dropper.c: dropper drop"per (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, drops. Specif.: (Fishing) A fly that drops from the leader above the bob or end fly.

dropping.c: Dropping Drop"ping (?), n. 1. The action of causing to drop or of letting drop; falling.

dropsical.c: Dropsical Drop"si*cal (?), a. [From Dropsy.] 1. Diseased with dropsy; hydropical; tending to dropsy; as, a dropsical patient.

dropsicalness.c: Dropsicalness Drop"si*cal*ness, n. State of being dropsical.

dropsied.c: Dropsied Drop"sied (?), a. Diseased with drops. Shak.

dropsy.c: Dropsy Drop"sy (?), n.; pl. Dropsies (#). [OE. dropsie, dropesie, OF. idropisie, F. hydropisie, L. hydropisis, fr. Gr.? dropsy, fr.? water. See Water, and cf. Hydropsy.] (Med.) An unnatural collection of serous fluid in any serous cavity of the body, or in the subcutaneous cellular tissue. Dunglison.

dropt.c: Dropt Dropt (?), imp. & p. p. of Drop, v. G. Eliot.

dropwise.c: Dropwise Drop"wise` (?), adv. After the manner of a drop; in the form of drops.

dropworm.c: Dropworm Drop"worm` (drŏp"wûrm`), n. (Zool.) The larva of any geometrid moth, which drops from trees by means of a thread of silk, as the cankerworm or inchworm. See inchworm and geometrid.

dropwort.c: Dropwort Drop"wort` (drŏp"wûrt`), n. (Bot.) An Old World species of Spiræa (Spiræa filipendula), with finely cut leaves.

drosera.c: Drosera ‖Dros"e*ra (drŏs"e*rȧ), n. [NL., fr. Gr. drosero`s dewy.] (Bot.) A genus of low perennial or biennial plants, the leaves of which are beset with gland-tipped bristles. See Sundew. Gray.

drosky.c: drosky dros"ky (drŏs"ky̆), n.; pl. Droskies (drŏs"kĭz). [Russ. drojki, dim. of drogi a kind of carriage, prop. pl. of droga shaft or pole of a carriage.] A low, four-wheeled, open carriage, formerly used in Poland and Russia, consisting of a kind of long, narrow bench, on which the passengers ride as on a saddle, with their feet reaching nearly to the ground. Other kinds of vehicles have been so called, esp. a kind of victoria drawn by one or two horses, and used as a public carriage in German cities. [Written also droitzschka, droshky and droschke.]

drosometer.c: Drosometer Dro*som"e*ter (?), n. [Gr. dro`sos dew + -meter: cf. F. drosomètre.] (Meteorol.) An instrument for measuring the quantity of dew on the surface of a body in the open air. It consists of a balance, having a plate at one end to receive the dew, and at the other a weight protected from the deposit of dew.

dross.c: Dross Dross (drŏs; 115), n. [AS. dros, fr. dreósan to fall. See Dreary.] 1. The scum or refuse matter which is thrown off, or falls from, metals in smelting the ore, or in the process of melting; recrement.

drossel.c: Drossel Dros"sel (?), n. [Cf. Drazel.] A slut; a hussy; a drazel. [Obs.] Warner.

drossless.c: Drossless Dross"less, a. Free from dross. Stevens.

drossy.c: Drossy Dross"y (?), a. [Compar. Drossier (?); superl. Drossiest (?).] Of, pertaining to, resembling, dross; full of dross; impure; worthless. “ Drossy gold.” Dryden. “Drossy rhymes.” Donne. -- Dross"i*ness, n.

drought.c: Drought Drought (drout), n. [OE. droght, drougth, druȝð, AS. drugað, from drugian to dry. See Dry, and cf. Drouth, which shows the original final sound.] 1. Dryness; want of rain or of water; especially, such dryness of the weather as affects the earth, and prevents the growth of plants; aridity.

droughtiness.c: Droughtiness Drought"i*ness (?), n. A state of dryness of the weather; want of rain.

droughty.c: Droughty Drought"y (?), a. 1. Characterized by drought; wanting rain; arid; adust.

droumy.c: Droumy Drou"my (?), a. [Cf. Scot. drum, dram, melancholy, Icel prumr a moper, W. trwm heavy, sad.] Troubled; muddy. [Obs.] Bacon.

drouth.c: Drouth Drouth (?), n. Same as Drought. Sandys.

drove.c: Drove Drove, n. [AS. drāf, fr. drīfan to drive. See Drive.] 1. A collection of cattle driven, or cattle collected for driving; a number of animals, as oxen, sheep, or swine, driven in a body.

Drove Drove (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Droved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Droving (?).] [Cf. Drove, n., and Drover.] 1. To drive, as cattle or sheep, esp. on long journeys; to follow the occupation of a drover.

drover.c: Drover Dro"ver (?), n. 1. One who drives cattle or sheep to market; one who makes it his business to purchase cattle, and drive them to market.

drovy.c: Drovy Dro"vy (?), a. [AS. drōf dirty; cf. D. droef, G. trübe, Goth. drōbjan to trouble.] Turbid; muddy; filthy. [Obs.] Chaucer.

drown.c: Drown Drown (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drowned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drowning.] [OE. drunen, drounen, earlier drunknen, druncnien, AS. druncnian to be drowned, sink, become drunk, fr. druncen drunken. See Drunken, Drink.] To be suffocated in water or other fluid; to perish in water.
Drown Drown, v. t. 1. To overwhelm in water; to submerge; to inundate. “They drown the land.” Dryden.

drownage.c: Drownage Drown"age (?), n. The act of drowning. [R.]

drowner.c: Drowner Drown"er (?), n. One who, or that which, drowns.

drowse.c: Drowse Drowse (drouz), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drowsed (drouzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Drowsing.] [AS. drūsian, drūsan, to sink, become slow or inactive; cf. OD. droosen to be sleepy, fall asleep, LG. drūsen, druusken, to slumber, fall down with a noise; prob, akin to AS. dreósan to fall. See Dreary.] To sleep imperfectly or unsoundly; to slumber; to be heavy with sleepiness; to doze. “He drowsed upon his couch.” South.
Drowse Drowse, v. t. To make heavy with sleepiness or imperfect sleep; to make dull or stupid. Milton.
Drowse Drowse, n. A slight or imperfect sleep; a doze.

drowsily.c: drowsily drow"si*ly, adv. In a drowsy manner.

drowsiness.c: drowsiness drow"si*ness, n. State of being drowsy. Milton.

drowsy.c: Drowsy Drow"sy (?), a. [Compar. Drowsier (?); superl. Drowsiest.] 1. Inclined to drowse; heavy with sleepiness; lethargic; dozy. “When I am drowsy.” Shak.

droyle.c: Droyle Droyle (?), v. i. See Droil. [Obs.] Spenser.

drub.c: Drub Drub (drŭb), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Drubbed; p. pr. & vb. n. Drubbing.] [Cf. Prov. E. drab to beat, Icel. & Sw. drabba to hit, beat, Dan. dræbe to slay, and perh. OE. drepen to strike, kill, AS. drepan to strike, G. & D. freffen to hit, touch, Icel. drepa to strike, kill.] To beat with a stick; to thrash; to cudgel.
Drub Drub, n. A blow with a cudgel; a thump. Addison.

drubber.c: Drubber Drub"ber (drŭb"bẽr), n. One who drubs. Sir W. Scott.

drudge.c: Drudge Drudge (drŭj), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drudged (drŭjd); p. pr. & vb. n. Drudging.] [OE. druggen; prob not akin to E. drag, v. t., but fr. Celtic; cf. Ir. drugaire a slave or drudge.] To perform menial work; to labor in mean or unpleasant offices with toil and fatigue.
Drudge Drudge, v. t. To consume laboriously; -- with away.
Drudge Drudge, n. One who drudges; one who works hard in servile employment; a menial servant. Milton.

drudger.c: Drudger Drudg"er (drŭj"ẽr), n. 1. One who drudges; a drudge.

drudgery.c: Drudgery Drudg"er*y (drŭj"ẽr*y̆), n. The act of drudging; disagreeable and wearisome labor; ignoble or slavish toil.

drudging.c: Drudging box Drudg"ing box` (?). See Dredging box.

drudgingly.c: Drudgingly Drudg"ing*ly, adv. In a drudging manner; laboriously.

druery.c: Druery Dru"er*y (?), n. [OF. druerie.] Courtship; gallantry; love; an object of love. [Obs.] Chaucer.

drug.c: Drug Drug (drŭg), v. i. [See 1st Drudge.] To drudge; to toil laboriously. [Obs.] “To drugge and draw.” Chaucer.
Drug Drug, n. A drudge (?). Shak. (Timon iv. 3, 253).

Drug Drug, n. [F. drogue, prob. fr. D. droog; akin to E. dry; thus orig., dry substance, hers, plants, or wares. See Dry.] 1. Any animal, vegetable, or mineral substance used in the composition of medicines.
Drug Drug, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drugged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drugging.] [Cf. F. droguer.] To prescribe or administer drugs or medicines. B. Jonson.
Drug Drug, v. t. 1. To affect or season with drugs or ingredients; esp., to stupefy by a narcotic drug. Also Fig.

drugget.c: Drugget Drug"get (?), n. [F. droguet, prop. dim. of drogue trash, stuff, perh, the same word as drogue drug, but cf. also W. drwg evil, bad, Ir. & Gael. droch, Arm. droug, drouk. See 3d Drug.] (a) A coarse woolen cloth dyed of one color or printed on one side; generally used as a covering for carpets. (b) By extension, any material used for the same purpose.

druggist.c: druggist drug"gist (?), n. [F. droguiste, fr. drogue. See 3d Drug.] 1. One who deals in drugs; especially, one who buys and sells drugs without compounding them; one who owns or operates a drugstore.

druid.c: Druid Dru"id (?), n. [L. Druides; of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. & Gael. draoi, druidh, magician, Druid, W. derwydd Druid.] 1. One of an order of priests which in ancient times existed among certain branches of the Celtic race, especially among the Gauls and Britons.

druidess.c: Druidess Dru"id*ess, n. A female Druid; a prophetess.

druidical.c: Druidical Druidic { Dru*id"ic (?), Dru*id"ic*al (?), } a. Pertaining to, or resembling, the Druids.

druidism.c: Druidism Dru"id*ism (?), n. The system of religion, philosophy, and instruction, received and taught by the Druids; the rites and ceremonies of the Druids.

drum.c: Drum Drum (?), n. [Cf. D. trom, trommel, LG. trumme, G. trommel, Dan. tromme, Sw. trumma, OHG. trumba a trumpet, Icel. pruma a clap of thunder, and as a verb, to thunder, Dan. drum a booming sound, drumme to boom; prob. partly at least of imitative origin; perh. akin to E. trum, or trumpet.] 1. (Mus.) An instrument of percussion, consisting either of a hollow cylinder, over each end of which is stretched a piece of skin or vellum, to be beaten with a stick; or of a metallic hemisphere (kettledrum) with a single piece of skin to be so beaten; the common instrument for marking time in martial music; one of the pair of tympani in an orchestra, or cavalry band.
Drum Drum, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Drummed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drumming.] 1. To beat a drum with sticks; to beat or play a tune on a drum.
Drum Drum, v. t. 1. To execute on a drum, as a tune.
Drum major Drum" ma"jor (?). 1. The chief or first drummer of a regiment; an instructor of drummers.

Drum winding Drum winding. (Elec.) A method of armature winding in which the wire is wound upon the outer surface of a cylinder or drum from end to end of the cylinder; -- distinguished from ring winding, etc.

drumbeat.c: Drumbeat Drum"beat` (?), n. The sound of a beaten drum; drum music.

drumble.c: Drumble Drum"ble (?), v. i. [See Drumly.] 1. To be sluggish or lazy; to be confused. [Obs.] Shak.

drumfish.c: Drumfish Drum"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) Any fish of the family Sciænidæ, which makes a loud noise by means of its air bladder; -- called also drum.

drumhead.c: Drumhead Drum"head` (?), n. 1. The parchment or skin stretched over one end of a drum.

drumlin.c: Drumlin Drum"lin (?), n. [Gael. druim the ridge of a hill.] (Geol.) A hill of compact, unstratified, glacial drift or till, usually elongate or oval, with the larger axis parallel to the former local glacial motion.

drumly.c: Drumly Drum"ly, a. [Cf. Droumy.] Turbid; muddy. [Scot. & Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Wodroephe (1623). Burns.

drummer.c: Drummer Drum"mer (?), n. 1. One whose office is to best the drum, as in military exercises and marching.

drumming.c: Drumming Drum"ming (?), n. The act of beating upon, or as if upon, a drum; also, the noise which the male of the ruffed grouse makes in spring, by beating his wings upon his sides.

drummond.c: Drummond light Drum"mond light` (?). [From Thomas Drummond, a British naval officer.] A very intense light, produced by turning two streams of gas, one oxygen and the other hydrogen, or coal gas, in a state of ignition, upon a ball of lime; or a stream of oxygen gas through a flame of alcohol upon a ball or disk of lime; -- called also oxycalcium light, or lime light.

drumstick.c: Drumstick Drum"stick` (?), n. 1. A stick with which a drum is beaten.

drunk.c: Drunk Drunk (?), a. [OE. dronke, drunke, dronken, drunken, AS. druncen. Orig. the same as drunken, p. p. of drink. See Drink.] 1. Intoxicated with, or as with, strong drink; inebriated; drunken; -- never used attributively, but always predicatively; as, the man is drunk (not, a drunk man).
Drunk Drunk, n. A drunken condition; a spree. [Slang]

drunkard.c: Drunkard Drunk"ard (?), n. [Drunk + -ard.] One who habitually drinks strong liquors immoderately; one whose habit it is to get drunk; a toper; a sot.

drunken.c: Drunken Drunk"en (?), a. [AS. druncen, prop., that has drunk, p. p. of drincan, taken as active. See Drink, v. i., and cf. Drunk.] 1. Overcome by strong drink; intoxicated by, or as by, spirituous liquor; inebriated.

drunkenly.c: Drunkenly Drunk"en*ly, adv. In a drunken manner. [R.] Shak.

drunkenness.c: Drunkenness Drunk"en*ness, n. 1. The state of being drunken with, or as with, alcoholic liquor; intoxication; inebriety; -- used of the casual state or the habit.

drunkship.c: Drunkship Drunkenship { Drunk"en*ship, Drunk"ship, } n. The state of being drunk; drunkenness. [Obs.] Gower.

drupaceous.c: Drupaceous Dru*pa"ceous (?), a. [Cf. F. drupacé.] (Bot.) Producing, or pertaining to, drupes; having the form of drupes; as, drupaceous trees or fruits.

drupe.c: Drupe Drupe (drüp), n. [F. drupe, L. drupa an overripe, wrinkled olive, fr. Gr. dry`ppa.] (Bot.) A fruit consisting of pulpy, coriaceous, or fibrous exocarp, without valves, containing a nut or stone with a kernel. The exocarp is succulent in the plum, cherry, apricot, peach, etc.; dry and subcoriaceous in the almond; and fibrous in the cocoanut.

drupelet.c: Drupelet Drupel { Drup"el (?), Drupe"let (?), } n. [Dim. of Drupe.] (Bot.) A small drupe, as one of the pulpy grains of the blackberry.

druse.c: Druse Druse (?), n. [Cf. G. druse bonny, crystallized piece of ore, Bohem. druza. Cf. Dross.] (Min.) A cavity in a rock, having its interior surface studded with crystals and sometimes filled with water; a geode.
Druse Druse (?), n. One of a people and religious sect dwelling chiefly in the Lebanon mountains of Syria.

drused.c: Drused Drusy { Dru"sy (?), Drused (?), } a. (Min.) Covered with a large number of minute crystals.

druxy.c: Druxy Druxey { Drux"ey, Drux"y } (?), a. [Etymol. uncertain.] Having decayed spots or streaks of a whitish color; -- said of timber. Weale.

dry.c: Dry Dry (drī), a. [Compar. Drier (?); superl. Driest.] [OE. druȝe, druye, drie, AS. dryge; akin to LG. dröge, D. droog, OHG. trucchan, G. trocken, Icel. draugr a dry log. Cf. Drought, Drouth, 3d Drug.] 1. Free from moisture; having little humidity or none; arid; not wet or moist; deficient in the natural or normal supply of moisture, as rain or fluid of any kind; -- said especially: (a) Of the weather: Free from rain or mist.

Dry Dry, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dried (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Drying.] [AS. drygan; cf. drugian to grow dry. See Dry, a.] To make dry; to free from water, or from moisture of any kind, and by any means; to exsiccate; as, to dry the eyes; to dry one's tears; the wind dries the earth; to dry a wet cloth; to dry hay.
Dry Dry, v. i. 1. To grow dry; to become free from wetness, moisture, or juice; as, the road dries rapidly.
Dry dock Dry" dock` (?). (Naut.) See under Dock.
Dry goods Dry" goods` (?). A commercial name for textile fabrics, cottons, woolens, linen, silks, laces, etc., -- in distinction from groceries. [U.S.]
Dry nurse Dry" nurse` (?). A nurse who attends and feeds a child by hand; -- in distinction from a wet nurse, who suckles it.

dryad.c: Dryad Dry"ad (?), n. [L. dryas, pl. dryades, Gr.?, pl.?, fr.? oak, tree. See Tree.] (Class. Myth.) A wood nymph; a nymph whose life was bound up with that of her tree.

dryandra.c: Dryandra ‖Dry*an"dra (?), n. [NL. Named after J. Dryander.] (Bot.) A genus of shrubs growing in Australia, having beautiful, hard, dry, evergreen leaves.

dryas.c: Dryas ‖Dry"as (?), n.; pl. Dryades (#). [L. See Dryad.] (Class. Myth.) A dryad.

drybeat.c: Dry-beat Dry"-beat` (?), v. t. To beat severely. Shak.

dryboned.c: Dry-boned Dry"-boned` (?), a. Having dry bones, or bones without flesh.

dryer.c: Dryer Dry"er (?), n. See Drier. Sir W. Temple.

dryeyed.c: Dry-eyed Dry"-eyed` (?), a. Not having tears in the eyes. Opposite of tearful.

dryfoot.c: Dryfoot Dry"foot (?), n. The scent of the game, as far as it can be traced. [Obs.] Shak.

drying.c: Drying Dry"ing, a. 1. Adapted or tending to exhaust moisture; as, a drying wind or day; a drying room.

dryly.c: Dryly Dry"ly, adv. In a dry manner; not succulently; without interest; without sympathy; coldly.

dryness.c: Dryness Dry"ness, n. The state of being dry. See Dry.

drynurse.c: dry-nurse Drynurse Dry"nurse`, dry"-nurse`, v. t. To feed, attend, and bring up without breastfeeding it. Hudibras.

dryobalanops.c: Dryobalanops ‖Dry`o*bal"a*nops (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. dry^s oak + ba`lanos acorn + 'o`psis appearance. The fruit remotely resembles an acorn in its cup.] (Bot.) The genus to which belongs the single species Dryobalanops Camphora, a lofty resinous tree of Borneo and Sumatra, yielding Borneo camphor and camphor oil.

dryrub.c: Dry-rub Dry"-rub` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dry-rubbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dry-rubbing.] To rub and cleanse without wetting. Dodsley.

drysalter.c: Drysalter Dry"salt`er (?), n. A dealer in salted or dried meats, pickles, sauces, etc., and in the materials used in pickling, salting, and preserving various kinds of food Hence drysalters usually sell a number of saline substances and miscellaneous drugs. Brande & C.

drysaltery.c: Drysaltery Dry"salt`er*y (?), n. The articles kept by a drysalter; also, the business of a drysalter.

dryshod.c: Dry-shod Dry"-shod` (?), a. Without wetting the feet; having or keeping the feet or shoes dry; as, a land bridge over which man and beasts could have crossed dry-shod.

drystone.c: Dry-stone Dry"-stone` (?), a. Constructed of uncemented stone. “Dry-stone walls.” Sir W. Scott.

drith.c: Drith Dryth { Dryth (?), or Drith }, n. Drought. [Obs.] Tyndale.

duad.c: Duad Du"ad (?), n. [See Dyad.] A union of two; duality. [R.] Harris.

dual.c: Dual Du"al (?), a. [L. dualis, fr. duo two. See Two.] Expressing, or consisting of, the number two; belonging to two; as, the dual number of nouns, etc., in Greek.

dualin.c: Dualin Du"a*lin (?), n. (Chem.) An explosive substance consisting essentially of sawdust or wood pulp, saturated with nitroglycerin and other similar nitro compounds. It is inferior to dynamite, and is more liable to explosion.

dualism.c: Dualism Du"al*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. dualisme.] State of being dual or twofold; a twofold division; any system which is founded on a double principle, or a twofold distinction; as: (a) (Philos.) A view of man as constituted of two original and independent elements, as matter and spirit. (Theol.) (b) A system which accepts two gods, or two original principles, one good and the other evil. (c) The doctrine that all mankind are divided by the arbitrary decree of God, and in his eternal foreknowledge, into two classes, the elect and the reprobate. (d) (Physiol.) The theory that each cerebral hemisphere acts independently of the other.

dualist.c: Dualist Du"al*ist, n. [Cf. F. dualiste.] 1. One who believes in dualism; a ditheist.

dualistic.c: Dualistic Du`al*is"tic (?), a. Consisting of two; pertaining to dualism or duality.

duality.c: Duality Du"al"i*ty (?), n. [L. dualitas: cf. F. dualité.] The quality or condition of being two or twofold; dual character or usage.

duan.c: Duan Du"an (?), n. [Gael. & Ir.] A division of a poem corresponding to a canto; a poem or song. [R.]

duarchy.c: Duarchy Du"ar*chy (?), n. [Gr.? two + -archy.] Government by two persons.

dub.c: Dub Dub (dŭb), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dubbed (dŭbd); p. pr. & vb. n. Dubbing.] [AS. dubban to strike, beat (“dubbade his sunu... to rīdere.” AS. Chron. an. 1086); akin to Icel. dubba; cf. OF. adouber (prob. fr. Icel.) a chevalier, Icel. dubba til riddara.] 1. To confer knighthood upon; as, the king dubbed his son Henry a knight.
Dub Dub (dŭb), v. i. To make a noise by brisk drumbeats. “Now the drum dubs.” Beau. & Fl.
Dub Dub, n. [Cf. Ir. dób mire, stream, W. dwvr water.] A pool or puddle. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

dubb.c: Dubb Dubb (?), n. [Ar.] (Zool.) The Syrian bear. See under Bear. [Written also dhubb, and dub.]

dubber.c: Dubber Dub"ber (?), n. One who, or that which, dubs.
Dubber Dub"ber, n. [Hind. dabbah.] A globular vessel or bottle of leather, used in India to hold ghee, oil, etc. [Also written dupper.] M'Culloch.

dubbing.c: Dubbing Dub"bing (?), n. 1. The act of dubbing, as a knight, etc.

dubiety.c: Dubiety Du*bi"e*ty (?), n.; pl. Dubieties (#). [L. dubietas, fr. dubius. See Dubious.] Doubtfulness; uncertainty; doubt. [R.] Lamb. “The dubiety of his fate.” Sir W. Scott.

dubiosity.c: Dubiosity Du`bi*os"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Dubiosities (#). [L. dubiosus.] The state of being doubtful; a doubtful statement or thing. [R.]

dubious.c: Dubious Du"bi*ous (?), a. [L. dubius, dubiosus, fr. duo two. See Two, and cf. Doubt.] 1. Doubtful or not settled in opinion; being in doubt; wavering or fluctuating; undetermined. “Dubious policy.” Sir T. Scott.

dubiously.c: Dubiously Du"bi*ous*ly, adv. In a dubious manner.

dubiousness.c: Dubiousness Du"bi*ous*ness, n. State of being dubious.

dubitable.c: Dubitable Du"bi*ta*ble (?), a. [L. dubitabilis. Cf. Doubtable.] Liable to be doubted; uncertain. [R.] Dr. H. More. -- Du"bi*ta*bly, adv. [R.]

dubitancy.c: Dubitancy Du"bi*tan*cy (?), n. [LL. dubitantia.] Doubt; uncertainty. [R.] Hammond.

dubitate.c: Dubitate Du"bi*tate (?), v. i. [L. dubitatus, p. p. of dubitare. See Doubt.] To doubt. [R.]

dubitation.c: Dubitation Du`bi*ta"tion (?), n. [L. dubitatio.] Act of doubting; doubt. [R.] Sir T. Scott.

dubitative.c: Dubitative Du"bi*ta*tive (?), a. [L. dubitativus: cf. F. dubitatif.] Tending to doubt; doubtful. [R.] -- Du"bi*ta*tive*ly, adv. [R.]. Eliot.

duboisine.c: Duboisine Du*bois"ine (?), n. (Med.) An alkaloid obtained from the leaves of an Australian tree (Duboisia myoporoides), and regarded as identical with hyoscyamine. It produces dilation of the pupil of the eye.

ducal.c: Ducal Du"cal (?), a. [F. ducal. See Duke.] Of or pertaining to a duke.

ducally.c: Ducally Du"cal*ly, adv. In the manner of a duke, or in a manner becoming the rank of a duke.

ducat.c: Ducat Duc"at (?), n. [F. ducat, It. ducato, LL. ducatus, fr. dux leader or commander. See Duke.] A coin, either of gold or silver, of several countries in Europe; originally, one struck in the dominions of a duke.

ducatoon.c: Ducatoon Duc`a*toon" (?), n. [F. or Sp. ducaton, fr. ducat.] A silver coin of several countries of Europe, and of different values.

duces.c: Duces tecum ‖Du"ces te"cum (?). [L., bring with thee.] A judicial process commanding a person to appear in court and bring with him some piece of evidence or other thing to be produced to the court.

duchess.c: Duchess Duch"ess (?), n. [F. duchesse, fr. duc duke.] The wife or widow of a duke; also, a lady who has the sovereignty of a duchy in her own right.

duchesse.c: Duchesse d'Angouleme ‖Du`chesse" d'An`gou`lême" (?). [F.] (Bot.) A variety of pear of large size and excellent flavor.

Duchesse lace Du`chesse" lace (?). A beautiful variety of Brussels pillow lace made originally in Belgium and resembling Honiton guipure. It is worked with fine thread in large sprays, usually of the primrose pattern, with much raised work.

duchy.c: Duchy Duch"y (dŭch"y̆), n.; pl. Duchies (#). [F. duché, OF. duchée, (assumed) LL. ducitas, fr. L. dux. See Duke.] The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom.

duck.c: Duck Duck (dŭk), n. [Cf. Dan. dukke, Sw. docka, OHG. doccha, G. docke. Cf. Doxy.] A pet; a darling. Shak.

Duck Duck, n. [D. doek cloth, canvas, or Icel. dūkr cloth; akin to OHG. tuoh, G. tuch, Sw. duk, Dan. dug.] 1. A linen (or sometimes cotton) fabric, finer and lighter than canvas, -- used for the lighter sails of vessels, the sacking of beds, and sometimes for men's clothing.

Duck Duck, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ducked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ducking.] [OE. duken, douken, to dive; akin to D. duiken, OHG. t?hhan, MHG. tucken, tücken, t?chen, G. tuchen. Cf. 5th Duck.] 1. To thrust or plunge under water or other liquid and suddenly withdraw.
Duck Duck (dŭk), v. i. 1. To go under the surface of water and immediately reappear; to dive; to plunge the head in water or other liquid; to dip.
Duck Duck, n. [OE. duke, doke. See Duck, v. t. ] 1. (Zool.) Any bird of the subfamily Anatinæ, family Anatidæ.

duckbill.c: Duckbill Duck"bill`, n. (Zool.) See Duck mole, under Duck, n.

duckbilled.c: Duck-billed Duck"-billed` (?), a. Having a bill like that of a duck; as, a duck-billed dinosaur..

ducker.c: Ducker Duck"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, ducks; a plunger; a diver.

ducking.c: Ducking Duck"ing, n. & a., from Duck, v. t. & i.

ducklegged.c: Duck-legged Duck"-legged` (?), a. Having short legs, like a waddling duck; short-legged. Dryden.

duckling.c: Duckling Duck"ling (?), n. A young or little duck. Gay.

ducksbill.c: Duck's-bill Duck's"-bill`, a. Having the form of a duck's bill.

ducksfoot.c: Duck's-foot Duck's"-foot` (?), n. (Bot.) The May apple (Podophyllum peltatum).

duckweed.c: Duckweed Duck"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) A genus (Lemna) of small plants, seen floating in great quantity on the surface of stagnant pools fresh water, and supposed to furnish food for ducks; -- called also duckmeat.

duct.c: Duct Duct (dŭkt), n. [L. ductus a leading, conducting, conduit, fr. ducere, ductum, to lead. See Duke, and cf. Douche.] 1. Any tube or canal by which a fluid or other substance is conducted or conveyed.

ductible.c: Ductible Duc"ti*ble (?), a. Capable of being drawn out [R.] Feltham.

ductile.c: Ductile Duc"tile (?), a. [L. ductilis, fr. ducere to lead: cf. F. ductile. See Duct.] 1. Easily led; tractable; complying; yielding to motives, persuasion, or instruction; as, a ductile people. Addison.

ductilimeter.c: Ductilimeter Duc`ti*lim"e*ter (?), n. [Ductile + -meter.] An instrument for accurately determining the ductility of metals.

ductility.c: Ductility Duc*til"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. ductilité.] 1. The property of a metal which allows it to be drawn into wires or filaments.

duction.c: Duction Duc"tion (?), n. [L. ductio, fr. ducere to lead.] Guidance. [Obs.] Feltham.

ductless.c: Ductless Duct"less (?), a. Having to duct or outlet; as, a ductless gland.

ductor.c: Ductor Duc"tor (?), n. [L., fr. ducere to lead.] 1. One who leads. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

dudder.c: Dudder Dud"der (?), v. t. [In Suffolk, Eng., to shiver, shake, tremble; also written dodder.] To confuse or confound with noise. Jennings.
Dudder Dud"der, v. i. To shiver or tremble; to dodder.
Dudder Dud"der, n. [From Duds.] A peddler or hawker, especially of cheap and flashy goods pretended to be smuggled; a duffer. [Eng.]

duddery.c: Duddery Dud"der*y (?), n. A place where rags are bought and kept for sale. [Eng.]

dude.c: Dude Dude (?), n. A kind of dandy; especially, one characterized by an ultrafashionable style of dress and other affectations. [Recent]

dudeen.c: Dudeen Du*deen" (?), n. A short tobacco pipe. [Written also dudheen.] [Irish]

dudgeon.c: Dudgeon Dudg"eon (?), n. 1. The root of the box tree, of which hafts for daggers were made. Gerarde (1597).
Dudgeon Dudg"eon, n. [W. dygen anger, grudge.] Resentment; ill will; anger; displeasure.

dudish.c: Dudish Dud"ish (?), a. Like, or characterized of, a dude.

duds.c: Duds Duds (?), n. pl. [Scot. dud rag, pl. duds clothing of inferior quality.] 1. Old or inferior clothes; tattered garments. [Colloq.]

due.c: Due Due (?), a. [OF. deu, F. dû, p. p. of devoir to owe, fr. L. debere. See Debt, Habit, and cf. Duty.] 1. Owed, as a debt; that ought to be paid or done to or for another; payable; owing and demandable.
Due Due, adv. Directly; exactly; as, a due east course.

Due Due, n. 1. That which is owed; debt; that which one contracts to pay, or do, to or for another; that which belongs or may be claimed as a right; whatever custom, law, or morality requires to be done; a fee; a toll.
Due Due, v. t. To endue. [Obs.] Shak.

duebill.c: Duebill Due"bill` (?), n. (Com.) A brief written acknowledgment of a debt, not made payable to order, like a promissory note. Burrill.

duel.c: Duel Du"el (?), n. [It. duello, fr. L. duellum, orig., a contest between two, which passed into the common form bellum war, fr. duo two: cf. F. duel. See Bellicose, Two, and cf. Duello.] A combat between two persons, fought with deadly weapons, by agreement. It usually arises from an injury done or an affront given by one to the other.
Duel Du"el, v. i. & t. To fight in single combat. [Obs.]

dueler.c: Dueler Du"el*er, n. One who engages in a duel. [R.] [Written also dueller.] South.

dueling.c: Dueling Du"el*ing, n. The act or practice of fighting in single combat. Also adj. [Written also duelling.]

duelist.c: Duelist Du"el*ist (?), n. [F. duelliste.] One who fights in single combat. [Written also duellist.]

duelo.c: Duelo ‖Du*e"lo (?), n. [It. See Duel.] A duel; also, the rules of dueling. [Obs.] Shak.

dueness.c: Dueness Due"ness (?), n. Quality of being due; debt; what is due or becoming. T. Goodwin.

duenna.c: Duenna Du*en"na (?), n.; pl. Duennas (#). [Sp. dueña, doña, fr. L. domina. See Dame.] 1. The chief lady in waiting on the queen of Spain. Brande.

duet.c: Duet Du*et" (?), n. [Duetto.] (Mus.) A composition for two performers, whether vocal or instrumental.

duettino.c: Duettino ‖Du`et*ti"no (?), n. [It., dim. fr. duetto a duet.] A duet of short extent and concise form.

duetto.c: Duetto ‖Du*et"to (?), n. [It., fr. It & L. duo two. See Two.] See Duet.

duff.c: Duff Duff (dŭf), n. [From OE. dagh. √67. See Dough.] 1. Dough or paste. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

Duff Duff (dŭf), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Duffed; p. pr. & vb. n. Duffing.] [Etym. uncertain.] [Colloq. or Slang] 1. To treat or manipulate so as to give a specious appearance to; to fake; hence, to cheat.

duffel.c: Duffel Duf"fel (?), n. [D. duffel, from Duffel, a town not far from Antwerp.] 1. A kind of coarse woolen cloth, having a thick nap or frieze. [Written also duffle.]
Duffel bag Duffel bag. A sack to hold miscellaneous articles, as tools, supplies, or the like.

duffer.c: Duffer Duf"fer (?), n. 1. A peddler or hawker, especially of cheap, flashy articles, as sham jewelry; hence, a sham or cheat. [Slang, Eng.] Halliwell.
Duffer Duf"fer, n. One who duffs cattle, etc. [Australia]

dufrenite.c: Dufrenite Du*fren"ite (?), n. [From??ierre Armand Dufrénoy, a French geologist.] (Min.) A mineral of a blackish green color, commonly massive or in nodules. It is a hydrous phosphate of iron.

dug.c: Dug Dug (dŭg), n. [Akin to Sw. dägga to suckle (a child), Dan. dægge, and prob. to Goth. daddjan. √66.] A teat, pap, or nipple; -- formerly that of a human mother, now that of a cow or other beast.
Dug Dug, imp. & p. p. of Dig.

dugong.c: Dugong Du*gong" (dụ*gŏg"), n. [Malayan dūyōng, or Javan. duyung.] (Zool.) An aquatic herbivorous mammal (Halicore dugong), of the order Sirenia, allied to the manatee, but with a bilobed tail. It inhabits the Red Sea, Indian Ocean, East Indies, and Australia. [Written also duyong.]

dugout.c: Dugout Dug"out` (dŭg"out), n. 1. A canoe or boat dug out from a large log. [U.S.]

dugway.c: Dugway Dug"way` (?), n. A way or road dug through a hill, or sunk below the surface of the land. [U.S.]

duke.c: Duke Duke (dūk), n. [F. duc, fr. L. dux, ducis, leader, commander, fr. ducere to lead; akin to AS. teón to draw; cf. AS. heretoga (here army) an army leader, general, G. herzog duke. See Tue, and cf. Doge, Duchess, Ducat, Duct, Adduce, Deduct.] 1. A leader; a chief; a prince. [Obs.]
Duke Duke (dūk) v. i. To play the duke. [Poetic]

dukedom.c: Dukedom Duke"dom (?), n. 1. The territory of a duke.

dukeling.c: Dukeling Duke"ling, n. A little or insignificant duke. Ford.

dukeship.c: Dukeship Duke"ship, n. The quality or condition of being a duke; also, the personality of a duke. Massinger.

dukhobortsy.c: Dukhobortsy Dukhobors { Du*kho*bors" (?), Du*kho*bor"tsy (?) }, n. pl. [Russ. dukhobortsy spirit wrestlers; dukh spirit + bortsy wrestlers.] A Russian religious sect founded about the middle of the 18th century at Kharkov. They believe that Christ was wholly human, but that his soul reappears from time to time in mortals. They accept the Ten Commandments and the “useful” portions of the Bible, but deny the need of rulers, priests, or churches, and have no confessions, icons, or marriage ceremonies. They are communistic, opposed to any violence, and unwilling to use the labor of animals. Driven out of Russia proper, many have emigrated to Cyprus and Canada. See Raskolnik, below.

dulcamara.c: Dulcamara Dul`ca*ma"ra (?), n. [NL., fr. L. dulcis sweet + amarus bitter.] (Bot.) A plant (Solanum Dulcamara). See Bittersweet, n., 3 (a).

dulcamarin.c: Dulcamarin Dul`ca*ma"rin (?), n. (Chem.) A glucoside extracted from the bittersweet (Solanum Dulcamara), as a yellow amorphous substance. It probably occasions the compound taste. See Bittersweet, 3(a).

dulce.c: Dulce Dulce (?), v. t. To make sweet; to soothe. [Obs.]

dulcet.c: Dulcet Dul"cet (?), a. [OF. doucet, dim. of dous sweet, F. doux, L. dulcis; akin to Gr.?. Cf. Doucet.] 1. Sweet to the taste; luscious. [Obs.]

dulciana.c: Dulciana ‖Dul`ci*an"a (?), n. [NL., fr. L. dulcis sweet.] (Mus.) A sweet-toned stop of an organ.

dulcification.c: Dulcification Dul`ci*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. dulcification.] The act of dulcifying or sweetening. Boyle.

dulcifluous.c: Dulcifluous Dul*cif"lu*ous (?), a. [L. dulcis sweet + fluere to flow.] Flowing sweetly. [R.]

dulcify.c: Dulcify Dul"ci*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dulcified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dulcifying.] [L. dulcis sweet + -fy: cf. F. dulcifier.] 1. (Pharm.) To sweeten; to free from acidity, saltness, or acrimony. Wiseman.

dulciloquy.c: Dulciloquy Dul*cil"o*quy (?), n. [L. dulcis sweet + loqui to speak.] A soft manner of speaking.

dulcimer.c: Dulcimer Dul"ci*mer (?), n. [It. dolcemele,r Sp. dulcemele, fr. L. dulcis sweet + melos song, melody, Gr.?; cf. OF. doulcemele. See Dulcet, and Melody.] (Mus.) (a) An instrument, having stretched metallic wires which are beaten with two light hammers held in the hands of the performer. (b) An ancient musical instrument in use among the Jews. Dan. iii. 5. It is supposed to be the same with the psaltery.

dulcinea.c: Dulcinea Dul*cin"e*a (?), n. [Sp., from Dulcinea del Toboso the mistress of the affections of Don Quixote.] A mistress; a sweetheart.

dulcite.c: Dulcite Dul"cite (?), n. [Cf. F. dulcite, fr. L. dulcis sweet.] (Chem.) A white, sugarlike substance, C6H8.(OH)2, occurring naturally in a manna from Madagascar, and in certain plants, and produced artificially by the reduction of galactose and lactose or milk sugar.

dulcitude.c: Dulcitude Dul"ci*tude (?), n. [L. dulcitudo, fr. dulcis sweet. Sweetness. [R.] Cockeram.

dulcorate.c: Dulcorate Dul"co*rate (?), v. t. [L. dulcoratus, p. p. of dulcorare, fr. dulcor sweetness, fr. dulcis sweet.] To sweeten; to make less acrimonious. [R.] Bacon.

dulcoration.c: Dulcoration Dul`co*ra"tion (?), n. [LL. dulcoratio.] The act of sweetening. [R.] Bacon.

duledge.c: Duledge Du"ledge (?), n. (Mil.) One of the dowels joining the ends of the fellies which form the circle of the wheel of a gun carriage. Wilhelm.

dulia.c: Dulia ‖Du*li"a (?), n. [LL., fr. Gr.? servitude, fr.? slave.] (R. C. Ch.) An inferior kind of veneration or worship, given to the angels and saints as the servants of God.

dull.c: Dull Dull (?), a. [Compar. Duller (?); superl. Dullest.] [AS. dol foolish; akin to gedwelan to err, D. dol mad, dwalen to wander, err, G. toll mad, Goth. dwals foolish, stupid, cf. Gr.? turbid, troubled, Skr. dhvr to cause to fall. Cf. Dolt, Dwale, Dwell, Fraud.] 1. Slow of understanding; wanting readiness of apprehension; stupid; doltish; blockish. “Dull at classical learning.” Thackeray.
Dull Dull, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Duller (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dulling.] 1. To deprive of sharpness of edge or point. “This... dulled their swords.” Bacon.
Dull Dull, v. i. To become dull or stupid. Rom. of R.

dullard.c: Dullard Dull"ard (?), n. [Dull + -ard.] A stupid person; a dunce. Shak. -- a. Stupid. Bp. Hall.

dullbrowed.c: Dull-browed Dull"-browed` (?), a. Having a gloomy look.

duller.c: Duller Dull"er (?), n. One who, or that which, dulls.

dulleyed.c: Dull-eyed Dull"-eyed` (?), a. Having eyes wanting brightness, liveliness, or vivacity. Shak.

dullhead.c: Dullhead Dull"head` (?), n. A blockhead; a dolt. Ascham.

dullish.c: Dullish Dull"ish, a. Somewhat dull; uninteresting; tiresome. “A series of dullish verses.” Prof. Wilson.

dullness.c: Dullness Dull"ness, n. The state of being dull; slowness; stupidity; heaviness; drowsiness; bluntness; obtuseness; dimness; want of luster; want of vividness, or of brightness. [Written also dulness.]

dully.c: Dully Dul"ly (?), adv. In a dull manner; stupidly; slowly; sluggishly; without life or spirit.

dulse.c: Dulse Dulse (dŭls), n. [Cf. Gael. duileasg; duille leaf + uisge water. Cf. Whisky.] (Bot.) A seaweed of a reddish brown color, which is sometimes eaten, as in Scotland. The true dulse is Sarcophyllis edulis; the common is Rhodymenia. [Written also dillisk.]

dulwilly.c: Dulwilly Dul"wil*ly (?), n. [Prob. imitative.] (Zool.) The ring plover. [Prov. Eng.]

duly.c: Duly Du"ly (?), adv. In a due, fit, or becoming manner; as it (anything) ought to be; properly; regularly.

dumal.c: Dumal Du"mal (?), a. [L. dumus bramble.] Pertaining to, or set with, briers or bushes; brambly. [R.]

dumb.c: Dumb Dumb (dŭm), a. [AS. dumb; akin to D. dom stupid, dumb, Sw. dumb, Goth. dumbs; cf. Gr.? blind. See Deaf, and cf. Dummy.] 1. Destitute of the power of speech; unable; to utter articulate sounds; as, the dumb brutes.
Dumb Dumb, v. t. To put to silence. [Obs.] Shak.

dumbbell.c: dumb-bell dumbbell dumb"bell`, dumb"-bell` (?), n. An exercising weight, consisting of two spheres or spheroids, connected by a short bar for a handle; used (often in pairs) for gymnastic exercise.

dumbledor.c: Dumbledor Dum"ble*dor` (?), n. [The first part is prob. of imitative origin. See Dor a beetle.] (Zool.) A bumblebee; also, a cockchafer. [Prov. Eng.]

dumbness.c: Dumbness Dumb"ness, n. The quality or state of being dumb; muteness; silence; inability to speak.

dumbwaiter.c: Dumb-waiter Dumb"-wait`er (?), n. A framework on which dishes, food, etc., are passed from one room or story of a house to another; a lift for dishes, etc.; also, a piece of furniture with movable or revolving shelves.

dumdum.c: Dumdum bullet Dum"dum bul"let (?). (Mil.) A kind of man-stopping bullet, designed to fragment inside the body and thus inflict a severed and painful wound; -- so named from Dumdum, in India, where bullets are manufactured for the Indian army.

dumetose.c: Dumetose Du"me*tose` (?), a. [From L. dumetum a thicket.] (Bot.) Dumose.

dumfound.c: Dumfound Dum"found` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dumfounded; p. pr. & vb. n. Dumfounding.] To strike dumb; to confuse with astonishment. [Written also dumbfound.] Spectator.

dumfounder.c: dumfounder dum"found`er (?), v. t. To dumfound; to confound. [Written also dumbfounder.]

dummerer.c: Dummerer Dum"mer*er (?), n. One who feigns dumbness. [Obs.] Burton.

dummy.c: Dummy Dum"my (?), a. [See Dumb.] 1. Silent; mute; noiseless; as a dummy engine.
Dummy Dum"my, n.; pl. Dummies (?). 1. One who is dumb. H. Smith.

dumous.c: Dumous Dumose { Du`mose" (?), Du"mous (?), } a. [L. dumosus, fr. dumus a thornbush, a bramble.] 1. Abounding with bushes and briers.

dump.c: Dump Dump (dŭmp), n. [See Dumpling.] A thick, ill-shapen piece; a clumsy leaden counter used by boys in playing chuck farthing. [Eng.] Smart.

Dump Dump, n. [Cf. dial. Sw. dumpin melancholy, Dan.dump dull, low, D. dompig damp, G. dumpf damp, dull, gloomy, and E. damp, or rather perh. dump, v. t. Cf. Damp, or Dump, v. t.] 1. A dull, gloomy state of the mind; sadness; melancholy; low spirits or a mild depression; despondency; ill humor; -- now used only in the plural.

Dump Dump (dŭmp), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dumped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dumping.] [OE. dumpen to throw down, fall down, cf. Icel. dumpa to thump, Dan. dumpe to fall suddenly, rush, dial. Sw. dimpa to fall down plump. Cf. Dump sadness.] 1. To knock heavily; to stump. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
Dump Dump, n. 1. A car or boat for dumping refuse, etc.

dumpage.c: Dumpage Dump"age (?), n. 1. The act of dumping loads from carts, especially loads of refuse matter; also, a heap of dumped matter.

dumpiness.c: Dumpiness Dump"i*ness (?), n. The state of being dumpy.

dumpish.c: Dumpish Dump"ish, a. Dull; stupid; sad; moping; melancholy. “ A... dumpish and sour life.” Lord Herbert.

dumple.c: Dumple Dum"ple (?), v. t. [See Dumpling.] To make dumpy; to fold, or bend, as one part over another. [R.]

dumpling.c: Dumpling Dump"ling (?), n. [Dimin. of dump an illshapen piece; cf. D. dompelen to plunge, dip, duck, Scot. to dump in to plunge into, and E. dump, v. t.] A roundish mass of dough boiled in soup, or as a sort of pudding; often, a cover of paste inclosing an apple or other fruit, and boiled or baked; as, an apple dumpling.

dumpy.c: Dumpy Dump"y (?), a. [Compar. Dumpier (?); superl. Dumpiest.] [1. From Dump a short ill-shapen piece. 2. From Dump sadness.] 1. Short and thick; of low stature and disproportionately stout.

Dumpy level Dump"y lev"el. (Surv.) A level having a short telescope (hence its name) rigidly fixed to a table capable only of rotatory movement in a horizontal plane. The telescope is usually an inverting one. It is sometimes called the Troughton level, from the name of the inventor, and a variety improved by one Gavatt is known as the Gavatt level.

dun.c: Dun Dun (dŭn), n. [See Dune.] A mound or small hill.
Dun Dun, v. t. To cure, as codfish, in a particular manner, by laying them, after salting, in a pile in a dark place, covered with salt grass or some like substance.

Dun Dun (dŭn), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Dunned (dŭnd); p. pr. & vb. n. Dunning (dŭn"nĭng).] [AS. dyne noise, dynian to make a noise, or fr. Icel. dynr, duna, noise, thunder, duna to thunder; the same word as E. din. √74. See Din.] To ask or beset (e.g., a debtor), for payment; to urge importunately.
Dun Dun, n. 1. One who duns; a dunner.
Dun Dun, a. [AS. dunn, of Celtic origin; cf. W. dwn, Ir. & Gael. donn.] Of a dark color; of a color partaking of a brown and black; of a dull brown color; swarthy.

dunbird.c: Dunbird Dun"bird` (?), n. [Named from its color.] (Zool.) (a) The pochard; -- called also dunair, and dunker, or dun-curre. (b) An American duck; the ruddy duck.

dunce.c: Dunce Dunce (?), n. [From Joannes Duns Scotus, a schoolman called the Subtle Doctor, who died in 1308. Originally in the phrase “a Duns man”. See Note below.] One backward in book learning; a child or other person dull or weak in intellect; a dullard; a dolt.

duncedom.c: Duncedom Dunce"dom (?), n. The realm or domain of dunces. [Jocose] Carlyle.

duncical.c: Duncical Dun"ci*cal (?), a. Like a dunce; duncish.

duncify.c: Duncify Dun"ci*fy (?), v. t. [Dunce + -fy.] To make stupid in intellect. [R.] Bp. Warburton.

duncish.c: Duncish Dun"cish (?), a. Somewhat like a dunce. [R.]

dunder.c: Dunder Dun"der (?), n. [Cf. Sp. redundar to overflow.] The lees or dregs of cane juice, used in the distillation of rum. [West Indies]

dunderhead.c: Dunderhead Dun"der*head` (?), n. [Prov. Eng. also dunderpoll, from dunder, same as thunder.] A dunce; a numskull; a blockhead. Beau. & Fl.

dune.c: Dune Dune (dūn), n. [The same word as down: cf. D. duin. See Down a bank of sand.] A low hill of drifting sand usually formed on the coats, but often carried far inland by the prevailing winds. [Written also dun.]

dunfish.c: Dunfish Dun"fish (?), n. Codfish cured in a particular manner, so as to be of a superior quality.

dung.c: Dung Dung (dŭng), n. [AS. dung; akin to G. dung, dünger, OHG. tunga, Sw. dynga; cf. Icel. dyngja heap, Dan. dynge, MHG. tunc underground dwelling place, orig., covered with dung. Cf. Dingy.] The excrement of an animal. Bacon.
Dung Dung, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dunged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dunging.] 1. To manure with dung. Dryden.
Dung Dung, v. i. To void excrement. Swift.

dungaree.c: Dungaree Dun`ga*ree" (?), n. 1. A coarse kind of unbleached cotton fabric; blue denim. [Written also dungari.] [India]

dungeon.c: dungeon dun"geon (dŭn"jŭn), n. [OE. donjoun highest tower of a castle, tower, prison, F. donjon tower or platform in the midst of a castle, turret, or closet on the top of a house, a keep of a castle, LL. domnio, the same word as LL. dominus lord. See Dame, Don, and cf. Dominion, Domain, Demesne, Danger, Donjon.] A close, dark prison, commonly, under ground, as if the lower apartments of the donjon or keep of a castle, these being used as prisons.
Dungeon Dun"geon, v. t. To shut up in a dungeon. Bp. Hall.

dungfork.c: Dungfork Dung"fork` (?), n. A fork for tossing dung.

dunghill.c: Dunghill Dung"hill` (?), n. 1. A heap of dung.

dungmeer.c: Dungmeer Dung"meer` (?), n. [Dung + (prob.) meer a pool.] A pit where dung and weeds rot for manure.

dungy.c: Dungy Dung"y (?), a. Full of dung; filthy; vile; low. Shak.

dungyard.c: Dungyard Dung"yard` (?), n. A yard where dung is collected.

dunker.c: Dunker Dun"ker (?), prop. n. [G. tunken to dip.] One of a religious denomination whose tenets and practices are mainly those of the Baptists, but partly those of the Quakers; -- called also Tunkers, Dunkards, Dippers, and, by themselves, Brethren, and German Baptists, and they call their denomination the Church of the Brethren.

dunlin.c: Dunlin Dun"lin (?), n. [Prob. of Celtic origin; cf. Gael. dun hill (E. dune), and linne pool, pond, lake, E. lin.] (Zool.) A species of sandpiper (Tringa alpina); -- called also churr, dorbie, grass bird, and red-backed sandpiper. It is found both in Europe and America.

dunnage.c: Dunnage Dun"nage (?), n. [Cf. Dun a mound.] (Naut.) Fagots, boughs, or loose materials of any kind, laid on the bottom of the hold for the cargo to rest upon to prevent injury by water, or stowed among casks and other cargo to prevent their motion.

dunner.c: Dunner Dun"ner (?), n. [From Dun to ask payment from.] One employed in soliciting the payment of debts.

dunnish.c: Dunnish Dun"nish (dŭn"nĭsh), a. Inclined to a dun color. Ray.

dunnock.c: Dunnock Dun"nock (?), n. [Cf. Dun,a.] (Zool.) The hedge sparrow or hedge accentor. [Local, Eng.]

dunt.c: Dunt Dunt (?), n. [Dint.] A blow. [Obs.] R. of Glouc.

duo.c: Duo Du"o (?), n. [It. duo, fr. L. duo two. See Duet.] (Mus.) A composition for two performers; a duet.

duodecahedron.c: Duodecahedron Duodecahedral Du`o*dec`a*he"dral (?), a., Du`o*dec`a*he"dron (?), n. See Dodecahedral, and Dodecahedron.

duodecennial.c: Duodecennial Du`o*de*cen"ni*al (?), a. [L. duodecennis; duodecim twelve + annus year.] Consisting of twelve years. [R.] Ash.

duodecimal.c: Duodecimal Du`o*dec"i*mal (?), a. [L. duodecim twelve. See Dozen.] Proceeding in computation by twelves; expressed in the scale of twelves. -- Du`o*dec"i*mal*ly, adv.
Duodecimal Du`o*dec"i*mal, n. 1. A twelfth part; as, the duodecimals of an inch.

duodecimfid.c: Duodecimfid Du`o*dec"im*fid (?), a. [L. duodecim twelve + findere to cleave.] Divided into twelve parts.

duodecimo.c: Duodecimo Du`o*dec"i*mo (?), a. [L. in duodecimo in twelfth, fr. duodecimus twelfth, fr. duodecim twelve. See Dozen.] Having twelve leaves to a sheet; as, a duodecimo from, book, leaf, size, etc.

Duodecimo Du*o*dec"i*mo, n.; pl. Duodecimos (?). A book consisting of sheets each of which is folded into twelve leaves; hence, indicating, more or less definitely, a size of a book; -- usually written 12mo or 12°.

duodecuple.c: Duodecuple Du`o*dec"u*ple (?), a. [L. duo two +? decuple.] Consisting of twelves. Arbuthnot.

duodenal.c: Duodenal Du`o*de"nal (?), a. [Cf. F. duodénal.] Of or pertaining to the duodenum; as, duodenal digestion.

duodenary.c: Duodenary Du`o*den"a*ry (?), a. [L. duodenarius, fr. duodeni twelve each: cf. F. duodénaire.] Containing twelve; twelvefold; increasing by twelves; duodecimal.

duodenum.c: Duodenum ‖Du`o*de"num (?), n. [NL., fr. duodeni twelve each: cf. F. duodenum. So called because its length is about twelve fingers' breadth.] (Anat.) The part of the small intestines between the stomach and the jejunum. See Illust. of Digestive apparatus, under Digestive.

duograph.c: Duograph Du"o*graph (?), n. [L. duo two + -graph.] (Photo-engraving) A picture printed from two half-tone plates made with the screen set at different angles, and usually printed in two shades of the same color or in black and one tint.

duoliteral.c: Duoliteral Du`o*lit"er*al (?), a. [L. duo two + E. literal.] Consisting of two letters only; biliteral. Stuart.

duomo.c: Duomo ‖Duo"mo (?), n. [It. See Done.] A cathedral. See Dome, 2.

duotone.c: Duotone Du"o*tone (?), n. [L. duo two + tone.] (Photoengraving) Any picture printed in two shades of the same color, as duotypes and duographs are usually printed.

duotype.c: Duotype Du"o*type (?), n. [L. duo two + type.] (Photoengraving) A print made from two half-tone plates made from the same negative, but etched differently.

dup.c: Dup Dup (dŭp), v. t. [Contr. fr. do up, that is, to lift up the latch. Cf. Don, Doff.] To open; as, to dup the door. [Obs.] Shak.

dupable.c: Dupable Dup"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being duped.

dupe.c: Dupe Dupe (dūp), n. [F., prob. from Prov. F. dupe, dube; of unknown origin; equiv. to F. huppe hoopoe, a foolish bird, easily caught. Cf. Armor. houpérik hoopoe, a man easily deceived. Cf. also Gull, Booby.] One who has been deceived or who is easily deceived; a gull; as, the dupe of a schemer.

Dupe Dupe, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Duped (dūpt); p. pr. & vb. n. Duping.] [Cf. F. duper, fr. dupe. See Dupe, n.] To deceive; to trick; to mislead by imposing on one's credulity; to gull; as, dupe one by flattery.

duper.c: Duper Dup"er (dūp"ẽr), n. One who dupes another.

dupery.c: Dupery Dup"er*y (dūp"ẽr*y̆), n. [F. duperie, fr. duper.] The act or practice of duping. [R.]

dupion.c: Dupion Du"pi*on (?), n. [F. doupion, It. doppione, fr. doppio double, L. duplus. See Double, and cf. Doubloon.] A double cocoon, made by two silkworms.

duple.c: Duple Du"ple (?), a. [L. duplus. See Double.] Double.

duplex.c: Duplex ‖Du"plex (?), a. [L., fr. duo two + plicare to fold. See Two, and Complex.] 1. Double; twofold.
Duplex Du"plex (?), v. t. [See Duplex, a.] (Teleg.) To arrange, as a telegraph line, so that two messages may be transmitted simultaneously; to equip with a duplex telegraphic outfit.

duplicate.c: duplicate du"pli*cate (?), a. [L. duplicatus, p. p. of duplicare to double, fr. duplex double, twofold. See Duplex.] Double; twofold.
Duplicate Du"pli*cate, n. 1. That which exactly resembles or corresponds to something else; another, correspondent to the first; hence, a copy; a transcript; a counterpart.
Duplicate Du"pli*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Duplicated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Duplicating.] 1. To double; to fold; to render double.

duplication.c: duplication du`pli*ca"tion (?), n. [L. duplicatio: cf. F. duplication.] 1. The act of duplicating, or the state of being duplicated; a doubling; a folding over; a fold.

duplicative.c: duplicative du"pli*ca*tive (?), a. 1. Having the quality of duplicating or doubling.

duplicature.c: duplicature du"pli*ca*ture (?), n. [Cf. F. duplicature.] A doubling; a fold, as of a membrane.

duplicity.c: duplicity du*plic"i*ty (?), n.; pl. duplicities (#). [F. duplicité, L. duplicitas, fr. duplex double. See Duplex.] 1. Doubleness; a twofold state. [Archaic]

dur.c: Dur ‖Dur (?), a. [G., fr. L. durus hard, firm, vigorous.] (Mus.) Major; in the major mode; as, C dur, that is, C major.

dura.c: Dura ‖Du"ra (?), n. Short form for Dura mater.

Dura mater ‖Du"ra ma"ter (?). [L., lit., hard mother. The membrane was called mater, or mother, because it was formerly thought to give rise to every membrane of the body.] (Anat.) The tough, fibrous membrane, which lines the cavity of the skull and spinal column, and surrounds the brain and spinal cord; -- frequently abbreviated to dura.

durability.c: Durability Du`ra*bil"i*ty, n. [L. durabilitas.] The state or quality of being durable; the power of uninterrupted or long continuance in any condition; the power of resisting agents or influences which tend to cause changes, decay, or dissolution; lastingness.

durable.c: Durable Du"ra*ble (?), a. [L. durabilis, fr. durare to last: cf. F. durable. See Dure.] Able to endure or continue in a particular condition; lasting; not perishable or changeable; not wearing out or decaying soon; enduring; as, durable cloth; durable happiness.

durableness.c: Durableness Du"ra*ble*ness, n. Power of lasting, enduring, or resisting; durability.

durably.c: Durably Du"ra*bly, adv. In a lasting manner; with long continuance.

dural.c: Dural Du"ral (?), a. (Anat.) Pertaining to the dura, or dura mater.

duramen.c: Duramen ‖Du*ra"men (?), n. [L., hardness, a hardened, i. e., ligneous, vine branch, fr. durare to harden. See Dure.] (Bot.) The heartwood of an exogenous tree.

durance.c: Durance Dur"ance (?), n. [OF. durance duration, fr. L. durans, -antis, p. pr. durare to endure, last. See Dure, and cf. Durant.] 1. Continuance; duration. See Endurance. [Archaic]

durancy.c: Durancy Dur"an*cy (?), n. Duration. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

durant.c: Durant Dur"ant (?), n. [F. durant, p. pr. of durer to last. Cf. Durance.] See Durance, 3.

durante.c: Durante ‖Du*ran"te (?), prep. [L., abl. case of the p. pr. of durare to last.] (Law) During; as, durante vita, during life; durante bene placito, during pleasure.

duration.c: Duration Du*ra"tion (?), n. [OF. duration. See Dure.] The state or quality of lasting; continuance in time; the portion of time during which anything exists.

durative.c: Durative Dur"a*tive (?), a. Continuing; not completed; implying duration.

durbar.c: Durbar Dur"bar (?), n. [Hind. darbār, fr. Per dar?ār house, court, hall of audience; dar door, gate + bār court, assembly.] An audience hall; the court of a native prince; a state levee; a formal reception of native princes, given by the governor general of India. [India] [Written also darbar.]

dure.c: Dure Dure (?), a. [L. durus; akin to Ir. & Gael. dur?, stubborn, W. dir certain, sure, cf. Gr.? force.] Hard; harsh; severe; rough; toilsome. [R.]
Dure Dure, v. i. [F. durer, L. durare to harden, be hardened, to endure, last, fr. durus hard. See Dure, a.] To last; to continue; to endure. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.

dureless.c: Dureless Dure"less, a. Not lasting. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.

durene.c: Durene Du"rene (?), n. [L. durus hard; -- so called because solid at ordinary temperatures.] (Chem.) A colorless, crystalline, aromatic hydrocarbon, C6H2(CH3)4, off artificial production, with an odor like camphor.

duress.c: Duress Du"ress (?), n. [OF. duresse, du?, hardship, severity, L. duritia, durities, fr. durus hard. See Dure.] 1. Hardship; constraint; pressure; imprisonment; restraint of liberty.
Duress Du*ress" (?), v. t. To subject to duress. “The party duressed.” Bacon.

duressor.c: Duressor Du*ress"or (?), n. (Law) One who subjects another to duress Bacon.

durham.c: Durham Dur"ham (?), n. One or a breed of short-horned cattle, originating in the county of Durham, England. The Durham cattle are noted for their beef-producing quality.

durion.c: Durion Durian { Du"ri*an (?), or Du"ri*on (?) }, n. (Bot.) The fruit of the durio. It is oval or globular, and eight or ten inches long. It has a hard prickly rind, containing a soft, cream-colored pulp, of a most delicious flavor and a very offensive odor. The seeds are roasted and eaten like chestnuts.

during.c: During Dur"ing (?), prep. [Orig., p. pr. of dure.] In the time of; as long as the action or existence of; as, during life; during the space of a year.

durio.c: Durio ‖Du"ri*o (?), n. [NL., fr. Malay d?ri thorn.] (Bot.) A fruit tree (Durio zibethinus, the only species known) of the Indian Archipelago. It bears the durian.

durity.c: Durity Du"ri*ty (?), n. [L. duritas, fr. durus hard.] [Obs.] 1. Hardness; firmness. Sir T. Browne.

durometer.c: Durometer Du*rom"e*ter (?), n. [L. durus hard + -meter.] An instrument for measuring the degree of hardness; especially, an instrument for testing the relative hardness of steel rails and the like.

durra.c: Durra Dur"ra (?), n. [Ar. dhorra.] (Bot.) A kind of millet, cultivated throughout Asia, and introduced into the south of Europe; a variety of Sorghum vulgare; -- called also Indian millet, and Guinea corn. [Written also dhoorra, dhurra, doura, etc.]

durst.c: Durst Durst (?), imp. of Dare. See Dare, v. i.

durukuli.c: Durukuli ‖Du`ru*ku"li (?), n. (Zool.) A small, nocturnal, South American monkey of the genus Aotus (formerly Nyctipthecus trivirgatus). The owl monkey. See douroucouli. [Written also douroucouli.]

durylic.c: Durylic Du*ryl"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, allied to, or derived from, durene; as, durylic acid.

duse.c: Duse Duse (?), n. A demon or spirit. See Deuce.

dusk.c: Dusk Dusk (?), a. [OE. dusc, dosc, deosc; cf. dial. Sw. duska to drizzle, dusk a slight shower.???.] Tending to darkness or blackness; moderately dark or black; dusky.
Dusk Dusk, n. 1. Imperfect obscurity; a middle degree between light and darkness; twilight; as, the dusk of the evening.
Dusk Dusk, v. t. To make dusk. [Archaic]
Dusk Dusk, v. i. To grow dusk. [R.] Chaucer.

dusken.c: Dusken Dusk"en (?), v. t. To make dusk or obscure. [R.]

duskily.c: Duskily Dusk"i*ly (?), adv. In a dusky manner. Byron.

duskiness.c: Duskiness Dusk"i*ness, n. The state of being dusky.

duskish.c: Duskish Dusk"ish, a. Somewhat dusky. “ Duskish smoke.” Spenser. -- Dusk"ish*ly, adv. -- Dusk"ish*ness, n.

duskness.c: Duskness Dusk"ness, n. Duskiness. [R.] Sir T. Elyot.

dusky.c: Dusky Dusk"y (?), a. 1. Partially dark or obscure; not luminous; dusk; as, a dusky valley.

dust.c: Dust Dust (dŭst), n. [AS. dust; cf. LG. dust, D. duist meal dust, OD. doest, donst, and G. dunst vapor, OHG. tunist, dunist, a blowing, wind, Icel. dust dust, Dan. dyst mill dust; perh. akin to L. fumus smoke, E. fume. √71.] 1. Fine, dry particles of earth or other matter, so comminuted that they may be raised and wafted by the wind; that which is crumbled to minute portions; fine powder; as, clouds of dust; bone dust.
Dust Dust (dŭst), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dusted; p. pr. & vb. n. Dusting.] 1. To free from dust; to brush, wipe, or sweep away dust from; as, to dust a table or a floor.

dustbrush.c: Dustbrush Dust"brush` (dŭst"brŭsh), n. A brush of feathers, bristles, or hair, for removing dust from furniture.

duster.c: duster dust"er (dŭst"ẽr), n. 1. One who, or that which, dusts; a utensil that frees from dust. Specifically: (a) (Paper Making) A revolving wire-cloth cylinder which removes the dust from rags, etc. (b) (Milling) A blowing machine for separating the flour from the bran. (c) A dustcloth or a brush used for removing dust from objects or surfaces.

dustiness.c: dustiness dust"i*ness (dŭst"ĭ*nĕs), n. The state of being dusty.

dustless.c: dustless dust"less (dŭst"lĕs), a. Without dust; as a dustless path.

dustman.c: dustman dust"man (dŭst"măn), n.; pl. dustmen (dŭst"mĕn). One whose employment is to remove dirt and refuse; a garbage man. Gay.

dustpan.c: dustpan dust"pan` (dŭst"păn`), n. A shovel-like utensil with a short handle used for conveying away dust brushed from the floor.

dustpoint.c: dust-point dust"-point` (dŭst"point`), n. An old rural game.

dusty.c: dusty dust"y (dŭst"y̆), a. [Compar. Dustier (dŭst"ĭ*ẽr); superl. Dustiest (dŭst"ĭ*ĕst).] [AS. dystig. See Dust.] 1. Filled, covered, or sprinkled with dust; clouded with dust; as, a dusty table; a dusty attic; also, reducing to dust.

dutch.c: Dutch Dutch (?), a. [D. duitsch German; or G. deutsch, orig., popular, national, OD. dietsc, MHG. diutsch, tiutsch, OHG. diutisk, fr. diot, diota, a people, a nation; akin to AS. peód, OS. thiod, thioda, Goth. piuda; cf. Lith. tauta land, OIr. tuath people, Oscan touto. The English have applied the name especially to the Germanic people living nearest them, the Hollanders. Cf. Derrick, Teutonic.] Pertaining to Holland, or to its inhabitants.
Dutch Dutch, n. 1. pl. The people of Holland; Dutchmen.

dutchman.c: Dutchman Dutch"man (?), n.; pl. Dutchmen (?). A native, or one of the people, of Holland.

dutchmansbreeches.c: Dutchman's-breeches Dutchman's breeches Dutchman's breeches, Dutchman's-breeches n. (Bot.), a delicate perennial spring-flowering herb (Dicentra cucullaria) of eastern U.S., having peculiar double-spurred white flowers. See Illust. of Dicentra

dutchmanspipe.c: Dutchman's-pipe Dutchman's-pipe n. a hardy deciduous American vine (Aristolochia durior) having large, heart-shaped leaves and bearing brownish-purple flowers which have their calyx tubes curved like the bowl of a tobacco pipe. Formerly classified as Aristolochia Sipho.

duteous.c: Duteous Du"te*ous (?), a. [From Duty.] 1. Fulfilling duty; dutiful; having the sentiments due to a superior, or to one to whom respect or service is owed; obedient; as, a duteous son or daughter.

dutiable.c: Dutiable Du"ti*a*ble (?), a. [From Duty.] Subject to the payment of a duty; as dutiable goods. [U.S.]

dutied.c: Dutied Du"tied (?), a. Subjected to a duty. Ames.

dutiful.c: Dutiful Du"ti*ful (?), a. 1. Performing, or ready to perform, the duties required by one who has the right to claim submission, obedience, or deference; submissive to natural or legal superiors; obedient, as to parents or superiors; as, a dutiful son or daughter; a dutiful ward or servant; a dutiful subject.

duty.c: Duty Du"ty (?), n.; pl. Duties (#). [From Due.] 1. That which is due; payment. [Obs. as signifying a material thing.]

duumvir.c: Duumvir ‖Du*um"vir (?), n.; pl. E. Duumvirs (#), L. Duumviri (#). [L., fr. duo two + vir man.] (Rom. Antiq.) One of two Roman officers or magistrates united in the same public functions.

duumviral.c: Duumviral Du*um"vi*ral (?), a. [L. duumviralis.] Of or belonging to the duumviri or the duumvirate.

duumvirate.c: Duumvirate Du*um"vi*rate (?), n. [L. duumviratus, fr. duumvir.] The union of two men in the same office; or the office, dignity, or government of two men thus associated, as in ancient Rome.

dux.c: Dux ‖Dux (?), n. [L., leader.] (Mus.) The scholastic name for the theme or subject of a fugue, the answer being called the comes, or companion.

duykerbok.c: Duykerbok ‖Duy"ker*bok (?), n. [D. duiker diver + bok a buck, lit., diver buck. So named from its habit of diving suddenly into the bush.] (Zool.) A small South African antelope (Cephalous mergens); -- called also impoon, and deloo.

dvergr.c: Dvergr ‖Dver"gr (?), n.; pl. Dvergar (#). [See Dwarf.] (Scand. Myth.) A dwarf supposed to dwell in rocks and hills and to be skillful in working metals.

dwale.c: Dwale Dwale (?), n. [OE. dwale, dwole, deception, deadly nightshade, AS. dwala, dwola, error, doubt; akin to E. dull. See Dull, a.] 1. (Bot.) The deadly nightshade (Atropa Belladonna), having stupefying qualities.

dwang.c: Dwang Dwang (?), n. [Cf. D. dwingen to force, compel.] 1. (Carp.) A piece of wood set between two studs, posts, etc., to stiffen and support them.

dwarf.c: Dwarf Dwarf (?), n.; pl. Dwarfs (#). [OE. dwergh, dwerf, dwarf, AS. dweorg, dweorh; akin to D. dwerg, MHG. twerc, G. zwerg, Icel. dvergr, Sw. & Dan. dverg; of unknown origin.] 1. An animal or plant which is much below the ordinary size of its species or kind.
Dwarf Dwarf, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Dwarfed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dwarfing.] To hinder from growing to the natural size; to make or keep small; to stunt. Addison.
Dwarf Dwarf, v. i. To become small; to diminish in size.

dwarfish.c: Dwarfish Dwarf"ish, a. Like a dwarf; below the common stature or size; very small; petty; as, a dwarfish animal, shrub. -- Dwarf"ish*ly, adv. -- Dwarf"ish*ness, n.

dwaule.c: Dwaule Dwaul { Dwaul, Dwaule } (?), v. i. [See Dull, Dwell.] To be delirious. [Obs.] Junius.

dwell.c: Dwell Dwell (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Dwelled (?), usually contracted into Dwelt (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Dwelling.] [OE. dwellen, dwelien, to err, linger, AS. dwellan to deceive, hinder, delay, dwelian to err; akin to Icel. dvelja to delay, tarry, Sw. dväljas to dwell, Dan. dvæle to linger, and to E. dull. See Dull, and cf. Dwale.] 1. To delay; to linger. [Obs.]
Dwell Dwell (?), v. t. To inhabit. [R.] Milton.

dweller.c: Dweller Dwell"er (?), n. An inhabitant; a resident; as, a cave dweller. “Dwellers at Jerusalem.” Acts i. 19.

dwelling.c: Dwelling Dwell"ing, n. Habitation; place or house in which a person lives; abode; domicile.

dwindle.c: Dwindle Dwin"dle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Dwindled (?); p. pr. & vb. n.
